paras.A: For centuries, sailors travelling near rocky coasts faced the danger of wrecking their ships in the dark. The solution, a tall tower with a bright light at the top, is known as a lighthouse. The most famous ancient example was the Pharos of Alexandria, built on an island off the coast of Egypt in the third century BC. It stood well over a hundred metres high, according to ancient writers, and was counted among the Seven Wonders of the ancient world. Fires burned at its top, and polished metal may have reflected the light out to sea. The tower served for many centuries until it was brought down by earthquakes.
paras.B: In the Middle Ages, coastal lights were few, and in many places, they were maintained by monks or by local lords who collected payment from passing ships. It was only in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, when trade by sea increased rapidly, that governments began to build lighthouses on a large scale. Many of these were built on dangerous rocks far from land, where waves could reach the top of the tower in a storm. Builders had to work for years, often landing on the rock only in calm weather, and some of the structures took a decade to finish.
paras.C: A major problem was the light itself. Early lighthouses burned wood or coal in open fires, which were smoky and unreliable, and then candles and oil lamps. The great improvement came in 1822, when the French physicist Augustin Fresnel invented a new kind of lens. Instead of a single thick piece of glass, it was made of many rings of glass, arranged so that the light was gathered and sent out in a narrow, powerful beam. The Fresnel lens was lighter and far brighter than earlier designs, and a light that once could be seen from perhaps ten kilometres could now be seen from more than thirty.
paras.D: To make each lighthouse recognisable, engineers gave every light its own pattern. One tower might send out a single flash every ten seconds, another two flashes every fifteen seconds, and a third a steady glow. A captain who looked at his chart and counted the flashes could identify the place and know precisely where his ship was. The towers were also painted in different colours and stripes so that they could be recognised in daylight.
paras.E: Life for the keepers was demanding. They had to climb the stairs to the top several times a night to trim the wicks, clean the lens and wind the clockwork that turned it. Families often lived at the base of the tower, and on isolated rocks keepers might spend weeks away from home. In fog, they sounded horns or rang bells to warn ships. Because the work was lonely, many keepers kept diaries, and these records give a vivid picture of weather, shipwrecks and rescue.
paras.F: In the twentieth century, electric lamps replaced oil, and later radio beacons and satellite navigation made the lighthouse less essential. Most lighthouses today are fully automatic, and the last keepers left their posts in the late twentieth century in many countries. Even so, lighthouses have not vanished. They still serve as a back-up when electronic systems fail, and many have been turned into museums, hotels or symbols of local identity. Visitors climb them to enjoy views of the sea, and the beam that once warned sailors of danger now welcomes tourists to the shore.
paras.G: Lighthouses have also left a mark on culture. Stories of storms and rescues have been told for generations, and the towers appear in paintings, poems and novels as symbols of safety, loneliness and hope. Many coastal communities hold festivals around their local light, and volunteers raise money to repair old towers. In several countries, the preservation of lighthouses is now treated as a part of national heritage, in the same way as castles and old bridges. For people who have never been to sea, these quiet towers still stand for the idea of a guiding light in the dark.

qs.title: Questions 10–13

ps.title: How a New Language Was Born

paras.A: Linguists have long debated how languages begin. Written records cover only the last five thousand years, and spoken languages leave no trace in the ground, so the origin of speech is hidden. Yet in one remarkable case, scientists were able to watch a new language come into being. It happened in Nicaragua, in Central America, among a group of deaf children, and it began in the 1970s.
paras.B: Before that time, deaf people in Nicaragua had little contact with each other. Most lived in isolated families, and each one used a few simple gestures, called 'home signs', to communicate with relatives. There was no shared language and no school for the deaf. In 1977, the government opened a school in the capital, Managua, and soon, hundreds of deaf children from across the country came together for the first time.
paras.C: The teachers did not know how to teach sign language. They tried to teach the children to lip-read and speak Spanish, with very little success. In the classrooms, the pupils sat in silence, but in the playground and on the school bus, something very different happened. The children combined their home signs, and by the early 1980s, a system had been created which all of them could use and understand.
paras.D: The first group of children created a basic system, but the real change came with the next generation. Younger children who joined the school learned the earlier system from older friends, and then they changed it. They made it more regular and more elegant: for example, instead of acting out a rolling ball with one long gesture, they broke the action into two signs, one showing the shape of the object and the other the way it moved. The same younger children were using grammar that nobody had taught them.
paras.E: In the 1980s, researchers from the United States, including the linguist Ann Senghas, began to study the signing of the children. They compared the signs used by different age groups and recorded how they changed. The results showed that the younger children signed faster and more fluently than the older ones, and that they used structure in a more complex way. Today, the language is known as Nicaraguan Sign Language, and it is used by thousands of people.
paras.F: Scientists found the story exciting because it supported an idea about the human brain: that children are born with a strong ability to create language. If given the opportunity to interact, they will not simply copy what they see but will build rules of their own. The idea is supported by similar studies of other communities in which deaf people have created languages, for example in a village in the Middle East where a sign language has developed over several generations.
paras.G: Critics, however, urge caution. They point out that the Nicaraguan children were not completely without influence: many had seen Spanish speakers and gestures, and some visited deaf clubs. Whether this shows that the ability to create grammar is inborn or merely that humans are very good at learning from the people around them is still debated. Whatever the explanation, the case remains one of the few opportunities we have had to observe the birth of a language.
paras.H: The story also carries a practical lesson for education. For many years, deaf children in several countries were discouraged from using sign language, because adults feared that it would prevent them from learning to speak. Studies of deaf communities have shown that this fear was mistaken. Children who have access to a full language from an early age, whether spoken or signed, tend to develop better thinking and reading skills later. The Nicaraguan example is therefore important not only to scientists, but also to teachers and parents who want to give every child the best start.

qs.title: Questions 23–26

paras.A: Every few decades, a new technology provokes the fear that machines will make human workers unnecessary. In the early nineteenth century, English weavers smashed the new looms that threatened their livelihoods. A century later, economists worried that tractors and factory machines would produce mass unemployment. Today, the same anxiety has returned in discussions of robots and artificial intelligence, and some forecasts claim that nearly half of present jobs could be automated within a generation.
paras.B: History, however, offers reasons for caution about such predictions. Technology has certainly destroyed particular jobs: few people now work as lamplighters, telephone operators or typists. Yet overall employment has not fallen; it has grown, because new technologies create new industries and new demand. A farmer's grandchild may now design software or manage a hospital, occupations that did not exist when her grandfather ploughed the field. The process is gradual, but it is not smooth for those who are affected.
paras.C: What is different this time, argue some economists, is the nature of the machines. Earlier technologies replaced physical strength, leaving humans to use their minds. Modern software, by contrast, can read documents, recognise faces, translate languages and even write passable text, abilities that were once regarded as the property of educated professionals. If machines can do mental as well as physical work, the argument runs, the usual refuge for human workers may disappear.
paras.D: Other experts reply that it is jobs, not tasks, that matter, and most jobs consist of many different tasks. A doctor spends time analysing scans, but also talking with patients, comforting families and making difficult judgements. Software may take over the first of these without replacing the doctor. Research suggests that in the majority of occupations only some activities can be automated, so that the more likely result is changed work rather than vanished work.
paras.E: Nevertheless, there are real dangers. The benefits of automation may not be shared evenly. Workers with a high level of education are often able to use new tools to increase their output and income, while those with fewer qualifications find that their tasks are taken over by machines. The result can be growing inequality, with rewards flowing to the owners of technology and to a small group of skilled workers. Some regions that depend on a single industry could suffer severe, long-lasting decline.
paras.F: How should societies respond? Most economists emphasise education and retraining, since workers who can learn new skills will adapt more easily. Others propose stronger safety nets, such as unemployment support, or even a basic income paid to everyone, though the cost and effect on motivation are fiercely debated. A third idea is to tax the use of robots so as to finance support for displaced workers. None of these proposals is free of difficulties, and there is little agreement about which is best.
paras.G: It may be wise to avoid both panic and complacency. The pace of change is hard to predict, and forecasts about technology have often been wrong, in both directions. What seems certain is that skills such as creativity, empathy and the ability to learn will remain valuable, and that the way a society manages the transition will matter as much as the technology itself. The question is not whether machines will change work, but who will benefit from the change.
paras.H: Individual workers, meanwhile, are not powerless. People can protect their position by treating learning as a lifelong habit rather than something that stops with school. Courses are now available online for many subjects, and some employers pay for staff to study. Choosing work that involves human contact, such as teaching, nursing or skilled repair, is another strategy, since these tasks are among the hardest to automate. The future will be shaped partly by decisions made in governments and companies, but also by the choices that millions of ordinary people make about how to prepare.

ps.title: Iceland: A Country Heated from Below

paras.A: Iceland lies in the North Atlantic, just below the Arctic Circle, and its name suggests a cold and empty land. Yet it is also one of the most volcanic countries on Earth. The island sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, the line where two enormous plates of the Earth's crust are slowly moving apart. Along this line, hot rock rises from deep underground, and the result is a landscape of volcanoes, hot springs, steaming vents and fields of black lava. The inhabitants have lived with this fire for over a thousand years, and in the last century they have learned to use it.
paras.B: The energy of the hot ground is called geothermal energy. In places, rain and melted snow seep deep into the rock, where they are heated to high temperatures and rise again as hot springs or as geysers, fountains of boiling water that shoot into the air. The word 'geyser' itself comes from the name of a famous spring in Iceland, Geysir. For centuries, Icelanders used the hot springs for washing clothes and bathing, and some farmers even baked bread by burying dough in warm ground.
paras.C: The first large-scale use came in the twentieth century. In the 1920s, a few houses in the capital, Reykjavik, were connected to a hot spring by a pipe. The experiment was a success, and in the 1930s, a system was built to pipe hot water to schools and a swimming pool. After the oil crisis of the 1970s, when imported fuel became very expensive, the country moved quickly. Today, around nine out of ten homes in Iceland are heated by geothermal water, which flows through pipes from boreholes sometimes two kilometres deep.
paras.D: Geothermal power is used for much more than heating. Steam from wells drives turbines in power stations, and together with hydroelectric dams, these provide almost all of the country's electricity. Hot water warms greenhouses where farmers grow tomatoes, cucumbers and even bananas, though the island is cold for much of the year. In winter, pipes under pavements and car parks melt snow and ice. Fish farms and factories use the heat as well, and some industries have been attracted to Iceland by cheap, clean energy.
paras.E: The tourist industry has also benefited. The Blue Lagoon, one of the country's most famous attractions, is a pool of warm, milky-blue water created from the outflow of a geothermal power station. Visitors bathe in it, and the minerals in the water are said to be good for the skin. Thousands of people also come each year to see geysers, volcanoes and glaciers, and to enjoy hot springs in the open air even when snow is falling around them.
paras.F: Using the heat of the Earth is not without difficulty. The hot water contains minerals that build up inside pipes, and engineers must clean them regularly. Some wells give off gases with an unpleasant smell like rotten eggs. Drilling can occasionally trigger small earthquakes, and a field that is used too heavily may cool down, so power companies have to manage it carefully. Furthermore, volcanoes can erupt without warning, as happened in 2010 when ash from one volcano stopped air traffic across Europe for several days.
paras.G: Other countries are now interested in the Icelandic experience. Geothermal energy is used in places such as Kenya, the Philippines, Indonesia and parts of the United States, and engineers are developing methods to reach hot rock in regions that have no hot springs. Icelandic experts help to train specialists and advise on projects abroad. They point out that the technology is not suitable everywhere, but where conditions are right, it can supply steady power day and night, in all weathers, with very little pollution.

qs.title: Questions 10–13

paras.A: Almost everyone has stood in a queue and felt the time pass slowly. Waiting in line at a bank, an airport or a supermarket is an ordinary part of modern life, yet it can produce surprisingly strong emotions. Researchers who study the experience have found that how long people actually wait often matters less than how long they feel they have waited. This insight has led businesses, airports and even theme parks to rethink how they treat their customers.
paras.B: One of the best-known observations is that unoccupied time feels longer than occupied time. When people have nothing to do, they watch the clock, and every minute seems to stretch. A famous story concerns the owners of an office building, who received complaints about the slow lifts. Instead of buying expensive new machines, they installed mirrors beside the doors. The complaints almost disappeared, because people used the waiting time to check their appearance and did not notice the delay.
paras.C: Uncertainty makes waiting worse. A person told that a train will arrive in five minutes feels calmer than one who has been given no information, even if the wait is the same. For this reason, many airports display the expected waiting time at security checks, and bus stops now use electronic signs that count down. Explanations also help: passengers on a delayed flight become less angry if they are told the cause. People can accept a delay more easily when they know that someone is in control.
paras.D: Fairness matters as much as speed. A single line that feeds several counters is considered fairer than separate lines at each counter, because nobody can see another line moving faster. Mathematically, the single line is also more efficient, since the next free server always takes the next customer. Many banks and post offices therefore use one 'snake' line. Customers dislike it when someone pushes ahead of them, and the anger caused by an unfair queue can be far greater than the annoyance of a long one.
paras.E: The beginning and the end of a wait are important too. Studies suggest that people are happier with a wait that seems to be moving, even slowly, than with one that is still. Some restaurants offer a drink or a menu to read while customers wait, so that the service has already begun. And experiments show that people remember the final moments of an experience best: a long wait that ends with a friendly greeting can leave a more positive memory than a short wait that ends with rudeness.
paras.F: Theme parks have become experts in managing queues. Lines are often arranged in winding paths, so that the crowd cannot be seen all at once, and rooms along the way are decorated with scenes related to the ride, which turns the waiting into part of the entertainment. Some parks give visitors a pager or an app which allows them to reserve a time and walk around, returning when their turn is near. Others sell a priority ticket, though this raises its own question of fairness, because it allows people with more money to avoid waiting.
paras.G: Digital technology is changing the picture. Many people now order food or book an appointment by phone, and queues have partly moved online, into virtual waiting rooms for concert tickets and popular websites. Yet the same psychological principles apply: people want to know how long the wait will be, to see that the process is fair and to feel that their time is respected. The lesson for any business is simple: a customer who feels respected will often wait longer, and complain less, than one who is ignored.

qs.title: Questions 23–26

paras.A: Museums in Europe and North America hold millions of objects from other parts of the world. Many were acquired during the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, when powerful nations ruled large empires, and some were taken in war or bought from people who had little choice. Today, a number of countries are asking for the return of famous items: sculptures, ancient inscriptions, royal regalia and the remains of ancestors. The debate has become one of the most discussed questions in the world of culture, and it divides experts.
paras.B: Supporters of return make a simple moral argument: what was taken unfairly should be given back. The objects, they say, are not just beautiful things but part of a community's history and identity, and the people who made them should have the right to see and care for them. Some items have religious meaning for living communities. Returning them is also seen as a way of acknowledging past wrongs, and in recent years, several museums and governments have agreed to hand over objects, especially human remains and items looted by soldiers.
paras.C: Those who oppose large-scale return offer several answers. One is legal: many objects were acquired under the laws of the time, and museum directors argue that they cannot simply reverse every transaction of the past. Another is practical, namely that museums in major cities are free or cheap to visit, and bring together works from many cultures so that visitors can compare them. A famous collection shown in one place, they say, helps to create a global audience for each culture.
paras.D: A third argument concerns safety. Critics of return have sometimes pointed to wars, theft and lack of funding in the countries of origin, and say that the objects are better preserved in well-funded institutions. This claim is strongly disputed. Representatives of the countries concerned reply that it is patronising, that modern museums have been built or are being built, and that no one would suggest that European objects should be held abroad because of their own countries' history of wars.
paras.E: Between the two positions, a number of compromises have been tried. Long-term loans allow objects to return to their home countries for display while remaining in the legal ownership of the museum. Some museums share expertise and help to train curators and build storage. Others have created digital copies using three-dimensional scanning, so that people everywhere can study an item, although the originals stay where they are. Not everyone is satisfied: those who demand return say that a copy or a loan is not the same as ownership.
paras.F: A further problem is how to decide which claims are legitimate. Borders have changed, and some objects were made in empires that no longer exist, so it is not always clear which modern nation, or which community inside it, should receive them. Items may also have been traded for centuries between different peoples. Some experts have proposed that each case should be judged individually, considering how the object was acquired, how important it is to the claimant, and whether it can be cared for properly.
paras.G: The debate shows no sign of ending soon. What is changing is the tone. Museums that once defended their collections without question are now more willing to discuss their origins, to research who owned each object and to show visitors a more complete history. Whatever the outcome in particular cases, the discussion has made people think about who tells the story of the past, and who has the right to keep its evidence.

ps.title: The Mysterious Journey of the Eel

paras.A: For more than two thousand years, the life of the European eel was a mystery. People knew the long, snake-like fish well, since it lived in rivers, ponds and ditches across the continent. But nobody had ever seen an eel egg, or a baby eel, or an adult eel with young. The Greek philosopher Aristotle, who studied animals closely, concluded that eels grew from mud, and for centuries, other writers suggested that they came from horse hairs or from the bodies of dead insects. In the 1870s, a young medical student named Sigmund Freud, later famous for other work, spent weeks dissecting hundreds of eels in an attempt to find their reproductive organs, without success.
paras.B: The breakthrough came from a Danish scientist, Johannes Schmidt. In the early twentieth century, he led several expeditions across the Atlantic, collecting tiny, transparent, leaf-shaped fish known as larvae. He noticed that the smaller the larvae were, the farther west he found them. Following the trail of ever smaller specimens for nearly twenty years, he arrived at the Sargasso Sea, a region of warm water in the western Atlantic, east of Florida. This, he concluded, was where European eels were born.
paras.C: The journey that follows is one of the longest in the animal world. The larvae drift eastwards on ocean currents, including the Gulf Stream, a voyage that takes between one and three years. As they approach Europe, they change into 'glass eels', small and almost clear, and swim into the mouths of rivers. They then grow into yellow eels, dull brown or yellow in colour, and may live in fresh water for ten, twenty or even more than forty years.
paras.D: When an eel is ready to breed, its body changes again. Its eyes grow larger, its skin turns silver and it stops eating. In autumn, on dark nights, these silver eels leave their rivers and swim back to the sea, travelling thousands of kilometres across the ocean to the place where they were born. They are believed to spawn and die there. Remarkably, no one has ever seen eels spawning in the wild, and scientists still do not fully understand how the fish find their way.
paras.E: Whatever the details, the species is now in serious trouble. Studies show that the number of young eels reaching Europe has fallen by as much as ninety per cent since the 1980s, and the European eel is classed as critically endangered. Many reasons are suspected. Dams and pumping stations block the rivers, so that eels can no longer travel up or down them. Pollution has contaminated their bodies, a parasite has spread through their swim bladders and changes in ocean currents may have affected the larvae.
paras.F: Fishing has also played a part. Glass eels are caught in large numbers and sold at high prices, because some of them are used to stock farms in Asia, and others are eaten as a delicacy. Because eels cannot yet be bred reliably in captivity, farms depend on wild-caught young. Illegal trade has become a serious problem, and authorities in Europe have found shipments of glass eels hidden in suitcases and cargo boxes.
paras.G: Measures to protect the species are under way. The European Union limits fishing and has banned the export of eels outside Europe. Engineers have built 'eel ladders' beside dams, where young eels can climb, and some countries release young eels into rivers where the way to the sea is clear. Conservationists argue that more is needed, including better control of trade and cleaner rivers. If the eel is to survive, the next stage of its mystery may depend on people, as much as on the ocean.

ps.title: Concrete: The Material That Built the Modern World

paras.A: After water, concrete is the most widely used substance on Earth. Roads, bridges, dams, airports, apartment blocks and stadiums around the world are made of it, and each year, more than four billion tonnes of cement, the key ingredient, are produced. Most people hardly notice concrete, because it is grey and plain, yet it has shaped the modern landscape more than almost any other material.
paras.B: The idea is not new. The ancient Romans made a strong, durable concrete from lime, water, stones and a volcanic ash found near Naples. Remarkably, the mixture even hardened under water, which made it ideal for harbours. The Pantheon in Rome, completed in the second century AD, has a concrete dome 43 metres across, which remained the largest unreinforced dome in the world for more than a thousand years. After the Roman Empire declined, the secret of making such concrete was largely forgotten in Europe.
paras.C: Modern concrete dates from 1824, when an English bricklayer, Joseph Aspdin, patented a cement made by heating limestone and clay to a very high temperature and grinding the result into powder. He called it Portland cement because it resembled a stone quarried on the Isle of Portland. When mixed with sand, gravel and water, the powder reacts chemically and sets into a hard solid. Because the mixture is liquid at first, it can be poured into any shape, which gave builders freedom to create new forms.
paras.D: Concrete has one weakness: it is strong when pressed, but weak when pulled or bent, and it can crack. In the nineteenth century, engineers solved the problem by placing steel bars inside it. Steel is strong in tension, and the two materials expand and contract at nearly the same rate, so they work together. This 'reinforced concrete' made possible tall buildings, long bridges and large dams in the twentieth century, such as the Hoover Dam in the United States.
paras.E: The success of concrete has created problems. Making cement requires great heat and also releases carbon dioxide from the limestone itself, so the industry is responsible for around eight per cent of global emissions of this gas. Concrete also needs enormous quantities of sand and gravel, and in some places the extraction of sand from rivers and beaches is damaging the environment. Dense, hard surfaces keep cities warm and prevent rainwater from soaking into the ground.
paras.F: Researchers are searching for greener alternatives. Some are developing cements that use industrial waste such as ash from power stations or slag from steel works, replacing part of the cement. Others capture carbon dioxide and store it inside the concrete as it hardens. A particularly interesting idea is 'self-healing' concrete, which contains dormant bacteria; when cracks open and water enters, the bacteria wake up and produce limestone that seals the gap. This could greatly extend the life of structures.
paras.G: There are also simple measures. Architects can design buildings that use less material, engineers can crush old concrete and reuse it as gravel, and planners can choose timber or other materials where they are suitable. Yet experts agree that no material can replace concrete entirely in the near future, since the world needs housing, clean water and transport for a growing population. The challenge is not to abandon it, but to make it more sustainable.

ps.title: Is Online Learning as Good as the Classroom?

paras.A: Before 2020, online education was a niche, used by adults studying while working and by those living far from schools. When the pandemic closed buildings, hundreds of millions of students moved to learning on screens almost overnight. The experience was remarkably uneven: some pupils thrived at home, others fell behind, and parents and teachers asked a question that had long been debated by researchers: is learning online as effective as learning in a classroom?
paras.B: The research gives a mixed answer. Studies comparing similar groups of students find that, when well designed, online courses can produce results close to those of face-to-face teaching, especially for adults who are motivated. But they also show higher rates of dropping out. Many students who begin an online course never finish it, and the problem is greater among those who need more support. Convenience, it seems, does not guarantee success.
paras.C: One reason is self-discipline. In a classroom, the timetable, the teacher and the presence of other students provide structure. At home, there are distractions, and nobody notices if a student stops listening. Younger children, who are still learning to organise themselves, find this especially hard. For this reason, most experts believe that online education works best for older, independent learners, while the youngest need the guidance of a person in the room.
paras.D: Another factor is the social side of schools. Children do not learn only facts; they also learn to cooperate, to resolve quarrels and to make friends. Research during the pandemic suggests that many students felt lonely and less motivated. At the same time, a small group, such as shy pupils or those who had been bullied, said they enjoyed learning more at home. These differences show that no single approach suits everyone.
paras.E: Access to technology is a further issue. A reliable connection, a suitable device and a quiet place to study cannot be taken for granted. In many countries, a large share of households lack one or more of these, and so online teaching can widen the gap between rich and poor students. Where governments supplied free devices and televised lessons, the gap was smaller, but the effort required was considerable.
paras.F: Technology, nevertheless, offers real advantages. Recorded lessons can be paused and repeated, programs can adapt exercises to a student's level, and learners in distant villages can reach teachers and courses that were once unavailable. Combining the two systems, in what is called blended learning, is increasingly popular. Students attend school for discussion, experiments and support, and use online materials for practice and revision.
paras.G: The most likely future is therefore a mixture. Rather than asking whether the screen or the classroom is better, schools may ask what each does best. If online tools handle explanation and practice, teachers may have more time for conversation and individual attention. Whether this potential is realised will depend on training, funding and, above all, on a clear view of what education is for.

paras.A: Along a narrow strip of the Pacific coast of North America grow the tallest trees on Earth. The coast redwood can reach more than a hundred metres in height, taller than a thirty-storey building. The record holder, a tree named Hyperion, was discovered in 2006 and measures about 116 metres. Its exact location is kept secret to protect it from the damage that thousands of visitors might cause. Redwoods can also live for a very long time: some individuals are more than two thousand years old, which means that they were already growing when the Roman Empire was at its peak.
paras.B: Redwoods grow only where the climate suits them, in a belt of coastal forest in northern California and southern Oregon. Here the winters are mild and wet, and in summer, when there is almost no rain, thick fog rolls in from the cold ocean. The fog is essential. The needle-like leaves absorb moisture directly from the air, and water dripping from the branches falls to the ground like rain. Scientists estimate that fog provides a large share of the water that the trees use in the dry season.
paras.C: Despite their height, redwoods have surprisingly shallow roots, usually not more than about twelve metres deep. To support such weight, the roots spread out sideways for thirty metres or more and become tangled with those of neighbouring trees. In this way, the trees in a grove hold on to one another, and a strong wind is less likely to blow down any single tree. The trunk is protected by bark which can be thirty centimetres thick and contains little resin, so it resists fire and insects.
paras.D: High above the ground, the forest contains a hidden world. On large branches, dead leaves and other material collect and form thick mats of soil, in which ferns, shrubs and even small trees take root. Researchers who have climbed into the canopy with ropes have discovered animals that spend their entire lives there, including a species of salamander that never touches the ground. A single old redwood can therefore be a miniature ecosystem, with creatures that live nowhere else.
paras.E: Redwoods were once much more widespread, but in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, the demand for their timber was enormous. The wood is light, straight-grained and resistant to rot, and it was used for houses, fences and railway tracks. By the end of the twentieth century, about ninety-five per cent of the original old forest had been cut down. The loss alarmed a group of citizens, who formed an organisation in 1918 to buy and protect the remaining groves.
paras.F: Their work led to the creation of parks, and in 1968, a national park was established to protect further areas. Today, the surviving old-growth forests attract visitors from all over the world. Foresters have learned that the trees can regrow from the stumps of felled trunks, and young forests are slowly recovering in areas that were logged. However, it will take many centuries before they resemble the original ones.
paras.G: Redwoods are sometimes confused with giant sequoias, a related species which grows in the Sierra Nevada mountains of California. The sequoia is not as tall, but its trunk is far wider, and it is the largest living thing on Earth by volume. Both species face a new threat in the form of climate change, which brings hotter, drier summers and more severe fires. Scientists are studying how the trees respond, in the hope that they can help these ancient giants survive the century.

paras.A: Most people think of an insect's eye as a simple device, but in fact, insects have some of the most sophisticated vision in the animal kingdom. Their eyes are built on principles that are very different from our own, and they allow insects to notice things that humans cannot. Understanding how insects see has helped scientists to explain the behaviour of bees, flies and dragonflies, and has even inspired the design of cameras and robots.
paras.B: The compound eye is the main structure. It is made of many tiny units, called facets, each with its own lens, and each facet looks in a slightly different direction. A house fly has several thousand facets in each eye, and a dragonfly may have around thirty thousand. The brain combines the information from all these units into a single image. Because the eyes bulge outward, the insect can see in nearly every direction at once, which makes it hard to approach unnoticed.
paras.C: One disadvantage of compound eyes is that they give a coarse picture. Because the facets are small and fixed, an insect's image is much less detailed than ours, and it cannot focus on objects in the way that a human eye can. To read this page from a normal distance, an insect with eyes of a similar size to ours would see only a blur. The compensation is speed. Insects are extremely good at detecting movement, and many can process visual changes several times faster than a person can.
paras.D: This is why a fly is so hard to swat. To a human, the world appears smooth because we see about sixty separate images every second, but a fly's brain may process more than two hundred. To the fly, the descending hand seems to move in slow motion, giving the insect time to escape. Dragonflies use their speed of vision to catch other insects in the air, and they calculate where the prey will be and fly to meet it, hitting their target in a large majority of attempts.
paras.E: Insects also see colours that we cannot. Bees, for instance, are blind to red but sensitive to ultraviolet light, which is invisible to us. Many flowers have markings that are visible only in ultraviolet, patterns of lines and spots that guide the bee towards the nectar, like the lights on an airport runway. To a bee, a flower that looks plain yellow to us may appear to have a striking target at its centre.
paras.F: Another ability is the detection of polarised light. Light from the sky is polarised in a pattern that depends on the position of the sun, and insects such as bees and desert ants have special cells in their eyes that detect this pattern. Using it, they can find their direction even when the sun is hidden by clouds, and they return in a straight line to their nests after wandering for hundreds of metres.
paras.G: In addition to compound eyes, many insects have three simple eyes, called ocelli, on the top of the head. These cannot form images, but they detect changes in the amount of light very quickly and help the insect to keep its balance in flight. Engineers have copied this idea in small flying robots, and researchers are still learning from the eyes of insects, which have been evolving for hundreds of millions of years.

ps.title: The Case for a Four-Day Working Week

paras.A: For more than a century, the five-day week has been the standard pattern of work in most of the world. It was introduced in the early twentieth century, at a time when many people worked six days, and it was considered a great advance. Now, a growing number of employers and researchers are asking whether the idea needs updating. Their proposal is simple: workers would do the same job in four days instead of five, for the same pay.
paras.B: The central argument concerns productivity. Supporters claim that people cannot concentrate for ever, and that a shorter week encourages them to work more efficiently, cutting unnecessary meetings and distractions. In several trials, companies reported that output stayed the same or even rose. In a large trial in Britain in 2022, involving about sixty companies and several thousand employees, most organisations judged the experiment successful, and the majority said that they would continue with the shorter week.
paras.C: A second argument concerns health. Long hours are linked to stress, exhaustion and illness, and many employees report feelings of burnout. In the trials, participants said they slept better, felt less anxious and had more time for exercise, family and hobbies. Some employers noted fewer days of sickness and less staff turnover, which saves the cost of recruiting and training new workers. Happier employees, it is argued, are also better employees.
paras.D: A third argument is environmental. When people travel to work on one day less each week, there are fewer journeys, which means less traffic and lower emissions. Offices may also use less energy. Some researchers suggest that a shorter week could reduce a country's carbon footprint, though the effect depends on what people do with their extra day. If they take long flights, the benefit disappears.
paras.E: Critics, however, point out that the idea is not suitable for every job. A hospital must be staffed every day of the week, and so must a fire station or a restaurant. In such sectors, a four-day week may mean hiring more staff, which is expensive, or asking people to work longer hours on the days they attend, which is tiring. There is a risk, too, that the benefits would go mainly to office workers, who already enjoy more flexibility than most.
paras.F: Some employers also fear that customers would be poorly served, or that competitors who continue to work five days would gain an advantage. Others believe that the experience of a trial group, which often consists of enthusiastic volunteers, may not be repeated in a typical workplace. They argue that more evidence, collected over a longer period and in a wider range of industries, is needed before a general change is made.
paras.G: The debate is likely to continue. In the past, the shortening of the working week came gradually, as productivity grew, and a further reduction would follow the same pattern. Yet it will not happen by itself. It requires agreement between employers, workers and governments about how the gains from technology should be shared: as higher profits, higher wages, or more time.

qs.title: Questions 39–40

paras.A: Few instruments are as familiar as the piano. It stands in schools, concert halls, churches and homes, and it has been the favourite instrument of composers for three hundred years. Yet the piano is a relatively recent invention. For most of musical history, the keyboard instruments were the organ, which produces a continuous sound from pipes, and the harpsichord, whose strings are plucked by small quills when a key is pressed.
paras.B: The harpsichord had a limitation that frustrated musicians: it could not change its volume. Whether the player pressed a key gently or with force, the sound was the same. Around the year 1700, an instrument maker named Bartolomeo Cristofori, who worked for a noble family in Florence, set out to solve this problem. His idea was to replace the quills with small hammers covered in leather, which strike the strings and then fall back, so that the strings can continue to vibrate.
paras.C: The result was an instrument on which the loudness of each note depended on the force of the player's fingers. Cristofori called it a 'gravicembalo col piano e forte', which means a harpsichord with soft and loud. The name was later shortened to 'pianoforte' and then to 'piano'. The invention was not an immediate success. It was expensive, and many players felt that the harpsichord, with its bright sound, was good enough.
paras.D: Over the next century, makers in Germany, Austria and England improved the design. They enlarged the keyboard, made the action of the hammers faster and more reliable and added pedals, which lengthen notes or soften them. Composers such as Mozart and Beethoven took up the new instrument, and the latter pushed it to its limits, demanding louder and more dramatic sounds than the instruments of his youth could provide. Makers responded by building stronger instruments.
paras.E: A key change came in the nineteenth century, when iron frames were introduced. The strings of a piano are under enormous tension, together pulling with a force of many tonnes, and a wooden frame could not withstand more. A frame of cast iron allowed thicker strings, tightened to a higher tension, and the sound became fuller, louder and richer. The modern concert piano, with its eighty-eight keys, took shape at this time.
paras.F: The piano became a symbol of middle-class life. Factories produced thousands of upright pianos, which take up less room than grand pianos because their strings are vertical, and families gathered around them in the evening to sing. Young people, especially girls, were often expected to learn to play. The piano also created a new profession, that of the travelling virtuoso, whose concerts drew huge audiences.
paras.G: In the twentieth century, recorded music and radio reduced the number of people who played at home, and today, electronic keyboards and digital pianos, which are cheaper and quieter, have taken part of the market. Even so, the acoustic piano has not disappeared. Pianists, teachers and composers still value its touch and tone, and millions of people continue to learn the instrument, finding that it offers a reward that no machine can quite replace.

ps.title: The Science of Taste and Smell

paras.A: When we eat, we usually say that we are tasting our food. In reality, what we call taste is a combination of several senses, and the sense of smell plays a leading role. Anyone who has had a bad cold knows the effect: food seems dull, and even a favourite dish seems to have lost its flavour. This is not because the tongue has stopped working, but because the nose is blocked.
paras.B: The tongue can detect only a small number of basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty and bitter, and a fifth known as umami, a savoury taste found in foods such as meat, cheese and tomatoes. Umami was identified in 1908 by a Japanese chemist, Kikunae Ikeda, who discovered that the flavour of a traditional seaweed soup came from a particular chemical. It was accepted by Western scientists only decades later.
paras.C: The sensors for these tastes are located in taste buds, tiny clusters of cells found mainly on the tongue but also on the roof of the mouth and the throat. An adult has several thousand of them, and each lives for only a week or two before it is replaced. A common textbook diagram once showed the tongue divided into zones, with sweet at the tip and bitter at the back. Modern research has shown that this 'tongue map' is wrong: all the tastes can be detected on all parts of the tongue.
paras.D: Smell is far more complex. Inside the upper part of the nose lies a patch of tissue containing millions of nerve cells with receptors. Humans have about four hundred different kinds of receptor, and each responds to particular molecules in the air. When we chew, odours travel from the back of the mouth up into the nose, which is how flavour is created. Together, the receptors can distinguish an enormous number of odours, probably far more than a trillion, according to one controversial estimate.
paras.E: Smell also has a special link to memory and emotion. The nerves that carry smell signals connect closely to parts of the brain that handle memory and feelings, which is why a sudden odour, such as the scent of a certain soup or soap, can bring back a childhood scene with remarkable clarity. Advertisers, shop owners and hotels make use of this connection by choosing fragrances that put customers in a positive mood.
paras.F: People differ greatly in their sensitivity. Some individuals, sometimes called 'supertasters', have more taste buds than average and find bitter flavours such as those in coffee or certain vegetables very strong. Genes affect these differences, so that two people can taste the same food very differently. Age matters as well: children generally dislike bitter tastes more than adults, and older people often lose some sensitivity to smell.
paras.G: There are evolutionary reasons for these abilities. A liking for sweet foods guided early humans towards ripe fruit, a source of energy, while an aversion to bitterness protected them from poisonous plants. Today, the same instincts can work against us, since sugar and salt are cheap and plentiful. Understanding how taste works is therefore not only a matter of curiosity, but also helps us to think about diet and health.

paras.A: In democratic countries, voting is usually regarded as a right, but in a few places it is also a duty. In Australia, for example, citizens have been required by law to vote since 1924, and anyone who fails to do so without a good reason may be fined a small amount. Belgium and some other countries have similar systems. The idea is controversial: supporters see it as strengthening democracy, and opponents see it as an unacceptable limit on freedom.
paras.B: The strongest argument in favour is turnout. In countries with voluntary voting, many people stay at home, and in some elections fewer than half of eligible citizens take part. Where voting is compulsory and the law is enforced, participation is often above ninety per cent. Supporters argue that a government elected by almost everyone has a stronger claim to represent the whole population than one chosen by a minority.
paras.C: They also argue that compulsory voting makes elections fairer. In voluntary systems, the people who vote are not a random sample of the population. They tend to be older, wealthier and better educated, and so politicians pay more attention to their interests. Poorer and younger citizens, who vote less, are ignored. If everyone must vote, parties have to appeal to all groups, and the policies they offer may be more balanced.
paras.D: A further argument concerns political style. When parties need not spend large sums persuading their supporters to go to the polls, they can concentrate on persuading undecided voters, and may avoid the harshest attacks on opponents. Some researchers suggest that compulsory systems may reduce extreme positions, though the evidence is not conclusive, since many other factors influence the tone of politics.
paras.E: Opponents begin from the principle of liberty. In their view, the right to vote includes the right not to vote, and a citizen who is not interested or who dislikes all the candidates should not be punished. Forcing people to the polls does not make them engaged. Some will vote carelessly, or choose names at random, and others will cast an empty or spoiled ballot as a form of protest, which may be counted as turnout but means little.
paras.F: There are practical objections, too. Compulsory voting needs a system of enforcement, with records, warnings and fines, and this costs money and affects mostly those with the least resources. It may also encourage parties to focus on the most easily persuaded voters rather than on serious debate. Critics add that a better remedy for low turnout is to remove the obstacles that discourage people from voting.
paras.G: Such obstacles include elections held on working days, long queues and complicated registration. Some countries have tried voting at weekends, early voting, postal ballots and automatic registration, and have increased turnout without compulsion. Civic education in schools can also help young people to understand why voting matters. The question is therefore whether democracy is better served by requiring participation, or by making it easier and more attractive.

ps.title: The Brothers Who Taught Humans to Fly

paras.A: For thousands of years, people looked at birds and dreamed of flying. Legends told of men with wings of feathers and wax, and inventors tried to copy the flapping of a bird with arms and artificial wings, usually with painful results. The first real success came not from imitating birds, but from a discovery about air. In the late eighteenth century, two French brothers, Joseph-Michel and Jacques-Étienne Montgolfier, found a way to lift a large object off the ground using nothing more than hot air.
paras.B: The brothers ran a family paper-making business in the small town of Annonay, in the south of France. According to a well-known story, Joseph-Michel noticed that a paper bag or a piece of cloth held above a fire tended to rise. The brothers began to experiment, building larger and larger bags of silk lined with paper, and burning straw and wool beneath them. They believed that the smoke contained a special gas that gave lift. In fact, the effect has a simpler cause: hot air is lighter than the cooler air around it.
paras.C: In June 1783, the brothers held a public demonstration in Annonay. A huge balloon, about eleven metres across, rose into the sky in front of a crowd of officials and spectators and travelled for several kilometres. News spread quickly, and soon the scientific academy in Paris was asking for a display. The brothers then built a more elaborate balloon, decorated in blue and gold, and in September they sent up the first passengers in front of the king, Louis XVI, and his court. They were a sheep, a duck and a rooster.
paras.D: The animals landed safely after about eight minutes, and the experiment showed that a living creature could survive in the air. The next step was to carry a person. In November 1783, two men, Jean-François Pilâtre de Rozier and the Marquis d'Arlandes, climbed into a basket under a Montgolfier balloon in Paris. They stayed aloft for about twenty-five minutes, flew across part of the city, and landed some nine kilometres away. They were the first humans to make a free flight.
paras.E: A rival design appeared only ten days later. The French scientist Jacques Charles, working with the Robert brothers, launched a balloon filled with hydrogen, a gas lighter than air. Hydrogen balloons could stay up longer, since there was no need to keep a fire burning, although the gas was expensive and dangerous. In 1785, a Frenchman, Jean-Pierre Blanchard, and an American, John Jeffries, used a hydrogen balloon to cross the English Channel, an achievement which made them famous.
paras.F: Ballooning became a craze. Crowds gathered to watch ascents, ladies wore hats shaped like balloons and the new invention appeared on plates, fans and clocks. It was also put to practical use. Balloons carried instruments to measure the weather and the air at height, and in the nineteenth century, armies used them to observe the enemy. During the siege of Paris in 1870, balloons carried letters and passengers out of the city.
paras.G: The balloon had one great weakness: it could not be steered, but drifted wherever the wind took it. This problem was solved in the twentieth century by aeroplanes, but ballooning has survived as a sport and a leisure activity. Modern hot-air balloons use nylon fabric and propane burners, and thousands of people enjoy flights each year. In 1999, two pilots completed the first non-stop flight around the world in a balloon, which took just under twenty days, proving that the dream of the Montgolfiers has not ended.

ps.title: How Bees Choose a New Home

paras.A: Every spring, a healthy colony of honeybees may become too large for its hive. When this happens, about half of the bees leave with the old queen in a swarm, while the other half stay behind with a new queen. The swarm, which may contain ten thousand bees, hangs from a branch in a great cluster for a few hours or days. It looks like a quiet rest, but in fact, it is a meeting where one of the most important decisions in the bees' lives is being made.
paras.B: The problem is to find a good place for a new nest. A poor choice can mean disaster, since the colony must be able to store enough honey to survive the winter. The ideal site is a cavity in a tree, with a small entrance, which is dry, high above the ground and about the size of a large bucket. Scientists have found that a swarm usually chooses the best site available within several kilometres, even though no single bee has seen all the options.
paras.C: The search is done by a small group of scouts, perhaps a few hundred, who fly out in different directions. When a scout finds a possible cavity, she inspects it carefully, walking around the inside and measuring its size. She then returns to the cluster and performs a 'waggle dance' on the surface of the swarm. The direction of the dance shows the direction of the site, the length of the dance shows the distance, and the energy of the dance reveals how good the scout thinks it is.
paras.D: Other scouts watch the dance, then fly out to examine the site for themselves. If they agree with the first scout, they return and dance in turn. In this way, a good site attracts more and more dancers, while a poor one soon loses support, because the scouts that visited it dance with little enthusiasm or not at all. Over a period of days, the number of dancers for the best sites grows, and those for weaker sites fall to zero.
paras.E: The biologist Thomas Seeley, who studied swarms for many years, discovered how the bees know when to stop. When the number of scouts at a particular site reaches a certain level, perhaps fifteen or twenty, a quorum has been reached. The scouts return to the swarm and begin to produce a high-pitched piping sound, which tells the other bees to warm their flight muscles. Within an hour, the whole swarm takes off and flies to the chosen cavity.
paras.F: The bees have a way of preventing hasty decisions as well. Scouts who disagree with a rival site sometimes butt their heads against dancers for other sites and make a short buzzing sound. This 'stop signal' reduces the dancing for that site, and it helps the colony to avoid a deadlock between two equally good places. The decision thus emerges from many small signals, rather than from a leader. The queen takes no part.
paras.G: Scientists see in this process a model for human groups. The bees search widely for options, share information honestly, and allow each member to judge for herself. Their decisions are not influenced by a loud voice or high status. Some experts on management have suggested that human committees could improve their own decisions by following similar rules: gather several options, encourage independent opinions and make the final choice only when support is clearly strong.

qs.title: Questions 23–26

paras.A: Antarctica is the coldest, windiest and driest continent on Earth, and it has no permanent population. Yet each summer, tens of thousands of tourists arrive, mostly on cruise ships, to see its ice cliffs, whales and penguins. The number has risen sharply in recent decades, from a few thousand a year in the early 1990s to over a hundred thousand in some recent seasons. This growth raises a difficult question: can a fragile wilderness protect itself from the people who come to admire it?
paras.B: Antarctica is governed by a special arrangement. The Antarctic Treaty, signed in 1959, reserves the continent for peaceful purposes and scientific research, and sets aside national claims to its territory. A later agreement, the Madrid Protocol of 1991, bans mining and sets strict rules for protecting the environment. Tourism, however, was not the main concern of the authors of these documents, and its rules are mostly voluntary. They are set by an association of tour operators, which sets limits such as the number of people who can land at a site at one time.
paras.C: Supporters of tourism emphasise its benefits. People who visit Antarctica often return home with a lasting concern for the environment and become what some operators call 'ambassadors', speaking about the continent to family and friends. Tourism also pays for part of the cost of studying and monitoring the region. Operators point out that their ships travel only along certain routes, and that visitors follow strict rules: they must not touch the animals, take stones or leave rubbish.
paras.D: Critics reply that the effects are real, even if each visit is small. Penguins and seals can be disturbed by the presence of people, particularly during the breeding season, when stress may cause parents to abandon their eggs or chicks. Footsteps can damage the thin layer of moss and lichen, which grows extremely slowly. There is also a danger that visitors may carry seeds, insects or microbes from other continents on their boots and clothing, introducing species that could displace native ones.
paras.E: Ships themselves cause concern. Burning fuel releases soot, which may settle on snow and ice and make them darker, so that they absorb more heat and melt faster. The risk of accidents is serious as well. Ships have struck icebergs and run aground, and a spill of oil in these cold waters could be disastrous because it would break down very slowly. Rescue is also difficult, since the nearest help may be several days away.
paras.F: A further complication is the growth of new kinds of tourism. Some companies now offer trips by air, camping on the ice, or even skiing to the South Pole, and there is interest in building permanent facilities. Because these activities take place away from the ships, they are more difficult to monitor. Environmental organisations have called for stricter rules, backed by law, and for limits on the total number of visitors.
paras.G: The challenge is to find the right balance. Total prohibition would be difficult, since the right to visit is accepted by many countries, and might weaken the support of people who learn to care about the continent. On the other hand, unlimited growth would almost certainly damage the very qualities that attract visitors. Most experts agree that decisions should be based on careful scientific studies of the cumulative impact of tourism, and that the precautionary principle should apply: when in doubt, protect.

paras.A: The Great Wall of China is among the best-known structures in the world, yet it is often misunderstood. It is not a single wall but a series of walls, built and rebuilt by different rulers over more than two thousand years. Some sections run across mountain ridges, others cross deserts and grasslands, and many have disappeared entirely. A Chinese survey completed in 2012 added up all the known sections, including trenches and natural barriers used for defence, and arrived at a total length of over twenty-one thousand kilometres.
paras.B: The earliest walls were built by rival states in the period before China was united. In about 221 BC, the first emperor, Qin Shi Huang, joined some of these walls together and extended them to defend his northern frontier against nomadic horsemen. Soldiers, prisoners and peasants were forced to build the wall, and the work was hard and dangerous. Later dynasties, including the Han, repaired and extended the wall westwards into the desert, to protect the trade routes that became known as the Silk Road.
paras.C: Most of the wall that tourists visit today is much younger. It was built by the Ming dynasty, which ruled from 1368 to 1644, after a long period of troubles on the northern border. The Ming builders used stone and bricks, which were stronger than the rammed earth of the earlier walls. Fired in kilns, the bricks were carried up the hills by workers and donkeys, and sticky rice was sometimes added to the mortar to make it stronger. The result was a high wall, in some places wide enough for several soldiers to march side by side.
paras.D: The wall was more than a barrier. Along it stood thousands of watchtowers, from which sentries could look over the land, and beacon towers, where smoke by day or fire by night could pass a warning along the line. In the best conditions, a message could travel hundreds of kilometres within hours. Garrisons lived in forts attached to the wall, with stores of food and weapons. Gates allowed merchants to pass, and officials collected taxes on goods going in and out.
paras.E: Historians debate how effective the wall was. It could not stop a determined army, and in 1644, the Manchu forces entered China after a rebel opened the gate at one of its passes. Yet it slowed raiders, helped to control movement and trade, and gave the defenders time to prepare. Perhaps its greatest value was symbolic, showing the power of the state and marking the line between the farming world and the grasslands beyond.
paras.F: A popular story claims that the Great Wall can be seen from space with the naked eye. This is a myth. The wall is long but narrow, and its colour is similar to the land around it, so astronauts looking from orbit have been unable to pick it out without help from a camera. Roads, cities and airports are often easier to see. The story persists, perhaps, because people want the largest thing ever built to be visible from the greatest distance.
paras.G: Today, the Great Wall is a World Heritage Site and attracts millions of visitors every year. Their numbers, however, are one of its problems. Many sections are crumbling because of wind, rain and the roots of plants, and some have been damaged by people who take bricks as souvenirs or build roads through them. The government has introduced laws to protect the wall, and local people are being trained as guards, but the task of preserving so long a structure is immense.

ps.title: Why We Need Sleep to Remember

paras.A: We spend about a third of our lives asleep, yet for centuries, sleep was thought of as a simple switching off of the brain. Modern research has shown the opposite. During sleep, the brain remains highly active, and some of its most important work, including the storage of memories, takes place in the dark hours. Understanding this has changed how scientists, teachers and doctors think about the value of a good night's rest.
paras.B: Sleep is not a single state. Over a night, a person passes through several cycles of about ninety minutes, each consisting of different stages. In light sleep, the body relaxes and brain activity slows. In deep sleep, the slowest brain waves appear, and it is very hard to wake a person. In REM sleep, named after the rapid eye movements that occur beneath the eyelids, the brain becomes active again, and most vivid dreams take place. A healthy adult goes through four to six cycles.
paras.C: The stages seem to have different jobs in memory. When we learn something new, the information is first held in a part of the brain called the hippocampus, which acts like a temporary store. During deep sleep, the brain replays the patterns of activity from the day, and the memories are gradually transferred to the outer layers of the brain for long-term storage. Experiments with rats have shown that nerve cells which fired as the animal ran through a maze fired in the same order, but faster, while it slept.
paras.D: Studies on people confirm the importance of this process. In a typical experiment, two groups learn a list of words or a skill, such as a sequence of finger movements on a keyboard. One group then sleeps, and the other stays awake for the same period. When tested later, the group that slept usually remembers more and performs better. Even a short nap of an hour or so seems to give some benefit, particularly if it includes deep sleep.
paras.E: REM sleep appears to play a different role, helping to process emotional memories and to link new information with older knowledge. Some researchers believe that this is why people sometimes wake with a solution to a problem that seemed impossible the night before. The chemist Dmitri Mendeleev is said to have seen the arrangement of his periodic table in a dream, although historians doubt that the story is quite so simple.
paras.F: Lack of sleep, by contrast, has clear costs. After a night with little sleep, people find it harder to concentrate, learn new material and control their emotions. Students who stay up all night to study may therefore be harming their results. Over longer periods, poor sleep is linked with health problems, including heart disease and weakened defences against infection. Teenagers, whose natural body clocks shift later, need around eight to ten hours but often get far fewer.
paras.G: Sleep experts offer simple advice. Keep regular hours, even at weekends, avoid caffeine in the afternoon and switch off bright screens an hour before bed. A cool, dark and quiet bedroom helps. Above all, they suggest, people should treat sleep as a part of learning, not as a waste of time. A student who sleeps after studying is not stopping the work; the brain is still doing it.

paras.A: In 2001, an American businessman named Dennis Tito became the first person to pay for a trip into space. He travelled to the International Space Station on a Russian rocket, spending about a week in orbit, and the price is believed to have been around twenty million dollars. For several years, only a handful of wealthy individuals followed him. In the 2020s, however, private companies began to offer shorter flights, and the idea of space tourism moved from fantasy towards reality.
paras.B: There are two main kinds of trip. Orbital flights carry passengers around the Earth for days or even weeks, and they are extremely expensive. Suborbital flights are much cheaper and shorter: a rocket or a rocket-powered plane takes passengers to the edge of space, about a hundred kilometres up, where they experience a few minutes of weightlessness and see the curve of the Earth before coming back. In 2021, two companies carried their first paying passengers on flights of this kind.
paras.C: Supporters of the industry make several claims. The first is that it accelerates technology. Competition between companies has encouraged reusable rockets and lowered the cost of launching, and these advances can also benefit science and communications. Second, they argue that tourism creates a market that makes space travel safer and cheaper over time, much as early airline passengers helped to turn flying from an adventure into a routine. Third, some astronauts report that seeing the Earth from space changes their sense of how fragile it is, an effect which tourists may share.
paras.D: Critics offer sharp objections. One concerns the environment. Rocket launches release gases and soot into the upper atmosphere, where they may remain for years, and researchers warn that a large increase in flights could affect the ozone layer and the climate. Although the total number of flights is small today, the emissions per passenger are very high. Critics also question the use of resources: should so much talent and money be devoted to entertainment for the rich when there are pressing problems on Earth?
paras.E: Questions of safety are also unresolved. Spaceflight is inherently dangerous, and accidents have occurred, in some cases killing crew members. In many countries, passengers are required to sign a statement that they accept the risk, and regulators have been reluctant to impose strict safety rules, fearing that they would slow down a young industry. Supporters say that the industry will improve as experience grows, but opponents note that early errors can cost lives.
paras.F: The law is another difficult area. The existing international treaties were written when only governments went into space, and they say little about private citizens, passengers or the rights of companies. Who is responsible if a vehicle crashes into a populated area, or if debris from a launch damages another satellite? Experts have called for clearer rules, but countries disagree on how far to restrict a business that many of them want to attract.
paras.G: For the moment, space tourism remains a luxury for a very small number of people. Prices may fall, but experts doubt that a trip to orbit will be affordable for ordinary travellers within the lifetime of most people alive today. Whether this is a cause for concern depends on one's view. For enthusiasts, the industry is the first step towards a future in which many people will live and work beyond the Earth; for critics, it is an expensive amusement that the planet can ill afford.

paras.A: For centuries, ships travelling between the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans had to make a long and dangerous journey around the southern tip of South America. The voyage took weeks, through some of the stormiest waters in the world. The narrow strip of land that joins North and South America, the Isthmus of Panama, seemed to offer a shortcut, and for four hundred years, engineers dreamed of cutting a channel across it.
paras.B: The first serious attempt began in 1881 under the French diplomat Ferdinand de Lesseps, who had successfully built the Suez Canal. He planned a canal at sea level, without locks. But Panama was very different from the Egyptian desert. The workers faced heavy rain, thick jungle, and enormous landslides which filled the channel as fast as it was dug. Worst of all, they suffered from diseases such as yellow fever and malaria. Tens of thousands died, the company went bankrupt in 1889 and the project was abandoned.
paras.C: The United States took over the project in 1904. American doctors, led by William Gorgas, had learned that mosquitoes carried both yellow fever and malaria. Gorgas organised a huge campaign to drain pools, cover water tanks and spray houses, and the diseases were brought under control within a few years. Chief engineer John Stevens, and then George Goethals, changed the plan. Instead of a sea-level channel, they proposed a canal with locks, which would lift ships over the highlands.
paras.D: The design was ingenious. A ship enters a chamber called a lock, whose gates are closed behind it. Water flows in from a higher chamber, purely by gravity, and the vessel rises. After three steps, it reaches an artificial lake, Gatun Lake, about twenty-six metres above sea level, and crosses the lake before descending in the same way on the other side. The canal, roughly eighty kilometres long, opened in August 1914, shortening a trip from New York to San Francisco by thousands of kilometres.
paras.E: Building the canal required one of the greatest earth-moving operations in history. Steam shovels dug away the hills, and trains carried the soil away to build dams and fill swamps. At the peak of construction, around forty thousand workers were employed, many of them from the Caribbean islands. Their labour was dangerous, and thousands lost their lives, though the toll was far lower than during the French attempt.
paras.F: The canal remained under American control for most of the twentieth century. In 1977, after years of protest in Panama, the two countries signed treaties which gave the canal to Panama, and the transfer was completed on 31 December 1999. Panama has since managed it successfully, and the canal now produces a significant share of the country's income. To meet the needs of larger ships, a wider set of locks was opened in 2016.
paras.G: Today, the canal faces new challenges. Each ship that passes uses a large amount of fresh water from the lake, which is replenished by rain, and in dry years, the authorities have had to limit the number of ships. Climate change may make droughts more common. Engineers are therefore studying ways to save water and to find new sources, because a canal built to save a journey of thousands of kilometres depends on a few lakes in the Panamanian rainforest.

paras.A: Look at a rainbow, and most English speakers will say they see red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet. But the rainbow is a continuous band of light, with no sharp lines between colours. The names we use are cultural choices, and different languages divide the spectrum in different ways. The study of colour words has become a classic area of research on the relationship between language, thought and perception.
paras.B: In 1969, two researchers at the University of California, Brent Berlin and Paul Kay, published a study of colour terms in about twenty languages. They found that the languages differed in the number of basic colour words they possessed, from only two to eleven, but that the differences followed a pattern. The order in which colour terms appear was surprisingly similar from one language to another. A language with only two terms always distinguishes dark from light, roughly like black and white.
paras.C: According to their theory, a third term, if one appears, is always red. The next to appear are green and yellow, in either order, and then blue. Later come brown, followed by purple, pink, orange and grey. Many linguists have disputed details of the scheme, and later studies found exceptions, but its main idea, that there is a typical sequence in which colour words evolve, is still widely accepted.
paras.D: Blue seems to be a latecomer in many cultures. The ancient Greek poet Homer described the sea as 'wine-dark', and he never used a word for blue in his works. Some scholars have concluded that the ancient Greeks could not see the colour, but this is unlikely, since the eyes of humans have not changed. A better explanation is that blue dyes were rare, and there was little need to name a colour that was not seen on objects, and could not be made easily.
paras.E: Does the vocabulary of a language influence the way its speakers perceive colour? Russian offers a test case, because it has two separate basic words for light blue and dark blue, 'goluboy' and 'siniy'. In experiments, Russian speakers were found to be faster at telling apart two shades of blue when they fell on different sides of the boundary between the two words. English speakers, who have only one word, showed no such advantage.
paras.F: Another study involved the Himba, a people of Namibia. Their language groups together colours that English speakers would call green and blue, but it separates several shades of green that look very similar to us. When the Himba were asked to pick out a square of a slightly different shade from a group of green squares, they were quicker than English speakers when the shade belonged to a different Himba category, and slower when the difference was between what English speakers call green and blue.
paras.G: These results do not mean that language determines what people see. All humans have the same basic visual system, and speakers of every language can learn new colour terms. The influence of words is better described as a small bias, which affects speed and memory rather than ability. The research suggests that language and perception are connected in subtle ways, but also that human experience of colour is largely shared.
