qs.title: Questions 23–26

paras.A: Modern life offers little opportunity to be bored. A phone in the pocket provides news, games, music and messages whenever there is a gap, whether at a bus stop, in a queue or even in the middle of a conversation. Many people say that this is a good thing, since boredom is unpleasant. But a growing number of psychologists question whether we are losing something valuable when we fill every spare moment.
paras.B: Boredom is usually defined as the uncomfortable feeling of wanting to do something but being unable to find anything satisfying to do. It is a common experience: surveys suggest that most people feel bored regularly, and it is particularly common among teenagers. It is not the same as laziness or depression, although long-lasting boredom is linked with both. The feeling seems to act as a signal, like hunger, urging us to look for something more meaningful.
paras.C: The idea that boredom might help creativity comes from experiments. In a well-known British study in 2014, researchers asked one group of volunteers to copy numbers from a telephone directory for a quarter of an hour, a dull task, while another group did nothing. All were then asked to think of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. The group that had been bored produced more ideas and more original ones, which suggested that the dull task had pushed their minds to wander.
paras.D: Brain scientists have an explanation. When people are not concentrating on a task, a set of brain regions, known as the default mode network, becomes active. It is involved in remembering the past, imagining the future and thinking about other people. In this state, the mind makes unexpected connections between ideas, which can lead to insights. Many writers, artists and scientists describe a sudden idea arriving while walking, bathing or staring out of a window.
paras.E: Children may benefit as well. Parents often feel they must keep their children busy, with lessons and activities, but educators argue that unstructured time allows young people to develop imagination and independence. A child who complains of boredom may soon invent a game, build a model or begin a story. If adults always provide entertainment, say psychologists, children may never learn to entertain themselves.
paras.F: This does not mean that all boredom is useful. Researchers have found that people who are often bored are more likely to take risks, to overeat or to turn to harmful habits in an effort to feel stimulated. Boredom at work or in school, where people have no choice, may be a sign that tasks are too easy, too hard or meaningless. In such cases, the solution is to change the task or the environment, not to accept the feeling.
paras.G: What, then, should we do? Some experts advise deliberately keeping short periods without screens: a walk without headphones, a journey without a phone, a few minutes of waiting without checking messages. The aim is not to suffer, but to give the mind a chance to wander. Boredom, it seems, is like a doorway: unpleasant to stand in for long, but sometimes leading to unexpected rooms.

ps.title: The Art and Science of Perfume

paras.A: Perfume is one of the oldest luxuries. Ancient Egyptians burned resins and fragrant woods in temples and wore scented oils, and perfume jars have been found in the tombs of kings. The word itself comes from the Latin phrase 'per fumum', meaning 'through smoke', which reminds us that the first perfumes were smoke from burning incense. In the Middle Ages, scent was important in the Islamic world, where rose water and other fragrant waters were used in homes, mosques and at celebrations.
paras.B: A key step in the history of perfume was distillation, in which plant material is heated with water and the steam, carrying the scent, is collected and cooled. Arab chemists refined the process in the early Middle Ages, and the philosopher and physician Ibn Sina is often credited with improving the method of obtaining rose water. Distillation made it possible to produce pure essences, which are far stronger than the flowers themselves. A thousand kilograms of rose petals may yield only about one kilogram of rose oil.
paras.C: In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, the centre of the European perfume trade moved to the town of Grasse, in the south of France, where flowers such as jasmine, rose and lavender grew in abundance. The town had been famous for its leather gloves, which were scented to hide the smell of the tanning process. Gradually, the makers realised that the scents were more valuable than the gloves, and perfume became the town's main industry, which it remains today.
paras.D: A perfume is not a single smell but a structure, which perfumers describe in terms of 'notes'. The top notes are the first impression: they are light, fresh and evaporate within minutes. The middle or heart notes, often floral, appear as the top notes fade and last for a few hours. The base notes, such as wood, vanilla and musk, are heavy, remain for many hours and give the perfume depth. A good perfumer blends all three so that the scent develops over time.
paras.E: Traditionally, perfumers used natural materials, including flowers, resins, spices and substances from animals, such as musk from deer and ambergris from whales. Many of these were rare and costly, and some involved cruelty to animals. In the late nineteenth century, chemists learned to make aromatic compounds in the laboratory. Synthetic ingredients are cheaper, more consistent and often more ethical, and today, most perfumes contain both natural and artificial materials.
paras.F: A famous example of this change is Chanel No. 5, launched in 1921. Its creator, the perfumer Ernest Beaux, used a group of synthetic chemicals called aldehydes to produce a bright, abstract scent unlike the simple flower perfumes of the time. It became one of the most successful perfumes in history, and it showed that a perfume need not imitate nature, but could be a work of imagination, like a painting or a piece of music.
paras.G: The strength of a perfume depends on the amount of essence dissolved in alcohol. A 'parfum' contains the most, often twenty to thirty per cent, and lasts the longest, while an 'eau de toilette' contains perhaps five to fifteen per cent. Scientists have also found that perfume affects the wearer differently from the observer, since a scent is influenced by the chemistry of the skin. This is why the same perfume may smell different on two different people.

ps.title: How Satellites Tell Us Where We Are

paras.A: A few decades ago, travellers relied on paper maps, compasses and the advice of passers-by. Today, most people carry a device that can show their position anywhere on Earth, usually to within a few metres. This is made possible by a network of satellites called the Global Positioning System, or GPS. Although most of us use it without a thought, the system relies on some remarkable science.
paras.B: GPS was developed by the United States military, which launched the first satellite in 1978, and became fully operational in the 1990s. For many years, the signal available to civilians was deliberately made less precise, but in 2000, the government removed this restriction, and the number of civilian uses grew rapidly. Other countries have built their own systems, including Russia, the European Union and China, and many phones now use signals from several of them.
paras.C: A navigation system of this kind requires a large number of satellites. The American system has about thirty, each orbiting at a height of roughly twenty thousand kilometres, and they are arranged so that at least four are above the horizon from almost any point on the Earth's surface. Each one broadcasts a continuous signal that includes its position and the exact time at which the signal was sent.
paras.D: A receiver, such as a phone, measures how long each signal takes to arrive. Since radio waves travel at the speed of light, the time delay reveals the distance from each satellite. With the distance from one satellite, the receiver knows that it lies somewhere on a huge imaginary sphere. With two, the possibilities narrow to a circle, and with three, to two points, one of which is usually in space. A fourth satellite is needed to correct the clock in the receiver, which is far less accurate than the clocks in the satellites.
paras.E: Accuracy of timing is therefore crucial. Light travels about thirty centimetres in a billionth of a second, so a timing error of just a millionth of a second would produce an error of 300 metres. The satellites carry extremely precise atomic clocks, and their time is checked regularly from the ground. Without such clocks, the system would drift into uselessness within hours.
paras.F: The theory of relativity also plays a part. According to Einstein, time passes more slowly for objects that move fast, and more quickly where gravity is weaker. Both effects act on the satellite clocks, and the net result is that they run faster than clocks on the ground by a small amount each day. The system corrects for this, and if engineers ignored relativity, errors would accumulate to several kilometres in a single day.
paras.G: GPS is now used in many fields. Farmers guide tractors with it, surveyors map land, scientists track animals and measure the slow movement of continents, and banks and power grids use its signals to keep accurate time. Its weak point is that the signals are faint and can be blocked by buildings, or jammed deliberately. Researchers are therefore developing backup systems, because society now depends on a technology which few people understand.

qs.title: Questions 23–26

paras.A: Few topics divide parents and researchers as sharply as video games. For many adults, a child bent over a screen suggests wasted time, aggression and isolation. For many young people, games are a normal form of play, a way to meet friends and to solve problems. Since games have become one of the largest entertainment industries in the world, with billions of players, the question of their effects is not only a matter for families but for society as a whole.
paras.B: The most frequent worry concerns violence. Many popular games involve fighting, and it seems natural to suppose that children who practise violence in a game will become more violent in life. Some laboratory studies have found that, immediately after playing a violent game, people respond slightly more aggressively in tests. However, reviews of the research by large groups of scientists have concluded that the evidence for a lasting effect on real-life violence is weak, and that other factors, such as family background, are far more important.
paras.C: A second concern is addiction. In 2019, the World Health Organization recognised 'gaming disorder' as a condition, characterised by loss of control over play, giving priority to games over other activities and continuing despite harm. The condition is real for some people, but experts stress that it affects only a small minority of players, and that heavy gaming is often a symptom of other problems, such as anxiety or loneliness, rather than the cause.
paras.D: Sleep and health are also at issue. Late-night playing may reduce sleep, which affects mood and school performance, and long hours of sitting are bad for the body. Parents are right to set limits. At the same time, researchers have not found strong evidence that moderate play, say an hour or so a day, does any harm to the average child, and some studies have found slightly higher wellbeing among those who play a little than among those who never play at all.
paras.E: Games can also have positive effects. Action games seem to improve certain visual skills, such as noticing details and tracking moving objects. Strategy and puzzle games exercise planning and problem-solving, and many games require teamwork and communication with other players, sometimes in different countries. Some games are designed for education, teaching history, mathematics or languages, and surgeons have been found to perform better in simulated operations after practising on games.
paras.F: The content of games matters, too. Age ratings exist to guide parents, but they are not always followed. Online games bring additional risks, including bullying, contact with strangers and pressure to spend money on in-game purchases. Experts advise parents to learn about the games their children play, to talk with them and, where possible, to play together, rather than to ban games outright, which can lead to secrecy.
paras.G: The scientific picture is therefore more nuanced than headlines suggest. For most children, moderate playing of suitable games appears to be harmless, and may bring benefits, while excessive play, harmful content or neglect of sleep and other activities can cause problems. As with other forms of entertainment, from books to films, the key questions are what, how much and with whom, and not simply whether children play.

ps.title: Pompeii: A City Frozen in Time

paras.A: In the year 79 AD, Pompeii was a prosperous Roman town on the Bay of Naples, with perhaps twelve thousand inhabitants. It had a forum, temples, a theatre, public baths and busy streets lined with shops and workshops. Behind the town rose a green mountain, Vesuvius, where farmers grew vines on the fertile slopes. Few people realised that it was a volcano. It had been silent for centuries, and the Romans had no word for what it was about to do.
paras.B: The eruption began around midday with a huge explosion. A column of ash and pumice, light volcanic stones, rose many kilometres into the sky and then spread out like the branches of a tree. For hours, the pumice fell on Pompeii like hail, piling up on roofs, until many of them collapsed. Some residents fled with whatever they could carry, and many survived. Others took shelter in their houses, hoping that the danger would pass.
paras.C: Our best eyewitness account was written by Pliny the Younger, a teenager at the time, who watched from across the bay. Many years later, he described the dark cloud and the panic in a pair of letters to the historian Tacitus. His uncle, Pliny the Elder, who commanded a fleet, sailed across the bay to rescue friends and to observe the phenomenon, and died on the shore. The letters are among the earliest descriptions of a volcanic eruption.
paras.D: During the night and the early morning, the second and more deadly phase began. The tall column of ash collapsed, and avalanches of burning gas, ash and rock, known as pyroclastic surges, rushed down the mountain at tremendous speed. They were hotter than any oven, and anyone still in the town died within moments. When the eruption ended, Pompeii lay buried under a layer of ash and pumice several metres deep, and the town was forgotten.
paras.E: The ruins were rediscovered by accident in the sixteenth century, when workers digging a channel found walls and paintings, but systematic excavation began only in 1748. The site was a revelation. Because ash had covered everything quickly, it preserved the town in an extraordinary way: loaves of bread were found in an oven, coins on a counter, and bright paintings on the walls of houses. Writing on the walls, from political slogans to jokes and love messages, shows how ordinary people lived.
paras.F: In the 1860s, an Italian archaeologist named Giuseppe Fiorelli devised a method of recording the victims. He noticed that the bodies had decayed, leaving hollow spaces in the hardened ash. By pouring liquid plaster into these hollows, he made casts which show people in the final moments of their lives, some crouched, some covering their faces. These casts are among the most moving objects ever discovered by archaeologists.
paras.G: Vesuvius is still active, and it is now one of the most dangerous volcanoes in the world, since around three million people live in the surrounding area. Scientists monitor it constantly with instruments that measure earthquakes, ground movement and gases, and the authorities have prepared an evacuation plan. Meanwhile, Pompeii itself faces different threats, including rain, plants growing in the walls and the footsteps of millions of tourists, which means that conservation work never stops.

qs.title: Questions 10–13

paras.A: At dawn in spring, the air fills with birdsong. To human ears, it is one of the most pleasant sounds in nature, and poets have praised it for thousands of years. For biologists, though, it is also a puzzle. Why do birds sing, how do they produce such complex sounds and how do they learn them? Over the last century, researchers have found answers to many of these questions, and the results have surprised even them.
paras.B: Birdsong has two main purposes. Males use it to defend a territory, warning rivals to keep away, and to attract females. In many species, the quality of a song seems to tell a female something about the male's health and experience: a long, complex and accurate song is difficult to produce, so it is an honest sign of fitness. In some species, females, too, sing, and pairs of birds sometimes sing together in duets so well coordinated that they sound like a single bird.
paras.C: The organ that makes the sound is not the throat, as in humans, but the syrinx, which lies deep in the chest where the windpipe divides into two tubes leading to the lungs. Each side of the syrinx can be controlled separately, so that a bird can produce two different notes at once, or sing one phrase with one side while breathing with the other. This allows songs of astonishing speed and complexity, which a human would be unable to imitate.
paras.D: Perhaps the most remarkable discovery is that many birds learn their songs, much as human children learn language. A young songbird first listens to adult birds, often its father, and stores the sounds in memory. Later, it starts to produce them, at first in a rough, wandering form called subsong, similar to the babbling of a baby, and gradually improves by comparing its own voice with the memory until the song is accurate.
paras.E: There is a sensitive period for this learning. If a young bird is raised in isolation, it sings a simple, strange song, and if it hears recordings only after a certain age, it may never learn the correct one. Different regions have local dialects, so that chaffinches in one valley may sing differently from those in the next. Scientists studying the zebra finch have found that the parts of the brain involved in song learning resemble those involved in human speech.
paras.F: Some birds are expert mimics. The lyrebird of Australia can copy the calls of other birds, and has even been recorded imitating the sounds of a camera shutter and a chainsaw. Mynas and parrots can imitate human words, although they do not understand them in the way we do. Why mimicry evolved is still debated, but it may help males to show off the size of their repertoire.
paras.G: Birdsong is now changing because of human activity. In noisy cities, birds such as blackbirds and great tits sing at a higher pitch than their country cousins, so that their songs are not drowned out by the low rumble of traffic. Others sing at night, when the streets are quieter. Researchers worry that if the noise becomes too great, some species may not find mates. The dawn chorus may therefore be an indicator of how well we are looking after the environment.

qs.title: Questions 23–26

paras.A: For most of history, children have played in streets, squares and fields near their homes. Today, in many cities, they rarely do. Busy roads, fears of crime and the attractions of screens mean that many young people spend much of their time indoors, and a child who is allowed to walk to school alone is now the exception in many countries. Planners and health experts increasingly ask whether cities can be redesigned to give children back some freedom.
paras.B: The idea has a long history, but it gained momentum in 1996, when the United Nations children's agency launched an initiative to encourage towns to put children's rights at the centre of local decisions. The initiative urges authorities to consult children about their neighbourhoods, to improve safety and to ensure that all children have access to parks, schools and health services. Hundreds of cities around the world have taken part, from large capitals to small towns.
paras.C: The case for child-friendly cities begins with health. Children who play outdoors tend to be more active and are less likely to become overweight. Contact with nature appears to reduce stress and to improve concentration. Independent movement through the neighbourhood also builds confidence, a sense of direction and the ability to judge risk. Researchers who compare generations note that children's independent mobility has fallen steeply in many countries over recent decades.
paras.D: Several practical measures have been tried. Some cities have created 'school streets', closing the road outside a school to cars at the start and end of the day, so that children can walk or cycle in safety. Others have lowered speed limits, widened pavements and built safer crossings. A number of cities close streets to traffic on certain days, allowing children and adults to play, ride and walk on the road. Playgrounds are being designed with natural materials and wild corners, not just standard equipment.
paras.E: Such measures, planners argue, benefit everyone. A street where a child can safely walk is also safe for the elderly, for people in wheelchairs and for parents with babies. A phrase popular among urban designers says that a city planned for the youngest and the oldest, the eight-year-old and the eighty-year-old, will be good for everyone in between. Less traffic means cleaner air and quieter neighbourhoods, which brings advantages to all residents.
paras.F: Not everyone is convinced. Drivers and shop owners sometimes object to the loss of parking spaces or the closing of roads, and in crowded cities, land for playgrounds competes with housing. Some parents worry that giving children freedom exposes them to danger, though studies suggest that the risk from traffic is far greater than the risk from strangers. Critics also note that child-friendly programmes are often more successful in wealthy districts than in poorer ones, where the needs are greatest.
paras.G: Perhaps the most important change is in attitudes. When children are asked what they want, they rarely mention expensive equipment. They ask for safe paths, green places, somewhere to meet friends and the right to be taken seriously. Cities that listen to them may discover that child-friendly design is less a matter of money than of imagination, and of the willingness to share public space more fairly.

paras.A: Salt is so common that we hardly think about it. It sits in a shaker on almost every table, and it costs very little. Yet for most of history, salt was a precious commodity, valued so highly that it was traded over thousands of kilometres and sometimes used as a form of payment. Wars were fought over salt sources, and empires taxed it. To understand why, we need to ask what salt does for us.
paras.B: The human body needs a small amount of sodium, one of the elements in salt, in order to keep the nerves, muscles and fluids working properly. In hot climates, people lose salt through sweat and must replace it. Animals need it, too, and wild herds often travel long distances to reach natural salt licks. Farmers who keep sheep, cattle and horses must provide extra salt for their animals.
paras.C: Before the invention of refrigeration, salt was also the main way of preserving food. Meat and fish packed in salt could be kept for months, because salt draws water out of the food and prevents the growth of the bacteria that cause rotting. This made it possible to store the harvest for winter, to feed armies on campaign and to sail on long voyages. Cheese, pickled vegetables and sausages are all examples of salt-preserved foods that people still enjoy.
paras.D: Salt can be obtained in two main ways. One is by evaporating sea water or water from salty springs, which is done in shallow pans using the heat of the sun. The other is by mining rock salt, the remains of ancient seas that dried up millions of years ago. The Wieliczka salt mine in Poland, which has been worked since the Middle Ages, contains underground chapels, statues and even a lake, all carved from salt by the miners.
paras.E: Because it was essential and sometimes scarce, salt shaped trade routes and politics. Caravans carried it across the Sahara, where blocks of salt were exchanged for gold. In Venice and in China, the state controlled salt production and earned a large part of its income from the salt tax. Some scholars connect the English word 'salary' with the Latin word for salt, although the exact story of the link is uncertain.
paras.F: The most famous protest about salt took place in India in 1930. At that time, British rulers had a monopoly on its production and made Indians pay a tax on it. Mahatma Gandhi led a march of about 390 kilometres from his home to the sea at Dandi, which took nearly four weeks. On arrival, he picked up a lump of natural salt, thus breaking the law. The act inspired thousands of people to follow, and it became a symbol of the struggle for independence.
paras.G: Today, salt is cheap and plentiful, and the concern is not shortage but excess. Too much sodium raises the blood pressure of many people, increasing the risk of heart disease and strokes. The World Health Organization recommends that adults eat less than five grams of salt a day, but many people consume far more, mostly from processed foods and restaurant meals, not from the shaker on the table. The treasure of the past has become something to be used with care.

qs.title: Questions 10–13

paras.A: Look closely at a sunflower, a pine cone, a snail shell or a honeycomb, and you will notice that nature is full of patterns. Spirals, hexagons, stripes and branching forms appear again and again in living things, in places that have nothing else in common. For centuries, scientists and artists have asked why. Some of the answers lie in mathematics, and others in the practical demands of survival.
paras.B: One of the best-known patterns involves a sequence of numbers named after the Italian mathematician Fibonacci, who described it in 1202. It begins 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, and each number is the sum of the two before it. These numbers appear remarkably often in the spirals of plants. The seeds in the head of a sunflower, for example, are arranged in two sets of spirals, one turning clockwise and the other anticlockwise, and the numbers of spirals in each set are usually neighbouring Fibonacci numbers, such as 34 and 55.
paras.C: The reason is efficiency. As a plant grows, each new leaf or seed appears at a certain angle from the last. If this angle is chosen well, the leaves are spaced so that none is shaded by those above, and the seeds are packed tightly without leaving gaps. The best angle, about 137.5 degrees, is called the golden angle, and it is closely linked to the Fibonacci numbers. Plants do not calculate; the pattern emerges from simple growth rules which have been favoured by evolution.
paras.D: Another familiar pattern is the hexagon. In a honeycomb, bees build rows of six-sided cells. Among shapes that can fit together without gaps, the hexagon encloses the largest area for a given length of wall, and so it saves wax. Bees do not know geometry; rather, the cells are built as round tubes that become hexagonal as neighbours push against each other while the wax is warm. The same shape appears in soap bubbles packed together, where surface tension works in a similar way.
paras.E: Some patterns repeat at different scales, a property known as self-similarity. A fern leaf consists of smaller leaflets, each of which resembles the whole leaf, and the branching of a tree is echoed in the branching of its twigs. Such shapes, called fractals, are found in coastlines, river networks, lightning and even the blood vessels of the lungs. They allow a structure to fill space efficiently, whether to collect sunlight, drain water or deliver oxygen.
paras.F: Animal markings are another puzzle. In 1952, the mathematician Alan Turing proposed that stripes and spots could arise when two chemicals spread through tissue at different speeds, one activating colour and the other inhibiting it. Computer models based on this idea can produce patterns resembling those of zebras, leopards and fish. Experiments have since shown that similar processes occur in the development of animals, although the details are more complex than Turing's simple model.
paras.G: Finding patterns in nature does not mean that nature follows a mathematical plan. Rather, mathematics describes the limits within which natural processes operate. Because shapes that save energy and materials tend to survive, the same solutions appear again and again. For people, studying them has practical value, and engineers now borrow ideas from honeycombs, shells and plants to design strong, light structures.

ps.title: Should Cars Be Banned from City Centres?

paras.A: In the middle of the twentieth century, planners in many countries designed their cities around the car. Wide roads were built, old streets were cleared for parking, and the motor vehicle became the symbol of freedom and progress. Today, many city leaders are reconsidering that choice. Some have limited or even banned private cars in their centres, and the results have attracted attention around the world.
paras.B: Supporters of such restrictions begin with air quality. Exhaust fumes contain fine particles and gases that damage the lungs and the heart, and the World Health Organization estimates that air pollution contributes to millions of early deaths every year. Cars are not the only source, but in dense city centres they are often the largest. Several cities that restricted traffic have recorded lower levels of pollution within a few years.
paras.C: A second argument concerns space. A private car is parked for most of its life, and each parked car occupies about the area of a small room. If streets and car parks were given to pedestrians, cyclists, trees and cafés, supporters say, the city would become more pleasant and healthier. They also point to safety: traffic accidents are a leading cause of death among young people, and lower speeds and fewer cars reduce injuries.
paras.D: There are several experiments to examine. In 2003, London introduced a charge for driving into its centre, which reduced traffic considerably, and later added a charge for the most polluting vehicles. Madrid created a low-emission zone in its centre in 2018, and Oslo has removed most on-street parking. In Paris, the mayor has expanded cycle lanes and closed some riverside roads to cars. In each case, cycling and use of public transport increased.
paras.E: Critics raise important objections. Shopkeepers often fear that customers who arrive by car will go elsewhere, and some people with limited mobility depend on cars to reach the centre. Delivery vehicles and emergency services must be able to enter. Residents of outer suburbs, who may have no good bus or train, argue that restrictions fall most heavily on people who have the fewest alternatives, and that wealthy central residents benefit most.
paras.F: Evidence on business is mixed but often reassuring. Studies of pedestrian streets in several countries show that shops frequently do as well or better after traffic is removed, since people who walk visit more often and linger longer. Shopkeepers tend to overestimate the number of their customers who arrive by car. Success, however, depends on good public transport, since a ban without alternatives may simply cause frustration.
paras.G: Most experts therefore favour a gradual, well-prepared approach. Cities can improve buses, trams and cycle routes first, consult residents and businesses, and make exceptions for people with disabilities and for deliveries at certain hours. Over time, as habits change, the area free of cars can grow. The aim is not to punish drivers, but to ask a simple question: who should the centre of a city be for?

ps.title: The Tulip: From the Mountains to Amsterdam

paras.A: The tulip is so closely linked to the Netherlands that many people assume it grew there naturally. In fact, wild tulips come from the mountains of Central Asia, especially the ranges that stretch through present-day Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, and from parts of Turkey and Iran. They flower in spring, when the snow melts, and their bulbs survive the hot, dry summers underground. People in this region admired them long before Europeans did.
paras.B: The Persians and the Ottoman Turks were the first to grow tulips in gardens. In the sixteenth century, the flower became a favourite of the sultans in Istanbul, who held tulip festivals and developed hundreds of varieties with long, narrow, pointed petals. The name 'tulip' is thought to come from the Persian and Turkish word for turban, because of the shape of the flower. One period of Ottoman history in the early eighteenth century is even known as the 'Tulip Era'.
paras.C: Tulips reached Western Europe in the sixteenth century. A diplomat named Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq, who served the Austrian emperor in Istanbul, sent bulbs and seeds home in the 1550s. Later, a botanist named Carolus Clusius took bulbs to the University of Leiden in the Netherlands, where he planted them in 1593 in the university's botanical garden. The flowers were admired, and Clusius refused to sell them, so some of them were stolen. The theft helped to spread tulips through Dutch gardens.
paras.D: Some tulips developed beautiful streaks and flames of colour on their petals. At that time, nobody understood the cause; we now know that the patterns were produced by a virus that weakened the bulbs. Bulbs of such 'broken' tulips were extremely rare, and collectors competed to buy them. In the 1630s, the Dutch republic was rich and optimistic, and a number of people began to trade tulip bulbs, sometimes even before the bulbs were dug up, as promises written on paper.
paras.E: Prices rose dramatically, and in the winter of 1636 to 1637, a single rare bulb might change hands for more than the cost of a house. Then, in February 1637, buyers failed to appear at an auction, and the market collapsed. The episode, known as 'tulip mania', has often been told as a warning about the madness of crowds, in which thousands of people were ruined. Modern historians, however, believe that the story has been exaggerated: only a small number of traders were involved, and few lost much money.
paras.F: Whatever the truth, the Dutch tulip industry survived. The sandy soil and mild, damp climate of the coast were ideal for growing bulbs, and farmers developed new varieties and methods. By the nineteenth century, bulb farming had become a major business. Today, the Netherlands produces billions of tulip bulbs every year, and exports them to countries all over the world, including their home region of Central Asia.
paras.G: Each spring, fields of tulips in red, yellow, pink and purple stretch for kilometres across the Dutch landscape, and the gardens of Keukenhof, which open for only a few weeks each year, attract hundreds of thousands of visitors. Meanwhile, in the mountains of Central Asia, wild tulips still bloom on the slopes. Some of the species are now rare, and conservationists remind visitors that the original flower of the East deserves protection too.

qs.title: Questions 10–13

paras.A: A plant cannot run away from a hungry animal, and it cannot hide. Rooted in one place, it must face insects, grazing mammals, fungi and bacteria, as well as drought and cold. It might seem that plants are helpless. In fact, over hundreds of millions of years, they have evolved an astonishing range of defences, some physical, some chemical and some that involve forming alliances with other creatures.
paras.B: The most obvious defences are physical. Thorns, spines and prickles prevent large animals from taking a bite. Many leaves are covered with tiny hairs, and some are so tough, or coated with wax, that insects find them difficult to chew. Stinging nettles carry hollow hairs filled with chemicals that cause pain when touched. In deserts, cactus spines also shade the plant and collect moisture, so a single feature may serve more than one purpose.
paras.C: Chemical defences are even more widespread. Plants produce thousands of substances that taste bitter, burn the mouth, or poison the animals that eat them. Nicotine in tobacco plants and caffeine in coffee plants are both thought to have evolved as protection against insects. Humans, however, have turned many of these substances to their own use as medicines, spices and drugs. Aspirin, for example, was developed from a compound found in willow bark.
paras.D: Some plants respond only when attacked. When a caterpillar begins to chew a leaf, the plant detects chemicals in its saliva and quickly increases its production of toxins. More surprising still, certain plants release a scent when damaged, which attracts wasps or other predators that attack the caterpillars. This may be thought of as a 'cry for help', although the plant does not, of course, act with intention; the ability has simply been favoured by evolution.
paras.E: Plants can warn one another, too. Studies show that when a plant is damaged, it releases airborne chemicals that neighbouring plants of the same species can detect, after which the neighbours begin to prepare their own defences. Some researchers also suggest that signals may pass between plants through networks of fungi in the soil, although scientists disagree about how important this is, and the claim is still being tested.
paras.F: Movement is rare in plants, but a few species use it to protect themselves. The sensitive plant, or mimosa, folds its leaves together within seconds when touched, which probably startles insects and makes the plant appear less attractive. The Venus flytrap goes further, catching insects with leaves that snap shut, and digesting them to obtain nutrients that are scarce in its poor soil.
paras.G: Understanding plant defences is of great practical importance. Farmers lose a large share of their crops to pests each year, and chemical sprays can harm the environment and human health. Scientists hope to breed crops that are better at defending themselves, using the natural strategies that wild plants have developed, and perhaps to find new medicines in the chemicals that plants make.

qs.title: Questions 23–26

paras.A: In many countries, the school day begins very early, at eight o'clock or even before. For adults, this seems natural, but for teenagers, it can be a daily struggle. Scientists who study sleep have found that adolescents are not simply lazy when they find it difficult to wake: their bodies are changing in ways that make early mornings especially hard. This has led to a growing debate about whether secondary schools should start later.
paras.B: The explanation lies in the body clock. During puberty, the release of the hormone melatonin, which makes us feel sleepy, shifts later in the evening. As a result, many teenagers do not feel tired until eleven at night or later, but they still need around eight to ten hours of sleep. If they must wake at six or seven to get to school, they may regularly lose two or more hours of sleep. This pattern is the result of biology, not of choice.
paras.C: The consequences of sleep loss are well documented. Tired students find it harder to concentrate and remember, and their moods are more changeable. Studies link too little sleep with a higher risk of depression, accidents and poor health. Many teenagers try to catch up at weekends, which further disturbs their body clocks. Some doctors have described the situation as a public health problem, and several medical associations recommend that schools start no earlier than half past eight.
paras.D: Some schools have already tried the change. In one American study, a school district in Seattle moved its high-school start time from about 7.50 to 8.45. Researchers who followed the students found that they slept on average about half an hour longer each night, and that their grades improved modestly. Attendance rose, and students were less often late. Similar results have been reported in other studies, though not all find a large effect.
paras.E: Opponents mention practical difficulties. School buses often serve students of different ages in turn, and changing the start of secondary schools may require changes for primary schools too, or additional buses, which cost money. Later finishing times can interfere with sports, part-time jobs and after-school activities, and some parents have jobs that begin early and cannot easily take their children to school later. Teachers, too, may have family obligations in the afternoon.
paras.F: Another objection is that some students would simply stay up even later if they could, and so gain no sleep. There is some truth in this: sleep depends on habits as well as on schedules. Experts therefore recommend combining later start times with advice about sleep, such as limiting the use of screens in the bedroom in the evening and avoiding caffeine. Schools can also teach students why sleep matters.
paras.G: The question is ultimately about priorities. A school timetable is a human choice, and it can be changed if there is good reason. Supporters of later starts argue that learning, health and safety are more important than convenience, and that the cost of adjusting schedules is small compared with the benefits. Whether communities agree will depend on their particular circumstances, but the science suggests that the question deserves to be taken seriously.

ps.title: The Giant Squid: Monster of the Deep

paras.A: For centuries, sailors told stories of enormous sea monsters with many arms that rose from the depths and dragged ships beneath the waves. The legend of the kraken, as it was called in Scandinavia, probably grew from sightings of a real animal: the giant squid. Dead specimens washed ashore from time to time, or were found floating at sea, and their size convinced scientists that the stories contained some truth. Yet the living animal remained unseen for a very long time.
paras.B: The giant squid is among the largest invertebrates on Earth. Females can reach a length of around thirteen metres, including the two long feeding tentacles, though most of this is arms and tentacles, and the body itself is about two metres long. The animal has eight arms and two tentacles lined with hundreds of suckers, each with a toothed ring. It also has the largest eyes of any animal, as wide as a dinner plate, which are believed to help it see in the dim light of the deep sea.
paras.C: Giant squid live in the ocean at depths of three hundred to a thousand metres, where sunlight barely penetrates and the water is cold. They are found in all the world's oceans, but mostly far from the coast. Because of this, scientists have learned about them chiefly from dead animals, the stomach contents of other creatures and the occasional unlucky individual caught in a fishing net. Much of our information comes from one predator in particular, the sperm whale.
paras.D: Sperm whales hunt giant squid, and the sharp, beak-like jaws of the squid, which cannot be digested, accumulate in the whales' stomachs. Researchers have found hundreds of these beaks in a single whale. The skin of many sperm whales also carries round scars, made by the suckers of squid during battles in the dark. These scars suggest a struggle between two of the largest animals on Earth, though no one has seen it directly.
paras.E: For a long time, no one had photographed a living giant squid. The first pictures of one in its natural habitat were taken in 2004, by Japanese researchers who lowered a camera attached to a long line baited with a small squid at a depth of nine hundred metres. Several years later, the same team succeeded in filming a giant squid with a submersible, and in 2012, they recorded video of an adult in its home. The animal appeared pale and silvery, and surprisingly graceful.
paras.F: These observations corrected some old ideas. The squid was not a violent monster hunting ships but a slow-moving predator that probably catches fish and other squid by ambushing them. Scientists also learned that it swims by pumping jets of water, and that it can change colour. Its lifespan seems short, perhaps only a few years, and its growth is fast. Questions remain about how it breeds, and how many individuals exist.
paras.G: There is also a heavier relative, the colossal squid, which lives in the cold waters near Antarctica. It is shorter than the giant squid, but has a bulkier body and hooks on its tentacles, and it may weigh more than four hundred kilograms. Only a few specimens have ever been seen. The deep sea is the least explored environment on our planet, and the story of the giant squid is a reminder that large animals can still remain hidden, and that our oceans hold many surprises.

paras.A: No language is entirely pure. Every language has borrowed words from others, usually many of them, and the vocabulary of a language tells the story of its people's contacts with the world. English, which has been called a magpie language because it collects shiny things from everywhere, is a famous example. Experts estimate that most of the words in a large English dictionary have origins outside the oldest English core.
paras.B: The largest single source of borrowing was the French language of the Normans, who conquered England in 1066. For several hundred years, the nobility spoke French while ordinary people spoke English, and so English words for animals in the field, such as 'cow' and 'sheep', come from the farmers, while the words for the meat on the table, 'beef' and 'mutton', come from the French of the rulers. Many words for law, government and art entered in the same way.
paras.C: Later waves of borrowing followed trade and exploration. From Arabic, English took words including 'algebra', 'coffee', 'sugar', 'cotton' and 'zero', reflecting the importance of Arab science and commerce in the Middle Ages. From Hindi came 'shampoo' and 'jungle', and from Persian, 'bazaar' and 'caravan'. In the same way, Uzbek, Russian and other languages have received hundreds of words from Persian, Arabic, Turkic neighbours and, in more recent times, from Russian and English.
paras.D: Why do languages borrow? The most common reason is need: when a new object or idea arrives, the language adopts the name that comes with it. Tea, tobacco and tomatoes arrived in Europe with their names, and in the twentieth century, words such as 'computer' and 'internet' spread around the world. Another reason is prestige. People may use a foreign word because it sounds modern, educated or fashionable, even when a native word exists.
paras.E: Borrowed words rarely arrive unchanged. Speakers adapt them to the sounds and spelling of their own language, so that the French word 'beefsteak' became the Japanese 'bifuteki' and the English word 'football' became 'futbol' in Spanish. Often, the meaning also changes. The English word 'pants' means trousers in American English but underwear in British English, and in Japanese, the borrowed word 'mansion' means an apartment block.
paras.F: Not everyone welcomes the flow of foreign words. Some governments and institutions try to protect their language from what they see as excessive influence. The French Academy, founded in 1635, publishes recommended native alternatives to English terms, and several other countries have similar bodies. Their success is limited, as ordinary speakers tend to use the words they find convenient. Language, as one linguist said, is a river that cannot be dammed.
paras.G: Linguists generally take a calm view of borrowing. They point out that it is a sign of a living language, and that borrowed words become part of the borrower's vocabulary. A serious problem arises only when a small language is under pressure from a large one, and speakers abandon their own words and grammar altogether. Then, a language does not simply borrow; it begins to disappear.

ps.title: Can the Economy Grow without Harming the Planet?

paras.A: For most of the last two centuries, economic growth has meant more factories, more energy and more goods. It has also meant rising incomes, longer lives and falling poverty in many parts of the world. At the same time, growth has been accompanied by pollution, the destruction of habitats and climate change. This raises one of the central questions of our time: is it possible to keep improving living standards without destroying the natural systems on which life depends?
paras.B: Optimists answer yes, and their key idea is 'decoupling'. The economy, they argue, can grow while its use of resources and its emissions fall, because of improved technology and a shift from heavy industry to services. There is some evidence for this. In a number of wealthy countries, including Britain and Germany, economic output has risen while carbon dioxide emissions have declined over the past few decades. Renewable energy has become cheaper, and efficient machines use less fuel.
paras.C: Sceptics reply that the evidence is less impressive than it looks. Part of the decline in emissions in rich countries results from moving production abroad: goods are made elsewhere, in factories whose emissions are not counted, and then imported. When these hidden emissions are included, the fall is smaller. Moreover, decoupling must be rapid and complete to protect the climate, and so far the reductions have not been fast enough. Resource use in general, including metals, sand and land, has continued to rise.
paras.D: A more radical group argues that wealthy countries should abandon growth as a goal altogether. Supporters of this 'degrowth' movement say that economic output is a poor measure of wellbeing, since it counts the cost of repairing disasters as a gain and ignores unpaid work and the health of the environment. They propose shorter working hours, more sharing and lower consumption of luxuries, while ensuring that everyone has enough for a good life.
paras.E: Critics of degrowth warn that it would be politically and socially risky. Without growth, they argue, it is much harder to pay for pensions, healthcare and education, or to reduce poverty, and unemployment could rise. Poorer countries, in particular, need to grow in order to provide decent housing and services for their citizens. Many economists add that history shows no example of a rich society that has deliberately accepted a smaller economy.
paras.F: A middle path is sometimes called 'green growth', or the pursuit of growth in activities that reduce harm, such as clean energy, public transport, recycling and restoration of nature. Governments can encourage this by making polluters pay, by ending subsidies for fossil fuels and by funding research. Proponents note that a carbon price changes the incentives for business, so that cleaner options become the more profitable ones.
paras.G: The disagreement is partly about facts and partly about values. How quickly can technology change? How much do people value more goods compared with more leisure or a healthy environment? It is possible that no single answer fits every country. What most observers accept is that continuing as before is unlikely to work, and that whichever path is chosen, the transition will need careful planning and fairness.

ps.title: The Taj Mahal: A Monument to Love

paras.A: On the southern bank of the Yamuna River in Agra, India, stands a white marble building that many regard as the most beautiful in the world. The Taj Mahal was built by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan as a tomb for his beloved wife, Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631 while giving birth to their fourteenth child. The emperor was heartbroken, and it is said that his hair turned white with grief. He decided to create a memorial that would be remembered for ever.
paras.B: The Mughal dynasty had its roots in Central Asia. Its founder, Babur, was born in the Fergana Valley, in what is now Uzbekistan, and was a descendant of Timur. After losing his homeland, he led an army south and in 1526 established a new empire in India. Mughal rulers brought with them the Persian language, a love of gardens and a style of architecture that combined Central Asian, Persian and Indian traditions. The Taj Mahal is the finest expression of this blend.
paras.C: Work began around 1632 and lasted more than twenty years. Roughly twenty thousand workers were employed, including masons, stone-cutters, carvers and calligraphers from many parts of India and beyond. The white marble was brought from quarries at Makrana, in Rajasthan, about three hundred kilometres away, on carts pulled by teams of oxen. Other materials came from even farther: jade and crystal from China, turquoise from Tibet and lapis lazuli from Afghanistan.
paras.D: The design follows a plan of perfect symmetry. The tomb stands on a raised platform, with a minaret at each corner, and is crowned by a great central dome surrounded by four smaller ones. The four minarets lean slightly outward, which probably protects the tomb if they were to fall, since they would collapse away from it. In front of the tomb lies a long garden divided by water channels into four equal parts, reflecting the Persian idea of paradise.
paras.E: The surface is decorated with great delicacy. Verses from the Quran are carved in elegant script around the arches, and the letters become slightly larger towards the top so that they appear the same size to a viewer on the ground. Flowers and vines are made from thin pieces of coloured stone set into the marble, in a technique known as pietra dura. Some single flowers contain dozens of tiny stones.
paras.F: One of the pleasures of the building is the way its appearance changes during the day. At dawn, the marble looks soft pink, in the full sun it glows white, and under the moon it seems to shine with a silver light. Visitors often come at sunrise to see this change. Each year, millions of people visit the monument, making it one of the most popular tourist attractions in the world.
paras.G: The building now faces threats from the modern world. Air pollution from factories and traffic has caused the marble to turn yellow in places, and acid rain damages the stone. The Yamuna River has been polluted and has sometimes dried up, which worries engineers because the foundations are made of wood that needs moisture. The government has restricted vehicles near the monument and closed some factories, and conservators regularly clean the marble with a special clay, in the hope that this masterpiece will survive for centuries more.

qs.title: Questions 10–13

paras.A: Every night, for about two hours, we dream. Most dreams are forgotten within minutes of waking, but some are vivid enough to be remembered for a lifetime. People have always been fascinated by dreams. The ancient Egyptians recorded them as messages from the gods, the Greeks consulted dream interpreters, and many cultures have treated dreams as a window to the future. Only in the last hundred years have scientists begun to study them systematically.
paras.B: The most famous early theory was proposed by Sigmund Freud, who published his book on the interpretation of dreams in 1899. He believed that dreams express wishes that we are unable to admit to ourselves, disguised in symbols. Although his ideas were very influential, they are difficult to test, and most scientists today regard them with scepticism. The symbols in dreams, they say, are usually less mysterious than Freud thought.
paras.C: A turning point came in the 1950s, when researchers discovered REM sleep, the stage of sleep with rapid eye movements, during which most vivid dreaming occurs. When people were woken during REM sleep, they reported dreams much more often than when woken at other times. This made it possible to study the brain during dreaming, and it showed that the brain is highly active during this stage, almost as active as when awake.
paras.D: In 1977, two Harvard psychiatrists, Allan Hobson and Robert McCarley, proposed the 'activation-synthesis' theory. According to this view, dreams arise when the sleeping brain produces random signals, and the higher parts of the brain try to make a story out of them. This explains why dreams are often strange and illogical. Later researchers have modified the theory, suggesting that dreams are not completely random but are influenced by our memories, worries and experiences.
paras.E: Other theories focus on function. One suggests that dreaming helps with memory, by replaying and reorganising the events of the day. Another proposes that dreams help to deal with emotions: in REM sleep, the levels of stress chemicals in the brain are low, so that upsetting memories can be reviewed in a safer state. Yet another idea, the threat simulation theory, suggests that dreams provide a rehearsal for dangerous situations, which helped our ancestors to survive.
paras.F: The content of dreams has been studied by collecting thousands of dream reports. Most dreams concern ordinary matters from daily life, and many include negative feelings such as anxiety or fear. People blind from birth dream in sounds, smells and touch rather than in pictures. Common themes, such as being chased, falling or arriving unprepared for an examination, occur across cultures, although the reasons are not known.
paras.G: Some people can become aware that they are dreaming and even control what happens. Known as lucid dreaming, this ability can be improved with practice, and some people use it to overcome nightmares. Scientists remain uncertain about the purpose of dreams, and it is possible that they serve several purposes, or none directly. What is clear is that sleep and dreaming are essential to health, and that much remains to be discovered.

qs.title: Questions 23–26

paras.A: Walk through any modern city centre, and you are likely to be filmed many times. Cameras watch shops, stations, streets and car parks, and in some places, one can be found every few metres. In Britain alone, there are estimated to be several million of them. They are usually installed for good reasons, such as preventing crime and helping police, but their growing number and power raise a question that societies are only beginning to answer: how much watching is too much?
paras.B: The case for cameras rests on security. Their presence may discourage some offenders, and their recordings can help to identify those who commit crimes. After terrorist attacks and serious crimes, images from cameras have often been crucial in tracing the culprits. Many shop owners, residents and transport operators say that cameras make them feel safer, and some insurance companies offer lower prices to buildings that have them.
paras.C: The evidence for crime prevention is, however, mixed. Reviews of numerous studies suggest that cameras reduce crime modestly in some settings, especially in car parks, but have little effect in city streets, where offenders may move to other places or do not consider the risk. Cameras are most effective when combined with other measures, such as better lighting and active monitoring. Simply putting up more of them does not guarantee a safer place.
paras.D: Technology has changed the nature of surveillance. In the past, a camera recorded pictures that someone had to watch. Today, software can analyse the images automatically, reading vehicle number plates and, with facial recognition, identifying individuals in a crowd. This makes it possible to search through recordings in seconds, and to track a person across a city. Supporters say that this helps find missing people and wanted criminals; critics see the first step towards constant monitoring.
paras.E: Privacy is the central worry. People feel differently when they know they are being watched, and may behave less freely, a effect sometimes called the 'chilling effect'. A person might hesitate to attend a protest, visit a clinic or meet a friend if the movement can be recorded and stored. Without clear rules, the information can be misused, shared with other organisations or stolen by criminals. History offers examples of governments using records to control opponents.
paras.F: There are also concerns about accuracy and fairness. Studies show that some facial recognition systems make more mistakes with women and with people with darker skin, so that innocent people may be wrongly identified. An error that results in a person being stopped by the police can be frightening and damaging. Critics argue that decisions of this kind should not be made by a program that nobody can inspect.
paras.G: Most experts do not call for removing all cameras, but for strict rules. Suggested safeguards include clear signs, limits on how long recordings are kept, independent supervision, and a ban or tight limits on the most intrusive technologies, such as live facial recognition in public places. Citizens should also have the right to know how their images are used. The aim is to enjoy the benefits of security without sacrificing the freedom that security is meant to protect.

ps.title: Marie Tharp and the Map of the Ocean Floor

paras.A: Until the middle of the twentieth century, the bottom of the ocean was one of the least known places on Earth. Scientists could map the surface of the Moon more accurately than the seabed. Most people imagined that the ocean floor was a flat, featureless plain covered in mud. The woman who changed this picture was an American scientist named Marie Tharp, whose maps revealed a hidden world of mountains and valleys.
paras.B: Tharp was born in 1920 and trained as a geologist. At that time, women were seldom welcomed in the sciences, but the Second World War had created opportunities, and she gained a degree and a job in a laboratory at Columbia University in New York. There she joined a geologist named Bruce Heezen, who collected measurements of the depth of the sea. Because women were not allowed to join research ships in those days, Tharp stayed ashore and worked with the data.
paras.C: Ships measured the depth of the ocean by sending out sound waves, which bounced from the bottom and returned, and the time they took revealed the depth. Every voyage produced long lines of numbers along its track. Tharp took thousands of these lines and, by hand, turned them into drawings of the seabed. It was patient, detailed work that took years. She had to decide how to join the dots between widely separated tracks, using her knowledge of geology.
paras.D: In 1952, she noticed something remarkable. In the middle of the Atlantic Ocean, a long chain of underwater mountains ran from north to south, and along its centre there was a deep valley, a rift. She realised that it might be a place where the Earth's crust was splitting apart, which would support the unpopular idea that continents move. Heezen did not believe her at first, dismissing the idea as 'girl talk'. At the time, most geologists rejected continental drift.
paras.E: Over the next few years, Heezen gathered further evidence. Records of earthquakes showed that they followed the line of the rift, exactly as Tharp had mapped it. Later, photographs of the seabed and other measurements confirmed the picture. By the 1960s, her discovery had become central to the theory of plate tectonics, which explains how the surface of the Earth is made of moving plates, and which is now the foundation of modern geology.
paras.F: Tharp and Heezen then worked on a series of maps of the world's seafloors. The most famous, published in 1977, was painted by an Austrian artist, Heinrich Berann, who used Tharp's data. It showed the ocean basins as if the water had been drained away, with mountain ranges, canyons and plains in vivid detail. The map was widely reproduced, and for many people, it was the first time that they had seen what the bottom of the sea really looks like.
paras.G: For many years, Tharp's contribution was not fully recognised, and Heezen's name was more often mentioned. Gradually, however, scientists recognised her role, and in the 1990s, she received honours including a place in the Library of Congress as one of the great mapmakers of the century. She died in 2006. Her story reminds us that important discoveries often depend on people whose work was not noticed at first.

qs.title: Questions 10–13

paras.A: Today, pepper and cinnamon sit in kitchen cupboards and cost very little. For much of history, however, spices were among the most valuable goods in the world. Worth their weight in silver or even gold at times, they came from distant places that few Europeans had ever seen, and their journey passed through many hands. The desire for spices drove explorers across oceans, enriched cities and kingdoms and, in the end, helped to reshape the map of the world.
paras.B: The most important spices came from Asia. Pepper grew in southern India, cinnamon in Sri Lanka, and cloves and nutmeg only on a few small islands in what is now Indonesia. Nutmeg, for instance, was grown on the tiny Banda Islands, and for centuries nobody outside the region knew where it came from. Traders from India, Arabia and China carried the spices to markets in the Middle East, where merchants sold them on to Europe.
paras.C: A popular belief holds that Europeans used spices to hide the taste of rotting meat. Most historians doubt this. Fresh meat was available to those who could afford spices, and the rich who bought them would hardly have eaten spoiled food. A better explanation is that spices were prized because they were rare and exotic, signs of wealth and sophistication, and because they made food taste better. They were also valued as medicines, perfumes and as offerings in religious ceremonies.
paras.D: Spices did have another useful property. Modern research has shown that many, such as cloves, cinnamon and garlic, contain chemicals that kill or slow the growth of bacteria. This may explain why dishes in hot countries, where food spoils quickly, tend to use more spice. Scientists suggest that early cooks discovered, by experience, that spiced food made people less likely to fall ill, long before anyone understood the reason.
paras.E: The high prices tempted Europeans to try to reach the source. In 1498, the Portuguese explorer Vasco da Gama sailed around Africa and reached Calicut in India, opening a sea route that avoided the Middle Eastern middlemen. Portugal quickly built a trading empire, with forts along the coasts of Africa and Asia. Spain, meanwhile, supported Columbus, who had hoped to reach the same lands by sailing west, and who instead reached the Americas.
paras.F: In the seventeenth century, the Dutch and English formed powerful companies to control the trade. The Dutch East India Company took the Banda Islands by force and ruthlessly eliminated the local population in order to control the nutmeg supply. In a famous exchange in 1667, the Dutch gave up a small colony in North America, later called New York, in return for the English giving up a claim to one of the spice islands.
paras.G: The monopoly eventually broke down. Seeds and seedlings were smuggled out and planted in other places, so that clove and nutmeg were grown in the Caribbean, East Africa and elsewhere. Prices fell, and spices became available to ordinary people. Yet the legacy remained: the cities of the spice trade, the languages and the global trading networks that began with the search for pepper and cloves are still part of the modern world.

qs.title: Questions 23–26

paras.A: A few decades ago, every child learned to write by hand, and most adults wrote shopping lists, letters and notes every day. Now, much of our writing takes place on screens, and it is common to go for weeks without picking up a pen. Some education systems have begun to reduce the time spent on handwriting, and a few have even removed the teaching of cursive, or joined-up writing. Is this a sensible adaptation to modern life, or a mistake?
paras.B: Those who support the change argue that typing is faster and easier for most adults, produces more legible text and is essential in the workplace. Children, they say, will need keyboard skills for the whole of their working lives, and time spent on elaborate handwriting could be better used for other subjects. In 2016, Finland, known for the success of its education system, reduced the teaching of cursive writing in favour of typing, a move that attracted international attention.
paras.C: Supporters of handwriting reply with research on the brain. In one study, young children who learned letters by writing them by hand later recognised them more easily than those who typed them. Brain scans showed greater activity in the areas linked to reading in children who had written by hand. The movements involved in forming a letter, it seems, help the brain to remember its shape and its sound. Typing involves pressing similar keys for different letters.
paras.D: Another line of research compares note-taking. In a widely quoted American experiment published in 2014, students listened to lectures and took notes either by hand or on laptops. Those who typed wrote more words, often copying the lecturer almost word for word, while those who wrote by hand had to summarise, since they could not write as fast. In tests of understanding afterwards, the handwriting group did better on questions about ideas.
paras.E: The finding should be treated with caution. Later attempts to repeat the experiment gave mixed results, and some found little difference. Typing can also help students who find handwriting painful or slow, including those with certain disabilities, and for them a keyboard may be a gateway to learning. Researchers agree that the effect depends on how the notes are used, and on whether students think about the material or merely copy it.
paras.F: There are cultural reasons to value handwriting, too. Handwritten letters, signatures and notes carry a personal touch that typed text lacks. Calligraphy is an art form in many cultures, including those of the Islamic world and East Asia, where beautiful writing has been admired for centuries. Teachers note that many children enjoy writing by hand, and that it can be a calming activity in a world of screens.
paras.G: The most balanced view is that both skills matter. Children should learn to write clearly by hand, because this supports reading and thinking, and should also learn to type efficiently. Some educators suggest that handwriting should be taught in short, regular sessions, while keyboard skills can be introduced later. In the end, the question is not whether one tool will replace the other, but how best to use each for its purpose.

ps.title: The Remarkable Life of a Butterfly

paras.A: Few animals change as dramatically during their lives as the butterfly. A creature that begins as a tiny egg becomes a hungry, crawling caterpillar, then a motionless case hanging from a twig, and finally a delicate insect with brightly patterned wings that can fly across continents. This process of total transformation is known as complete metamorphosis, and it is shared by beetles, flies, bees and many other insects.
paras.B: The cycle begins when a female butterfly lays her eggs, usually on a particular kind of plant. She chooses with care, because the caterpillars that hatch will feed on the leaves of that plant alone, and they cannot travel far. Some species lay their eggs singly and others in clusters. The eggs are very small, often no larger than a pinhead, and in warm weather they may hatch within a few days.
paras.C: The caterpillar's job is to eat. It spends nearly all of its time chewing leaves, and in a few weeks, it may increase its weight by several thousand times. Since its skin does not stretch, it must shed it, a process called moulting, usually four or five times as it grows. Many caterpillars are protected from birds by their colours: some look like twigs or bird droppings, and others are brightly coloured to warn that they taste unpleasant.
paras.D: When the caterpillar is fully grown, it finds a safe place, attaches itself and changes into a pupa, or chrysalis. From outside, it seems that nothing is happening. Inside, however, much of the caterpillar's body breaks down into a kind of liquid, and groups of special cells that were present from the beginning use this material to build the parts of the adult: the wings, the long legs and the compound eyes. The process takes about ten days to a few weeks, though some species spend the entire winter in this stage.
paras.E: The adult butterfly emerges, pumps fluid into its crumpled wings to expand them and waits for them to dry. Its main aims now are to find food and a mate. Butterflies drink nectar from flowers through a long tongue, which is coiled up like a spring when not in use, and they pollinate plants as they move from flower to flower. Most adult butterflies live for only a few weeks, though some species that hibernate may live for several months.
paras.F: Some butterflies make astonishing journeys. The monarch of North America travels up to four thousand kilometres from Canada and the northern United States to spend the winter in the mountain forests of Mexico. No individual makes the entire round trip: the return journey in spring takes several generations, each of which flies a part of the way. How the new generations find their way to the same forests, which they have never seen, is still not fully understood.
paras.G: Many butterfly populations are declining because of the loss of meadows, the use of pesticides and climate change. The monarch, for example, depends on milkweed plants, which have been removed from many farms. Conservation efforts include protecting habitats, planting the right flowers and leaving wild corners in gardens. Because butterflies are sensitive to changes in the environment, their numbers are used by scientists as a measure of the health of natural areas.

paras.A: Deep inside the great ice sheets of Antarctica and Greenland lies a record of the climate of the past. Every winter, snow falls and settles on the surface. In the following years, new snow buries it, and the older layers are squeezed into solid ice. Because the process has continued for hundreds of thousands of years in the coldest places, the ice at the bottom of the sheet may be older than the human species. Scientists drill into the ice and bring up long cylinders called ice cores to read this history.
paras.B: The drilling is difficult work. Teams camp for months in freezing conditions, using specialised drills that cut a core a few metres long at a time. To reach the bottom of an ice sheet, which can be more than three kilometres thick, may take several seasons. The cores are cut into sections, packed in insulated boxes and flown to laboratories, where they are stored at temperatures far below freezing. Even a short section of core is precious, and scientists try to extract as much information as possible from each piece.
paras.C: The first clue is in the layers themselves. In places where snowfall is heavy, summer and winter snow differ in appearance, so that the layers can be counted much like the rings of a tree. In this way, a particular depth can be given an age. Where the layers are too thin, scientists use other methods, including ash from volcanic eruptions of known date, which appears as thin dark lines in the ice and acts as a marker.
paras.D: The second clue is air. When snow turns to ice, it traps tiny bubbles of the atmosphere. By crushing the ice and analysing the gas, researchers can measure the amount of carbon dioxide and methane in the air at the time the bubbles were sealed. These measurements, going back 800,000 years in the oldest Antarctic core, show that the levels of the gases rose and fell together with temperature through the ice ages and warm periods.
paras.E: Temperature itself can be estimated from the water. Water molecules come in slightly different forms, depending on the weight of the oxygen atoms they contain. In colder conditions, the snow that falls contains less of the heavier form, so by measuring the proportions in each layer, scientists can calculate the temperature at which the snow formed. This method has produced a continuous record of temperature in Antarctica, with surprising precision.
paras.F: The cores have provided important discoveries. They show that the climate has alternated between long ice ages and shorter warm periods, in a pattern linked to small changes in the Earth's orbit around the sun. They also reveal that sudden changes can occur: in Greenland, the temperature at one time rose by several degrees in a few decades. Most significant today is the finding that current levels of carbon dioxide are higher than at any time in the past 800,000 years.
paras.G: Ice cores are also being used to track human activities. Layers from the Roman period contain traces of lead from ancient mining, and layers from the twentieth century show the effect of nuclear tests and pollution. As glaciers melt, however, some of this archive is being lost. Scientists have therefore begun to collect cores from endangered mountain glaciers and to store them in an ice vault in Antarctica, so that future generations can study the past even when the original ice has gone.
