paras.A: In many countries, students go to school in a uniform: a jacket and tie, a skirt or trousers, a particular colour of shirt. In others, they wear whatever they choose. The question of whether school uniforms are a good idea has been debated for generations by parents, teachers and governments, and it is more complicated than it seems. The arguments touch on fairness, discipline, freedom and cost.
paras.B: The most common argument in favour is equality. When everyone dresses the same, it is claimed, differences in wealth are less visible, and students who cannot afford fashionable clothes are less likely to be teased. A uniform may also create a sense of belonging, a shared identity with the school, and some teachers believe that it helps pupils to feel part of a community. For this reason, many schools use their uniform as a symbol of pride.
paras.C: Supporters add practical points. A uniform saves time in the morning, since children do not need to decide what to wear, and it may reduce the amount of attention given to appearance in the classroom. In some places, school clothes make it easy for staff to recognise strangers who enter the grounds, and for the public to identify students on school trips. Parents may also find it cheaper, as a small number of items can last for a year.
paras.D: Critics reply that uniforms are not as cheap as claimed. Specialised items sold only by approved suppliers can be expensive, and children who grow quickly need new ones often. For poor families, the cost can be a heavy burden, and in some countries, charities help to pay. There is also the question of comfort: stiff or hot clothes can make it difficult to concentrate, especially in warm climates.
paras.E: A second criticism concerns freedom of expression. Clothes are a way for young people to explore their identity and to show their personality, and opponents argue that schools should respect this. Rules about uniforms can also raise difficult issues, for example when they require girls and boys to dress differently, or when they conflict with the religious dress of some students. Schools must handle these cases with sensitivity.
paras.F: What does the research say? A number of studies have tried to measure the effects of uniforms on behaviour and results, but the findings are inconsistent. Some report small improvements in attendance or discipline, while others find no effect. It is hard to be sure, because schools with uniforms often differ from others in many ways, such as the background of the pupils or the leadership of the school, and these may explain the results.
paras.G: The evidence therefore does not settle the matter. It seems likely that a uniform does not on its own raise standards, nor does it harm them seriously. The decision may depend on local conditions and on how the policy is carried out: whether it is affordable, flexible and developed after discussion with students and families. A well-designed rule may bring some benefits, but a uniform cannot replace good teaching.

paras.A: Easter Island, known to its inhabitants as Rapa Nui, is one of the most isolated inhabited places on Earth. It lies in the Pacific Ocean, more than three thousand kilometres from the coast of South America, and the nearest inhabited island is about two thousand kilometres away. This small triangle of volcanic rock, only about twenty-four kilometres long, is famous for its nearly nine hundred giant stone statues, called moai, which gaze across the land with solemn faces.
paras.B: The island was settled by Polynesian sailors, who crossed thousands of kilometres of open ocean in double-hulled canoes. Most researchers now believe that they arrived around the year 1200, although some propose an earlier date. They brought chickens, sweet potatoes and the Polynesian rat, and they found a land covered with forest, including a large species of palm. The settlers divided the island among clans, each of which built platforms along the coast.
paras.C: The moai were carved from soft volcanic stone in a quarry on the slopes of an extinct volcano. They represent ancestors and chiefs, and were placed on platforms with their backs to the sea, watching over the villages. The largest ever erected is about ten metres high and weighs more than seventy tonnes. Some carved figures were fitted with eyes of white coral, and a few wore massive hats of red stone. Hundreds of unfinished statues remain in the quarry, left where the carvers stopped.
paras.D: How were the statues moved across the island, sometimes for many kilometres? A long-standing explanation was that islanders rolled them on logs, cutting down the forest in the process. Experiments in recent years suggest another method: with ropes tied to a statue, teams of people could rock it from side to side so that it 'walked' forward in an upright position. Oral traditions say that the statues walked, and this experiment shows the story may be less fanciful than it sounds.
paras.E: By the time European sailors arrived, the island had few trees. A Dutch captain, Jacob Roggeveen, who landed on Easter Day in 1722 and gave the island its name, found a treeless landscape and perhaps two or three thousand people. A popular theory, which became famous through books and films, says that the islanders destroyed their own environment by cutting down the forest to move statues. The collapse of the forest then caused famine and war, and the society fell apart.
paras.F: Recent research has challenged this account. Some scientists have found evidence that the rats brought by the settlers multiplied rapidly and ate the seeds of palm trees, preventing the forest from regenerating. Others point out that the islanders were skilful farmers who used stones to protect their crops from wind and to keep the soil rich. On this view, the population did not collapse before the arrival of Europeans, but remained stable.
paras.G: The worst damage came after contact. Diseases brought by visitors spread among people who had no immunity, and in the 1860s, slave raiders from Peru carried off around a thousand islanders, including many leaders. By 1877, only about a hundred and eleven people remained. Today, several thousand live on the island, most of them descended from the survivors. Easter Island is therefore a story of ingenuity and survival, as well as a warning about the fragility of small ecosystems.

ps.title: From Candles to LEDs: The Story of Light

paras.A: For most of history, the main light after dark came from fire. Torches, candles and oil lamps provided a dim and flickering glow, and they were costly, smoky and dangerous. A single candle gives far less light than even a small modern bulb, and wealthy households burned dozens of them each evening. The invention of better sources of light has therefore been among the most significant advances in everyday life.
paras.B: The first great change came in the nineteenth century with gas lamps in streets and homes, and then electric light. In 1879, the British inventor Joseph Swan and the American Thomas Edison, working separately, produced practical electric bulbs. In these, an electric current heats a thin wire, the filament, until it glows white. The idea was simple, but it took years to find a material that could glow for hundreds of hours without burning out. Edison and his team tested thousands of materials.
paras.C: The incandescent bulb, as it is called, has a serious weakness: it wastes most of the energy it uses. Only around five per cent of the electricity is converted into light, and the rest becomes heat. A bulb that you cannot touch for a few minutes after switching off is turning most of its electricity into warmth. Nevertheless, it dominated homes for well over a century because it was cheap and gave pleasant light.
paras.D: The next step was the fluorescent tube, which passes electricity through a gas and uses the resulting ultraviolet light to make a coating on the glass glow. It was several times more efficient than the bulb, and it became common in offices and shops. Later, compact versions were made which could be screwed into ordinary lamps. They were efficient, but they took a moment to warm up, and they contained small amounts of mercury, which made disposal a concern.
paras.E: The most important recent development is the light-emitting diode, or LED. It is a tiny piece of semiconductor that gives off light when an electric current flows through it, without a hot filament. The first visible LED, which was red, was made in 1962, and for decades, LEDs were used only for small indicators on equipment. White light needed a blue LED, which proved extremely difficult to make.
paras.F: Three Japanese scientists, Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano and Shuji Nakamura, succeeded in the early 1990s, and they received the Nobel Prize in Physics for their work in 2014. Blue LEDs, combined with a coating that adds yellow light, produce white light of high quality. LED bulbs use about one fifth of the electricity of an old incandescent bulb to produce the same amount of light, and they last twenty thousand hours or more, a lifetime of many years.
paras.G: Because lighting accounts for a significant share of the world's electricity use, the change to LEDs has important effects. It lowers bills and reduces pollution, and it has brought light to remote villages through small solar-powered lamps. There are, however, some drawbacks. Cheap, bright lights have encouraged an increase in outdoor lighting at night, which wastes energy and affects wildlife and human sleep. Cities are therefore learning to use light more carefully, directing it only where and when it is needed.

paras.A: For more than a century, animals have been used in research to test the safety of medicines, chemicals and cosmetics and to study diseases. Each year, many millions of animals, mostly mice and rats but also rabbits, fish, dogs and monkeys, are used in laboratories around the world. Many people regard this as a necessary price for medical progress; others consider it cruel and unjustifiable. The debate raises difficult questions about science, ethics and the rights of animals.
paras.B: Those who defend animal research make a case based on human benefit. Many of the medicines, vaccines and surgical methods in use today were developed using animals, from insulin for diabetes to treatments for cancer and operations to replace hearts. Before a new drug is given to people, regulators require evidence on its effect in living bodies, which a test tube cannot provide. Researchers also say that the animals they use are protected by strict laws and are looked after carefully.
paras.C: Opponents answer on moral grounds. Animals are capable of feeling pain and fear, they argue, and it is wrong to cause suffering for human advantage, however great the advantage may be. Some philosophers hold that animals have rights that should not be overridden. They also note that conditions in some laboratories fall short of what the law demands, and that animals may be kept in small cages and subjected to painful procedures.
paras.D: There is also a scientific objection: animals are not small humans. A substance that is harmless to a rat may be harmful to a person, and the reverse is also true. Critics point out that a large share of drugs that seem safe and effective in animals fail when tried on people, and that the use of animals may have delayed or blocked treatments that would have worked. Defenders reply that animal tests nevertheless remove many dangerous drugs before they reach humans.
paras.E: Since 1959, many researchers have followed the principle of the 'three Rs', proposed by two British scientists: replacement, reduction and refinement. Researchers should replace animals with other methods wherever possible, reduce the number of animals used and refine procedures to cause as little suffering as possible. In several countries, these principles are now written into law, and ethics committees must approve each experiment.
paras.F: Alternatives are developing quickly. Scientists can grow human cells and tissues in dishes, and they have built tiny 'organs on a chip', devices that imitate the function of a lung or a liver. Computer models can predict how a chemical will behave, and volunteers can take extremely small doses of a drug in studies under close supervision. In 2013, the European Union banned the sale of cosmetics tested on animals, and several other countries have followed.
paras.G: A complete ban on all animal research is not yet practical, say many scientists, since there are still areas, such as the study of the brain or the whole body's response to infection, where alternatives are not good enough. The better strategy, they suggest, is to fund the development of alternatives and to move gradually away from animal experiments. Public opinion tends to be more relaxed about research that saves lives and more critical about tests for products such as cosmetics.

paras.A: In October 1883, a train left the Gare de l'Est in Paris with a small group of passengers, including journalists, bound for Constantinople, now Istanbul. It was the first journey of a service that would become the most famous train in the world: the Orient Express. Behind the venture was a Belgian engineer, Georges Nagelmackers, who had been inspired by sleeping cars he had seen in the United States and wanted to bring such comfort to Europe.
paras.B: Until then, travelling across the continent by rail was a slow business. Passengers had to change trains at borders, where they were checked by officials, and each country had its own timetable. Nagelmackers's company, the International Sleeping Car Company, arranged for a single train, with its own luxurious carriages, to run across several countries. The journey took about eighty hours, a great saving compared with the weeks of an earlier age.
paras.C: The interior was designed to dazzle. Compartments had polished wood panels, silk curtains and soft beds with fine linen. In the dining car, waiters in uniform served multi-course meals on china plates, with wine and crystal glasses, while the train rattled through the night at speed. Passengers dressed formally for dinner. The train quickly attracted rich travellers, nobles, diplomats and, it was rumoured, spies, who enjoyed its mixture of comfort and mystery.
paras.D: The route changed over the years. At first, it ran through Vienna and Budapest to Bucharest in Romania, where passengers continued by ferry and a short train to the Black Sea, and then by ship to Istanbul. In 1889, a direct line to the city was opened. After the First World War, a new route called the Simplon Orient Express passed through Switzerland and Italy, avoiding Germany and Austria, and served Milan, Venice, Belgrade and Istanbul.
paras.E: The train gained world fame from literature. In 1934, the writer Agatha Christie published a detective novel, 'Murder on the Orient Express', in which a murder takes place on a train trapped in snow. The author had travelled on the train and, it is said, drew on her experiences. Films and television series have since made the story familiar to millions, and the name of the train has become a symbol of romance, luxury and intrigue.
paras.F: Politics and technology eventually reduced the importance of the service. After the Second World War, the Iron Curtain divided Europe, and the line had to cross several border controls. Cars, motorways and especially aeroplanes offered faster journeys, and the Orient Express lost many of its customers. The original service stopped in 1977, and later versions were reduced to shorter distances until even those were discontinued.
paras.G: However, the legend did not die. In 1982, a private company restored a set of old carriages from the 1920s and 1930s and began running a luxury train from London to Venice, and on other routes, calling it the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express. Passengers pay high prices to relive the golden age of travel. The story of the Orient Express shows how a means of transport can become a legend, a symbol of an age when the journey was as important as the destination.

paras.A: Within a few years of birth, almost every child learns to speak a complex language fluently, without lessons, textbooks or formal teaching. Adults who try to learn a second language often find it difficult by comparison. How children achieve this feat has been one of the central questions of psychology and linguistics, and the answer is still being debated.
paras.B: Language learning begins long before the first word. Newborn babies prefer the sound of their mother's voice, which they heard in the womb, and within months they can tell apart the sounds of their own language from others. Around the age of six months, babies begin to babble, repeating syllables such as 'ba-ba' and 'ma-ma'. Babbling is not random: deaf babies who are exposed to sign language babble with their hands.
paras.C: The first real words usually appear around the age of one year. Typically, the first words name familiar people and objects, such as 'mama', 'ball' or 'dog'. For several months, the vocabulary grows slowly, but at about eighteen months, many children experience a 'vocabulary spurt', learning several new words each day. By the age of two, most children begin to join two words together, as in 'more milk', and by three, they speak in simple sentences.
paras.D: Children's mistakes reveal what they are doing. A child may say 'I goed' or 'two foots', forms she could not have heard from adults. These errors show that the child is not simply copying but discovering rules, in this case the rule for forming the past tense and the plural, and applying them even where they do not fit. Later, as she hears more language, she learns the exceptions and the errors disappear.
paras.E: What role does the environment play? The linguist Noam Chomsky argued in the 1950s that the speech children hear is too limited and too messy for them to learn grammar without some inborn guidance. He proposed that humans are born with an innate capacity for language. Others believe that children learn mainly from experience, using general abilities such as noticing patterns, and recent studies show that babies are surprisingly good at detecting regularities in sounds.
paras.F: The quantity and quality of speech matter. Children who are spoken to frequently, in warm and responsive conversation, tend to learn words faster than those who hear less. A well-known study in the 1990s reported a large difference in the number of words heard by children from different family backgrounds, although later research has questioned the size of this gap. Conversation, rather than television, seems to be what helps, since children learn little from screens alone.
paras.G: There also seems to be a sensitive period for language. Children who are not exposed to any language until adolescence rarely achieve full mastery of grammar, and children who learn a second language early generally speak it with a native accent. This does not mean that adults cannot learn a language, but that the task is different for them. Parents who talk, read and play with their babies are giving them the best possible help.

paras.A: Competition is everywhere in children's lives: in sport, in school examinations, in music contests and even in the playground. Many adults believe that it prepares young people for the real world, builds character and encourages them to do their best. Others fear that too much competition causes stress and damages friendships. Psychologists and educators have studied the question for decades, and their answer is more subtle than a simple yes or no.
paras.B: Supporters point to several benefits. A goal, such as winning a race or beating a score, can motivate children to practise harder than they otherwise would. Competition teaches them to deal with both success and disappointment, and learning to lose gracefully is a valuable skill. Team competitions, in particular, develop cooperation, since players must work together to win. And some children simply find contests exciting, a source of pleasure and energy.
paras.C: There are, however, risks. A child who loses repeatedly may decide that he or she is no good at the activity, and give up. Pressure from parents and coaches can turn play into anxiety, and some young athletes burn out and stop playing sport altogether. In classrooms where marks are ranked publicly, weaker pupils may feel humiliated and lose interest in learning, while the best pupils may become afraid of failure, preferring easy tasks to difficult ones.
paras.D: Research suggests that the effect depends heavily on how competition is organised and what children are encouraged to focus on. Psychologists distinguish between a 'performance' goal, which is about being better than others, and a 'mastery' goal, which is about improving one's own skills. Children who focus on mastery tend to persist longer, enjoy the activity more and recover from setbacks more quickly than those who are mainly concerned with winning.
paras.E: Age matters, too. Very young children do not clearly understand competition, and they may be upset by losing. Many experts therefore advise that for children under about eight, activities should emphasise fun and learning of basic skills, with little attention to results. As children grow older, they can handle formal contests, provided that these are fair, with players of similar ability matched against each other, and that every participant receives encouragement.
paras.F: The behaviour of adults has a large effect. Parents who show interest in effort and progress, and not just in results, tend to have children who enjoy the activity more. Coaches who criticise harshly or treat only the best players well can cause lasting harm. In contrast, a coach who praises effort, teaches the rules of fair play and gives all children a chance to play can make competition a positive experience.
paras.G: Competition itself is therefore neither good nor bad. It can bring out effort and teamwork or it can create fear and envy. The task for parents and teachers is to make sure that it serves children's development rather than the pride of adults. Some of the best learning, as many teachers observe, takes place when children compete not against each other but against their own earlier record.

paras.A: Yazd, an ancient city in the desert of central Iran, is one of the hottest places in the country. In summer, daytime temperatures often rise above forty degrees, and rain is rare. Yet for many centuries, people have lived in the city in comfort, without electricity or machines. The secret lies in an ingenious system of passive cooling, the most visible part of which is a forest of tall, square towers rising above the flat roofs of the old houses.
paras.B: These towers are called badgirs, a Persian word that means 'wind catcher'. A badgir is a chimney-like structure, often between five and fifteen metres high, with openings near the top that face the direction of the prevailing wind. The wind enters the openings and is directed down through channels inside the tower into the rooms below. Some towers have vertical dividers that divide the space into compartments, so that wind from any direction can be captured.
paras.C: The effect on temperature can be enhanced by water. In many houses, the base of the tower opens above a small pool or a fountain in a basement room. As the wind passes over the water, some evaporates, which takes heat from the air, and the cooled air flows into the living rooms. Scientists have measured temperature drops of ten degrees or more between the outside and the cooled room. The system also brings fresh air into the house.
paras.D: On days with no wind, the towers still work. During the day, the walls of the tower are heated by the sun, and the hot air inside rises and escapes through the top, drawing cooler air in from other openings. At night, the process works in reverse: the tower cools quickly, and the cool, heavy air sinks down into the rooms. The thick walls of mud brick also absorb heat during the day and release it slowly after dark.
paras.E: Water for these systems came from an underground channel system called a qanat. A qanat is a gently sloping tunnel that carries water from the foothills to a town, sometimes over many kilometres, without pumps. Because the water flows underground, little evaporates, which is important in the desert. Yazd's qanats, some of which are over a thousand years old, supplied water to houses, gardens and the pools in basements.
paras.F: The people of Yazd also solved the problem of keeping things cold. Large domed buildings, known as yakhchals, or ice pits, stored ice through the summer. Ice was made in shallow pools on winter nights, when the water froze in the dry air, and then cut into blocks and kept in a deep underground chamber with thick insulating walls. It was used to preserve food and make cold drinks and desserts for the people of the city.
paras.G: Today, most buildings in the region use electric air conditioning, which consumes large amounts of energy. Some architects and engineers, however, have turned back to the traditional methods. Modern buildings in the Middle East have been designed with wind towers and shaded courtyards, and researchers are testing how they could reduce the use of electricity. The old houses of Yazd, protected as a World Heritage Site, offer lessons in how to live well in a hot climate with little energy.

paras.A: Every living thing grows old, yet there is nothing in the laws of physics that says it must. Some animals, such as the Greenland shark, live for centuries, and certain trees survive for thousands of years. Humans live much longer than most mammals of their size, but they too show a gradual decline in strength, memory and health. Why this happens is one of the great questions of biology, and scientists have proposed several explanations.
paras.B: One of the oldest ideas is that the body simply wears out, like a machine. Over a lifetime, cells accumulate damage from chemicals, radiation and the normal processes of living. Repair systems exist, but they are imperfect, and as the damage accumulates, the tissues of the body work less well. The idea fits everyday experience, but it leaves unanswered a question: why do some species repair themselves so much better than others?
paras.C: Another theory focuses on the cells. In the 1960s, American biologist Leonard Hayflick showed that normal human cells in a dish can divide only a limited number of times, and then stop. The reason, it was later discovered, lies in telomeres, protective caps at the ends of chromosomes, which become a little shorter each time a cell divides. When they are too short, the cell stops dividing or dies. Cells that have stopped dividing may remain in the body and release substances that harm their neighbours.
paras.D: The evolutionary explanation is perhaps the most fundamental. Natural selection acts strongly on traits that influence survival and reproduction in early life, but weakly on events that happen late, after most animals have already had young or died of accidents or disease. A gene that gives an advantage when young but causes harm in old age may therefore spread through a population. Ageing, in this view, is not a programme but a result of selection having little power over late life.
paras.E: This idea explains patterns in nature. Animals that face few dangers, such as those that fly or live in protected places, tend to live longer than similar animals that are easily caught. Bats, for example, live many years for their size. Species that have many predators and breed fast, such as mice, age quickly. Experiments in which animals have been bred to reproduce later have produced individuals that live longer, which supports the theory.
paras.F: How long can a human live? The longest confirmed lifespan is that of a French woman, Jeanne Calment, who died in 1997 at the age of 122. Only a tiny number of people have lived beyond 115, and the average life expectancy has risen mainly because fewer people die young. Some researchers think there is a natural limit near 120 years, while others believe that future advances might extend it.
paras.G: Research on ageing is now moving quickly. Scientists have shown that limiting calories can extend the life of animals such as worms and mice, and drugs that clear damaged cells have improved health in old mice. Whether such treatments will work in people is not yet known. Many experts argue that the main aim should not be to prolong life at any cost but to extend the years in which people are healthy, so that old age is a time of independence and not of illness.

paras.A: For most of human history, eating meat was normal and seldom questioned. Today, in many countries, more people are asking whether it is right. Some have given up meat altogether, others eat less, and many more are uncertain. The debate involves three main concerns: the welfare of animals, the health of people and the state of the planet. Each raises its own difficult questions, and they do not always point in the same direction.
paras.B: The first and oldest concern is the treatment of animals. Most meat today comes from intensive farms, where large numbers of animals are kept indoors in crowded conditions. Critics argue that this causes suffering for creatures that are capable of feeling pain, and that the pleasure of eating meat cannot justify it. Some philosophers go further, claiming that killing animals for food is wrong in itself, since animals, like humans, have an interest in continuing to live.
paras.C: Defenders of meat-eating make several replies. Some argue that humans have always eaten meat and that it is a natural part of our diet. Others accept that cruelty is wrong but say that the answer is better welfare standards, not abstinence. Farming that allows animals to graze outside and live a natural life, they claim, can be both humane and sustainable. A third view is that humans are morally different from animals, though philosophers disagree about the reasons.
paras.D: The second concern is health. Meat is a source of protein, iron, zinc and vitamin B12, and well-planned diets that include it can be healthy. However, research suggests that high consumption of red meat and especially processed meat, such as sausages and bacon, is linked to a greater risk of heart disease and some cancers. Many dietary guidelines advise people to limit these foods. At the same time, studies of vegetarian diets generally find lower rates of some illnesses.
paras.E: The third concern is the environment. Livestock farming produces a significant share of greenhouse gases, especially from cattle, which release methane. It requires large areas of land for grazing and for growing animal feed, and in some regions it is a cause of forest clearance. Producing a kilogram of beef takes far more land and water than producing a kilogram of vegetables or grain. Replacing some meat with plants, studies indicate, would reduce emissions and free land.
paras.F: Yet the picture is not simple. In some parts of the world, particularly dry or mountainous regions where crops cannot grow, herding animals is the only way to produce food. For many poor families, meat and milk are an important source of nutrition and income. Critics of calls to reduce meat consumption argue that rich countries, which eat the most meat, should lead the change, and that poor communities should not be asked to give up what they need.
paras.G: Individuals reach different conclusions. Some choose to be vegetarian or vegan for ethical reasons, some adopt a 'flexitarian' approach, eating meat rarely and choosing higher-welfare products, and others see no reason to change. Most experts agree that the issue is not only a personal one, since farming rules, subsidies and prices shape the choices available. Whatever one decides, the debate encourages people to think about where their food comes from.

qs.title: Questions 39–40

ps.title: Alexander von Humboldt: The Man Who Saw Nature Whole

paras.A: Alexander von Humboldt was born in Berlin in 1769 into a wealthy Prussian family. As a boy he was restless and curious, collecting plants, insects and rocks, and his tutors despaired of making him study. After his mother's death, which left him a considerable inheritance, he abandoned a career in mining administration and resolved to devote himself to exploration. His dream was to travel to distant lands and to understand how the whole natural world fitted together.
paras.B: In 1799, with the French botanist Aimé Bonpland, Humboldt sailed for Latin America. Over the next five years, they travelled through what are now Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Cuba and Mexico, covering many thousands of kilometres by canoe, mule and on foot. They suffered from fevers, hunger and attacks by insects, and they once nearly drowned. Throughout the journey, Humboldt measured everything: temperature, air pressure, magnetism, the height of mountains and the colour of the sky.
paras.C: One of his most famous adventures was an attempt to climb Chimborazo, a volcano in Ecuador that was then believed to be the highest mountain in the world. In 1802, Humboldt and his companions climbed to about 5,900 metres, higher than anyone had recorded before. They were stopped by a deep crevasse, and suffered from altitude sickness. Despite failing to reach the top, Humboldt noticed that plants changed in distinct bands as the altitude increased.
paras.D: This observation led to an important idea. Humboldt saw that the plants on the slopes of a mountain near the equator corresponded to those found in different climate zones at sea level from the tropics to the poles. He drew a famous diagram of Chimborazo showing the plants at each height, together with measurements of temperature and pressure. The picture illustrated his view that nature is a web of connections, in which climate, plants and animals are linked.
paras.E: Humboldt was also among the first to notice that human beings can harm the environment. Near Lake Valencia in Venezuela, he observed that the water level had fallen, and he concluded that the cause was the clearing of forests for farming, which changed the local climate. He warned that destroying forests could cause problems for future generations. Today, he is sometimes called a pioneer of the study of environmental change.
paras.F: On his return to Europe, Humboldt settled in Paris and spent many years writing up his discoveries in a long series of volumes. He became one of the most famous men in the world and was admired by scientists and rulers. He was generous with his fortune, helping young researchers, and he corresponded with thousands of people. In his later years, he wrote 'Cosmos', a vast work that aimed to describe the whole universe, and which became a bestseller.
paras.G: His ideas influenced many other thinkers. Charles Darwin carried Humboldt's books on the voyage of the Beagle and said they inspired him to travel. American writers such as Henry David Thoreau and John Muir were also affected by Humboldt's view of nature as unified and beautiful. Humboldt died in 1859 at the age of eighty-nine. Many places, plants, animals and even a current in the Pacific Ocean carry his name, and his vision of a connected natural world feels more relevant than ever.

qs.title: Questions 10–13

paras.A: Imagine that you must remember a list of twenty unrelated items, such as 'bread, lamp, hammer, river, coin' and so on. Most people, trying by simple repetition, will do poorly. Yet for more than two thousand years, a technique has existed that allows ordinary people to recall long lists, speeches and even thousands of digits. It is called the method of loci, and more popularly the memory palace.
paras.B: According to a legend told by the Roman writer Cicero, the method was discovered by the Greek poet Simonides. He was giving a recital at a banquet when he was called outside. While he was away, the roof of the hall collapsed and crushed the guests so badly that they could not be identified. Simonides, however, found that he could recall where each person had been sitting, and so he was able to name the dead. He concluded that order and place are powerful aids to memory.
paras.C: The method works by linking things to be remembered with places in a familiar setting. First, the person chooses a place that he or she knows well, such as the home or the route to school, and imagines a path through it with several distinct locations: the front door, the hallway, the kitchen table and so on. Then each item is imagined in a particular spot. To remember the list, the person simply walks mentally along the route and 'sees' each object in its place.
paras.D: The pictures should be vivid and unusual, since the brain remembers the strange better than the ordinary. To remember 'bread', for instance, one might imagine a giant loaf blocking the front door, with steam rising from it. To remember a 'hammer', one might picture it hammering the hallway mirror. The more senses are engaged, with colour, sound and smell, and the more action in the picture, the stronger the memory.
paras.E: In ancient Rome, orators used the technique to deliver long speeches without notes, placing each section in a different part of an imagined building. In the Middle Ages, scholars and monks employed it to remember texts. The method still has followers today: the competitors in memory championships, who can memorise the order of a shuffled pack of cards in under a minute, almost all use some variation of it.
paras.F: Scientists have studied these memory athletes with interest. In a study in 2002, researchers examined the brains of several top competitors and compared them with those of ordinary people. They found no difference in structure or intelligence. The athletes' skill came from training: when they memorised, they used regions of the brain that deal with spatial memory and navigation, exactly as the method suggests. The control group, when taught the technique for a few weeks, improved considerably.
paras.G: The technique has limits. It is useful for remembering ordered lists or facts, but less so for understanding. A student who memorises dates in a memory palace is not necessarily a better historian. Nevertheless, it demonstrates that human memory is not fixed and can be trained. It also shows something about our minds: we are made for places and stories, and we remember best what we can picture.

qs.title: Questions 23–26

paras.A: In 2018, a portrait created by a computer program was sold at a famous auction house for more than four hundred thousand dollars. The picture, which showed a blurred figure in dark clothes, had been produced by an algorithm trained on thousands of historical portraits. Its sale caused astonishment and debate. Could a machine be an artist? And if a program can write music, paint pictures and compose poems, what does that mean for human creativity?
paras.B: The technology behind such works has advanced rapidly. Modern systems learn by analysing huge collections of existing images, texts or sounds, identifying patterns, and then producing new material that resembles what they have learned. A user can type a short description, such as 'a castle on a hill at sunset in the style of a watercolour', and within seconds the program produces a picture. The results can be strikingly beautiful, and sometimes, difficult to distinguish from the work of skilled artists.
paras.C: Supporters see this as a new tool, comparable to the camera. When photography appeared in the nineteenth century, many painters feared that it would end their art, and critics denied that a photograph could be art at all. Yet photography became an art form of its own, and it freed painters to explore new directions. In the same way, supporters argue, artificial intelligence can extend human abilities, allowing people without technical training to realise ideas.
paras.D: Critics raise several objections. The first is about originality. Because the programs learn from existing works, often taken from the internet without permission, many artists feel that their style and labour are being copied. Several artists and writers have started legal actions, claiming that their rights have been violated. Courts in some countries have decided that a work with no human author cannot be protected by copyright, which leaves the status of such pieces unclear.
paras.E: The second objection concerns meaning. Many people believe that art is not merely a pleasing arrangement of colours but an expression of human experience: love, grief, protest, hope. A machine, which has no feelings or life, cannot have anything to express, they say. Others reply that the meaning of a work is created partly by the viewer, and that if a picture moves someone, it does not matter whether its maker was a person or a program.
paras.F: The third concern is economic. If companies can produce illustrations and music cheaply with software, they may stop employing human illustrators and composers, and many creative workers fear for their living. Some professionals already report losing work. Others are adopting the new tools to speed up routine tasks, such as producing rough sketches, so that they can concentrate on the aspects of the work that require judgement and taste.
paras.G: What is likely to happen? Probably, a mixture. Machines will take a part in many creative processes, but the value that people place on human skill, personality and story is unlikely to disappear, just as handmade objects remain valued in a world of factories. A growing number of experts propose clear labelling of machine-made work, fair payment for the creators whose work is used for training, and an open discussion of what we want art to be.

paras.A: In the thirteenth century, the Mongol Empire stretched from the Pacific coast of Asia to the borders of Europe, the largest land empire in history. Governing such a vast area was an enormous challenge. A command issued in the capital might have to travel for thousands of kilometres before reaching a distant governor, and without quick communication, the empire could easily fall apart. The solution was a relay system of messengers that the Mongols called the yam.
paras.B: The idea of relay stations was not new, but the Mongols organised it on an unprecedented scale. Stations were built along the main roads at intervals of a few tens of kilometres. Each one kept fresh horses, food and places for riders to rest. A messenger arriving at a station handed over his message or changed horses and continued at once, so that a message could travel day and night without the animals becoming exhausted. The system was maintained by local families, who provided the horses and supplies instead of paying some taxes.
paras.C: Official riders carried a metal or wooden tablet, known as a paiza, which served as a passport. It showed that the holder was on the business of the khan and entitled to the use of horses and food at any station. The tablets were of different ranks, some made of silver or gold for important officials, and anyone who refused to help a rider or used a tablet falsely could be punished severely. Urgent messages were fastened with bells, so that people along the way would clear the road.
paras.D: The speed was remarkable for the time. In normal circumstances, a rider could cover between 200 and 300 kilometres a day, and in an emergency, according to some accounts, even more. By comparison, an ordinary traveller on horseback might cover thirty or forty kilometres in a day. A message from one end of the empire to the other, which would have taken many months, could arrive in a few weeks. This allowed rulers to react quickly to rebellions and enemy movements.
paras.E: The yam was not intended only for the government. Merchants and travellers could use the stations with permission, and the roads were patrolled to keep them safe. In an age when robbers were a constant danger, this made long journeys much more secure. The Venetian traveller Marco Polo, who visited China in the late thirteenth century, wrote with admiration of the number of the stations and of the comfort they provided.
paras.F: The relay system helped to support the exchange of goods and ideas across Eurasia, a period historians sometimes call the 'Pax Mongolica', or Mongol peace. Silk, spices and porcelain moved westward, and new crops, technologies and religious ideas travelled in both directions. Some historians even suggest that the same routes helped to spread the plague which devastated Europe and Asia in the fourteenth century, though the evidence is still being debated.
paras.G: The system did not last for ever. When the empire divided into separate states, the coordinated network weakened, and many stations were abandoned. Yet its influence continued, and later rulers, including those of Russia, China and the Ottoman Empire, adopted similar systems. The yam shows that a state which controls information can control distance, and that the speed of communication has always been a source of power.

paras.A: Few sights in nature are as lovely as a rainbow. After a shower, when the sun breaks through, a curved band of colours appears in the sky, usually with red on the outside and violet on the inside. For thousands of years, people explained rainbows in terms of myth. Today, we know that they are produced by a combination of three simple processes: refraction, reflection and dispersion of sunlight in raindrops.
paras.B: Sunlight looks white, but it is made of light of many colours. When a ray of light passes from air into water, it changes direction, or is refracted, because light travels more slowly in water. Different colours bend by different amounts: violet light bends the most and red the least. This spreading of colours is called dispersion, and it is the same effect that occurs when light passes through a glass prism.
paras.C: A raindrop is a tiny, almost round ball of water. Light entering it is refracted and separated into its colours. It then travels across the drop and strikes the back surface, where part of it is reflected, and returns across the drop to the front, where it is refracted a second time and leaves. The result is that the light emerges from the drop at an angle, with its colours spread out. Red light leaves at about forty-two degrees from the original direction, and violet at around forty degrees.
paras.D: A rainbow is therefore seen only when the sun is behind the observer and the rain is in front. Each drop sends light of different colours in different directions, and the observer sees one colour from each drop, depending on its position. Drops at the higher level send red towards the eye and those at the lower level send violet, forming the bands. Because the geometry depends on the position of the eye, every person sees a slightly different rainbow, and no two people see exactly the same one.
paras.E: The shape of a rainbow is a circle, although the ground normally cuts off the lower part. From an aircraft or a mountain top, it is sometimes possible to see a complete circle. Often, a fainter second rainbow can be seen outside the first. This arises when light is reflected twice inside the drops, and the order of the colours is reversed, with violet on the outside. The sky between the two bows looks darker than elsewhere.
paras.F: The English scientist Isaac Newton studied the matter in the 1660s. By passing a beam of sunlight through a glass prism, he showed that white light is made up of colours, and that the colours cannot be further divided. He decided to name seven: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet. Some historians believe he chose seven because of an old belief about a connection between colours and the seven notes of the musical scale; in reality, the spectrum has no clear dividing lines.
paras.G: Rainbows are not limited to rain. They can appear in the spray of a waterfall or a garden hose, in mist and even around the moon, where faint 'moonbows' occur on bright nights. Sometimes, light also produces thin extra bands inside the main rainbow, which can only be explained by treating light as waves. The rainbow is a reminder that beauty in nature often follows from the application of simple laws.

paras.A: At many famous sites around the world, there are two prices. Local citizens pay a small fee, or nothing at all, while foreign visitors are charged many times as much. At some temples, palaces and national parks, the difference can be ten times or more. The practice, called two-tier or dual pricing, is common in Asia, Africa and Latin America, and it has become the subject of an ethical argument. Is it fair?
paras.B: Supporters give a number of reasons. The first is affordability. The incomes of people in many countries are far lower than those of visitors from richer ones, and a ticket that a foreign tourist hardly notices could represent a day's wages to a local resident. If everyone had to pay the same, they argue, local people could be priced out of their own heritage, and children might never see the monuments of their country.
paras.C: A second argument is that heritage sites cost money to maintain, and local taxpayers have already contributed to their upkeep. A visitor from abroad has not, and so it seems reasonable to expect that visitor to pay a fair share. The additional income can be used to repair buildings, pay guards and guides and pay for improvements to facilities. In some countries, a large part of the money for conservation comes from foreign ticket sales.
paras.D: A third point concerns crowding. Higher prices for foreigners may help to limit the number of visitors, protecting delicate places. Since foreign tourists tend to be willing to pay more, the site can earn a good income from fewer people. A system in which the price varies according to the time of year or day can also spread visitors through the week and reduce crowding at peak periods.
paras.E: Critics offer several objections. The first is simple fairness: it seems wrong to charge people differently for the same experience because of their passport. Some visitors feel that they are being treated as walking wallets, and may leave with bad feelings, which can damage a country's reputation. Foreign residents, students and workers who live in the country for years may also be asked to pay the higher price, though they contribute to its economy and its taxes.
paras.F: Another objection is practical. Checking nationality requires staff and documents, and it may create opportunities for corruption or disputes at the gate. Systems that depend on identity cards can also exclude citizens who lack them. And if prices rise too high, some visitors will simply choose to go elsewhere, so the plan may lose rather than gain income. Evidence on how tourists respond is limited and varies between places.
paras.G: Some governments have chosen a middle way: the same price for everybody, plus free or reduced entry for local residents, or free days for citizens. Others charge according to the services provided, such as guides or special areas. A discussion of fairness, in the end, must consider what the money is for, how it is spent and who benefits. If visitors can see that their fees protect the places they enjoy, and that local people are not shut out, they are more likely to accept the cost.

paras.A: Rising from the plains of northern Tanzania, Mount Kilimanjaro is the highest mountain in Africa, standing 5,895 metres above sea level. It is a huge volcano, and it is also the highest freestanding mountain in the world, meaning that it rises on its own and is not part of a range. Its summit, near the equator, has long been capped with snow and ice, a startling sight above the warm savanna. Ernest Hemingway made it famous in his story 'The Snows of Kilimanjaro'.
paras.B: The mountain has three volcanic cones, of which the highest, Kibo, carries the ice. Climbers who ascend it pass through different zones of vegetation. At the foot lie farms, growing coffee and bananas. Above them is a belt of rainforest, home to monkeys and many birds. Higher up are open moorland with giant heather, then a stony desert, and finally the ice-covered summit. A walk of several days takes the visitor through what is equivalent to a journey from the equator to the polar regions.
paras.C: The ice on Kilimanjaro has been shrinking for over a century. Measurements and photographs show that in 1912, the glaciers covered about twelve square kilometres. By the early twenty-first century, the area had fallen to less than two square kilometres, and some scientists have estimated that most of the ice could disappear within a few decades. Many of the smaller glaciers have vanished already, and the remaining ones are retreating from year to year.
paras.D: What is the cause? Warming of the climate is part of the explanation, but it is not the whole story. The ice of Kilimanjaro is exceptional because it sits in a very dry, tropical environment. Studies suggest that a drying of the climate in East Africa since the late nineteenth century, associated with changes in the surrounding oceans, has reduced snowfall on the mountain. With less new snow to replace what is lost, the ice has gradually disappeared.
paras.E: There is also a physical reason. Most of the ice on Kilimanjaro does not melt; it turns directly from solid to vapour, in a process called sublimation, when the sun is strong and the air is thin and dry. The loss of forest on the lower slopes may also have changed local weather, because trees recycle moisture. Researchers therefore consider several factors, and the relative importance of each is still being argued.
paras.F: The loss of the ice matters to people. The glaciers are a symbol of the mountain, and tourism is a major source of income, with tens of thousands of climbers and visitors each year. Some worry that fewer tourists will come if the snow disappears. Local people who farm on the slopes also depend on streams, but studies indicate that the ice contributes a rather small fraction of their water. The main source is rain and the moisture caught by the mountain forest.
paras.G: That is why protecting the forest is considered at least as important as the ice. Fires, often started by honey collectors or careless people, destroy large areas of the forest each year, and the damage reduces the amount of water that flows to the plains. Programmes to plant trees and stop fires are being organised by local communities and the national park. Kilimanjaro thus has a warning and a lesson: even a mountain that looks eternal can change, and the way to look after it begins on its lower slopes.

paras.A: Humans are social animals, and friendship is one of the most valued parts of life. Ask people what makes them happy, and most will mention friends and family before money or possessions. For a long time, however, friendship was neglected by scientists, who studied romantic love and family ties but treated friends as a minor matter. In recent decades, that has changed, and researchers have begun to measure what friends do for us and how friendships work.
paras.B: The benefits are large. One of the best-known pieces of evidence comes from a series of studies that followed thousands of people for years. These showed that people with strong social connections lived longer, on average, than those with few, and that the effect was comparable with the benefits of giving up smoking. Friends reduce stress, offer practical help and provide a feeling of belonging. People with good friends also tend to recover from illness more quickly.
paras.C: How many friends can a person have? The British anthropologist Robin Dunbar argued that our brains limit the number of stable relationships we can maintain, to about 150 for most people. Within this circle, he said, friends are arranged in layers: perhaps five very close ones, fifteen good friends and fifty friends, with the rest as acquaintances. Researchers who studied phone calls and social networks found patterns that were roughly consistent with these numbers, though the exact figures are debated.
paras.D: Friendships need time. Studies suggest that it takes around fifty hours of shared activity for an acquaintance to become a casual friend, and about two hundred hours for a close friend. This helps to explain why friends are often made at school, at work or in the neighbourhood, where people meet again and again without effort. After adults leave these settings, making new friends becomes harder, and many report feeling lonelier in middle age.
paras.E: People tend to become friends with those who resemble them, a principle known as homophily. Friends often share age, education, interests and values. Similarity makes conversation easier and builds trust. Yet researchers also point out that mixed friendships have special benefits. A friend from a different background can offer new ideas, information and experiences, and diverse networks have been linked to success in finding work.
paras.F: What about friendship online? Social media allows people to keep in touch across distance, and many value it for that reason. But studies suggest that online contacts are not always a substitute for meeting face to face. Seeing a smile, hearing a voice and sharing an experience in the same room seem to deepen bonds more than messages do. Having many online 'friends' is not the same as having a few people who can be relied on.
paras.G: Friendships also change and can end. People move, marry or change jobs, and some friendships fade without any quarrel. Psychologists find that friendships are more likely to last when both people make an effort, show appreciation and offer support in difficult moments. In this sense, friendship is not only a gift of chance but also a skill that can be practised. A simple message or a short call may be enough to keep a connection alive.

qs.title: Questions 23–26

paras.A: Every year, millions of students sit for examinations that are the same for everyone in a country or region: tests that decide who enters a university, who receives a scholarship or who graduates from school. These standardised tests have the advantage of apparent simplicity, since all candidates answer the same questions under the same conditions. But how fair are they? The question has produced strong opinions on both sides.
paras.B: Supporters argue that such tests are the fairest method available. Because they are marked according to fixed criteria, often by computers or by examiners who do not know the candidate, they reduce the influence of personal bias. A student from a poor family or a small town can compete on the same terms as one from a rich school. Before the introduction of national exams in many countries, jobs and university places often depended on connections, and tests were seen as a way of opening opportunities on the basis of merit.
paras.C: A second argument is comparability. A national exam gives a standard measure, so that universities and employers can compare candidates from different schools. In its absence, they would have to rely on school marks, which vary in strictness, and on recommendations, which are subjective. Governments also use test results to monitor the quality of education and to see which schools need help.
paras.D: Critics, however, argue that the tests measure a narrow range of skills. Multiple-choice questions can assess knowledge and some reasoning, but they are poor at measuring creativity, persistence, teamwork and practical skills. A student with a gift for art, music or building may not be recognised. Teachers also complain of 'teaching to the test': when results matter greatly, lessons are reduced to practice for the exam, and subjects that are not tested receive less time.
paras.E: There is evidence, too, that results are linked to family background. Students from wealthy families often do better, not necessarily because they are more able but because they can afford private tutors, books and quiet places to study. In some countries, a whole industry of preparation courses has grown up. This means that the playing field is not truly level, even if the questions are the same for all.
paras.F: Test anxiety is another problem. Some students perform well below their ability under the stress of a single, high-stakes examination, and a bad day can change the course of a life. Several education systems have responded by offering more than one opportunity to take an exam, or by combining exam results with coursework and teacher assessments, so that a decision does not depend on three hours.
paras.G: Few experts propose abolishing standardised tests altogether. Most suggest that they should be one measure among several, and that their use should be accompanied by support for disadvantaged students. A fair system, they say, must also ask whether the tests assess what society truly values. If a test is easy to mark but does not measure what matters, then its fairness is a limited virtue.

paras.A: On Salisbury Plain in southern England stands one of the most famous prehistoric monuments in the world. Stonehenge consists of a circle of huge standing stones, some of them capped with horizontal stones, set on a grassy hill. It was built in several stages over more than a thousand years, beginning about five thousand years ago, at a time when the people of Britain were farmers who used tools of stone and bone and had no writing.
paras.B: The first monument was a circular bank and ditch with a ring of pits, built around 3000 BC. The great stones came later. The largest, known as sarsens, are a hard sandstone that was brought from an area about twenty-five kilometres to the north. A typical sarsen weighs around twenty-five tonnes, and the heaviest may exceed thirty. Moving them without wheels or metal tools, over land, must have required the effort of hundreds of people, using ropes, sledges and timber rollers.
paras.C: Smaller stones, the bluestones, have an even more remarkable story. Scientists have traced their origin to the Preseli Hills in west Wales, about 240 kilometres away. Whether they were carried by human beings or by the movement of ice thousands of years earlier was once debated, but most researchers now believe that people transported them, perhaps partly by water. Why Neolithic communities carried the stones so far is unknown, but it suggests that the Welsh hills had a special meaning.
paras.D: The purpose of Stonehenge has been argued for centuries. In the seventeenth century, writers claimed that it was built by the Romans or the Druids, priests of the Celtic peoples, although it is far older than either. Today, the evidence points to a place of ceremony and burial. Excavations have uncovered the remains of hundreds of people, whose bones were cremated and buried there, suggesting that it served as a cemetery for a long period.
paras.E: The monument is also aligned with the sun. At the midsummer solstice, in June, the sun rises over a stone outside the circle, called the Heel Stone, and its first rays shine into the centre. At midwinter, the sun sets at the opposite side. Archaeologists believe that the winter solstice may have been more important for the builders, since nearby settlements show evidence of great winter feasts. For farmers, the turning of the seasons was a matter of life and death.
paras.F: Stonehenge was not isolated. In the surrounding landscape, there are other monuments, including a huge earth circle and many burial mounds, as well as a long avenue that links the stones with the River Avon. Recent research, using ground-scanning instruments, has revealed hidden pits and structures beneath the grass, showing that the area was a great ritual centre of its day, used by people from distant places.
paras.G: Today, Stonehenge is a World Heritage Site and attracts more than a million visitors each year. Many people gather there for the solstices, when the site is opened to the public. Visitors can no longer walk among the stones except on special occasions, as the damage from many feet and from souvenir hunters had become severe. Despite thousands of years of study, the monument still holds secrets, and each new discovery raises fresh questions.

paras.A: Many people imagine foxes as creatures of woods and fields, living far from towns. Yet in many countries, the red fox has become a familiar resident of cities. At night, foxes can be seen trotting along suburban streets, crossing gardens and walking over railway lines. They have made themselves at home in places that, a century ago, they rarely visited, and their success offers lessons about how wild animals can adapt to a world dominated by humans.
paras.B: In Britain, foxes first began to settle in towns in the 1930s, when a wave of house-building created suburbs with large gardens, hedges and sheds. The animals found that these places offered good shelter and abundant food. By the 1980s, foxes were established in nearly all major British cities. Estimates suggest that a city such as London may have about ten thousand foxes, which means a density in some districts higher than in the surrounding countryside.
paras.C: The success of the fox is due to its flexible habits. It is an omnivore, which means that it eats almost anything: insects, worms, fruit, small mammals and birds, as well as scraps from bins, food left for pets and even sandwiches dropped in parks. In the countryside, it has to search for its meals over wide areas, but in a city, food is concentrated and reliable. Foxes can therefore live in smaller territories than their rural cousins.
paras.D: Urban foxes also seem to be bolder. Where they are not hunted, they lose some of their fear of people and may be seen in daylight. Researchers have found that city foxes are more likely to approach new objects than country foxes, which suggests that boldness is an advantage in this environment and may be passed from parents to young. Their dens may be found under garden sheds, beneath buildings or in thick bushes, and cubs are born in early spring.
paras.E: The relationship between foxes and people is mixed. Many residents enjoy seeing wild animals so close to their homes, and some put out food for them, which is not generally recommended since it may increase the number of animals and attract rats. Others complain about noise at night, since foxes scream during the breeding season, about damage to gardens and about the dirt from rubbish bags that they tear open. There are also worries about pets, although cats are rarely attacked.
paras.F: A greater danger to foxes themselves comes from cars. Traffic accidents kill many of them each year. They are also affected by diseases, particularly a skin infection called mange, which causes hair loss and leaves animals weak in winter. In some towns, wildlife organisations have begun to treat sick foxes, while others argue that nature should be left to take its course.
paras.G: Foxes are not alone in their move to cities. Coyotes in North American cities, wild boar in some European towns, raccoons in Japan and leopards on the edge of Indian cities have all adapted to urban life. Scientists study these animals to learn how species respond to rapid change. As cities grow, the challenge is to find ways to share space, for example by keeping rubbish secure and protecting green corridors where wildlife can move.

paras.A: Not long ago, paying for goods meant handing over coins and notes. Today, in many countries, people tap a card or a phone, or pay online, and may go for days without touching cash. In Sweden, less than ten per cent of payments are now made with banknotes and coins, and some shops no longer accept them. The trend is spreading, and it raises the question of whether we are moving towards a cashless society, and whether that is desirable.
paras.B: Supporters of digital payments list many advantages. They are fast and convenient, they remove the need to carry money or give change, and they leave a record, so that spending can be tracked and budgeted. For businesses, handling cash is costly, with the need for secure storage, counting and transport. Digital payments can also be safer from robbery. And during the recent pandemic, many people preferred contactless payment because it avoided the handling of notes.
paras.C: There are also arguments connected with crime and the economy. Cash is hard to trace, and criminals use it for illegal trade, bribes and tax evasion. A society with little cash makes these activities more difficult. In some countries, governments have encouraged digital payments to raise tax collection and bring more people into the official economy. Central banks, too, are developing digital forms of national currency, which they believe could make payments cheaper and more efficient.
paras.D: Critics respond that a cashless society leaves some people behind. Older people, the poor, migrants and people living in remote areas are less likely to have bank accounts, smartphones or reliable connections. If shops and public services stop accepting cash, these groups may find it hard to buy food or pay bills. For them, notes and coins are not a relic but a necessity. Even in rich countries, millions of adults rely on cash for daily needs.
paras.E: Privacy is another concern. A cash purchase leaves no trace, whereas a card payment records what was bought, where and when. This information can be used by companies to target advertising, or may be accessed by governments and criminals. Some people feel that the freedom to spend without being watched is a basic right, and cash is the only means to achieve it. Defenders of digital systems say that good laws and security can protect personal data.
paras.F: Resilience is a third worry. Digital payments depend on electricity, networks and computers, and if they fail, a country can be unable to buy anything. Natural disasters, power cuts and cyber-attacks have shown the danger. In response, several governments, including those of Nordic countries that were early adopters of digital payment, now advise citizens to keep some cash at home and have urged banks to ensure that notes and coins remain available.
paras.G: What is likely to happen? Probably, cash will decline further, but will not disappear soon. Many experts suggest that the best course is to make sure it remains available, for example by requiring shops to accept it and banks to provide access, while also developing safe and inclusive digital alternatives. Money is not just a technology but a public service, and the way in which we pay affects who is included in the economy.

paras.A: The cheetah is the fastest land animal on Earth. In short bursts, it can reach speeds of around a hundred kilometres an hour, accelerating from a standstill faster than most sports cars. The cat's whole body is designed for running. It has a light frame, long legs, a deep chest and a narrow waist, and a small head with large nostrils that allow it to take in great quantities of air. Even the black 'tear marks' that run from the eyes to the mouth are thought to reduce glare from the sun.
paras.B: The cheetah's running style is unique among big cats. Its spine is extremely flexible, acting like a spring: at each stride, the back bends and straightens, which lengthens the animal's reach. For part of each stride, all four feet are off the ground. Unlike other cats, a cheetah cannot fully retract its claws, so they serve like the spikes of a running shoe, giving grip on the ground. The long tail, flattened near the tip, works like a rudder, helping the animal to make sharp turns while running.
paras.C: Speed has its price. A cheetah can sustain a top-speed chase for only a few hundred metres, and its body heats up so quickly that it must rest after a chase for perhaps half an hour. During this time, it is vulnerable, as it may be robbed of its prey by stronger predators such as lions and hyenas. Some studies suggest that cheetahs lose a significant share of their kills in this way. Cheetahs also depend on their sight, and usually hunt in the daytime, avoiding the hours when lions are most active.
paras.D: The hunt itself is a sequence of stages. The cheetah first spots a target, usually a gazelle or impala, from a high place such as a termite mound or a low branch. It then creeps closer, keeping its body low and using cover, until it is within about fifty metres or so. Only then does it sprint. When it reaches its prey, it knocks it down with a paw and kills with a bite to the throat. Despite its speed, a cheetah's chase fails about as often as it succeeds.
paras.E: Cheetahs once ranged across Africa and much of Asia, including the Middle East and Central Asia, but they have disappeared from most of this area. A small population, perhaps fewer than a hundred, survives in Iran, and the animal has vanished from Uzbekistan and the neighbouring region. In Africa, the number has fallen to roughly seven thousand adults, living mostly in a few countries in the east and south. The main threats are the loss of habitat to farms and settlements, the hunting of their prey and conflicts with farmers.
paras.F: Another problem is the lack of genetic variety. Studies show that cheetahs are much more similar to one another than most wild animals, probably because their species passed through a narrow bottleneck, when very few individuals survived, around ten thousand years ago. With such a small gene pool, the animals are more vulnerable to disease, and fewer cubs survive. In captivity, breeding has been difficult.
paras.G: Conservationists are working on several solutions. They help farmers protect livestock by using guard dogs, which scare cheetahs away without harm. Others fit radio collars to track the animals' movements and identify areas that need protection. Education programmes teach children and farmers about the value of the species. The cheetah is a symbol of grace, and if the effort succeeds, future generations will be able to watch this magnificent runner in the wild.

paras.A: Deserts cover roughly a third of the Earth's land surface, and they are found on every continent. Many people think of them as seas of sand and dunes, but in fact, only about a fifth of the world's desert area is covered with sand. The rest consists of bare rock, gravel plains and salt flats. What these varied landscapes share is not heat but dryness: a desert is defined as a region that receives very little rain, generally less than 250 millimetres a year.
paras.B: The reasons why some places are dry vary. The largest hot deserts, such as the Sahara and the Arabian Desert, lie in two belts at around thirty degrees north and south of the equator. They are the result of the pattern of air movement in the atmosphere. Near the equator, intense sunshine heats the air, which rises and loses its moisture as heavy rain. The now dry air moves away from the equator, cools and sinks at about thirty degrees, where it warms again and absorbs moisture rather than releasing it.
paras.C: A second cause is the shadow of mountains. When moist winds meet a mountain range, they are forced to rise, cool and drop their rain on the windward side. By the time the air descends on the far side, it has lost most of its moisture. This 'rain shadow' effect has produced the deserts of the Great Basin in North America and the Patagonian desert in Argentina, which lies to the east of the Andes.
paras.D: A third cause is a cold ocean current along a coast. The Atacama Desert in Chile, one of the driest places on Earth, lies beside the cold Humboldt Current. The cold water cools the air above it, which then holds little moisture and brings fog rather than rain. In parts of the Atacama, no rain has been recorded for years at a time. A similar process creates the Namib Desert in southwestern Africa.
paras.E: Finally, some deserts lie deep inside continents, far from the sea. Moist air from the ocean loses most of its water before it travels thousands of kilometres inland. The Gobi Desert in Mongolia and China and the Karakum and Kyzylkum deserts of Central Asia belong to this type. They have extreme temperatures: scorching summers, and freezing winters when the thermometer may drop far below zero.
paras.F: Life in a desert is difficult but not impossible. Plants such as cacti store water in their stems, and others have long roots or a seed that waits for years for rain. Animals have also adapted: camels can drink huge amounts of water at once, and many small creatures spend the day underground and emerge at night. A desert, after a rare storm, can burst into bloom within days.
paras.G: Deserts are not fixed. Some have been growing because of drought, overgrazing and cutting trees, a process called desertification, which affects hundreds of millions of people. The shrinking of the Aral Sea created a new desert of salt and dust in Central Asia. Yet efforts to stop the spread, such as planting trees in belts and restoring grazing land, have achieved success in some regions. Deserts have been shaped by nature, but the human hand now plays a part in changing them.
