ps.title: Should the Voting Age Be Lowered to 16?

paras.A: In most countries, citizens must be eighteen before they can vote. Yet in a growing number of places, the age has been lowered to sixteen, at least for some elections. Austria introduced it for all elections in 2007, and Scotland allowed sixteen-year-olds to vote in the independence referendum of 2014 and has kept the rule for local and national parliament elections. Countries such as Brazil and Argentina also allow voting at sixteen. The idea has supporters and critics in many other places.
paras.B: Supporters begin with fairness. At sixteen, they say, young people can work, pay taxes and, in some countries, join the army or marry, but they cannot vote for the government that makes the rules. Decisions about education, the climate and the economy affect the young for longer than they affect older voters, and yet the young have the smallest voice. Allowing them to vote would give them a say in their own future.
paras.C: A second argument is about habit. Studies of voters suggest that voting is a habit: a person who votes in the first election is likely to vote in later ones, and the opposite is also true. At eighteen, many young people leave home for university or work and are busy with other matters; at sixteen, most still live with their families and attend school, where they can be encouraged to vote. In Austria, research has found that turnout among sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds was higher than among those a little older, who were just starting independent lives.
paras.D: Supporters also dispute the claim that sixteen-year-olds are too immature. Research on political knowledge finds that sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds know about as much as young adults in their twenties, and in some tests, they are better informed than older voters. Their reasoning skills for such decisions seem broadly similar to those of adults, though it is acknowledged that emotional control continues to develop into the twenties. Many adults, after all, vote without deep knowledge.
paras.E: Opponents have objections. They argue that the age of eighteen marks the transition to full adulthood in most legal matters, and that it would be inconsistent to give young people the vote but not other rights, such as buying alcohol. Teenagers, they claim, are more easily influenced by parents, friends or social media, and may not have the experience to judge political promises. A lower voting age might also give some parties an unfair advantage if they appeal strongly to the young.
paras.F: Another worry is that turnout could fall. Critics point to evidence that young voters often vote less than older ones, and an increase in the number of eligible young voters who stay at home might reduce the overall rate. Supporters reply that this is an argument for better civic education, rather than against the right to vote. In Scotland, schools introduced lessons about politics and elections before the referendum, and many young people took part.
paras.G: The question may in the end depend on what voting is seen to be: a reward for maturity or a right belonging to those who live under a government's decisions. If the second view is accepted, there is a strong case for lowering the age, provided that schools prepare young people. Countries are experimenting, and the results of their experience will probably decide whether the idea spreads or fades.

paras.A: In 1974, farmers digging a well near the city of Xi'an in central China struck something hard. What they uncovered was one of the greatest archaeological finds of the twentieth century: an army of life-sized clay soldiers, buried for more than two thousand years. Since then, archaeologists have found thousands of figures in several pits, and the work of excavation still continues today.
paras.B: The army was made for Qin Shi Huang, who united China in 221 BC and became its first emperor. He began planning his tomb soon after taking the throne of the state of Qin at the age of thirteen, and it is said that around 700,000 workers laboured on it over nearly four decades. The soldiers were meant to guard him in the afterlife, and the main tomb, a great mound that has not yet been opened, is believed to contain a model of his palace and empire.
paras.C: The scale of the figures is remarkable. Estimates suggest that there are about eight thousand soldiers, together with some one hundred and thirty chariots, more than five hundred horses and many other figures including officials, acrobats and musicians. The soldiers stand between 1.8 and 2 metres tall, taller than the average man of the time. No two faces are exactly alike, which has led some scholars to suggest that the sculptors used real soldiers as models.
paras.D: The method of manufacture was organised like a modern factory. Workshops made the bodies in standard parts: legs, torsos, arms and hands were produced from moulds and then joined together. The heads were finished by hand, with individual ears, moustaches and hairstyles added by craftsmen before the figures were fired. Each piece was then painted in bright colours. Traces of purple, red and green can still be found, but the paint began to flake and fade within minutes of exposure to the air when the figures were first excavated, which remains a challenge for conservators.
paras.E: The weapons were real. Bronze swords, spears and crossbow triggers have been recovered, and many of them were still sharp. Some blades have a thin surface layer containing chromium, which a number of researchers believe helped to protect them from rust. The standardisation of the weapons shows how efficient the Qin state was in organising production, a skill that helped it to defeat its rivals.
paras.F: The pits were not left in peace. Not long after the emperor's death in 210 BC, rebels attacked the site, and a fire probably burned the wooden roofs, which collapsed onto the soldiers and smashed most of them. As a result, almost every figure that visitors see today has been painstakingly put together from fragments. Restoration is slow work: a single warrior may take months to reassemble.
paras.G: Today the site is a World Heritage Site and welcomes millions of visitors a year. Archaeologists have deliberately left the emperor's tomb unopened, partly because ancient texts describe rivers of mercury inside it, and soil tests around the mound have indeed shown high levels of mercury. Many experts argue that excavation should wait until technology is able to protect what is found, so the army's greatest secret remains underground.

paras.A: Every day we are asked to buy, believe or agree. Advertisers, politicians, colleagues and friends all try to change what we think or do, and most of us believe that we make up our own minds. Psychologists who study persuasion have shown, however, that our decisions are often shaped by simple mental shortcuts, which we use because we are busy and cannot examine every choice carefully. Understanding these shortcuts does not make us immune, but it helps us to notice when they are being used.
paras.B: One of the best-known principles is reciprocity: when someone gives us something, we feel obliged to give something back. Charities know this well. In several experiments, people who received a small gift, such as a free pen or a few sweets, were more likely to make a donation than those who received nothing. Shops that offer free samples are using the same idea, since a customer who has accepted a taste often feels uncomfortable about walking away without buying.
paras.C: A second principle is social proof. When we are unsure what to do, we look at what others are doing. In one famous study, hotel guests were asked to reuse their towels. A card that said most guests in the hotel reused their towels was more effective than a card that spoke only about protecting the environment. Online, the same effect appears in star ratings and the number of people who have bought a product, which is why reviews are so valuable to sellers.
paras.D: Authority is a third influence. People tend to obey those who seem to be experts, whether or not the expertise is relevant. Advertisements often show actors dressed as doctors, and a uniform or a title can raise the chance that a request will be followed. In the 1960s, an American psychologist, Stanley Milgram, showed how far obedience could go. In his experiment, ordinary volunteers were told to give what they believed to be painful electric shocks to another person, and a majority continued to the highest level when a scientist in a white coat told them to carry on.
paras.E: Scarcity also has power. Things seem more valuable when they are rare or when time is running out. Phrases such as 'only three left' or 'offer ends tonight' push people to decide quickly, with less thought. Researchers have found that shoppers who were told that a product was in short supply rated it as more desirable, even though the product itself had not changed.
paras.F: Commitment and consistency form a further principle. Once we have agreed to a small request, we tend to agree to larger ones, because we want to act in line with what we have already done. A well-known study asked homeowners to place a large sign supporting safe driving on their lawns. Few agreed, but among those who had first agreed to display a tiny sticker in a window, the number who accepted the big sign was far higher.
paras.G: None of this means that persuasion is always harmful. Doctors who use social proof to encourage vaccination, or governments that remind citizens to pay taxes on time, are applying the same principles for the public good. The ethical question is whether people are given honest information and a real choice. The best defence against manipulation is awareness: when we feel a sudden pressure to act, it is wise to stop and ask why.

qs.title: Questions 24–27

paras.A: A decade ago, a wave of campaigns urged everyone to learn to program. Governments added coding to school curricula, charities ran free classes, and well-known figures declared that writing software was the literacy of the twenty-first century. In England, computing became a compulsory subject for children from the age of five in 2014, and similar reforms followed in several other countries. Today, however, the enthusiasm has been replaced by a more careful debate about who needs which skills.
paras.B: Supporters offer several arguments. The first is economic. Software now runs hospitals, banks, farms and factories, and employers in almost every sector complain that they cannot find enough people with digital skills. A country that teaches programming early, the argument goes, will have a workforce ready for the jobs of the future, and its young people will have access to well-paid careers whatever their background.
paras.C: A second argument concerns understanding. Even if a person never works as a programmer, knowing how programs are built helps them to understand the technology that shapes their lives. Someone who has written a simple program is less likely to think of an app as magic, and more likely to ask who designed it, what data it collects and what rules it follows. In this view, coding is less a job skill than a form of citizenship.
paras.D: Coding is also said to train the mind. Writing a program requires breaking a large problem into small steps, testing each step and finding the mistakes, a process known as debugging. Teachers report that pupils learn persistence, because a program that does not run is a puzzle that must be solved. Whether these habits transfer to other subjects is less clear, however, since research on the question has produced mixed results.
paras.E: Critics begin by pointing out that most people will never need to write code. Just as one can drive without being able to repair an engine, they say, one can use software skilfully without building it. The time spent on programming in school is time not spent on reading, mathematics or the arts. Moreover, the tools are changing quickly. New systems can already produce working code from a plain-language description, and some experts believe that the ability to describe a problem clearly will soon matter more than the ability to type instructions in a particular language.
paras.F: There is also a problem of quality. Many schools lack teachers who are confident in the subject, since people with programming skills can earn far more in industry than in a classroom. A poorly taught course may leave pupils bored and convinced that computing is not for them, which defeats the purpose of the policy. Some reports have found that girls, in particular, lose interest when lessons are dull or the classroom culture is unwelcoming.
paras.G: In my view, the best answer lies between the two positions. Every child should meet the basic ideas of computing, such as how data is stored, how an algorithm works and why a computer follows instructions exactly, in the same way that every child meets basic science. But it is unrealistic to expect everyone to become a skilled programmer, and it would be unwise to promise young people that a coding course is a guaranteed route to a good job. Schools should aim for understanding first, and leave deeper specialisation to those who choose it.

paras.A: Most rivers flow to the sea, but the Okavango does not. Rising in the highlands of Angola, it travels south for around a thousand kilometres, crosses the narrow Caprivi Strip of Namibia and then spreads out across the flat sands of northern Botswana. There, instead of reaching the ocean, it disappears into the Kalahari Desert. The result is one of the largest inland deltas in the world, a vast maze of channels, lagoons and islands in the middle of dry country.
paras.B: The most surprising feature of the delta is its timing. The rain that feeds the river falls in Angola in the summer months, but the water travels so slowly across the almost level land that it takes four or five months to arrive. The flood therefore reaches the delta in the dry season, usually between June and August, just when the surrounding country is at its driest. Animals from a wide area move towards the water at this time, and the delta becomes crowded with life.
paras.C: The size of the delta changes dramatically from year to year. In a dry year, the permanently flooded area may cover about six thousand square kilometres, while in a wet year it can more than double. Very little of the water leaves the system. Scientists estimate that around ninety-five per cent is lost to the air, either through evaporation from the surface or through the leaves of plants, and only a small fraction leaves the delta through seasonal rivers.
paras.D: The islands of the delta have an unusual origin. Many began as termite mounds. According to one explanation, when the termites abandoned a mound, seeds carried by birds and wind took root on it, and the trees that grew there absorbed water from the surrounding channels. As the trees took up the water, salts that had been dissolved in it were left behind in the soil, and over many years the islands grew larger. The salt in the centre of an island may eventually become so concentrated that trees can no longer survive there, leaving a bare, white patch.
paras.E: Wildlife has adapted to the changing waters in remarkable ways. Hippopotamuses move through the reeds at night and keep channels open, which allows water to flow and prevents the delta from becoming choked with plants. The red lechwe, an antelope with long hooves, can run through shallow water that would slow most predators, and it escapes lions by leaping into deeper lagoons. In the delta, some lions have even learned to swim in order to reach prey on distant islands.
paras.F: People have lived in the delta for centuries. They travel in the mokoro, a narrow canoe traditionally carved from a single tree trunk and pushed through the shallows with a long pole. Today many mokoros are made of fibreglass, which protects the forests. Fishing and small-scale farming remain important, but the main source of income is now tourism. The government of Botswana has chosen a policy of attracting fewer visitors who pay high prices, rather than large crowds, in order to protect the environment.
paras.G: The delta's survival depends on events far beyond its borders. The river is shared by three countries, and plans for dams or for removing large amounts of water upstream could reduce the flood. A shift in rainfall patterns caused by climate change is another risk. In 2014, the Okavango Delta was named a World Heritage Site, the thousandth place to receive this status. Its protection now requires cooperation between Angola, Namibia and Botswana, which created a shared commission to manage the river basin.

paras.A: Almost every living thing on Earth depends, directly or indirectly, on photosynthesis. Plants, algae and some bacteria use the energy of sunlight to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugar, releasing oxygen as a by-product. The sugar fuels the growth of the organism, and it passes along food chains to the animals that eat plants and to the animals that eat those animals. The oxygen we breathe is also a product of the process. Yet it took scientists more than two centuries to understand how it works.
paras.B: In the seventeenth century, a Belgian physician, Jan van Helmont, performed one of the first careful experiments on plant growth. He planted a young willow tree in a pot containing a measured quantity of soil and watered it for five years. At the end, the tree had gained around seventy kilograms, but the soil had lost only a tiny amount of its weight. Van Helmont concluded that the tree had been built from water. He was partly right, but he did not know that the air also played a part.
paras.C: A century later, the English chemist Joseph Priestley discovered that air could be 'restored'. In the 1770s, he found that a candle burning in a closed jar would soon go out, and that a mouse in the jar would die, but that a sprig of mint placed in the jar kept the air fresh for much longer. Some years afterwards, a Dutch scientist, Jan Ingenhousz, repeated the experiments and noticed that plants restored the air only when they were placed in sunlight. Light, he concluded, was essential.
paras.D: Today we know that the process takes place inside tiny structures in plant cells, called chloroplasts. They contain a pigment, chlorophyll, which absorbs light very well in the red and blue parts of the spectrum but reflects green light. That is why most leaves look green. Carbon dioxide enters the leaf through microscopic openings called stomata, and water is drawn up from the roots through the stem. When the stomata open to admit carbon dioxide, water vapour escapes, so the plant must balance its need for gas against the danger of drying out.
paras.E: Photosynthesis happens in two stages. In the first, light energy is captured and used to split water molecules, releasing oxygen and storing energy in small chemical carriers. In the second, known as the Calvin cycle, this stored energy is used to build sugar from carbon dioxide. The second stage does not need light directly, though it depends on the products of the first. At the centre of the cycle is an enzyme called Rubisco, which is thought to be the most abundant protein on Earth, but it works slowly and sometimes captures oxygen by mistake.
paras.F: Photosynthesis is very old. The first organisms to produce oxygen in this way were bacteria, called cyanobacteria, which appeared more than two billion years ago. Over a long period, the oxygen they released changed the atmosphere and the chemistry of the oceans, making possible the evolution of animals that breathe air. Today, microscopic floating algae in the oceans produce roughly half of the oxygen in the atmosphere.
paras.G: Scientists are now looking for ways to make photosynthesis more efficient. Even in good conditions, a crop plant converts only a few per cent of the sunlight it receives into stored energy. Some plants, such as maize and sugar cane, have evolved a more efficient method, and researchers are trying to introduce it into rice and other crops. Others are developing 'artificial leaves', devices that use sunlight to split water and produce fuel. If either approach succeeds, it could help to feed a growing population and to reduce our dependence on fossil fuels.

paras.A: When a famous footballer wears a particular brand of boots, sales of those boots rise. When a singer mentions a book, it can top the bestseller list within days. The power of celebrities to shape what we buy, eat and even believe has never been greater, thanks to social media, where a single post can reach tens of millions of followers. This influence raises a question that is rarely asked directly: why do we listen to people who are famous for something unrelated to the advice they give?
paras.B: The practice is far from new. In the eighteenth century, the potter Josiah Wedgwood won a surge of orders after the queen approved his tableware, and he advertised the fact widely. In the twentieth century, film stars appeared in advertisements for soap and cigarettes, and sports champions endorsed everything from breakfast cereal to cars. What has changed is the closeness. Followers see celebrities in their kitchens and bedrooms, and this feeling of friendship makes recommendations seem more personal and more honest than a traditional advertisement.
paras.C: Psychologists call this feeling a 'parasocial relationship': a one-sided bond in which the fan feels that he or she knows the celebrity, although the celebrity does not know the fan. Such relationships are not necessarily unhealthy. They can offer comfort and a sense of belonging, especially to lonely people. But they also lower our guard. We are less likely to question an opinion from someone we feel we know, which is precisely why companies are willing to pay large sums for endorsements.
paras.D: Defenders of celebrity influence point to real benefits. Famous people have raised huge sums for charity and drawn attention to diseases and disasters that might otherwise have been ignored. When a well-known actor spoke openly about a medical test, studies showed a rise in the number of people who booked the same test. Celebrities can also challenge stereotypes and give young people role models who look and sound like them.
paras.E: Yet the same power can do harm. Celebrities have promoted diets, supplements and financial products that experts consider useless or dangerous. In several countries, regulators have ruled that influencers must state clearly when a post is paid advertising, but studies show that many do not, and that followers often fail to notice the small print that does appear. Younger audiences, who spend the most time online, are the most vulnerable.
paras.F: Some argue that the problem lies with audiences rather than with celebrities. People, they say, are responsible for their own choices, and it is patronising to treat fans as if they cannot think. This view has some force, but it ignores the way that advertising is designed. Companies employ researchers to study exactly which messages change behaviour, so it is hardly a fair contest between a teenager and a professional campaign.
paras.G: My own view is that celebrity influence is neither good nor bad in itself; it is a form of power, and power needs rules. Honest labelling of paid posts should be strictly enforced, and schools should teach young people to ask who benefits from a recommendation. Famous people, for their part, should recognise that a large audience brings a duty of care. They have not earned the right to be believed on every subject, only the right to be heard.

paras.A: In June 1325, a young legal scholar named Ibn Battuta left his home town of Tangier, in Morocco, to make the pilgrimage to Mecca. He was twenty-one years old and expected to be away for about a year and a half. In fact, he did not return to Morocco for nearly a quarter of a century. By the end of his travels, he had covered more than a hundred thousand kilometres, a distance that few people in history had equalled before the age of steam.
paras.B: After Mecca, Ibn Battuta did not go home. He joined caravans to Iraq and Persia, sailed down the coast of East Africa as far as Kilwa, and later crossed the Black Sea to the lands of the Golden Horde. Wherever he went, he looked for fellow Muslims who could offer a meal, a bed and, if he was fortunate, a gift of money. Travelling Muslim scholars were respected, and the network of mosques, schools and guest houses that stretched across the Islamic world made long journeys possible.
paras.C: According to his own account, he then travelled through Central Asia, passing through Khwarazm, Bukhara and Samarkand, in what is now Uzbekistan, before crossing the mountains into Afghanistan and reaching the valley of the Indus in 1333. He described the cities of Central Asia as rich and full of mosques and colleges, though he also saw the ruin that Mongol armies had left behind.
paras.D: In India, the sultan of Delhi, Muhammad bin Tughluq, made the visitor a judge, and he stayed for several years. The post brought him wealth, but also danger, because the sultan was famously unpredictable, and Ibn Battuta was once placed under house arrest. In 1341, the sultan chose him as an envoy to China, but the expedition ended in disaster when a storm sank the ships carrying the gifts. Fearing the sultan's anger, he did not return to Delhi, and instead went to the Maldives, where he again served as a judge.
paras.E: He did not reach China on the intended mission, but he claimed to have visited its ports later. Modern historians doubt some of these claims, noting that the descriptions of China are less detailed than those of other regions and that parts of his story seem to have been borrowed from earlier writers. Nevertheless, his accounts of the Maldives, of Sri Lanka and of the Indian Ocean trade are considered reliable and valuable.
paras.F: Ibn Battuta returned to Morocco in 1349, to find that his mother had died only a few months earlier. In Damascus, the year before, he had seen the plague killing thousands. Restless, he soon set out again, first to Spain and then across the Sahara to the empire of Mali, where he visited Timbuktu. He was impressed by the safety of the roads, but he complained about the bad food and the strange habits of the court.
paras.G: At the request of the Sultan of Morocco, Ibn Battuta dictated the story of his journeys to a scholar named Ibn Juzayy in 1355. The book, known as the Rihla, or 'Journey', was little read outside the Islamic world until the nineteenth century, when European scholars translated it. Today it is a major source for historians, who value it for its detail about food, clothing, markets and customs in dozens of societies. The date of his death is uncertain, but he is thought to have died in Morocco in about 1369.

ps.title: The Hidden World Beneath Our Feet

paras.A: We walk on it, build on it and grow our food in it, yet most people give soil very little thought. A handful of healthy soil contains billions of living organisms, from bacteria and fungi to tiny worms and insects. Together they form one of the most complex habitats on Earth. A single teaspoon may hold more microorganisms than there are people in the world. Without this hidden life, plants could not grow, and the world's food supply would collapse.
paras.B: Soil is made very slowly. It begins when rock is broken down by wind, rain, ice and the roots of plants, and then mixes with dead leaves and animals. Scientists estimate that it may take hundreds of years to form a single centimetre of fertile topsoil. A mature soil is arranged in layers, called horizons: a dark upper layer rich in decaying matter, a paler layer below where minerals collect, and finally the broken rock from which the soil came.
paras.C: The creatures of the soil perform tasks that no machine can match. Bacteria break down dead material and release nutrients so that plants can use them again. Some bacteria live in swellings on the roots of peas, beans and clover, where they convert nitrogen from the air into a form that the plant can absorb. This is why farmers have traditionally grown these crops in rotation with others, in order to restore the fertility of the field.
paras.D: Earthworms are among the most important soil animals. In the nineteenth century, Charles Darwin spent forty years observing them, and in his last book, published in 1881, he argued that they had a large effect on the landscape. Their tunnels allow air and water to reach roots, and as they eat their way through the earth, they mix the layers and leave behind droppings rich in nutrients. He estimated that earthworms bring many tonnes of soil to the surface on every hectare each year.
paras.E: Fungi form an underground network that is only now being understood. Thin threads, called hyphae, surround the roots of most plants and extend far into the soil. In exchange for sugar that the plant produces, the fungus delivers water and minerals such as phosphorus. Some researchers believe that these threads also connect neighbouring plants, allowing them to share resources or even warnings about attack, though this idea remains debated among scientists.
paras.F: Soil is also a vast store of carbon. It contains more carbon than all the plants and the atmosphere combined, and healthy soils help to slow climate change by keeping this carbon out of the air. When forests are cleared and fields are ploughed repeatedly, however, much of that carbon is released as carbon dioxide. Ploughing also exposes the soil to wind and rain, which carry it away.
paras.G: Soil can be lost far faster than it is made. In the 1930s, drought and poor farming in the central United States turned millions of hectares into dust, forcing many families to leave their farms. This disaster, known as the Dust Bowl, led to the first national soil conservation programmes. Today, the United Nations warns that around a third of the world's soils are degraded. Methods such as planting cover crops, reducing ploughing and adding compost can rebuild soil, but the process takes years, and prevention is better than cure.

ps.title: Should Social Media Be Regulated for Children?

paras.A: In 2024, Australia passed a law to prevent children under sixteen from holding accounts on major social media platforms, one of the strictest measures of its kind in the world. Other countries have since considered similar rules, and the debate has divided parents, teachers, doctors and the technology companies themselves. The question is no longer whether social media affects young people, but whether the state should set limits, and, if so, how.
paras.B: Supporters of regulation begin with evidence of harm. Surveys in many countries link heavy use of social media among teenagers with poor sleep, anxiety and low self-esteem, especially among girls. Young users may also meet bullying, violent images or strangers with bad intentions. Platforms are designed to keep people on the screen for as long as possible, using endless feeds and notifications, and children have less self-control than adults.
paras.C: A second argument concerns responsibility. Societies already restrict children's access to alcohol, tobacco and gambling, not because every child will be harmed but because the risks are too great and the products are made by companies that profit from sales. Why, supporters ask, should an app be treated differently? They add that parents cannot do the job alone. One family that bans a platform may leave its child isolated if all the child's friends are still online.
paras.D: Critics reply that the evidence is less clear than it seems. Many studies show correlation but not cause: unhappy teenagers may use social media more, rather than social media making them unhappy. Some researchers find that the overall effect on well-being is small, while others find that moderate use is no worse than none. Critics also point out that for many young people, especially those who are shy, disabled or belong to minorities, online communities provide friendship and information that they cannot find locally.
paras.E: There are practical problems, too. To enforce an age limit, platforms must check the age of every user, which may require people to upload identity documents or have their faces scanned. This raises privacy concerns for adults as well as children. Determined teenagers can often avoid controls by lying, borrowing an older sibling's account or using a virtual private network. If young people are driven to less regulated corners of the internet, the policy might leave them less safe than before.
paras.F: Between a complete ban and no rules at all lie other options. Some countries require platforms to switch off addictive features for young users, such as endless scrolling and late-night notifications, and to set the strictest privacy settings by default. Others demand that companies be open about how their systems recommend content. Schools in several countries have banned phones during lessons, and early reports suggest improvements in attention and a fall in bullying, though research is still limited.
paras.G: In my view, an age limit alone is a blunt instrument, but doing nothing is not an acceptable alternative. The companies have the data and the engineers to make their products safer for children, and they should be required to do so. Parents and schools also have a role in teaching young people to use these tools wisely. Whatever approach is chosen, governments should measure the results honestly and be ready to change course if the evidence shows that a policy is not working.

paras.A: The Dead Sea is not really a sea, but a salt lake lying between Jordan to the east and Israel and the West Bank to the west. Its surface is about 430 metres below sea level, which makes the shore the lowest point on dry land anywhere on Earth. The lake is fed mainly by the River Jordan, but there is no outlet. Water leaves only by evaporation, and under the fierce desert sun a great deal of it does so, leaving the minerals behind.
paras.B: As a result, the water is extraordinarily salty: roughly ten times saltier than the ocean. Swimmers float effortlessly because the dense water pushes upwards on the body, and visitors are often photographed reading a newspaper while lying on the surface. The salt, however, stings cuts and the eyes, and swallowing even a small amount of the water is dangerous. Only simple microscopic organisms can live in it, which explains the name 'Dead Sea'.
paras.C: People have valued the lake for thousands of years. In ancient times, the Egyptians imported bitumen, a black sticky substance that floats up from the lake bed, to use in the preparation of mummies. King Herod built a fortress at Masada on a cliff overlooking the western shore, and the Greek philosopher Aristotle wrote about the lake's strange water. Even today, many tourists come for the black mud, which they spread on their skin, and for the dry, mineral-rich air, which some doctors recommend for people with certain skin and breathing conditions.
paras.D: In 1947, according to the usual story, a shepherd searching for a lost animal found a cave near the northwestern shore in which there were clay jars containing ancient scrolls. Over the following years, thousands of fragments were discovered in eleven caves near the settlement of Qumran. The Dead Sea Scrolls, as they are known, include the oldest known copies of many books of the Hebrew Bible, and they have given scholars a rare view of Jewish life some two thousand years ago.
paras.E: The lake is now in serious danger. Since the 1960s, water from the River Jordan has been diverted for farms and cities, and the flow that reaches the lake is only a small fraction of what it was. The level has fallen by about a metre a year, and the shoreline has retreated by hundreds of metres, leaving wide stretches of dry salt. Mineral companies that pump water into evaporation ponds to produce potash and other chemicals have made the loss worse.
paras.F: The falling water has had unexpected effects. As the sea retreats, fresh groundwater flows into the empty salt layers underground and dissolves them, creating hollows. The ground above collapses suddenly, forming sinkholes, of which thousands have appeared along the shores. They have swallowed roads, farm buildings and parts of hotels, and they make some beaches unsafe.
paras.G: Proposals to save the lake include a pipeline to carry seawater from the Red Sea, about 200 kilometres to the south. Supporters say it would stop the fall in the level and provide fresh water through desalination. Critics fear that mixing Red Sea water with the lake's unique chemistry could change its colour and produce algae or white crystals. Some environmentalists argue that the simplest answer is to return more water from the River Jordan, a solution that needs cooperation between neighbouring countries.

paras.A: Few things are more thrilling than the moment when a firework explodes high in the night sky into a ball of colour. Behind the beauty lies chemistry. The first fireworks were probably made in China more than a thousand years ago, after alchemists mixing sulphur, charcoal and a salt called saltpetre discovered a black powder that burned fiercely. Before that, people had made noise at festivals by throwing green bamboo onto fires, where trapped air and sap made it burst with a bang.
paras.B: Black powder, later called gunpowder, remains at the heart of a modern firework. It contains three ingredients: charcoal as the fuel, sulphur to help it ignite, and potassium nitrate, which supplies oxygen. Because the oxygen comes from within the mixture, the powder can burn even in a sealed container, and the gas that it produces so quickly creates enormous pressure.
paras.C: A typical aerial shell is a paper or plastic sphere packed with small pellets known as stars. At the base is a charge of black powder that is lit by a fuse and launches the shell from a tube. As it climbs, a second fuse, timed to burn for a few seconds, ignites a small explosive in the centre of the shell, which breaks it open and throws the burning stars outwards in all directions. The pattern depends on how the stars are arranged: a ring, a heart or a willow-like shower of gold.
paras.D: The colours come from metal compounds mixed into the stars. When heated, the atoms of each metal absorb energy, and electrons jump to higher energy levels. As the electrons fall back, they release this energy as light of a particular colour. Strontium compounds give a deep red, sodium gives yellow, barium produces green, and copper produces blue. Each metal has its own light 'signature', which is why the same effect is used by scientists to identify elements in a laboratory flame test.
paras.E: Blue is the most difficult colour to create. Copper compounds give a good blue only within a narrow temperature range: if the star burns too hot, the compound breaks down and the colour is lost, and if it is too cool, the light is too weak to be seen. Firework designers must therefore control the temperature of the burning mixture with great care, and a really clear deep blue is considered a mark of skill.
paras.F: Other effects need other ingredients. Fine particles of aluminium, magnesium or titanium burn with a brilliant white light and produce sparks, while charcoal and iron give the long, golden trails of the 'willow'. The crackle of some fireworks comes from small grains that explode in rapid succession as the stars fall. Combinations of these ingredients produce the mixed colours and changing effects that fill modern displays.
paras.G: Fireworks also have costs. The smoke contains fine particles that can irritate the lungs, and metals and chemicals such as perchlorates, which provide oxygen in many modern mixtures, may fall into lakes and rivers. Some cities now use drones or laser shows instead, which have no smoke and little noise, but fans of traditional fireworks insist that nothing yet matches the sound and the smell of a real display. Manufacturers meanwhile are developing cleaner mixtures that produce less smoke.

ps.title: Is Working from Home Here to Stay?

paras.A: Before 2020, only a small share of office workers in most countries worked from home regularly. Then the pandemic forced millions of people to move their desks to kitchens and bedrooms almost overnight. What was meant to be a short emergency measure turned into one of the largest unplanned experiments in the history of work. Now that the emergency has passed, many companies are asking their staff to return to the office for at least part of the week, and many staff are resisting.
paras.B: Employees give clear reasons for their preference. The first is time and money. Without a daily commute, a worker may save an hour or more each day, as well as the cost of fares or fuel. Parents and carers value the flexibility to be at home when children return from school. People living far from big cities, or with disabilities that make travel difficult, can apply for jobs that were once out of reach.
paras.C: Employers, on the other hand, worry about performance. Early studies of home working produced encouraging results, with many staff reporting that they could concentrate better without interruptions. Yet some managers remain unconvinced. They argue that new employees learn more quickly when they sit beside experienced colleagues, and that creative ideas often arise from unplanned conversations in corridors or at the coffee machine, which are hard to reproduce on a video call.
paras.D: Researchers have tried to measure the difference. In one well-known experiment, a Chinese travel company allowed call-centre staff to work from home for nine months. Productivity rose by about thirteen per cent, and fewer employees left their jobs. But when employees were given a choice, a significant number chose to return to the office, which suggests that the experience was not suited to everyone.
paras.E: A more cautious finding comes from studies of fully remote work in jobs that depend on teamwork. These often show that communication becomes more formal and that people are less likely to form links with colleagues in other departments. Employees working from home may also be passed over for promotion simply because their managers see them less often, a problem that researchers call 'proximity bias'.
paras.F: Many organisations have therefore chosen a hybrid model, in which staff spend some days in the office and some at home. In theory, this offers the benefits of both. In practice, it can be difficult to manage. If a team's members choose different days, a meeting may include some people in the room and others on screen, and those on screen can feel left out. Companies that have succeeded tend to set clear rules about which days everyone should attend.
paras.G: Looking ahead, it seems unlikely that work will return fully to the pre-2020 pattern. Technology has made remote cooperation easier, and many workers now regard flexibility as a right, not a favour. However, I do not believe that the office will disappear. Humans are social beings, and many valuable things, such as training, trust and a sense of belonging, are best developed in person. The best arrangement is likely to differ from one job and one person to another, and the wisest employers will experiment and listen.

ps.title: Venice: A City Built on Water

paras.A: Venice is built in a way that no sensible planner would have chosen. Its palaces, churches and houses stand on more than a hundred small islands in a shallow lagoon in northeastern Italy, linked by hundreds of bridges and divided by canals that serve as its streets. Cars are impossible; people walk, or travel by boat. Yet this improbable city was for centuries one of the richest and most powerful places in Europe.
paras.B: According to tradition, the city was founded in the year 421, but it grew mainly in the sixth and seventh centuries, when people from the mainland fled from invading armies and found safety among the marshy islands. Enemies on horseback could not easily reach them, and ships could not easily navigate the shallow waters without local knowledge. The settlers lived by fishing and by collecting salt, and then, as their skills improved, by trade.
paras.C: The foundations of Venice are one of the wonders of medieval engineering. Builders drove millions of wooden piles, mostly of alder, oak and larch, deep into the soft mud until they reached a layer of hard clay. On top of the piles, they laid platforms of timber and then blocks of stone. Because the wood is buried in mud with almost no oxygen, it does not rot. Over centuries, minerals in the water have gradually hardened some of it into a stone-like material.
paras.D: For about a thousand years, until Napoleon ended it in 1797, Venice was an independent republic ruled by a leader called the doge, who was chosen by a council of noble families. Its fleet, built in a huge state shipyard called the Arsenal, controlled trade routes to the eastern Mediterranean. Spices, silk and other goods from Asia came through Venice on the way to Europe, and the city became one of the richest in the world. Its merchants, such as Marco Polo, travelled as far as China.
paras.E: Wealth produced art. Painters like Titian and Tintoretto, architects and musicians were drawn to the city. The glassmakers of Murano, a nearby island to which they were moved in 1291 because of the danger of fire, guarded the secrets of their craft so closely that, it is said, a glassmaker who left the republic could be pursued by the authorities.
paras.F: The greatest threat today is water. Venice is slowly sinking while the sea level is rising. Flooding, known as acqua alta, or 'high water', occurs regularly in autumn and winter, when tides are pushed up by winds. In 2019, the water reached almost two metres above its normal level, the second highest on record, and flooded most of the city. A barrier system known as MOSE, consisting of seventy-eight hinged gates on the seabed at the entrances to the lagoon, was first used in October 2020 after years of delay and rising costs. When a high tide is forecast, the gates fill with air and rise to block the water. Some experts doubt that it will be enough as the sea continues to rise.
paras.G: Venice has a second problem: too many visitors. The historic centre, which had around 175,000 residents in the 1950s, now has fewer than 50,000, while millions of tourists arrive each year. Shops that once served local people have been replaced by souvenir stands, and rents have risen beyond the reach of many families. In 2024, the city began to charge day visitors an entry fee on selected days, an experiment that other crowded destinations are watching closely.

paras.A: Every day, billions of messages, photographs and videos travel around the world in a fraction of a second, yet few people can explain how. The internet is not a single machine or a single company but a 'network of networks': millions of smaller networks, owned by universities, businesses, governments and service providers, which have agreed to exchange data using common rules. No one person or organisation owns the whole system, and more than five billion people now use it.
paras.B: The idea began in the 1960s, when American researchers wanted computers in different places to share scarce and expensive resources. In October 1969, a message was sent between computers at two universities in California for the first time on a network called ARPANET. The researchers planned to type the word 'login', but the system crashed after the first two letters, so the first message ever sent was simply 'lo'.
paras.C: In the early network, different systems could not easily talk to each other. The solution was a set of standard rules, called protocols. The most important, known as TCP/IP, was adopted across the network on 1 January 1983, a date some people regard as the real birthday of the internet. Under these rules, a message is broken into small pieces called packets. Each packet carries the address of its destination and is sent separately.
paras.D: On the way, packets pass through devices called routers, which read the address and send each packet on to the next router that is closest to its destination. The packets of a single message may travel by different routes and arrive in a different order; at the destination, they are reassembled. This design makes the internet resilient. If one connection is broken, the packets simply find another way. It also makes it possible for many users to share the same cables at once.
paras.E: Humans prefer names to numbers, so a system called the Domain Name System works like a global telephone directory. When you type a website's name into a browser, your computer asks a server for the numerical address, known as an IP address, that belongs to the name. The answer comes back in a few milliseconds, and the browser then requests the page from the computer at that address.
paras.F: Physical cables, not satellites, carry most of the traffic. More than ninety-five per cent of international data travels through cables laid on the ocean floor, each about as thick as a garden hose and containing hair-thin fibres of glass that carry pulses of light. Ships lay the cables, and occasionally they are damaged by anchors, fishing nets or earthquakes, which can slow the internet in entire regions.
paras.G: The internet is often confused with the World Wide Web, but the two are different. The web is a service that runs on the internet, a system of linked pages invented by the British scientist Tim Berners-Lee at CERN in 1989. Email, online games and video calls also use the internet but are not part of the web. Together, they have changed the way that people work, learn and communicate, although they also raise urgent questions about privacy, security and who should decide the rules.

qs.title: Questions 22–26

paras.A: Few debates in the cultural world are as persistent as the question of whether museums should charge for entry. In Britain, many national museums have been free to enter since 2001, with the exception of special exhibitions, and visitor numbers rose sharply afterwards. In the United States, by contrast, most large museums charge entry fees of twenty to thirty dollars, and in many other countries the price depends on the visitor's age, nationality or income. Each system has its supporters, and each has weaknesses.
paras.B: The case for free entry begins with principle. The collections of a public museum, supporters argue, belong to the public, having been bought or preserved with public money. Charging for admission is like charging a citizen to enter a library. Free entry also breaks down the idea that museums are for the wealthy and educated. Surveys have shown that when tickets are free, more people from poorer areas and from minority groups walk through the doors.
paras.C: Free entry can also change the way people visit. Without a ticket to justify, visitors feel able to come for twenty minutes to look at a single painting, or to shelter from the rain, or to bring a restless child. Many museum directors say that this casual, repeated contact does more to create lifelong interest in culture than a single expensive visit that visitors feel they must make last for hours.
paras.D: Opponents respond that museums are expensive to run. Conservation, security, research and the care of fragile objects cost large sums, and governments do not always provide enough money. Without income from tickets, museums may have to depend more heavily on gifts from rich donors and corporate sponsors, who may influence what is exhibited. Charging, say critics, also makes visitors value what they see. People who have paid are more likely to pay attention.
paras.E: There is also evidence that free admission does not always bring in the groups it is meant to attract. Studies of British museums after 2001 found that most of the increase in visitors came from people who already visited museums and now came more often. A free ticket, it seems, is not enough on its own to overcome the barriers of distance, time and the feeling that a museum is not 'for people like us'.
paras.F: Middle paths exist. Some museums are free on one day or evening each week, or free to children, students and local residents, while charging foreign tourists. Others suggest a donation, but leave the amount to the visitor. A growing number offer free access to the permanent collection but charge for special exhibitions. These systems combine access with income, though they can be complicated to administer, and the rules sometimes confuse visitors.
paras.G: Having weighed the arguments, I am persuaded that permanent collections should be free wherever possible, at least for residents. A museum that has paid its way with public funds should be open to the public, and the cost of free entry is small compared with the benefits to education and civic pride. But free entry is not enough. Museums must also reach out through schools, local events and clear, friendly displays that invite everyone to take part. It would be a mistake to think that opening the door is the same as welcoming the visitor.

paras.A: Few animals have shaped human history as deeply as the horse. Horses carried armies, farmers and messengers; they pulled ploughs, carts and chariots; and until little more than a century ago they were the fastest means of land travel available. Yet for a long time, nobody knew when or where they were first tamed. The mystery has only recently begun to be solved, with the help of ancient DNA.
paras.B: For many years, archaeologists pointed to the Botai culture, which lived on the steppes of what is now northern Kazakhstan about 5,500 years ago. At Botai sites, researchers found huge numbers of horse bones, as well as signs of fenced areas and traces of horse milk fat on pottery. Some scholars concluded that the Botai people were the first to keep horses. In 2018, however, a genetic study showed that the Botai horses were not the ancestors of modern domestic horses, but of the wild Przewalski's horses.
paras.C: A larger study, published in 2021, compared the DNA of 273 ancient horses from across Europe and Asia. It found that the ancestors of modern domestic horses first appeared in the grasslands north of the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea, in the region of the lower Volga and Don rivers, about 4,200 years ago. Within a few centuries, these horses had spread across Eurasia, replacing all other local populations. The speed of this spread suggests that they had a quality that people prized.
paras.D: What was that quality? The researchers found two genetic changes in the new horses. One affected the skeleton, probably making the back stronger, and the other was linked to behaviour, and perhaps made the animals calmer. A strong back and a gentle temperament are exactly what is required in a horse that is ridden. The evidence therefore supports the view that riding, rather than meat or milk, was the key to the horse's success.
paras.E: Physical evidence of riding is hard to find, but it exists. Skeletons of people buried about 5,000 years ago in Eastern Europe show injuries to the hips and spine that are similar to those suffered by modern riders. Also, horse teeth from sites of a later period show wear that was caused by bits, the metal or bone bars placed in the mouth to control the animal.
paras.F: With riding came changes in warfare and travel. By about 2000 BC, light chariots with spoked wheels were being driven across the steppes, and by about 900 BC, the Assyrians and other peoples had trained cavalry. A great invention was the stirrup, which appeared in China in the early centuries AD and gave the rider a firm seat from which to fight and shoot. Mounted peoples of the steppe, such as the Mongols, used these advantages to build the largest land empires in history.
paras.G: In the Americas, horses had died out thousands of years earlier, and they returned only when Spanish settlers brought them across the Atlantic in the 1490s. Within a few generations, Native American nations of the Great Plains had become some of the finest riders in the world. Today, machines have replaced horses for most work, but the unit of power in an engine, horsepower, still remembers the animal, and horses remain valued for sport, tourism and companionship.

paras.A: Colour in the animal kingdom is rarely decoration alone. For most species, it is a matter of survival: a way to hide, to warn, to attract a partner or to control body temperature. The colours themselves are produced in two quite different ways, and understanding the difference helps to explain why some of the most brilliant creatures in nature are not coloured by pigment at all.
paras.B: The first way is pigment. Chemicals such as melanin, which gives black, brown and grey, or carotenoids, which give red, orange and yellow, absorb some wavelengths of light and reflect others. Animals cannot make carotenoids themselves and must obtain them from food. Flamingos are born grey and become pink as they eat shrimps and algae rich in these chemicals; in a zoo, they will fade unless their diet is adjusted.
paras.C: The second way is structure. Many blues and iridescent greens are created not by pigment but by microscopic structures on the surface of feathers, scales or wings, which reflect light in such a way that waves of certain colours reinforce each other. A blue jay's feather, if ground into powder, would look brown, since the blue disappears when the structure is destroyed. The brilliant blue of Morpho butterflies and the shimmering tail of a peacock are produced in the same way.
paras.D: The best-known function of colour is camouflage. The stripes of a tiger break up its outline in tall grass, and the skin of a flatfish copies the pattern of the sea floor on which it lies. Many animals are darker on top and lighter underneath, an effect known as countershading, which cancels out the shadow produced by sunlight and makes the body look flat. Some, such as the cuttlefish, can change their colour in less than a second to match their surroundings.
paras.E: Other animals do the opposite, and advertise themselves. Bright colours in wasps, poison frogs and some caterpillars warn predators that they are poisonous or dangerous, and a predator that has had a bad experience will avoid the same pattern in future. This strategy has been copied. Harmless hoverflies have yellow and black stripes like those of wasps, so that predators avoid them too, a trick called mimicry.
paras.F: Colour is also used to attract a partner. A male peacock's tail is heavy and conspicuous, and it makes escape from predators harder. Peahens, however, prefer males with the most brilliant tail feathers, which may be a sign of good health. Over many generations, females' choices have driven the evolution of ever more spectacular displays. In some species of bird, the brightness of a male's colours reflects the quality of his diet.
paras.G: Colour can change over time with the environment. The peppered moth is a famous example. In industrial Britain in the nineteenth century, trees were blackened by soot, and dark moths, once rare, became common because birds found it harder to see them against the dark bark. When the air became cleaner in the twentieth century, pale moths became common again. More recently, scientists studying zebras have suggested that their stripes may help to confuse biting flies, showing that the purposes of colour are still being discovered.

ps.title: Is Happiness the Right Goal for Governments?

paras.A: For most of history, governments measured success by wealth. Gross domestic product, the total value of goods and services produced in a country, became the standard measure in the twentieth century, and politicians have competed to make it grow. In recent decades, however, a different idea has gained support: that the aim of policy should be the happiness of citizens. The small Himalayan kingdom of Bhutan has long spoken of 'Gross National Happiness', and countries such as New Zealand and the United Arab Emirates have introduced well-being budgets or even a minister for happiness.
paras.B: Supporters begin by pointing out that wealth is only a means to an end. People want a higher income because they expect it to make their lives better, not for its own sake. Why not, then, measure the result directly? Surveys of life satisfaction are now conducted regularly in most rich countries, and the World Happiness Report ranks nations every year, with the Nordic countries consistently near the top.
paras.C: Research also suggests that, beyond a certain level, more money brings smaller gains in happiness. Within a country, the rich are on average happier than the poor, but when a nation's income rises, its average happiness often rises slowly or not at all. This pattern, noted by the economist Richard Easterlin in the 1970s, is known as the Easterlin paradox, although later studies have disputed it.
paras.D: Happiness research has also revealed causes of unhappiness that economic data hide. Long commutes, unemployment, loneliness and poor mental health reduce life satisfaction by more than most people expect, and such findings can guide spending. A government that learns that loneliness is a major source of misery might fund community centres rather than a new motorway.
paras.E: Critics raise several objections. First, happiness is hard to measure. Responses to a survey can be affected by the weather, the wording of the question or what happened that morning, and people from different cultures understand the word differently. In some societies, it is considered boastful to say that you are very happy. Comparisons across countries may therefore be unreliable.
paras.F: A deeper objection is philosophical. Some argue that a good life is not simply a happy one. A person may sacrifice comfort for a cause, devote years to a difficult skill or care for a sick relative, and be less cheerful than they would otherwise have been, yet most of us would not say that the life was wasted. There is also a danger that governments will use happiness figures to avoid hard questions about justice and freedom. A population can be content and still be badly treated.
paras.G: My conclusion is that happiness should be one of the measures a government uses, but not the only one. It is a useful corrective to the obsession with growth, and it directs attention to the neglected areas of life such as friendship, health and time. Yet a society should also care about fairness, freedom and the rights of minorities, which cannot be reduced to a single number. The wisest policy-makers will look at a dashboard of indicators, rather than at any one dial.

paras.A: The Silk Road was not a single road but a network of routes that, for more than a thousand years, linked China with India, Central Asia, Persia and the Mediterranean. Its name is quite modern. It was invented in 1877 by a German geographer, Ferdinand von Richthofen, who wanted a simple phrase for the trade that had carried Chinese silk to the West. Few merchants ever travelled the whole distance; goods were passed from one trader to another, becoming more expensive at each stop.
paras.B: The routes began to flourish in the second century BC. The Chinese emperor of the Han dynasty sent an envoy, Zhang Qian, to find allies against nomadic raiders in the west. Zhang Qian was held captive for ten years, but when he returned he brought detailed reports of the kingdoms of Central Asia, including Ferghana, which was famous for its powerful horses. China wanted these animals for its army, and the exchange of horses for silk helped to open the road.
paras.C: Silk was the most celebrated product, and for centuries its production was a secret closely guarded by the Chinese. Wealthy Romans paid enormous sums for the cloth, and some officials complained that it drained gold from the empire. According to a well-known story, in the sixth century two monks hid silkworm eggs in hollow walking sticks and carried them to the Byzantine emperor, ending the Chinese monopoly. Whether or not the story is exactly true, silk was soon being produced outside China.
paras.D: Many other goods travelled along the routes. From the east came tea, porcelain, paper and spices; from the west came glass, wine, gold and silver, and from India came cotton and pepper. Cities on the way, such as Samarkand and Bukhara in what is now Uzbekistan, grew rich as meeting places where merchants rested, exchanged goods and changed animals in great inns called caravanserais. The Sogdians, whose homeland lay in this region, became the most successful traders and interpreters of the Silk Road.
paras.E: Ideas moved as well as goods. Buddhism travelled from India to China along the road, and Buddhist monks left carvings and paintings in cave temples along the way. Islam spread through Central Asia in the eighth century, and Muslim scholars later carried mathematics and astronomy in both directions. The technology of papermaking also moved west. According to tradition, Chinese prisoners captured in a battle near the Talas River in 751 taught the art to the people of Samarkand, which became a famous centre of paper production.
paras.F: Travel was dangerous. Caravans crossed deserts such as the Taklamakan, whose name is sometimes said to mean 'go in and you will not come out', and they climbed high passes through the Pamir and Tian Shan mountains. Travellers risked thieves, storms, thirst and disease. Diseases also moved along the routes, and many historians believe that the plague that killed millions of people in the fourteenth century travelled from Asia to Europe by way of trade.
paras.G: The Silk Road declined from the fifteenth century, when sailors found sea routes between Europe and Asia that were cheaper and safer for large cargoes. Many of the oasis cities lost their wealth. In recent years, however, the idea has returned. Governments have promoted new railways, roads and ports under the name of a modern Silk Road, and in 2014 a section of the ancient network, running through China, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, was named a World Heritage Site.

paras.A: Every day our bodies are attacked by viruses and bacteria. Most are stopped by the skin, the stomach acid or the immune system before we notice them. The immune system is a network of cells and chemicals that recognises invaders and destroys them. Its weakness is speed. When it meets a new germ, it can take several days to build an effective defence, and in that time a serious disease may do great harm. Vaccines are designed to give the body a head start.
paras.B: The principle is simple. A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless piece or version of a germ, so that the body learns to recognise it. The distinctive molecules on the surface of a germ are called antigens. When white blood cells detect an unfamiliar antigen, they make proteins called antibodies, which attach themselves to the invader and mark it for destruction. Afterwards, some of the cells remain in the body for years as 'memory cells'. If the real germ appears, they recognise it at once and react within hours.
paras.C: The first vaccine was developed in England in 1796 by Edward Jenner, a country doctor. He had heard that milkmaids who caught cowpox, a mild illness, seemed to be protected from smallpox, which killed or disfigured millions of people. Jenner took fluid from a cowpox sore on a milkmaid and introduced it into the arm of an eight-year-old boy, James Phipps. When he later exposed the boy to smallpox, the child did not become ill. The word 'vaccine' comes from the Latin word for cow, vacca.
paras.D: Modern vaccines take several forms. Some contain a live but weakened germ, which can cause a mild infection and a strong response; the vaccine against measles is of this kind. Others contain a germ that has been killed, or only a fragment, such as a protein from its surface. A newer type uses a molecule called messenger RNA, which carries instructions that make the body's own cells produce a harmless piece of the germ. The immune system then reacts to that piece in the usual way.
paras.E: No vaccine is perfect. Most produce mild side effects such as a sore arm or a slight fever for a day or two, which show that the immune system is working. Serious reactions are very rare. Protection can also fade, which is why some vaccines require 'boosters' after a few years, and why some germs, such as the influenza virus, change so quickly that a new vaccine is needed every year.
paras.F: Vaccines protect communities as well as individuals. When enough people are immune, a disease finds it hard to spread, and those who cannot be vaccinated, such as newborn babies or people with weak immune systems, are indirectly protected. This effect is called herd immunity. The proportion of people who need to be immune varies; for a highly infectious disease like measles, it is more than ninety per cent.
paras.G: The results have been dramatic. Smallpox, which killed hundreds of millions of people in the twentieth century alone, was declared eradicated by the World Health Organization in 1980, the only human disease so far to be defeated in this way. Polio has been reduced by more than 99 per cent since the 1980s, and every year vaccines prevent millions of deaths. Yet there are still areas where immunisation is incomplete, because of poverty, war or distrust, and the diseases quickly return where coverage falls.

paras.A: Every year, hundreds of millions of people visit zoos. For many, a trip to see a giraffe or a tiger is a childhood memory. Yet attitudes are changing. Surveys in several countries show that a growing number of people feel uneasy about keeping wild animals in captivity, and a few countries have banned certain kinds of animal from entertainment. The question is whether zoos still have a place in the modern world.
paras.B: Defenders of zoos begin with conservation. Some species have survived only because zoos kept and bred them. The Arabian oryx, which was hunted to extinction in the wild in the early 1970s, was brought back from small groups in zoos and private collections and has since been returned to the deserts of Oman and elsewhere. The California condor and the black-footed ferret were saved in a similar way. Without the zoos, supporters say, these animals would have disappeared.
paras.C: Zoos also claim an educational role. Seeing a living animal, they argue, creates a bond that no film can match, and people who care about animals are more likely to support their protection. Many zoos fund research and projects to protect habitats in the wild. Critics reply that studies of the educational value of zoos are weak, and that most visitors spend only a few minutes in front of each enclosure.
paras.D: The strongest objections concern the animals' welfare. Wild animals that travel long distances, such as elephants, polar bears and big cats, may suffer when they are confined. Some develop repetitive behaviours, such as pacing back and forth, which scientists consider a sign of stress. Elephants in zoos tend to live shorter lives than those in protected reserves. Better design can reduce these problems, but critics doubt that it can remove them for the largest and most intelligent species.
paras.E: Another objection is that only a small number of zoo animals contribute to conservation. Most species kept in zoos are not endangered, and very few are ever released into the wild. Raising animals in captivity can also be difficult because they must learn the skills needed for survival, such as finding food and avoiding predators. For many species, protecting the natural habitat is a far better use of money than keeping animals in cages.
paras.F: In response, some zoos have changed. Modern designs give animals larger and more natural spaces, and a number of zoos have stopped keeping species, such as elephants, that they cannot house well. Others have turned to 'safari parks' or sanctuaries for rescued animals, where visitors can observe animals in more natural groups. Whether such places are zoos or something new is a matter of definition.
paras.G: My own view is that the case for the traditional zoo has weakened, but the case for well-run conservation centres is strong. A zoo should be judged by how much it contributes to saving species and by the quality of life it offers its animals, not by the number of tickets it sells. Zoos that cannot meet this standard should be closed or reformed. At the same time, I do not think that all zoos should be abolished immediately, since some species depend on them.

paras.A: The Amazon rainforest is the largest tropical forest on Earth. It covers more than five million square kilometres, an area many times larger than France, and it stretches across nine countries, although about sixty per cent of it lies in Brazil. Through the forest flows the Amazon River, which carries more water than any other river in the world; roughly one-fifth of all the fresh water that rivers deliver to the oceans comes from this one system.
paras.B: Nowhere else on land contains so many kinds of living things. Scientists estimate that the Amazon is home to about one in ten of all the species known to science, including more than two thousand kinds of fish, more than 1,300 kinds of bird and countless insects, many of them still unnamed. A single hectare of forest may contain several hundred species of tree. New animals and plants are discovered there so often that, by one count, a new species has been described every two days in recent years.
paras.C: The forest is arranged in layers. At the top, a few giant trees called emergents rise forty or fifty metres above the rest. Below them, the closed roof of the canopy blocks most of the sunlight, and the animals that live there, such as monkeys, sloths and parrots, rarely descend to the ground. Beneath the canopy is a dim, humid understory, and on the forest floor, only about two per cent of the light arrives. Plants of the floor have large leaves to catch what little light there is.
paras.D: Surprisingly, the soil of the Amazon is poor. Heavy rain washes the minerals out of the ground, so most of the forest's nutrients are held in the living plants rather than in the earth. When leaves fall, they are broken down within weeks by fungi and insects, and the roots, which spread close to the surface, absorb the nutrients at once. This efficient cycle explains why cleared land quickly loses its fertility, and why farms made from rainforest are often abandoned after a few years.
paras.E: The forest also creates its own weather. Trees draw up water from the ground and release it into the air through their leaves, and this vapour forms clouds that fall again as rain further to the west. Scientists call the streams of moisture that travel through the sky 'flying rivers'. Rainfall in distant regions, including farmland in southern Brazil and Argentina, may depend on them. The idea that the Amazon is 'the lungs of the Earth' is less accurate: the forest uses almost as much oxygen as it produces.
paras.F: Over 400 Indigenous peoples live in the Amazon basin, and some groups have almost no contact with the outside world. They have developed detailed knowledge of the plants of the forest, and many medicines come from it. Research indicates that, in areas where Indigenous people manage the land, deforestation rates are lower than elsewhere. Their rights to the land are therefore important both for justice and for the protection of the forest.
paras.G: The greatest threat is clearing. About a fifth of the original forest in Brazil has been cut down, mostly to create pastures for cattle and fields of soya. Scientists warn of a 'tipping point': if too much is lost, the remaining forest may no longer produce enough rain to survive, and large areas could turn into dry savanna. In recent years, deforestation has fallen when governments enforced laws, and risen when they did not, which suggests that the future of the Amazon depends strongly on political decisions.
