ps.title: Earthquakes and How We Measure Them

paras.A: The ground beneath our feet seems solid, but the outer layer of the Earth is broken into huge pieces called tectonic plates, which move slowly over the hot rock below, at about the speed that fingernails grow. In most places they slide past or push against each other so gradually that no one notices. Occasionally, however, the rock at the edge of a plate becomes stuck, and stress builds up for years or decades. When it finally breaks, the stored energy is released in seconds as an earthquake.
paras.B: The break takes place along a crack in the rock known as a fault. The point underground where the rock first slips is called the focus, and the point on the surface directly above it is the epicentre. Most earthquakes occur around the edges of plates; about 90 per cent happen along the 'Ring of Fire' around the Pacific Ocean, where several plates meet. Earthquakes also occur in the interior of continents, though they are less frequent.
paras.C: The energy travels outwards as vibrations, called seismic waves. The fastest, known as P waves, push and pull the rock in the direction in which they travel and arrive first. S waves, which are slower, shake the ground from side to side, and they cannot travel through liquid. By studying how these waves pass through the Earth, scientists discovered in the early twentieth century that the planet has a liquid outer core. The slowest and most destructive waves travel along the surface.
paras.D: The ancient Chinese were the first to try to detect earthquakes. According to records, in AD 132 a scholar named Zhang Heng built a bronze vessel with dragon heads around the outside, each holding a ball; when the ground shook, a ball dropped from the mouth of a dragon into the mouth of a bronze toad below, pointing in the direction of the quake. Modern instruments, called seismometers, use a heavy weight suspended from a frame. When the ground moves, the weight stays almost still, and the difference is recorded.
paras.E: The size of an earthquake is described by its magnitude. In 1935, the American scientist Charles Richter devised a scale in which each whole number represents a tenfold increase in the amplitude of the waves, which corresponds to about thirty-two times more energy. Thus, a magnitude 7 earthquake releases roughly a thousand times more energy than a magnitude 5. Scientists now use a refined version, the moment magnitude scale, but the numbers are similar. The largest earthquake ever recorded, in Chile in 1960, had a magnitude of 9.5.
paras.F: Magnitude does not tell the whole story about damage. A moderate earthquake directly beneath a city can do more harm than a larger one far away. In 1966, an earthquake of magnitude of only about 5 struck Tashkent, in Uzbekistan. Because its focus was very shallow and lay almost directly below the city, it destroyed much of the centre and left many thousands of families homeless. The city was rebuilt in a few years with the help of builders from across the Soviet Union.
paras.G: Scientists cannot predict earthquakes, but they can reduce the danger. Maps of faults show where risk is highest. Warning systems detect the fast P waves and send alerts to phones and trains a few seconds before the damaging waves arrive, which is enough time to stop trains and open fire-station doors. Above all, buildings designed to flex rather than to break save lives. Most people who die in earthquakes are killed by falling buildings, not by the ground itself.

ps.title: Is Tourism Good for Local Communities?

paras.A: Tourism is one of the world's largest industries. Before the pandemic, it accounted for roughly one job in ten around the world, and in some countries, such as the Maldives and Croatia, it provides a large share of national income. Governments often welcome visitors as a source of foreign money. But in recent years, residents of popular destinations have begun to protest, and in cities such as Barcelona and Amsterdam, banners reading 'tourists go home' have appeared. Is tourism a blessing or a burden for those who live in the places that tourists visit?
paras.B: The economic argument is strong. Hotels, restaurants, guides, taxi drivers and shopkeepers all earn a living from visitors, and tourism often creates work in remote places where there are few other opportunities. It tends to employ a high proportion of women and young people. Money spent by tourists spreads through the local economy, supporting farmers who supply food and craftspeople who sell souvenirs. For many poor regions, tourism is the easiest path to growth.
paras.C: Tourism can also protect culture and nature. Entrance fees pay for the upkeep of historic buildings and national parks, and the interest of visitors encourages communities to preserve traditional crafts, music and festivals that might otherwise disappear. In East Africa, income from safaris gives local people a reason to protect wild animals rather than hunt them. In such cases, tourism and conservation support each other.
paras.D: Yet the benefits are not shared equally. A large part of the money spent on a package holiday often goes to international airlines and hotel chains rather than to local people, a loss that economists call 'leakage'. Jobs in tourism are frequently seasonal and poorly paid, and the best positions go to people from outside. In some places, local people are excluded from beaches that have been bought by luxury resorts.
paras.E: Crowds create further problems. In popular cities, short-term holiday rentals have reduced the supply of housing, so that rents rise and residents are pushed out of the centre. Shops that serve everyday needs are replaced by souvenir stands. Fragile sites also suffer; footpaths erode, coral reefs are damaged by careless divers, and some beaches are covered with rubbish. Visitors to a small town may outnumber the residents many times over in the summer.
paras.F: Possible solutions exist. Some cities limit the number of days that a home can be rented to visitors, charge an entrance fee to day-trippers, or cap the number of daily visitors to the most fragile sites. Others encourage tourists to visit less crowded places or to travel outside the peak season. A 'community-based' model, in which villages own and run guest houses and keep the profits, has proved successful in parts of Asia and Latin America.
paras.G: My view is that tourism is neither good nor bad in itself; what matters is who decides and who benefits. When communities are consulted and their share of the income is fair, tourism can be a powerful force for good. When the industry is allowed to grow without limits, it can destroy the very qualities that attracted visitors in the first place. Tourists, too, have a responsibility: to spend money locally, to respect local customs and to choose their destination with care.

ps.title: Machu Picchu: The Lost City of the Inca

paras.A: High in the Andes of Peru, on a narrow ridge between two peaks, stands the ruined city of Machu Picchu. Its name means 'old peak' in Quechua, the language of the Inca. At about 2,430 metres above sea level, the site is surrounded by steep forested mountains, and the Urubamba River curves far below. For centuries it was known only to local farmers; today it is one of the most visited archaeological sites in South America.
paras.B: Machu Picchu was probably built as a royal estate for Pachacuti, the ruler who transformed the Inca from a regional power into an empire in the middle of the fifteenth century. A study published in 2021, which used radiocarbon dating of human remains, suggested that the site was occupied from about 1420, a few decades earlier than historians had believed. Perhaps a few hundred people lived there permanently, serving the emperor and his family when they visited.
paras.C: The Inca were master builders. The walls of the finest buildings were made of blocks of granite cut so precisely that they fit together without any mortar; in some places, it is impossible to push a knife blade between the stones. Doors and windows are trapezoid-shaped, narrower at the top than at the bottom, a form that resists earthquakes. Peru is a country of earthquakes, and the walls of Machu Picchu have survived many, which is one reason why so much remains today.
paras.D: Another achievement was the management of water and land. The steep slopes were cut into hundreds of stone terraces, which prevented soil from sliding and made small fields for crops such as maize and potatoes. Under the terraces, layers of stones and gravel allow rainwater to drain away. A system of channels carried spring water to fountains in the city. The engineers also understood the mountain: the city sits on the meeting point of fault lines, and its builders used the broken rock for the walls.
paras.E: Many buildings seem to have religious functions. The Temple of the Sun has a curved wall and a window that is positioned so that the sunrise at the June solstice shines through it on a carved stone. A rock known as the Intihuatana, or 'hitching post of the sun', is thought to have been used to observe the sun's movement. The Inca worshipped the sun as the source of life, and their calendar of festivals and farming depended on watching the sky.
paras.F: The Spanish conquered the Inca Empire in the 1530s, but they never found Machu Picchu. The site was abandoned, perhaps because of disease or the collapse of the empire, and the forest slowly covered it. In 1911, the American explorer Hiram Bingham, a lecturer at Yale University, was led there by local guides. Bingham photographed the ruins and published his findings in a famous magazine, which brought the site to the attention of the whole world. Local people had known of it all along.
paras.G: Today Machu Picchu is a World Heritage Site and, since 2007, one of the 'New Seven Wonders of the World'. The popularity has brought problems. More than a million visitors a year walk over the stones, erosion has damaged the paths, and heavy rain has caused landslides. Peru now limits the daily number of visitors and requires them to follow fixed routes with guides. Experts disagree about the right number, but most agree that the fragile site cannot support unlimited crowds.

paras.A: A battery stores energy in chemical form and releases it as electricity when needed. From the tiny cell in a watch to the huge packs of an electric car, all batteries work on the same principle: a chemical reaction that pushes electrons from one place to another. The idea is more than two hundred years old. In the 1780s, the Italian scientist Luigi Galvani noticed that the leg of a dead frog twitched when touched by two different metals, and he believed that the electricity came from the animal.
paras.B: His countryman Alessandro Volta disagreed. He suspected that the metals themselves were the source, and in 1800 he proved it by building a tower of zinc and copper discs separated by paper soaked in salt water. This 'voltaic pile' produced a steady electric current for the first time. The unit of electrical pressure, the volt, is named in his honour.
paras.C: Every battery has the same three basic parts. Two electrodes, one called the anode and the other the cathode, are made of different materials. Between them is an electrolyte, a liquid or gel that contains charged particles called ions. When a device is connected, the anode reacts chemically and gives up electrons. These cannot pass through the electrolyte and must travel through the wire of the circuit to the cathode, and it is this flow of electrons that powers the device.
paras.D: A small barrier called a separator keeps the two electrodes from touching each other, which would cause a short circuit and possibly a fire. Meanwhile, ions move through the electrolyte to balance the charge. When the chemicals are used up, a disposable battery is dead. In a rechargeable battery, however, the reaction can be reversed: an external current pushes the electrons and ions back to where they started.
paras.E: The first practical rechargeable battery was the lead-acid battery, invented by the French physicist Gaston Planté in 1859. It is heavy, but cheap and capable of delivering a large current, and it is still used to start car engines. Much lighter is the lithium-ion battery, which became common after a Japanese company began to sell it in 1991. In it, lithium ions travel between a graphite electrode and an electrode made from a metal oxide. For this work, three scientists shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2019.
paras.F: Lithium-ion batteries store a large amount of energy for their weight, which makes them ideal for phones, laptops and electric vehicles. They have disadvantages. They lose capacity over time, they can overheat, and they contain materials such as cobalt, mined in conditions that have been criticised. Only a small proportion of used batteries is currently recycled, although the metals inside them are valuable and recycling would reduce the need for new mining.
paras.G: Researchers are therefore searching for improvements. Sodium-ion batteries, which use a common and cheap element in place of lithium, are already entering the market. 'Solid-state' batteries, in which the liquid electrolyte is replaced by a solid, promise greater safety and energy storage. As more electricity is generated from the sun and wind, which do not produce power constantly, large batteries to store energy for the grid are becoming just as important as those in vehicles.

paras.A: Few subjects divide families and teachers as sharply as homework. In some countries, children as young as six are given tasks to complete after school; in others, such as Finland, primary pupils have little or none, and the country's students still perform well in international tests. In recent years, a few schools, and even some local governments, have moved to ban homework altogether. Is it a valuable habit, or an unnecessary burden?
paras.B: Supporters say that homework reinforces learning. Practising a skill, such as solving equations or writing in a foreign language, helps to fix it in the memory, and the school day is too short for all the practice that pupils need. Homework also teaches habits of independent work: planning time, working without supervision and completing tasks on a deadline. These skills, supporters say, will be needed in university and employment.
paras.C: Parents are sometimes included in this case. When children work at home, parents see what is being taught and can support their progress. Homework can provide a link between school and family. However, this benefit assumes that families have the time, knowledge and quiet space to help. Many do not. A child who shares a single room with several brothers and sisters, or who has to look after younger children, may find it almost impossible to work.
paras.D: Research on the effects of homework is mixed. A well-known review of many studies found that in secondary schools, a moderate amount of homework is linked to higher results, but the link was much weaker in primary schools, where it was barely noticeable. After about two hours a night, additional work did not seem to help and might even lower results. The studies, however, show correlation rather than cause, since stronger students may simply do more homework.
paras.E: Critics point to costs. Surveys of teenagers in several countries show that many sleep too little because of the amount of work they take home, and report high stress. Time spent on homework is time not spent playing, reading for pleasure, exercising or being with family, activities that also contribute to development. For a young child, an hour of drawing or free play may be worth more than an hour of worksheets.
paras.F: Homework may also increase inequality. Pupils from wealthier homes tend to have private tutors, computers, internet access and parents who can explain difficult ideas. Those from poorer homes may have none of these. As a result, homework can widen the gap between rich and poor, instead of narrowing it. Some schools have tried to solve the problem by creating homework clubs, where pupils can work after lessons with a teacher's help.
paras.G: I believe that complete abolition would be a mistake, but so would the heavy loads that are common today. Younger children should have very little homework, and what they do should be short, enjoyable and connected to what they are learning, such as reading a book of their choice. Older pupils can be given more demanding tasks, but teachers should coordinate so that no pupil is overloaded. Above all, schools should ask whether each task has a clear purpose; if it does not, it should not be set.

paras.A: The Nile is one of the longest rivers on Earth, about 6,650 kilometres from its farthest sources to the Mediterranean Sea. Unusually, it flows northwards, and for much of its course it crosses desert where it is the only source of water. The ancient Greek historian Herodotus called Egypt 'the gift of the Nile', and this was no exaggeration: even today, the great majority of Egyptians live within a few kilometres of the river.
paras.B: The river has two main branches. The White Nile begins in the highlands near Lake Victoria in East Africa and flows slowly through swamps and Sudan. The Blue Nile rises at Lake Tana in the highlands of Ethiopia, and it is a faster stream. The two meet at Khartoum, the capital of Sudan, and continue north as a single river. Although the White Nile is the longer, the Blue Nile contributes most of the water during the summer flood.
paras.C: Before modern dams, the Nile rose every year. Summer rains in Ethiopia sent floodwater downstream, and from July to October the river overflowed its banks. When the water retreated, it left a layer of rich black silt. The Egyptians called their fertile country 'Kemet', or 'the black land', and the desert beyond it 'Deshret', or 'the red land'. Their whole calendar was divided into three seasons: flooding, planting and harvest.
paras.D: The ancient Egyptians were careful to measure the flood. At places along the river, they built nilometers, which were stairways or pillars marked with measurements. A low flood meant hunger, because there would not be enough water for crops, while an extremely high one could destroy villages. Priests used the readings to forecast the harvest, and officials set taxes accordingly. In this way, the river guided the economy as well as the farming.
paras.E: Using the river also shaped Egyptian transport. Because the current flows north and the wind usually blows from the north, boats could drift downstream with the current and sail upstream with the wind. Barges carried granite from the quarries at Aswan to build the pyramids and temples. The plant papyrus, which grew in the marshes, was made into paper, boats and sandals. Fishing, the hunting of birds and the growing of wheat made the river valley one of the richest societies in the ancient world.
paras.F: In the twentieth century, Egypt tried to control the river. The Aswan High Dam, completed in 1970, created a huge reservoir, Lake Nasser, and ended the yearly flood. This brought benefits: farmers could harvest more than one crop a year, and the dam produced electricity. But there were also costs. The silt that once fertilised the land now collects behind the dam, so farmers need artificial fertilisers, and the Nile Delta, no longer fed with sediment, is slowly shrinking as the sea eats away at the coast.
paras.G: Today, the main question is who owns the water. Eleven countries share the basin, and Egypt, which receives almost no rain, depends on the river for nearly all of its fresh water. When Ethiopia built a very large dam on the Blue Nile, the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, to generate electricity, Egypt and Sudan feared that their supplies would be reduced. Negotiations have continued for years. The case shows that a river which supports civilisation can also be a cause of conflict.

paras.A: Inside every human digestive system lives a crowded community of microscopic organisms. This community, known as the gut microbiome, includes bacteria, viruses and fungi. Estimates suggest that the body contains about as many bacterial cells as human cells, in total somewhere around forty trillion, and that they weigh together a few hundred grams. The first person to observe such creatures was the Dutch lens-maker Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, who described the 'animalcules' he saw in the late seventeenth century.
paras.B: For a long time, these microbes were regarded mainly as a threat. Only in recent decades have scientists realised that most of them are helpful, and that we cannot do without them. A healthy gut contains hundreds of species, and a variety of species seems to be a sign of good health. People with illnesses such as obesity, diabetes and inflammatory bowel disease often have a less varied microbiome, although it is difficult to tell whether this is a cause or a result of the illness.
paras.C: One important job of the microbiome is to digest the food that our own bodies cannot. Human enzymes cannot break down dietary fibre, the tough parts of fruit, vegetables and grains. Bacteria in the large intestine ferment it, producing short-chain fatty acids, which feed the cells of the gut wall and reduce inflammation. Gut bacteria also make several vitamins, including vitamin K.
paras.D: The microbiome also trains the immune system. A large share of the body's immune cells are found in the gut, where they must learn to tolerate friendly bacteria and to fight dangerous ones. Babies receive their first microbes from their mothers during birth and from breast milk. Studies suggest that infants born by caesarean section, or given antibiotics early, have a different microbiome from others, and some researchers link this with a higher risk of allergies, though the evidence is not conclusive.
paras.E: Surprisingly, the gut seems to communicate with the brain. A long nerve, the vagus nerve, links the two organs, and bacteria produce chemicals that act as messengers. About ninety per cent of the body's serotonin, a chemical that affects mood, is made in the gut. Experiments in which the gut bacteria of mice were changed have altered the behaviour of the animals, making them more anxious or more adventurous. Whether the same effects occur in humans is still being investigated.
paras.F: Antibiotics, which are life-saving drugs, kill harmful bacteria but also damage friendly ones. Usually the microbiome recovers within weeks or months, but sometimes a dangerous bacterium called Clostridioides difficile takes over. In severe cases, doctors have treated patients with a faecal transplant, in which a small amount of processed stool from a healthy donor is placed in the patient's intestine. The treatment cures the majority of the cases that do not respond to antibiotics, and researchers are testing it for other conditions.
paras.G: Can we improve our own microbiome? The best evidence supports a varied diet that is rich in fibre: vegetables, beans, whole grains and fruit. A study in 2021 found that people who ate plenty of fermented foods, such as yoghurt and kimchi, for ten weeks had a more varied microbiome and lower levels of inflammation. Probiotic pills, which contain living bacteria, are popular but the evidence for them in healthy people is limited, and experts advise that food is a better investment.

qs.title: Questions 22–26

paras.A: Nuclear power produces about ten per cent of the world's electricity. In France, it provides roughly two-thirds. In recent years, interest has returned as governments search for ways to cut carbon emissions without losing reliable supply. Yet memories of Chernobyl in 1986 and Fukushima in 2011 remain strong, and in Germany the last reactors were shut down in 2023. Is nuclear power a necessary tool in the fight against climate change, or a risk that is not worth taking?
paras.B: Supporters begin with the climate. A nuclear plant releases almost no carbon dioxide while operating, and studies that count emissions from the whole life of the plant place nuclear among the lowest sources, similar to wind and lower than solar. Unlike wind and sun, a reactor works day and night regardless of the weather. A single plant can supply a large city, and the land it needs is small compared with a solar or wind farm of the same output.
paras.C: They also point to safety statistics. Measured by deaths per unit of electricity produced, nuclear power is among the safest sources, far safer than coal, oil or gas, whose air pollution causes millions of premature deaths each year. According to such comparisons, even the accidents at Chernobyl and Fukushima caused far fewer deaths than the air pollution from fossil fuels over the same period.
paras.D: Opponents reply that statistics cannot capture the nature of the risk. Accidents are rare, but when they happen, they can force hundreds of thousands of people from their homes and make land unusable for decades. Insurance companies do not cover the full cost, so governments, and therefore taxpayers, carry the risk. The public's fear, critics add, is not irrational; it reflects a reasonable dislike of damage that is invisible, long-lasting and beyond individual control.
paras.E: Waste is a second concern. Spent fuel remains dangerously radioactive for thousands of years. Most countries store it temporarily at the plant, and only Finland has so far built a permanent underground repository for it. Supporters note that the total amount is small, since all the waste from decades of operation could fit in a few large buildings, but the problem of guaranteeing safety for so long is without precedent.
paras.F: Cost is the third objection. New plants in Europe and North America have been built years late and billions over budget, and the price of electricity from wind and solar has fallen sharply. Critics argue that the money would reduce more emissions if it were spent on renewables and batteries. Supporters answer that cheap renewables are only cheap when the wind blows and the sun shines, and that a system based on them also needs backup.
paras.G: I do not think the debate should be a choice between all or nothing. Countries that already have safe, well-run reactors would be foolish to close them early and replace them with fossil fuels. Building new plants is more difficult to justify unless costs can be controlled, and the question of waste must be taken seriously. Governments should compare all low-carbon options honestly, with real costs, and avoid decisions based on fear or on enthusiasm alone.

qs.title: Questions 39–40

paras.A: Leonardo da Vinci is best known as the painter of the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, but he considered himself an engineer, an inventor and a student of nature as much as an artist. His curiosity is recorded in thousands of pages of notes and drawings that he made over some forty years. About 7,000 pages survive, perhaps half of what he wrote, and they are among the most remarkable documents of the Renaissance.
paras.B: The notebooks were not written to be read by others. Leonardo wrote from right to left, in 'mirror writing', which can be read easily only with a mirror. Some people think he did this to keep his ideas secret; the more likely explanation is practical, since he was left-handed, and writing from right to left stopped his hand from smudging the wet ink. His notes are a jumble of subjects: a shopping list may appear beside a sketch of a machine, and an anatomical study beside a drawing of a flower.
paras.C: Anatomy was one of his passions. Leonardo is believed to have dissected about thirty human bodies, and his drawings of the muscles, the bones and the heart are of astonishing accuracy. He studied how blood flows through the heart. In the twentieth century, doctors using modern scanning confirmed that his sketches of the swirling movement of blood behind the aortic valve were correct, even though no one else would understand this movement for centuries.
paras.D: The notebooks are full of designs for machines. Leonardo studied the flight of birds for years, and he drew gliders, a flying machine with beating wings and a spiral device that resembles a modern helicopter rotor. He designed a pyramid-shaped cloth parachute; in 2000, a British skydiver built one according to the drawing and jumped from a balloon, showing that it worked. Many of his other designs, for tanks, bridges and giant crossbows, were military, since he worked for rulers who needed weapons.
paras.E: Leonardo also puzzled over the Earth. In what is now called the Codex Leicester, he recorded observations about rivers, waves and the movements of water. He noticed fossil seashells high in the mountains of northern Italy and rejected the common explanation that they had been carried there by the biblical flood. Instead, he reasoned that the sea must once have covered the land, an idea that anticipated modern geology.
paras.F: Despite his genius, Leonardo rarely finished projects. He left no more than about twenty paintings that are widely accepted as his, and he never published his notebooks. After his death in 1519, they passed to his pupil Francesco Melzi and were later sold, split up and scattered in many collections. Some were lost entirely. Other notebooks resurfaced much later: two were found in the National Library of Spain in 1966, having been catalogued wrongly for years.
paras.G: Today the notebooks are guarded by libraries and private owners. The largest collection, the Codex Atlanticus, is kept in Milan. The Codex Leicester is the only major notebook in private hands; it was bought in 1994 by Bill Gates, who allows it to be displayed in museums from time to time. Because the paper is fragile, most pages can be seen only for short periods, but many have been digitised, so that anyone with a computer can now look into the mind of the world's most famous polymath.

qs.title: Questions 9–13

paras.A: A volcano is an opening in the Earth's crust through which molten rock, gas and ash escape from deep underground. There are more than a thousand potentially active volcanoes on land, and many more beneath the sea. Some erupt quietly, producing rivers of glowing lava that people can watch from a safe distance. Others explode with such violence that they change the climate of the entire planet. What decides which kind of eruption will occur?
paras.B: The raw material is magma, rock that has melted deep below the surface where the temperature is more than 1,000 degrees Celsius. Because magma is lighter than the solid rock around it, it rises and collects in a magma chamber, a huge underground reservoir. As it travels upwards, the pressure around it falls. Gases that were dissolved in the magma, mostly water vapour, carbon dioxide and sulphur dioxide, begin to form bubbles, in the same way that bubbles appear when a bottle of fizzy drink is opened.
paras.C: The key difference lies in the thickness, or viscosity, of the magma. Magma that is low in silica, as it is beneath Hawaii, is runny, and gas can escape easily. The result is a gentle eruption in which lava flows out and spreads, building a wide, gently sloping 'shield volcano'. Magma that is rich in silica is thick and sticky, like cold honey. Gas bubbles cannot escape, pressure builds up and eventually the rock bursts apart in an explosion.
paras.D: Explosive eruptions throw out huge quantities of ash, rock fragments and gas, sometimes to a height of tens of kilometres. The most dangerous product is the pyroclastic flow, a fast-moving cloud of hot gas and ash that rushes down the slopes at speeds that can exceed 100 kilometres an hour and temperatures of several hundred degrees. Explosions also build steep, cone-shaped 'stratovolcanoes' from alternating layers of lava and ash, such as Mount Fuji in Japan and Mount Vesuvius in Italy.
paras.E: Some eruptions have changed history. In 1815, Mount Tambora in Indonesia produced the largest eruption in recorded history. Its ash and sulphur gas spread around the globe and reflected sunlight, lowering temperatures. The following year, 1816, became known as 'the year without summer' in Europe and North America, when crops failed and food prices rose. In 1883, the explosion of Krakatoa, also in Indonesia, was heard nearly 5,000 kilometres away, and the tsunamis that it caused killed over thirty thousand people.
paras.F: Volcanoes are not all destructive. Ash and lava break down over time to make some of the most fertile soil in the world, which is why farmers have always settled around volcanoes. Heat from underground is used to generate electricity and to warm homes; in Iceland, geothermal energy supplies most of the heating. Volcanic gases also created the atmosphere and oceans of the early Earth, and the minerals in volcanic rocks include valuable metals.
paras.G: Scientists cannot say exactly when a volcano will erupt, but they can often give warning. Before an eruption, the ground may swell as magma moves beneath it, small earthquakes become more frequent, and the mixture of gases from vents changes. Instruments on and above the volcano record these signs, and satellites measure tiny movements of the surface. Evacuations based on such monitoring have saved thousands of lives, for example, at Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines in 1991.

paras.A: Around the world, the number of people with obesity has risen sharply. The World Health Organization estimates that the number of obese adults has more than doubled since 1990. Excess weight raises the risk of diabetes, heart disease and some cancers, and the cost of treating these illnesses is a heavy burden on health services. Governments have therefore started to look for ways to change what people eat, and one of the most debated is the tax on unhealthy food and drink.
paras.B: The best-known example is the tax on sugary drinks. Mexico introduced one in 2014, and the United Kingdom followed in 2018 with a levy that increased in proportion to the sugar content. In the UK, many manufacturers reduced the sugar in their products rather than pay the tax, so the amount of sugar consumed from soft drinks fell without any need for people to change their habits. In Mexico, purchases of taxed drinks fell by several per cent in the first two years.
paras.C: Supporters argue that such taxes are justified because the costs of unhealthy diets are shared by everyone. Taxpayers pay for treatment, and the economy loses working time. Taxing harmful products is not a new idea; tobacco and alcohol have long carried high taxes, with a clear effect on consumption. The revenue can be used for a good purpose: some governments spend the money from sugar taxes on school meals or on sports facilities for children.
paras.D: Opponents raise several objections. The first is fairness. Poorer households spend a larger proportion of their income on food, so a tax on food falls most heavily on them. Critics call it a regressive tax. Many poor families also live in areas with few shops that sell fresh food, and healthy options such as fruit, fish and vegetables are often more expensive per calorie than cheap processed foods. For these families, higher prices may mean simply paying more, not eating better.
paras.E: A second objection concerns definition. Where should the line be drawn? A tax on chocolate would be easy to understand, but what about cheese, which is high in fat but nutritious, or fruit juice, which contains natural sugar? In Denmark, a tax on saturated fat introduced in 2011 was repealed after a year, partly because it was complicated for businesses and partly because consumers bought food across the border.
paras.F: Finally, some people see taxes as an intrusion by the state. Adults, they say, have the right to decide what they eat, and the government should provide information and not punish choices. Yet supporters reply that people's decisions are already shaped by powerful marketing and by the way that foods are placed in shops. In their view, a tax is a small counterweight to a great deal of commercial pressure.
paras.G: I am in favour of a carefully designed tax on sugary drinks, because the evidence from several countries shows that it works and that it can encourage companies to improve recipes. I am less convinced by wider taxes on food groups, which are difficult to define and risk hurting poorer families. Taxes alone will not solve the problem of obesity. They need to be accompanied by cheaper healthy food, better food labels, restrictions on advertising to children and more opportunities for exercise.

paras.A: Off the north-east coast of Australia lies the largest living structure on the planet. The Great Barrier Reef stretches for about 2,300 kilometres and covers an area bigger than Italy. It is not a single reef but a collection of almost 3,000 separate reefs and around 900 islands, and it is so large that it can be seen from space. The reef was declared a World Heritage Site in 1981.
paras.B: The reef is built by tiny animals called coral polyps, each no bigger than a pinhead. A polyp takes calcium from the sea water and uses it to build a hard skeleton of limestone around its soft body. When it dies, its skeleton stays, and new polyps grow on top, so that over thousands of years the structure becomes immense. The present reef began to grow on older foundations roughly 8,000 years ago, when the sea rose at the end of the last ice age.
paras.C: Corals could not survive without a partnership with microscopic algae that live inside their tissues. The algae use sunlight to make sugar and share most of it with the coral, and in return they receive shelter and nutrients. The algae also give corals their bright colours. This arrangement allows corals to grow quickly in clear, shallow tropical water that has few nutrients of its own, but it makes them sensitive to light and to temperature.
paras.D: The reef supports an extraordinary variety of life. It is home to about 1,500 species of fish, about 400 types of coral, six of the world's seven species of sea turtle and more than thirty kinds of whale and dolphin. Every year, a few nights after the full moon in late spring, millions of coral colonies release eggs and sperm at the same time, in a mass spawning that turns the water into something resembling an underwater snowstorm.
paras.E: For many thousands of years, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have lived beside the reef and used it for food, travel and ceremony. Their traditions include stories about the creation of the islands and rules about when and where fish may be caught. Today, many Indigenous rangers work with scientists to monitor the health of the reef, combining traditional knowledge with modern technology.
paras.F: The reef faces several threats. Run-off from farms carries fertiliser and mud to the sea, which harms corals and encourages the crown-of-thorns starfish, a species that eats living coral. Cyclones break the reef apart. The most serious danger, however, is warming water. When the sea becomes too hot, corals expel their algae and turn white, a process called bleaching. Bleached corals are not dead, and can recover if the temperature falls, but if the heat lasts too long, they starve.
paras.G: Mass bleaching has occurred repeatedly since 1998, including in 2016, 2017, 2020, 2022 and 2024, and in some years, large sections of the reef were affected. Authorities have limited fishing, improved the quality of water entering the reef and supported efforts to grow heat-tolerant corals. Most scientists agree, however, that these measures can only buy time: the future of the reef depends mainly on whether the world manages to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

paras.A: An airliner weighing several hundred tonnes lifts off a runway and climbs into the sky. To many passengers, this seems almost impossible, yet the science is well understood. Four forces act on every aircraft in flight: weight, which pulls it down; lift, which pushes it up; thrust, which drives it forward; and drag, the resistance of the air, which holds it back. To fly steadily, lift must equal weight, and thrust must equal drag.
paras.B: Lift is produced by the wings. A wing has a curved upper surface and a flatter lower surface, a shape known as an aerofoil. As the aircraft moves forward, air flows over and under the wing, and the wing is tilted slightly upwards, at an angle called the angle of attack. The wing pushes the air downward, and, as Isaac Newton's third law says, the air pushes the wing upward with an equal force.
paras.C: There is also a difference in pressure. The air above the curved upper surface moves faster than that below, and fast-moving air has lower pressure. The higher pressure beneath the wing pushes upward more strongly than the lower pressure above it pushes down. Popular explanations often say that this alone creates lift and that the air above must 'catch up' with the air below, but that is incorrect: both the pressure difference and the downward deflection of air are descriptions of the same process.
paras.D: Thrust comes from engines. In a jet engine, a large fan draws in air, which is compressed and mixed with fuel and burned. The hot gases expand violently and rush out of the back of the engine, pushing the aircraft forward, while also turning a turbine that drives the fan. Older aircraft use engines that turn a propeller, which acts like a rotating wing and pulls the plane through the air.
paras.E: Pilots steer the aircraft using movable surfaces. Ailerons on the rear edges of the wings make the plane roll to one side or the other. Elevators on the tail make the nose go up or down. The rudder, on the vertical fin of the tail, turns the nose left or right. For slow flight, such as during take-off and landing, flaps extend from the wings to increase their area and curvature, giving more lift at lower speeds.
paras.F: Wings can fail to work. If the angle of attack becomes too large, the smooth flow of air over the wing breaks up and lift is suddenly lost, a condition called a stall. Pilots are trained to recognise the warning signs and to recover by lowering the nose to regain speed. Airliners typically cruise at around ten thousand metres, where the air is thin, there is less drag and engines are more efficient, so the cabin must be pressurised to allow passengers to breathe normally.
paras.G: Humans first flew in an engine-powered aircraft in 1903, when Orville and Wilbur Wright's Flyer travelled about 37 metres in twelve seconds at Kitty Hawk in North Carolina. The brothers had built their own wind tunnel to test wing shapes, and they discovered that earlier published tables of lift were wrong. Within a lifetime, aircraft have grown to carry hundreds of passengers across oceans at speeds around 900 kilometres an hour.

qs.title: Questions 23–26

ps.title: Is Space Exploration Worth the Cost?

paras.A: In 2024, the combined budgets of the world's space agencies were well over a hundred billion dollars. Since the first satellite, Sputnik, orbited the Earth in 1957, people have landed on the Moon, sent robots to every planet in the solar system and built a permanent laboratory in orbit. Now, plans for returning to the Moon and travelling to Mars have revived an old debate: should so much money be spent beyond the Earth when there are so many problems on it?
paras.B: Supporters argue that space exploration brings practical benefits. Satellites provide weather forecasts, navigation, communications and early warning of storms and floods. They monitor the climate, the melting of ice and the health of forests, providing data that could not be obtained in any other way. Some products developed for space, including water-purification systems, lightweight materials and medical imaging techniques, have found everyday uses. The money, they note, is spent on Earth, on salaries and equipment, not launched into space.
paras.C: A second argument concerns knowledge and inspiration. Telescopes and probes have revealed the age of the universe, the existence of planets around other stars and signs that water once flowed on Mars. Space missions also inspire young people to study science and engineering. The Apollo programme, for example, is widely believed to have encouraged a generation of students to follow careers in technology.
paras.D: Some also see space as insurance. Asteroids have struck the Earth in the past, and one such impact, 66 million years ago, helped to end the age of the dinosaurs. Scientists are developing the ability to detect dangerous objects and to alter their paths; in 2022, a spacecraft deliberately crashed into a small asteroid and changed its orbit. In the longer term, some argue that humanity should become a species living on more than one planet.
paras.E: Critics, however, argue that the money could be better used. The cost of a single mission to Mars may be tens of billions of dollars, enough to pay for clean water, vaccines or school meals for millions of people. They add that many of the 'spin-off' products would have been invented anyway, and that robotic probes can do much of the exploration at a fraction of the cost and without risking human lives.
paras.F: Others raise concerns about pollution and fairness. Thousands of satellites and large amounts of debris now circle the Earth, and collisions are a growing danger. Astronomers complain that bright satellite constellations spoil observations of the night sky. There are also questions about who has the right to use resources on the Moon or on asteroids, and whether commercial companies, rather than public agencies, should decide.
paras.G: Having considered the arguments, I believe that space exploration deserves public support, but at a measured level and with clear priorities. Spending on satellites that observe the Earth and on robotic science gives obvious returns. Crewed missions to Mars are far more difficult to justify now, and the claim that they will rescue humanity from disaster seems exaggerated, since no other planet is more hospitable than the Earth after climate change. Our first duty is to protect the one planet we know can support us.

paras.A: Few institutions have captured the imagination like the Library of Alexandria. Founded in Egypt in the third century BC, it aimed to collect all the knowledge of the world. The city of Alexandria, named after Alexander the Great, had been built on the Mediterranean coast in 331 BC, and after Alexander's death, it came under the rule of one of his generals, Ptolemy, and his descendants, who made it a centre of wealth and learning.
paras.B: The library was part of a larger institution called the Museion, or 'house of the Muses', which resembled a modern research institute. Scholars received a salary, meals and housing, and they were free to study and discuss without having to teach. Estimates of the library's collection vary widely, from forty thousand to several hundred thousand scrolls, each of which was handwritten on papyrus. Nobody knows the true figure, because no complete catalogue survives.
paras.C: The Ptolemies were determined collectors. According to ancient writers, ships that docked in Alexandria were searched for books. The scrolls were taken to the library and copied, and the owners received the copies, while the library kept the originals. The rulers also sent agents abroad with large sums of money to buy manuscripts, and they asked other kings to lend them important works. A famous scholar, Callimachus, compiled a catalogue of the collection in 120 volumes.
paras.D: The scholars of Alexandria made lasting discoveries. The mathematician Euclid, who worked there around 300 BC, wrote the Elements, a textbook of geometry that remained in use for more than two thousand years. Eratosthenes, the chief librarian in the third century BC, calculated the circumference of the Earth by comparing the lengths of shadows in two Egyptian cities, and his result was remarkably close to the modern figure. Another scholar, Aristarchus, suggested that the Earth moves around the Sun, an idea that was ignored for nearly eighteen centuries.
paras.E: Medicine also advanced. Doctors at Alexandria studied the human body by dissection, which was rare in the ancient world, and they identified the nerves and distinguished them from tendons. Literature also flourished: scholars edited and compared different copies of Homer's epic poems, establishing texts that have lasted until today and creating the first systematic grammar and dictionaries. In this way, the library helped to preserve not just books, but a method of careful scholarship.
paras.F: How did the library end? Popular accounts blame a single catastrophe. According to one story, Julius Caesar's soldiers set fire to the city in 48 BC and burned the library; according to another, an Arab commander destroyed the books in AD 642, supposedly because they were either unnecessary or contrary to the Koran. Modern historians regard the second story as a later invention, and they doubt that Caesar's fire destroyed more than a warehouse of scrolls near the harbour.
paras.G: The truth seems to be a slow decline. Rulers cut the funding. In 145 BC, one Ptolemy expelled many of the foreign scholars. Wars and rebellions damaged the city, and later Roman emperors showed little interest in the institution. By the fourth century AD, the great collection had probably disappeared. A new library, the Bibliotheca Alexandrina, opened in 2002 beside the sea near the site of the ancient one, and it has space for millions of books. The lesson, perhaps, is that knowledge is not destroyed in a single night but lost when societies stop supporting it.

qs.title: Questions 10–13

paras.A: The human heart is a muscle about the size of a clenched fist, and it never rests. On average, it beats around 100,000 times a day, pumping about five litres of blood around the body every minute at rest. During an average lifetime, it will beat more than two billion times. Its job is simple to state but difficult to perform: it must deliver oxygen and nutrients to every cell and carry away waste.
paras.B: For centuries, doctors misunderstood how the heart works. The ancient Greek physician Galen taught that blood was made in the liver and consumed by the body, ebbing and flowing in the veins. His view dominated medicine for around 1,400 years. In 1628, the English physician William Harvey published a book showing that the heart pumps blood in a continuous circuit. He calculated that the heart pushes out more blood in an hour than the body could possibly make, so the same blood must be going round and round.
paras.C: The heart has four chambers. The two upper chambers, the atria, receive blood, and the two lower chambers, the ventricles, pump it out. The right side of the heart sends oxygen-poor blood to the lungs, where it collects oxygen. This blood returns to the left side of the heart, which pumps it with great force through the body. Because the left ventricle must push blood further, its muscular wall is much thicker than that of the right.
paras.D: Four valves keep blood flowing in one direction. They open to let blood through and then snap shut to prevent it from flowing backwards. The familiar 'lub-dub' sound of a heartbeat is the noise of these valves closing. A doctor listening through a stethoscope, an instrument invented in France in 1816 by René Laennec, can detect murmurs when a valve leaks or becomes stiff.
paras.E: Each heartbeat is triggered by electricity. A small cluster of cells in the upper right chamber, the sinoatrial node, acts as a natural pacemaker, sending out a signal that spreads across the heart and makes the muscle contract in the correct order. The brain can speed up or slow down the rate, for example when we exercise or sleep. If the natural pacemaker fails, a small battery-powered device can be implanted under the skin to take over its job.
paras.F: From the heart, blood travels through arteries, which have thick, elastic walls to withstand pressure, and then into branching, ever-thinner vessels until it reaches the capillaries. These are so narrow that red blood cells must pass through them in single file, and their walls are thin enough for oxygen and nutrients to pass into the tissues. Veins carry the blood back to the heart; they contain valves of their own to stop blood from running backwards, especially in the legs. If laid end to end, all the body's blood vessels would stretch for many tens of thousands of kilometres.
paras.G: Heart disease remains the leading cause of death in the world. It is often caused by atherosclerosis, in which fatty deposits narrow the arteries and reduce the flow of blood. Smoking, high blood pressure and a diet rich in saturated fat increase the risk, while regular exercise reduces it. Treatment has advanced greatly. In 1967, the South African surgeon Christiaan Barnard performed the first human heart transplant in Cape Town, and today operations to replace valves and to bypass blocked arteries are common.

ps.title: Is a University Degree Still Worth It?

paras.A: For generations, a university degree has been seen as the safest route to a good career. Graduates, on average, earn more than those without degrees and are less likely to be unemployed. Yet in many countries, the value of a degree is being questioned. Tuition fees have risen sharply, graduates often start their working lives with large debts, and some employers say that many degrees do not prepare students for real jobs. Is higher education still worth the time and money?
paras.B: Supporters point to the evidence. Studies in many countries find that graduates earn considerably more over a lifetime than non-graduates, even after the costs of study are taken into account. In the United States, for example, the difference in median earnings between a bachelor's degree holder and someone with only a school diploma is more than a million dollars over a career by some estimates. Graduates also tend to enjoy better health, longer lives and greater job security.
paras.C: Beyond money, universities provide a broad education. Students learn to analyse evidence, to argue clearly and to work with people from different backgrounds. These abilities are valued by employers even if the course is not directly connected with a job. A university can also be a place of personal growth, where young people leave home, make lasting friendships and discover interests they did not know they had.
paras.D: Critics reply that average figures hide huge differences. Graduates in medicine or engineering usually earn much more than those who study some other subjects, and in some cases, a degree from a weak institution may bring little financial benefit at all. In some countries, a large number of graduates take jobs that do not need a degree, which suggests that the number of graduates exceeds the number of graduate jobs. Meanwhile, shortages of electricians, plumbers and technicians push up the wages of skilled workers.
paras.E: A second criticism concerns cost and debt. In England, students who start university today may owe tens of thousands of pounds on graduation, and in the United States, total student debt exceeds a trillion dollars. Many graduates will not repay their loans in full. Debt influences decisions about careers, housing and starting a family, and critics say that governments are using students to pay for a system that is too expensive.
paras.F: Alternatives are growing. Apprenticeships allow people to earn a wage while learning a trade, and in countries such as Germany and Switzerland, they have high status and lead to well-paid careers. Short courses and online certificates, offered by technology companies and universities, can provide specific skills at a fraction of the cost. Some large employers have stopped asking for degrees from applicants for many jobs and now examine skills instead.
paras.G: My own view is that a degree remains a good investment for most people who choose their subject and institution with care, but it should not be the only respected path. Societies need engineers and nurses, but they also need electricians and carpenters, and young people should be given honest information about the costs and returns of all options. The real mistake would be to treat university as the right choice for everyone, or as a waste for everyone.

paras.A: Mount Everest rises 8,849 metres above sea level on the border between Nepal and the Tibet region of China, and it is the highest mountain on Earth. The peak is part of the Himalayas, which formed over the past fifty million years as the Indian plate pushed northward into Asia. The collision is not finished: Everest is still rising by a few millimetres a year.
paras.B: The mountain has many names. The Tibetans call it Chomolungma, which is usually translated as 'Goddess Mother of the World', while in Nepal it is Sagarmatha. The English name was given in 1865 in honour of Sir George Everest, a former Surveyor General of India, although Everest himself had never seen the mountain and objected to the use of his name. It was only in the 1850s that surveyors in India, using measurements taken from a great distance, realised that the peak known as 'Peak XV' was the highest in the world.
paras.C: Among the mountain's surprises is the rock at its summit. It is limestone, containing the fossils of small sea creatures that lived on the floor of an ancient ocean hundreds of millions of years ago. The ocean disappeared as the plates collided and the sea floor was lifted to the roof of the world. Climbers who reach the top stand, in a sense, on the bottom of a prehistoric sea.
paras.D: Many attempts to climb Everest failed in the early twentieth century. In 1924, the British climber George Mallory and his partner Andrew Irvine disappeared near the summit, and nobody knows whether they reached it. Mallory is famous for answering the question of why he wanted to climb Everest with the words 'Because it's there.' His body was found in 1999, but the mystery of his success has never been solved.
paras.E: The first confirmed ascent took place on 29 May 1953, when the New Zealand beekeeper Edmund Hillary and the Sherpa climber Tenzing Norgay reached the top as part of a British expedition. Others followed. In 1975, Junko Tabei of Japan became the first woman to reach the summit, and in 1978 Reinhold Messner and Peter Habeler of Italy and Austria climbed it without bottled oxygen, something many experts had thought to be impossible.
paras.F: The dangers are severe. Above about 8,000 metres, an area known as the 'death zone', there is so little oxygen that the human body cannot survive for long, and climbers suffer from altitude sickness, frostbite, exhaustion and sudden storms. The route through the Khumbu Icefall, a moving river of ice with deep cracks and towers that may collapse without warning, kills more people than any other part of the climb. In 1996, eight climbers died in a single storm, an event that was later described in several famous books.
paras.G: Today, Everest has become a commercial business. In a good season, hundreds of people reach the summit, led by experienced Sherpa guides who carry equipment, fix ropes and often take the greatest risks. Critics complain of crowding, queues at the summit, discarded tents and oxygen bottles, and the bodies of those who died that remain on the mountain. Authorities in Nepal and China have introduced rules for cleaning up rubbish and for making climbers prove their experience.

ps.title: The Water Cycle and the Making of Rain

paras.A: The water in a glass on your table is very old. It has probably been rain, a cloud, a river and an ocean many times over, because the Earth's supply of water is constantly moving between the sea, the air and the land in a process known as the water cycle. About 97 per cent of the planet's water is in the oceans; of the rest, most is frozen in ice caps and glaciers, and only a tiny part is the fresh water in rivers, lakes and underground that people use every day.
paras.B: The cycle is driven by the sun. Its heat turns liquid water at the surface of the sea, lakes and rivers into invisible water vapour, a process called evaporation. Plants also release vapour through their leaves, which is known as transpiration. Most evaporation takes place over the tropical oceans, where the sun is strongest. The warm, moist air then rises, because warm air is lighter than cold air.
paras.C: As the air rises, it cools, and cool air cannot hold as much water vapour as warm air. At a certain point, the vapour condenses, turning into tiny droplets of liquid. However, droplets need something to form on. The surfaces provided by dust, smoke, pollen or sea salt, known as condensation nuclei, allow them to form. Millions of such droplets together make a cloud. They are so light, about a hundredth of a millimetre across, that they float in the air.
paras.D: To fall as rain, the droplets must grow. In warm clouds, droplets collide and join together, and in cold clouds, they freeze onto tiny ice crystals, which grow heavy and begin to fall. It takes about a million cloud droplets to make one raindrop. If the air near the ground is warm, the crystals melt and fall as rain; if it is below freezing, they arrive as snow. Hail forms when strong currents carry ice up and down inside a storm cloud, so that it collects layers of ice.
paras.E: Rain is caused in different ways. Convectional rain occurs when the sun heats the ground and warm air rises quickly, often creating sudden afternoon thunderstorms in tropical regions and in summer. Frontal rain falls when a mass of warm air meets a mass of cold air and is forced to rise over it. Relief rain occurs when moving air meets mountains and is forced up their slopes. The far side of the mountains, in the 'rain shadow', is often dry.
paras.F: When rain reaches the ground, some of it soaks into the soil and slowly moves through the rock as groundwater, which may emerge months or years later in springs. Some runs over the surface into streams and rivers, which carry it to the sea. In mountains, much of the precipitation falls as snow, and stores water until spring. The great rivers of Central Asia, such as the Amu Darya and Syr Darya, depend on the melting of snow and glaciers in the high mountains.
paras.G: The water cycle is changing as the climate warms. Warmer air can hold more vapour, which produces heavier downpours and more flooding in some regions, while evaporation from soils increases drought in others. Glaciers that act as natural water tanks are shrinking. Understanding the cycle is therefore not merely a matter of scientific curiosity; it is the foundation for managing water for farms, cities and ecosystems in the decades ahead.

paras.A: Every minute, around the world, up to a million plastic bags are used, and most are used for only a few minutes before being thrown away. Light and strong, the plastic bag was welcomed when it spread through supermarkets in the 1970s and 1980s. Today it is a symbol of waste. Bags choke drains, hang from trees and drift in the sea, and dozens of countries have introduced bans or charges on them. Do such measures work, and are they fair?
paras.B: The case for a ban starts with litter. A plastic bag can take hundreds of years to break down, and when it does, it becomes smaller pieces of plastic called microplastics that spread through soil and water. Sea turtles may mistake floating bags for jellyfish and die after eating them, and seabirds and whales have been found with their stomachs filled with plastic. Clean-up campaigns regularly find bags among the most common items on beaches.
paras.C: Evidence shows that charges can change behaviour quickly. After Ireland introduced a small charge in 2002, the use of bags fell by more than ninety per cent within a few months. England's charge on large shops in 2015 was followed by a drop of about ninety-five per cent in the number of bags handed out by the main supermarkets. People who must pay a few pence discover that they can remember to bring a bag.
paras.D: Yet critics note that banning plastic is not automatically good for the environment. Paper bags need more energy and water to manufacture, produce more greenhouse gases, and tear more easily. A cotton tote bag must be used many times, with some studies suggesting hundreds of times, before its total environmental impact becomes lower than that of a plastic bag. If people buy dozens of cloth bags and leave them in cupboards, the policy may do more harm than good.
paras.E: A further objection is that bags are only a small part of the plastic problem. They make up a tiny share of plastic waste when compared with packaging, bottles, fishing nets and clothing fibres. Some critics argue that a ban gives politicians an easy success while larger problems remain untouched. The reply from supporters is that the bag is a symbol, and that people who change their habits in one area may be more willing to accept other measures.
paras.F: There are also questions of fairness and practicality. Small shopkeepers worry about the cost of alternatives, and some poorer shoppers rely on cheap bags to carry goods. In several countries, strong bans have led to illegal trade: in Kenya, where possession of a plastic bag was punished by fines or prison, bags were smuggled across borders. Governments need to enforce rules, offer affordable options and exempt essential uses, such as bags for hygiene and medicine.
paras.G: I believe that a charge is better than a ban in most countries, since it allows people to choose and raises money for environmental projects. Charges should be high enough to change behaviour but should be accompanied by clear information about reuse. In the long run, the aim must be a general reduction in disposable packaging, not simply the replacement of one throwaway item with another. The humble plastic bag is a small step in a long journey.

paras.A: Before the fifteenth century, every book in Europe was copied by hand. A skilled monk might spend months producing one Bible, and the result was so expensive that only churches, universities and the very rich could own books. Around 1450, in the German city of Mainz, a goldsmith named Johannes Gutenberg began to print using movable metal type. Within fifty years, the way that knowledge was stored and shared in Europe had changed completely.
paras.B: Printing itself was not new. Chinese printers had carved whole pages in wooden blocks for centuries; the oldest dated printed book, the Diamond Sutra, was produced in China in AD 868. Around 1040, a man named Bi Sheng made movable characters of baked clay, and in Korea, printers were casting metal type by the thirteenth century; the oldest surviving book printed with metal type there dates from 1377. Gutenberg may not have known of these inventions.
paras.C: Gutenberg's genius was to combine several technologies into a practical system. The alphabet needs only a few dozen letters, so a printer could use small blocks, each carrying a single letter, rearranged for every page. He developed an alloy of lead, tin and antimony that melted at a low temperature, set quickly and was hard enough for thousands of impressions. He also invented an oil-based ink that stuck to the metal, and he adapted the screw press used for making wine to press the paper against the inked type.
paras.D: The most famous product was the Gutenberg Bible, finished in about 1455. About 180 copies were printed, some on vellum and the rest on paper, and about 50 survive. Each page has 42 lines of text, in two columns, in a style that imitated the best handwriting. Gutenberg himself, however, did not profit. He borrowed money from a businessman, Johann Fust, and when he could not repay it, Fust took the equipment through the courts.
paras.E: The technology spread with astonishing speed. By 1500, printing presses were working in more than 200 European cities, and an estimated twenty million volumes had been printed. As the supply increased, the price of books fell sharply, and the number of readers grew. Printers, who were also businessmen, published works that sold: schoolbooks, calendars, romances, religious texts and practical manuals.
paras.F: The effects on society were profound. When Martin Luther criticised the Church in 1517, printers turned his ideas into pamphlets and distributed hundreds of thousands of copies in a few years, helping to start the Reformation. Scientists could now exchange detailed diagrams and tables without introducing copying errors; in 1543, Vesalius published an anatomy book with precise illustrations of the human body, and Copernicus published his theory of a Sun-centred universe. Standard spellings and grammar emerged, as did national languages.
paras.G: Not everyone welcomed the change. Some rulers and church leaders feared that unlimited reading would encourage dangerous ideas, and they introduced censorship and lists of forbidden books. The Ottoman Empire permitted books in Arabic script to be printed only much later, in the eighteenth century, although minority communities printed earlier. Even so, there was no turning back. Many historians regard Gutenberg's press as one of the most important inventions in human history, a forerunner of the internet in its power to spread information.

qs.title: Questions 10–13

paras.A: Every living thing carries a set of instructions that tells its cells how to grow and function. In humans and most other organisms, these instructions are written in a molecule called DNA, which is found in nearly every cell. If the DNA from a single human cell were unwound, it would stretch for about two metres, yet it is packed into a nucleus far smaller than a speck of dust.
paras.B: The study of heredity began in the nineteenth century with an Augustinian monk, Gregor Mendel, who spent years growing pea plants in the garden of his monastery in what is now the Czech Republic. By counting how traits such as height and flower colour were passed on in thousands of plants, he concluded in the 1860s that characteristics are carried by separate 'factors', now called genes. His work was ignored for decades and was rediscovered only around 1900.
paras.C: The structure of DNA was discovered in 1953. James Watson and Francis Crick in Cambridge proposed that the molecule is a double helix, resembling a twisted ladder. Their model depended on X-ray images taken by Rosalind Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling in London, and on data from Maurice Wilkins. The sides of the ladder are made of sugar and phosphate, and the rungs are pairs of chemical units called bases.
paras.D: There are four bases, known by the letters A, T, G and C, and they pair in a strict way: A always joins with T, and G always joins with C. The order of the letters along the DNA forms a code. A gene is a stretch of this code that contains the instructions for making a protein, and proteins do most of the work in the body, building structures, speeding up chemical reactions and carrying signals. Humans have about twenty thousand genes.
paras.E: When a cell divides, it must copy all of its DNA. The two strands of the ladder separate like a zip, and each strand serves as a pattern for building a new partner. Because of the strict pairing rules, the copy is almost perfect. Occasionally, mistakes occur; these are called mutations. Most mutations have no effect, some are harmful, and a few are useful, and over many generations, the useful changes provide the raw material for evolution.
paras.F: Reading the code became possible in the second half of the twentieth century. The Human Genome Project, an international effort that started in 1990, produced the first complete sequence of human DNA in 2003; it contains about three billion letters. The project showed that people are, on average, 99.9 per cent identical in their DNA. The small differences, however, explain inherited traits and also how likely we are to develop certain diseases.
paras.G: The knowledge has produced new technologies. In 1984, Alec Jeffreys in Leicester developed DNA fingerprinting, which is now used to identify criminals and victims and to establish family relationships. Genetic tests can identify inherited diseases in embryos and adults. In 2012, scientists described CRISPR, a tool that can cut DNA at precise places and change the code, and it has already led to approved treatments for diseases of the blood. These developments raise ethical questions about privacy, fairness and how far humans should alter their own inheritance.

qs.title: Questions 22–26

paras.A: For more than a century, driving has meant a person at a wheel. That may be about to change. Several companies now operate taxis with no driver in a few cities, and many new cars already steer, brake and keep their lane on motorways with little human help. Engineers have defined six levels of automation, from Level 0, where the human does everything, to Level 5, where a vehicle can drive anywhere in any conditions without a person. No car for sale to the public has reached the top level.
paras.B: The best argument for self-driving cars is safety. Human error is a factor in the great majority of road accidents, which kill about 1.2 million people every year worldwide. People drive when tired, drunk or distracted by phones. A computer never gets tired, never drinks and watches in every direction at the same time. If automated vehicles were only a little safer than the average person, supporters say, thousands of lives could be saved.
paras.C: Automation could also make roads more efficient. Vehicles that communicate with each other can travel close together at steady speeds, reducing congestion and fuel use. The elderly and people with disabilities, who cannot drive, would gain independence. Cars that drive themselves could drop passengers off and park far away, freeing space in city centres now used for parking. Some experts even imagine a future in which most people no longer own a car, but call one when they need it.
paras.D: The technology has not yet reached that point. Self-driving systems rely on cameras, radar and laser scanners, together with software trained on millions of kilometres of driving. They cope well with clear roads and clear markings, but can be confused by heavy snow, glare, unusual objects or the unpredictable behaviour of pedestrians and cyclists. In several well-known accidents, vehicles in automated mode have failed to recognise dangers that a human driver would have seen.
paras.E: Accidents raise difficult questions of responsibility. If a car with no driver causes a crash, who is to blame: the owner, the manufacturer or the programmer? Laws in most countries were written for human drivers. There is also the question of how a vehicle should choose in rare situations in which harm cannot be avoided. Philosophers have debated such dilemmas for years, but in practice, engineers say that the best approach is to prevent them by driving cautiously.
paras.F: Economic effects could also be large. In many countries, millions of people earn a living as taxi, lorry or bus drivers. If their jobs disappear, many will need to retrain, and the transition may be painful. At the same time, new jobs may appear in technology, maintenance and services. Critics also worry that connected vehicles collect data about where people go, and that hackers could take control of them.
paras.G: My own opinion is that self-driving cars will arrive gradually rather than suddenly. They will probably appear first in controlled settings: on motorways, in specific districts of cities, in delivery services and in shuttles that follow fixed routes. I doubt that fully automated vehicles will be common in every town for decades. Whether the change is a success will depend less on the technology than on regulation, public trust and decisions about how the benefits are shared.

paras.A: Almost a thousand kilometres west of Ecuador, in the Pacific Ocean, lies a group of volcanic islands that changed the way humans understand life. The Galápagos Islands are young in geological terms. They were formed by volcanoes rising from the sea floor over the last few million years, and some, like Fernandina, are still erupting. No part of them was ever connected to a continent, so all their plants and animals arrived by crossing the sea.
paras.B: The newcomers came by chance. Seeds floated on the water or were carried in the feathers or stomachs of birds. Reptiles probably crossed on rafts of vegetation washed down the rivers of South America. Mammals, most of which cannot survive a long journey on the ocean, rarely arrived, so the islands were dominated by reptiles and birds. Those that survived found empty habitats with few enemies and few competitors for food, and over time they adapted.
paras.C: In 1835, the young naturalist Charles Darwin visited the islands for five weeks aboard HMS Beagle. He collected birds, plants and animals, but at first he did not realise how important they were. Later, an expert in London told him that the small birds he had gathered, which he had believed were blackbirds, finches and wrens, were all closely related finches. Each island seemed to have its own kind, with a beak suited to its particular food: some thin for catching insects, others strong for cracking seeds.
paras.D: Darwin also heard from the islands' vice-governor that the giant tortoises differed from island to island, so that he could tell where any tortoise came from by the shape of its shell. These observations, and others, helped him to develop the theory of natural selection, which he described in 1859 in On the Origin of Species. Individuals with traits that help them survive and reproduce pass on those traits, and over many generations, populations change.
paras.E: Today the animals of the Galápagos are as remarkable as in Darwin's time. The giant tortoises can weigh over 250 kilograms and live for more than a hundred years. The marine iguana is the only lizard in the world that feeds in the sea, diving for seaweed and then basking on black rocks to warm up. Flightless cormorants, which have lost the ability to fly because they have no need to escape from land predators, dive for fish. Because the animals evolved with no human enemies, many show little fear of visitors, and tourists often walk within a metre of nesting birds.
paras.F: The unique wildlife is vulnerable. Species brought by humans, such as goats, rats, cats and ants, have eaten native plants and preyed on eggs and young animals. Goats on some islands stripped the vegetation until tortoises starved. A project completed in 2006 removed more than a hundred thousand goats from islands in the north, using hunters, dogs and helicopters, and the vegetation has recovered. The last Pinta Island tortoise, a male known as Lonesome George, died in 2012 without leaving young.
paras.G: The islands were declared a national park in 1959, and they became one of the first World Heritage Sites in 1978. Ninety-seven per cent of the land is protected, and visitors must follow marked paths with licensed guides. Yet around thirty thousand people now live on the inhabited islands, and hundreds of thousands of tourists come each year, so the demand for water, food and energy is growing. The challenge is to allow people to appreciate the islands without damaging what they came to see.
