paras.A: Imagine an object so dense that nothing, not even light, can escape from it. That is a black hole. The idea is older than most people think. In 1783, an English clergyman and natural philosopher, John Michell, suggested that a star massive enough could have gravity so strong that light would fall back to it, and he called such an object a 'dark star'. For more than a century, however, the idea was regarded as a curiosity.
paras.B: Albert Einstein's theory of general relativity, published in 1915, gave it a firm basis. According to the theory, mass bends space and time, and a very large mass in a small space bends them so strongly that a region is created from which nothing can return. A few months after the theory appeared, the German physicist Karl Schwarzschild found a mathematical solution describing exactly this situation, though Einstein himself doubted whether such objects could exist in nature. The name 'black hole' became popular only in the 1960s, thanks to the American physicist John Wheeler.
paras.C: The boundary around a black hole is called the event horizon. It is not a solid surface but a point of no return: once something crosses it, it cannot get out, because it would have to travel faster than light, which is impossible. For a black hole with the mass of our Sun, the event horizon would be only about three kilometres in radius. The Sun itself will never become a black hole, because it does not have enough mass.
paras.D: Most black holes form when a massive star dies. A star shines because the energy from nuclear reactions in its core pushes outwards and balances the pull of gravity. When the fuel is used up, the balance is lost. If the star was more than about twenty times the mass of the Sun, its core collapses into a black hole, while the outer layers are blown into space in a huge explosion called a supernova. Astronomers think that there may be millions of such black holes in our galaxy alone.
paras.E: Much bigger black holes lie at the centres of most large galaxies. The one at the heart of our own, the Milky Way, is known as Sagittarius A* and has a mass of about four million Suns. How such giants grew so large is one of the great puzzles of astronomy. Some may have started as smaller black holes that swallowed gas and stars and merged with each other over billions of years.
paras.F: Since black holes give out no light, how can we know that they exist? Astronomers detect them by their effects on their surroundings. Stars near the centre of the Milky Way can be seen moving at great speed around an invisible point. Gas that falls towards a black hole forms a spinning disc, which becomes so hot that it shines brightly in X-rays. In 2015, a different method succeeded: two detectors in the United States recorded gravitational waves, ripples in space-time produced when two black holes merged more than a billion years earlier.
paras.G: In 2019, a worldwide network of radio telescopes called the Event Horizon Telescope produced the first image of a black hole, in the galaxy M87. It showed a bright ring of glowing gas around a dark centre. In 2022, the same team released a picture of Sagittarius A*. Many questions remain, including what lies at the very centre, where the known laws of physics seem to break down. In 1974, Stephen Hawking showed that black holes should slowly lose energy by emitting faint radiation and eventually evaporate, but the effect is far too small to be observed.

paras.A: Prisons exist for several purposes: to punish offenders, to protect the public by keeping dangerous people away, to deter others from crime and, in theory, to help offenders to change. Yet in many countries, a large share of prisoners return to prison within a few years of release. In England and Wales, for example, around a quarter of adults released from custody are convicted of another offence within a year. This record has led to a long debate about whether prisons should concentrate more on rehabilitation, or whether punishment should remain their first purpose.
paras.B: Supporters of rehabilitation point to the practical results. Most prisoners will one day be released. If they leave with the same problems as when they went in, such as addiction, lack of education or lack of skills, they are likely to commit crimes again. Programmes that treat addiction, teach reading and offer training can reduce reoffending. A large analysis of many studies found that prisoners who take part in education programmes are significantly less likely to return to prison.
paras.C: Countries that emphasise rehabilitation provide striking examples. Norway has a reoffending rate of about twenty per cent after two years, one of the lowest in the world. Prisoners live in small units with their own rooms, cook their own meals and take part in education or work. Staff are trained for several years, and they talk with prisoners, rather than simply guarding them. The maximum sentence for most crimes is twenty-one years. Supporters say that the approach treats prisoners as future neighbours.
paras.D: Opponents respond that justice requires punishment. Victims and their families expect that those who commit serious crimes will suffer consequences, and a system that seems comfortable may not reflect the seriousness of the harm that was done. Some people also worry that comfortable prisons will fail to deter, though studies suggest that the length and harshness of a sentence matter less for deterrence than the chance of being caught.
paras.E: There is also an argument about cost. Rehabilitation programmes require trained staff, more space and time, and in countries with overcrowded prisons, these resources are scarce. Critics ask why money should be spent on offenders when schools and hospitals are short of funds. Supporters reply that the real cost is of failure: each person who reoffends brings new victims, new trials and more years in prison, which cost far more than a course in a workshop.
paras.F: Public safety is a concern on both sides. Opponents argue that dangerous prisoners must be kept away from society for as long as necessary, and that any change risks releasing people who will commit crimes again. Reformers do not deny this, but they point out that nearly everyone will leave one day, and that it is better for society if they have a job and a home waiting for them than if they return to the street with a bus ticket and a small payment.
paras.G: I think that the debate often creates a false choice. Prisons have a duty to punish, and the main punishment is the loss of liberty, but they also have a duty to prepare prisoners for release. A sentence which ends with the prisoner more dangerous than at the beginning is a failure for everyone. Serious offenders should serve long sentences, but every prisoner should have access to education, work and treatment. Rehabilitation, in other words, should be seen as part of public safety, not as a favour.

paras.A: The Great Pyramid of Giza, near modern Cairo, is the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, and the only one that still stands. It was built as a tomb for the pharaoh Khufu around 2560 BC. For nearly four thousand years afterwards, it was the tallest structure ever made by human beings, until the spire of Lincoln Cathedral in England overtook it in the fourteenth century.
paras.B: Originally the pyramid stood about 147 metres high; erosion and the loss of its top and outer casing have reduced it to about 139 metres. Its base is a square with sides of around 230 metres, and these sides are aligned with the points of the compass with an error of a fraction of a degree. It contains an estimated 2.3 million blocks of stone, with an average weight of about two and a half tonnes, though some of the blocks in the interior chambers weigh far more.
paras.C: Who built it? The ancient Greek historian Herodotus, writing two thousand years later, claimed that 100,000 slaves laboured for twenty years. Modern archaeology paints a different picture. In the 1990s, archaeologists found the remains of a town near the pyramids, with bakeries, breweries and sleeping quarters for thousands of workers. The skeletons in nearby cemeteries show that the workers were given medical care, and some were buried near the pyramids in tombs with food and beer for the afterlife. It seems that the pyramid was built by Egyptian labourers, perhaps 20,000 to 30,000 at a time, many of whom worked in rotation.
paras.D: The stone came from different sources. Most of the limestone for the core was quarried a few hundred metres south of the pyramid, but the smooth white casing stones came from Tura, across the Nile, and the granite for the King's Chamber was brought from Aswan, more than 800 kilometres away. In 2013, archaeologists discovered papyri at a Red Sea port, including the logbook of an official called Merer, who describes crews transporting limestone blocks by boat along the river and canals to Giza.
paras.E: How the blocks were raised is still debated. Most experts believe that ramps of mud brick, stone and rubble were used, but opinions differ on their shape: a single straight ramp, a ramp that spiralled round the pyramid, or ramps inside it. The workers moved the heavy blocks on wooden sledges. A wall painting from a later tomb shows a man pouring water on sand in front of a sledge, and experiments have shown that wet sand halves the force needed to pull a load.
paras.F: The inside of the pyramid is a maze of passages. A narrow entrance on the north side leads to a descending corridor, a rising passage called the Grand Gallery and three chambers, of which the King's Chamber, built of red granite, contains an empty stone coffin. In 2017, scientists using cosmic-ray detectors discovered a large hidden void above the Grand Gallery, although its purpose is unknown. Robbers had entered the pyramid long before modern times, so the treasures that were buried with Khufu have never been found.
paras.G: Khufu's pyramid is one of three at Giza, built by him and by his son Khafre and his grandson Menkaure. Each of the later pyramids is smaller, perhaps reflecting a decline in royal resources or power. Beside Khafre's pyramid stands the Great Sphinx, a limestone statue with a lion's body and a human head. Today, the site is surrounded by the suburbs of Cairo, and a huge new museum, the Grand Egyptian Museum, has been built nearby to house the treasures of ancient Egypt.

paras.A: The eye works rather like a camera, but with a difference: what we call seeing happens mostly in the brain. Light bounces off objects, enters the eye and is focused to form an image on a layer of cells at the back. These cells convert the light into electrical signals, and the brain interprets the signals as a picture of the world. For many centuries, people did not understand this process at all.
paras.B: Ancient Greek thinkers, including Euclid and Ptolemy, believed that the eye sends out invisible rays that touch objects and bring back information. The idea was overturned in about 1021 by the scholar Ibn al-Haytham, known in Europe as Alhazen, who worked in Cairo. In his Book of Optics, he used experiments with light and darkened rooms to show that vision occurs when light from objects enters the eye. His book influenced European scientists for centuries, and he is often called the father of modern optics.
paras.C: Light first passes through the cornea, the transparent dome at the front of the eye, which does about two-thirds of the focusing. It then reaches the pupil, the dark opening in the centre of the coloured iris. The iris is a ring of muscle that widens the pupil in dim light and narrows it in bright light, controlling the amount that enters. Behind the pupil is the lens, which fine-tunes the focus. To see close objects, tiny muscles make the lens thicker and rounder; for distant objects, it becomes flatter.
paras.D: The image falls on the retina, a thin layer at the back of the eye that contains about 126 million light-sensitive cells of two kinds. Rods, which number about 120 million, work in dim light but cannot distinguish colours, which is why the world looks grey at night. Cones, about six million, need brighter light but give us colour vision. There are three kinds of cone, sensitive mainly to red, green and blue light, and the brain combines their signals to produce the millions of colours we can tell apart.
paras.E: Most of the cones are packed in a tiny pit in the centre of the retina called the fovea, where vision is sharpest. When you read, your eyes make quick movements to bring each word in turn to the fovea. Away from the centre, the image is blurred and colourless, although we are not aware of it. The signals from the retina travel along the optic nerve to the visual cortex at the back of the brain. The point at which the nerve leaves the eye contains no cells at all, which creates a blind spot, but the brain fills the gap using information from the surroundings.
paras.F: The image on the retina is upside down, and the brain turns it the right way up. In fact, the brain does much more than that. It combines the pictures from two eyes to judge distance, ignores the movement of our own eyes and uses past experience to interpret what it sees. This explains why optical illusions work: the brain makes a best guess, and sometimes the guess is wrong.
paras.G: Problems with the eye are common. In short-sightedness, the eyeball is too long, so distant objects are focused in front of the retina and look blurred; glasses or contact lenses correct the focus. About eight per cent of men, but less than one per cent of women, have some form of colour blindness, usually because one type of cone does not work normally. Eye diseases such as cataracts, in which the lens becomes cloudy, can be treated by surgery, which replaces the lens with an artificial one.

qs.title: Questions 22–26

ps.title: Is It Right to Keep Pets?

paras.A: In many countries, more than half of all households keep a pet. Dogs and cats are the most common, but people also keep rabbits, birds, fish, reptiles and even insects. Pets give pleasure and company to millions of people, and the pet industry is worth hundreds of billions of dollars a year. But a growing number of writers and philosophers ask whether keeping animals for our own enjoyment is ethically justified.
paras.B: Defenders of pet-keeping begin with the benefits to humans. Studies suggest that pet owners, especially dog owners, take more exercise, and that stroking an animal can lower blood pressure and reduce stress. For children, a pet can teach responsibility and empathy. For lonely or elderly people, an animal may provide companionship and a reason to get up in the morning. Some animals, such as guide dogs, perform essential work.
paras.C: Many also argue that pets benefit as well. Domestic dogs and cats have lived with people for thousands of years. They have been bred to enjoy our company, and, if well cared for, they receive food, shelter and medical treatment that wild animals do not have. Millions of unwanted animals are rescued each year, and adopting one can save a life. In this view, a loving home is better than a life on the streets.
paras.D: Critics reply that the relationship is not truly equal. Pets live where, and eat what, their owners decide. Many breeds have been shaped for appearance with little regard for health: flat-faced dogs may struggle to breathe, and some large breeds suffer from joint problems. Animals can be left alone for long hours, and when owners lose interest, they may be abandoned. In some countries, millions of animals are put down in shelters each year.
paras.E: The trade in animals raises other concerns. Puppies are bred in poor conditions to be sold, and wild animals such as parrots, monkeys and reptiles are captured and taken from their natural habitats; many die during transport. Exotic species require specialised care that few owners can provide. Meanwhile, domestic cats kill huge numbers of wild birds and small mammals. In the United States alone, they are estimated to kill billions of birds each year.
paras.F: There are also environmental costs. Feeding a dog or cat requires meat, and one study estimated that the food eaten by pets in the United States produces tens of millions of tonnes of greenhouse gases a year. Waste, litter and the chemicals used against fleas end up in the environment. Defenders respond that most pet food is made from parts of animals that humans do not eat, and that the benefits of companionship outweigh the costs.
paras.G: My own view is that keeping pets can be justified, but only with responsibility. Animals that have been bred over thousands of years to live with humans, such as dogs and cats, can have good lives in homes that meet their physical and emotional needs. Keeping wild animals is much harder to defend. People should adopt from shelters rather than buy from breeders when they can, choose animals whose needs they can meet and think carefully before acquiring any animal, remembering that a pet is a commitment for ten, fifteen or twenty years.

paras.A: In the autumn of 1347, a small fleet of ships arrived at the Sicilian port of Messina. Many of the sailors on board were dead; others were gravely ill, covered with black swellings and fever. Within days, the disease had spread through the city. This was the beginning of the Black Death, the worst pandemic in recorded history, which over the next four years killed an estimated one-third to one-half of the population of Europe.
paras.B: The disease was caused by a bacterium, Yersinia pestis, which was identified in 1894 by the Swiss-born scientist Alexandre Yersin, working in Hong Kong during a later outbreak. The bacterium normally lives in fleas that feed on rodents. When rats died, hungry fleas jumped to human beings and bit them, passing on the infection. In its most common form, the bubonic plague, victims developed painful swellings, called buboes, in the groin or armpits, followed by fever, and most died within a week.
paras.C: Where did the plague begin? For years, historians thought of China or Central Asia. In 2022, scientists studying DNA from the teeth of people buried in cemeteries near Lake Issyk-Kul, in what is now Kyrgyzstan, found the earliest known strain of the bacterium in graves dated to 1338 and 1339, when many tombstones recorded death from 'pestilence'. The evidence suggests that the epidemic began there. From Central Asia, the disease probably travelled along the trade routes of the Silk Road to the Black Sea, where in 1346 it reached the port of Caffa.
paras.D: From the ports of Italy, the plague spread north and west with astonishing speed, carried by ships, traders and armies. By 1348 it had reached France, Spain and England, and by 1350, Scandinavia and Germany. Cities, where people lived close together, were hit hardest, but villages did not escape. In some places, so many people died that the living could not bury the dead, and bodies were piled in mass graves. Contemporary writers like the Italian author Boccaccio described the horror in vivid detail.
paras.E: People had no idea what caused the disease. Some blamed bad air, the position of the stars or the anger of God. Groups of religious believers called flagellants marched from town to town, whipping themselves in public to ask for forgiveness. Terrible violence was directed at minorities, particularly Jews, who were falsely accused of poisoning wells, and many were murdered. The Pope, Clement VI, condemned the attacks, but they continued in several regions.
paras.F: Yet some of the measures were effective. The Italian city of Venice appointed officials to inspect ships and bodies, and in 1377, the port of Ragusa required travellers from infected areas to wait thirty days before entering. This was later extended to forty days, giving us the word 'quarantine', from the Italian for 'forty'. Although nobody understood the role of fleas, the idea that isolation could prevent the spread of disease turned out to be sound.
paras.G: The consequences lasted for generations. With so many workers dead, those who survived could demand higher wages, and landowners in England and elsewhere found it harder to keep peasants tied to the land. Resentment led to protests, such as the Peasants' Revolt in England in 1381. The Church lost some of its authority, since its prayers had not stopped the disease. Historians continue to debate how much change the plague caused, but many believe that it weakened the system of serfdom and opened the way to a more mobile society. The plague did not disappear; it returned in waves for centuries, and still causes a small number of cases each year, but it can now be treated with antibiotics.

paras.A: Some of the earliest magnets were found in nature. Lodestone, a naturally magnetic form of iron ore, was known in ancient Greece and China, where people noticed that it attracted small pieces of iron. Around the eleventh century, Chinese scholars described a needle rubbed with lodestone that pointed north-south when floated on water. Within a century or two, sailors in Asia and Europe were using compasses to navigate.
paras.B: Every magnet has two ends, or poles, called north and south. Opposite poles attract each other, and like poles push each other away. Around the magnet is a region in which its force can be felt, called a magnetic field, and the field can be shown by scattering iron filings on a sheet of paper over a magnet. The filings arrange themselves in curved lines running from one pole to the other.
paras.C: Why are some materials magnetic and others not? In iron, nickel and cobalt, each atom behaves like a tiny magnet. In ordinary iron, these atomic magnets are grouped in small regions, called domains, which point in random directions and cancel each other out. When the iron is placed in a strong magnetic field, the domains line up, and the metal becomes a magnet. If it is heated above a certain temperature, the order is destroyed and the magnetism disappears.
paras.D: The Earth itself is a giant magnet. Its field is produced by the movement of molten iron in the planet's outer core, which acts like a generator. The field extends far into space and protects the surface from the stream of charged particles from the Sun, the solar wind. When some of these particles are guided to the poles and strike gases in the atmosphere, they create the glowing curtains of light known as the aurora. The magnetic poles slowly wander, and about every few hundred thousand years, on average, they reverse; the last complete reversal happened around 780,000 years ago.
paras.E: For a long time, people thought that electricity and magnetism were separate subjects. In 1820, the Danish physicist Hans Christian Ørsted noticed, during a lecture, that a compass needle moved when he switched on an electric current in a nearby wire. This was the first evidence that an electric current produces a magnetic field. Within weeks, the French scientist André-Marie Ampère had developed the mathematics, and soon after, inventors discovered that winding the wire into a coil and placing iron inside it made a powerful electromagnet that could be switched on and off.
paras.F: In 1831, the English scientist Michael Faraday found the reverse effect. When he moved a magnet into a coil of wire, a current flowed in the wire, but only while the magnet was moving. This is called electromagnetic induction. It is the principle behind almost all the electricity that we use: in a power station, steam, water or wind turns huge magnets inside coils of wire, and the changing magnetic field pushes electric current through the wire.
paras.G: Electromagnets are everywhere. Electric motors use them to turn electrical energy into movement, in everything from toothbrushes to trains. Cranes in scrapyards lift cars by switching on an electromagnet. Magnetic levitation trains, which float above the track with no contact, can travel at more than 400 kilometres an hour. Hospitals use MRI machines, which employ strong magnetic fields and radio waves to produce detailed pictures of the inside of the body without using X-rays.

paras.A: Walk into a high-street clothing shop and the prices can seem astonishing: a shirt for the price of a sandwich, a dress for less than a taxi ride. 'Fast fashion', the business of copying catwalk designs quickly and selling them cheaply, has changed the way people buy clothes. A new collection may reach the shops in two or three weeks, and some online retailers add thousands of new styles every day. Consumers buy more than ever, but critics ask who is paying the real cost.
paras.B: The industry's supporters point to its advantages. Low prices allow people on small incomes to dress well and enjoy the pleasure of changing styles. The industry also employs tens of millions of workers, mostly women, in countries such as Bangladesh, Vietnam and Cambodia, where jobs in factories can provide a first source of independent income. For some countries, garment exports are the largest source of foreign earnings, and the development of the industry has helped to pull people out of poverty.
paras.C: Critics, however, point to the conditions in which clothes are made. In 2013, the Rana Plaza building in Bangladesh collapsed, killing more than 1,100 garment workers, many of whom had been ordered back to work although cracks had appeared in the walls. After this disaster, international brands signed agreements to improve safety, and thousands of factories have been inspected. But campaigners report that wages in many countries remain below a living wage and that workers who protest risk dismissal.
paras.D: The environmental costs are also high. Producing a single cotton shirt requires thousands of litres of water, and dyeing and finishing release chemicals into rivers. Most modern clothes also contain synthetic fibres such as polyester, made from oil, which release tiny plastic fibres into the water with every wash. The fashion industry is estimated to be responsible for several per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions, more than aeroplanes and shipping combined by some estimates.
paras.E: Another problem is waste. The average garment is worn fewer times than in the past, and many items are discarded after only a few uses. In some countries, the equivalent of a lorry load of clothes is thrown away or burned every second. Donated clothes are often shipped to poorer countries, where markets are overloaded with low-quality items, and what cannot be sold ends up on rubbish heaps. In Chile's Atacama Desert, a mountain of discarded clothing is so large that it can be seen in satellite images.
paras.F: Defenders respond that consumers have a choice and that companies are responding to demand. Some brands have launched collections made from recycled materials, started schemes to take back old clothes and promised to reduce emissions. Critics call this 'greenwashing', arguing that producing fewer clothes is the only real solution, and that selling more items, even recycled ones, cannot be sustainable. Second-hand shops and online resale have grown fast, which suggests that some customers are changing their attitudes.
paras.G: Overall, I think that fast fashion in its present form is hard to defend. The jobs it provides are valuable, but this cannot excuse unsafe workplaces, wages that do not cover basic needs or the pollution of rivers. Governments should enforce safety and environmental standards and require companies to take responsibility for their supply chains. Consumers, meanwhile, can make a difference by buying fewer, better-made items, repairing clothes and using second-hand shops. The cheapest shirt is not the cheapest if someone else has paid for it.

paras.A: The Sahara is the largest hot desert in the world. It covers about nine million square kilometres, roughly the size of China or the United States, and it stretches across North Africa from the Atlantic Ocean to the Red Sea, passing through eleven countries. Most people imagine endless sand dunes, but they cover only about a quarter of the area. The rest is a mixture of bare rock plateaus, gravel plains, dry river beds, salt flats and rugged mountains such as the Tibesti and the Ahaggar.
paras.B: The Sahara is a land of extremes. By day in summer, temperatures regularly exceed 45 degrees Celsius in the shade; at night they can fall sharply, and in winter, frost occurs in the mountains. Rain is rare and unpredictable. Some places receive only a few millimetres a year and may go several years without any. Yet life is found there: in oases, where underground water reaches the surface, date palms grow, and farmers cultivate crops in their shade.
paras.C: The desert has not always been dry. Around 11,000 years ago, a slow change in the wobble of the Earth's axis strengthened the African monsoon, and rain returned to the region. Over the next five thousand years, the Sahara became a landscape of grassland, lakes and rivers. Rock paintings from this period in the Tassili n'Ajjer, in Algeria, show cattle, giraffes, crocodiles and people swimming, and fossil bones of hippopotamuses have been found in what is now deep desert.
paras.D: About 5,000 years ago, the wobble changed again, the monsoon moved south, and the region dried over a few centuries. Scientists argue about how quickly this happened. Some evidence suggests that the change was sudden, while other studies point to a slow decline, in which human herding and the loss of plants may have made the drying worse. People moved to the Nile Valley, where the first great kingdoms of Egypt developed. The desert, in this sense, may have helped to shape the history of civilisation.
paras.E: For centuries, the Sahara was crossed by caravans of camels, which were introduced to North Africa from Arabia about 2,000 years ago. Camels can go for days without water, and their broad feet do not sink in sand. Traders carried salt from desert mines such as Taghaza to the south, where it was valuable, and brought back gold, ivory and slaves. Cities on the southern edge of the desert, such as Timbuktu, became wealthy centres of trade and learning.
paras.F: The nomadic Tuareg, who guided the caravans, developed methods for survival that are still used. They read the stars and the shapes of dunes to navigate, travelled at night in the hottest season and knew the location of every well. Today many Saharan people still live as herders, although droughts, wars and borders have made the old routes difficult. Many young men now work in towns far from the desert.
paras.G: The desert influences places far away. Winds lift enormous quantities of Saharan dust, and storms carry it across the Atlantic Ocean, where it fertilises the Amazon rainforest and the Caribbean with minerals, particularly phosphorus. Meanwhile, the desert's edge is changing. A study published in 2018 found that the Sahara had expanded by about ten per cent since 1920, partly due to natural cycles and partly due to climate change. African governments have started the Great Green Wall, a project to plant a belt of trees and restore land along the southern border of the desert, although progress has been slower than hoped. Others see the desert's intense sunshine as an opportunity for solar power.

paras.A: Long before people knew about microbes, they were using them. Fermentation, the process by which microorganisms change one substance into another, is behind bread, cheese, yoghurt, wine, beer, vinegar, soy sauce and kimchi. Archaeologists have found traces of fermented drinks made from rice, honey and fruit in a Chinese village dated to about 7000 BC, and wine-making in the Caucasus is at least 8,000 years old. For most of history, nobody could explain how it worked.
paras.B: In the 1850s, the French scientist Louis Pasteur was asked to find out why some barrels of wine in his region turned sour. Looking through a microscope, he saw that healthy wine contained round yeast cells, while spoiled wine contained rod-shaped bacteria. He concluded that fermentation was caused by living organisms. Later, in 1897, the German chemist Eduard Buchner showed that dead yeast extract could also ferment sugar, revealing that the actual work is done by chemical catalysts called enzymes.
paras.C: There are several kinds of fermentation, depending on the microbe. In alcoholic fermentation, yeast, a single-celled fungus, feeds on sugar and produces alcohol and carbon dioxide. It happens when yeast is added to grape juice or to a mixture of grain and water. In lactic fermentation, bacteria change sugars into lactic acid. In a third type, acetic fermentation, bacteria turn alcohol into acetic acid, the sour ingredient of vinegar.
paras.D: Bread makers use the gas. When yeast is mixed with flour, water and a little sugar, it produces carbon dioxide, which forms bubbles in the sticky dough and makes it rise. The alcohol evaporates during baking, and the heat kills the yeast. Sourdough bread is made without commercial yeast, using a mixture of wild yeasts and lactic-acid bacteria that is kept alive from one loaf to the next. Some bakers keep such a mixture, called a starter, for decades.
paras.E: Dairy products are the best-known examples of lactic fermentation. To make yoghurt, milk is warmed to about forty degrees Celsius and mixed with two kinds of bacteria. They feed on lactose, the sugar in milk, and produce lactic acid, which makes the milk proteins thicken and gives a sour taste. Cheese-making adds an enzyme, rennet, to curdle the milk before microbes ripen the curds over weeks or years. In Central Asia, similar processes give qatiq and kurt, as well as kumis, made from fermented mare's milk.
paras.F: Fermentation is also one of the oldest methods of preserving food. Lactic acid makes the surroundings acidic, which stops harmful bacteria from growing. This is why cabbage fermented as sauerkraut or kimchi can be kept for months without a refrigerator. Fermented foods may also be easier to digest and contain living bacteria that may help the gut, although scientists are still studying how much benefit they bring.
paras.G: Today, fermentation is used on an industrial scale. Huge steel tanks hold microbes that make medicines such as antibiotics and insulin, food additives such as citric acid, and ethanol for fuel. Some scientists use fermentation to produce proteins that resemble milk or egg white without the need for animals. These developments suggest that this ancient art may become increasingly important as the world looks for food and energy produced with a lower impact on the planet.

ps.title: Should Athletes Be Paid Like Stars?

paras.A: In 2023, the best-paid footballers earned more than 100 million dollars a year, and several of the top basketball and tennis players earned similar sums when advertising was added. Meanwhile, the nurse treating an injured player may earn in a year what the player earns in a day. Is it fair that sports stars receive so much? Or are they simply paid what the market will pay for rare talent?
paras.B: Defenders of high salaries start with economics. Sport is a business, and clubs, leagues and broadcasters earn huge revenues from fans who pay to watch the best. Television rights to major competitions are worth billions. A star athlete helps to produce this income by filling stadiums and selling shirts, and it is natural that she or he should receive a share. In a free market, the argument goes, people are paid according to the value they create.
paras.C: Others emphasise the unusual nature of an athlete's career. Most professional sports careers are short: a footballer may retire in his mid-thirties, and injuries can end a career at any time. Only a very small percentage of young people who aspire to play professionally ever succeed. A star earns for the few years of his career what an ordinary professional earns over a lifetime. In addition, years of training, sacrifice and risk go into reaching the top.
paras.D: Critics reply that the argument from the market is not a moral argument. A teacher or a doctor may contribute more to society than a footballer, yet receive far less. High salaries, they say, reflect not only talent but also the way the sports industry is organised: only a handful of top performers capture most of the rewards, while thousands of professionals in lower leagues earn modest wages or struggle to find work. In many sports, women are still paid much less than men for the same level of achievement.
paras.E: A second criticism concerns the effect on sport itself. When wealthy clubs, or clubs owned by billionaires or states, can buy the best players, smaller clubs cannot compete. Fans of a team may see their best players sold to richer rivals every season. Ticket prices rise, and ordinary supporters find it more difficult to attend matches. Some leagues, like the American NFL, use salary caps to limit spending, and argue that this makes competition more exciting.
paras.F: There is also the question of role models. Supporters of high pay argue that stars inspire young people to take up sport and to work hard, and many athletes donate money to charity or run foundations. Critics respond that excessive wealth and scandals involving stars send a different message. The relationship between stardom and social responsibility is complicated, and the evidence that success in sport leads children to be more active is mixed.
paras.G: My view is that high salaries are an inevitable result of the modern sports industry, but they are not a law of nature, and they can be influenced. Salary caps, fairer sharing of television income between clubs and equal pay for women and men would make the system fairer without removing the rewards for excellence. Societies should also ask whether the money going into elite sport might be better balanced by investment in grassroots facilities, where most people actually play.

paras.A: The Trans-Siberian Railway is the longest railway line in the world. It runs for 9,289 kilometres from Moscow to the Pacific port of Vladivostok, crossing seven time zones and some of the emptiest and most beautiful land on Earth. The full journey takes about a week. For passengers, it is a trip through forests, steppe, mountains and lakes; for Russia, it was the means by which an enormous country was tied together.
paras.B: Before the railway, travel across Siberia was slow and exhausting. Travellers used horses, boats on rivers or carts on roads which turned to mud in spring and autumn; a journey from Moscow to the Pacific could take months. By the 1880s, Russia's rulers had come to see the lack of transport as a political and military problem, since the empire's eastern lands were thinly settled and rivals such as Japan and Britain were expanding their influence in Asia.
paras.C: Construction began in 1891, when the heir to the throne, the future Tsar Nicholas II, ceremonially laid a stone at Vladivostok. Work went on from both ends. Thousands of soldiers, peasants and convicts, as well as foreign workers, built the line using hand tools, horses and explosives. The builders faced swamp, solid rock, and winter temperatures below minus forty degrees. In the north, the ground is permafrost, which melts in summer and turns to mud, so engineers had to find ways to stop track and bridges from sinking.
paras.D: The most difficult section was around Lake Baikal, the deepest lake in the world, which holds about one-fifth of the planet's fresh water. At first, there was no track around its southern shore, which was cut by cliffs; in the meantime, a steam ferry carried entire trains across the lake. In winter, rails were even laid on the ice. The Circum-Baikal line, with its 38 tunnels and many bridges, was completed in 1905 and is still considered one of the most beautiful pieces of railway engineering.
paras.E: The railway changed Siberia. Millions of farmers from European Russia moved east to settle the land in the decades after it opened, and towns such as Novosibirsk, which did not exist before 1893, grew into great cities. Mines, factories and wheat farms developed along the route. The line also allowed Russia to send troops to the east, and its military importance was proved in the war with Japan in 1904–1905, when the single-track line struggled to carry enough supplies.
paras.F: Over the years, the line has acquired branches. The Trans-Manchurian runs to Beijing through north-eastern China, while the Trans-Mongolian passes through Ulan Bator in Mongolia before reaching the Chinese capital. A later line, the Baikal-Amur Mainline, runs further north. The Turkestan–Siberia, or Turksib, line, completed in 1930, links the system with Central Asia, so that travellers can continue south towards cities such as Tashkent.
paras.G: Today the railway carries freight as well as passengers. Containers travelling between China and Europe, oil, coal and timber all use it, and the line is electrified along its whole length, a task completed in 2002. For the traveller, the carriage has become a way to see ordinary life: stations where grandmothers sell pies and pickles, villages of wooden houses with painted shutters, and long hours when the only sound is the rhythm of the wheels. It remains, more than a century after its opening, one of the great journeys of the world.

paras.A: The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite and the brightest object in our night sky, yet it is a small and lifeless world: its diameter of 3,474 kilometres is about a quarter of Earth's, and it has no air, no liquid water on its surface and no weather. It lies on average 384,400 kilometres away, a distance that light crosses in a little over a second. The Moon has fascinated humans for as long as there have been humans to look at it.
paras.B: The most widely accepted explanation of the Moon's origin is the giant impact hypothesis. About 4.5 billion years ago, soon after the Earth formed, a body about the size of Mars is believed to have struck the young planet. The collision threw enormous amounts of molten rock into orbit, and this material gradually gathered together to form the Moon. Analysis of lunar rocks brought back to Earth supports the idea, since they closely resemble the rocks of the Earth's outer layers.
paras.C: The surface of the Moon is covered with craters, made by asteroids and comets that have struck it over billions of years. Because there is no wind, rain or life to wear them away, the craters remain unchanged for ages. The dark patches that we see with the naked eye, called maria, which is Latin for 'seas', are not seas at all but vast plains of volcanic rock, formed when lava flooded huge basins early in the Moon's history.
paras.D: The Moon always shows the same face to the Earth. This is because the time it takes to spin once on its axis equals the time it takes to orbit the Earth, a state called tidal locking. The 'far side', as a result, was unseen by human beings until a Soviet spacecraft photographed it in 1959. Contrary to popular belief, the far side is not permanently dark; it receives as much sunlight as the near side. Because of the lack of an atmosphere, temperatures swing from about 120 degrees Celsius in the lunar day to minus 170 at night.
paras.E: The Moon affects the Earth in several ways. Its gravity pulls on the oceans and produces the tides, with the sea rising and falling twice a day. This pull also slows down the Earth's rotation very slowly, making each day slightly longer, and the Moon is drifting away from Earth by about 3.8 centimetres a year. Many scientists also believe that the Moon stabilises the tilt of the Earth's axis, which helps to keep the climate fairly steady over long periods.
paras.F: Humans first landed on the Moon on 20 July 1969, when the American astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the surface during the Apollo 11 mission. Between 1969 and 1972, twelve people in total walked on the Moon in six missions and brought back 382 kilograms of rock and soil. Then the programme ended, and no human has been there since. The samples are still being studied and continue to surprise scientists.
paras.G: Interest in the Moon is now growing again. Probes from China, India and Japan have landed there in recent years; in 2019, China's Chang'e-4 made the first soft landing on the far side, and in 2023, India's Chandrayaan-3 landed near the south pole. Scientists believe that frozen water exists in craters that are permanently in shadow, and this could provide drinking water and fuel for future bases. The United States and its partners aim to return astronauts to the lunar surface under the Artemis programme.

paras.A: Around the world, about half of all people use two or more languages in their daily lives, and in countries such as India, Switzerland and Uzbekistan, a child often grows up hearing several. Yet schools differ greatly in how they handle language. Some teach all subjects in one language and treat others as separate lessons; others use two languages to teach the main subjects. Is it better for children to be educated in two languages?
paras.B: Supporters of bilingual education point first to language results. Children who learn a subject in two languages become more fluent in both than those who study the second language as a separate subject for only a few hours each week. Canada's immersion programmes, in which English-speaking children are taught mainly in French from kindergarten, have been studied for over fifty years. The pupils typically reach high levels of French with no loss in their English or in other subjects.
paras.C: A second argument is about the brain. Studies suggest that people who speak two languages from a young age are better at switching attention between tasks and ignoring distractions, perhaps because they constantly select between two languages. Some research even suggests that bilingualism may delay the symptoms of dementia by several years. However, other studies find no such effect, and scientists still debate how strong the advantages are.
paras.D: A third argument concerns culture and identity. For children from minority communities, education in their home language shows respect for their background and keeps contact with grandparents and traditions. Research on immigrant children suggests that those who continue to develop their first language often do better at school than those who are forced to give it up early, since the home language provides a basis for learning new ideas.
paras.E: Critics raise practical problems. Bilingual programmes need teachers who are fluent in two languages and also trained to teach subjects such as science or history, and many countries have a shortage of such teachers. The materials are expensive, and programmes may be hard to organise in classes in which pupils speak many different home languages. When programmes are badly run, pupils may fail to master either language, and some parents fear that the second language will slow progress in the first.
paras.F: A further worry is about equality. In some countries, the best bilingual schools are private and charge high fees, giving wealthy children an advantage in a global language such as English. Critics argue that investing in them does little for children in poor areas, who often have the least access to good teaching in any language. The solution, according to supporters, is to expand good programmes in state schools, not to abandon them.
paras.G: On balance, I believe the evidence favours bilingual education, provided that it is well designed and well taught. The most successful programmes begin early, use both languages for real learning and not just for translation, and have teachers who are respected and properly trained. Governments that want their citizens to be comfortable in the global economy would be wise to invest in such programmes. But no method works without good teaching, and a well-taught monolingual class is better than a poorly run bilingual one.

paras.A: Long before the Spanish arrived in the Americas, a remarkable civilisation flourished in the jungles and highlands of what are now southern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize and Honduras. The Maya never formed a single empire. Instead, they lived in dozens of independent city-states, each ruled by a king, which traded, fought and made alliances with each other. The 'Classic' period of their culture lasted from about AD 250 to 900.
paras.B: Maya cities were centres of religion, government and trade. The largest, such as Tikal in Guatemala, had temple-pyramids rising above the forest, palaces, plazas and courts for a ball game played with a heavy rubber ball. In 2018, researchers using laser scanning from aircraft, called lidar, found the outlines of more than 60,000 buildings, roads and defensive walls hidden under the jungle in northern Guatemala, suggesting that the population had been much larger than previously thought.
paras.C: The Maya were skilled farmers. They cleared forest for fields of maize, beans and squash, built terraces on hillsides and raised fields in swamps. Maize was so important that, according to the Popol Vuh, a sacred text of the Maya, the gods made the first people from maize dough. The Maya were also among the first to prepare chocolate, drinking a bitter, frothy beverage made from ground cacao beans, spices and water. Cacao beans were even used as a form of money.
paras.D: The Maya developed the most advanced writing system in the pre-Columbian Americas. Its signs, called glyphs, were carved on stone monuments and painted in books made from bark paper. For centuries, the script could not be read. In 1952, the Soviet linguist Yuri Knorozov showed that many glyphs represent syllables, and gradually, scholars learned to read most of the texts, which describe the lives of kings, wars and rituals. Sadly, in 1562, a Spanish bishop ordered the burning of Maya books, and only four are known to survive.
paras.E: In mathematics and astronomy, the Maya also achieved a great deal. They used a number system based on twenty and had a symbol for zero, a concept that was unknown in Europe at that time. Maya astronomers watched the movements of the sun, the moon and the planet Venus so carefully that they could predict eclipses. They created several calendars: one of 365 days for the farming year, another of 260 days for religious ceremonies, and a long count which allowed them to record dates thousands of years apart.
paras.F: Around AD 800, the great cities of the southern lowlands began to be abandoned one after another. Historians have suggested many causes. Long periods of drought, shown by evidence from lake sediments and cave formations, could have destroyed harvests. Warfare between cities intensified, and forests were cut down to provide wood and farmland, which may have increased the effects of drought. Most likely, a combination of several pressures overwhelmed rulers who could no longer keep their promises of prosperity.
paras.G: The Maya did not disappear, however. Cities in the northern Yucatán, such as Chichén Itzá, continued to flourish for centuries, and the last independent Maya kingdom fell to the Spanish only in 1697. Today, around six million people speak one of the Mayan languages, and many continue to practise traditional farming, weaving and religion alongside Christianity. Their ancestors' monuments, now protected as World Heritage Sites, attract millions of visitors every year.

ps.title: The Greenhouse Effect and Climate Change

paras.A: Without the atmosphere, the Earth would be a frozen planet, with an average temperature of about minus 18 degrees Celsius. In fact, it is about 15 degrees. The difference of 33 degrees is due to the greenhouse effect, a natural process that keeps the planet warm enough for life. The effect itself is not a problem. What worries scientists is that human activity is making it stronger.
paras.B: The process works like this. Sunlight passes through the atmosphere and warms the surface of the Earth. The warm surface sends heat back towards space as infrared radiation. Some gases in the air, called greenhouse gases, absorb a part of this heat and send some of it back to the ground. The most important are water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide. Nitrogen and oxygen, which make up most of the air, do not absorb infrared radiation in this way.
paras.C: The idea is almost two hundred years old. In the 1820s, the French mathematician Joseph Fourier proposed that the atmosphere acts like a blanket. In 1859, the Irish scientist John Tyndall measured how strongly different gases absorb heat and found that water vapour and carbon dioxide are powerful absorbers. In 1896, the Swedish chemist Svante Arrhenius calculated that doubling the amount of carbon dioxide would raise the temperature of the Earth by several degrees. He thought, however, that the change would take thousands of years and might even be welcome.
paras.D: Since the Industrial Revolution, people have been burning coal, oil and gas, and each year they release billions of tonnes of carbon dioxide. The concentration of the gas in the air has risen from about 280 parts per million before 1800 to more than 420 today, a level not seen for millions of years. Measurements taken on the volcano Mauna Loa in Hawaii since 1958 show a steady rise, with a seasonal rhythm as plants in the northern hemisphere take up carbon dioxide in summer and release it in winter.
paras.E: Other human activities add to the problem. Cutting down forests removes trees that absorb carbon dioxide. Farming animals such as cattle produces methane, a gas which, over twenty years, traps much more heat per tonne than carbon dioxide, and flooded rice fields and leaking gas pipelines also release it. Fertilisers release nitrous oxide. As a result, the global average temperature has risen by about 1.2 degrees Celsius since the late nineteenth century, and the last ten years have been the warmest on record.
paras.F: The consequences are already visible. Glaciers and the ice sheets of Greenland and Antarctica are melting, and the average sea level has risen by about twenty centimetres since 1900, threatening low-lying coasts. Heatwaves, droughts and heavy rainstorms have become more frequent or more intense in many regions. The oceans absorb about a quarter of the carbon dioxide that we release, which makes the water more acidic and harms shellfish and corals.
paras.G: Governments responded in 2015 with the Paris Agreement, in which nearly every country agreed to keep warming well below 2 degrees above pre-industrial levels and to try to limit it to 1.5. Reaching these goals means reducing emissions rapidly: replacing coal and gas with solar, wind and other clean sources, improving efficiency, protecting forests and changing farming. Scientists say that each fraction of a degree matters, and that the choices made in the coming decades will shape the climate for centuries.

ps.title: Should Genetically Modified Crops Be Allowed?

paras.A: Since the 1990s, farmers around the world have grown crops whose genes have been altered in the laboratory. These genetically modified, or GM, crops include maize, soybeans, cotton and rapeseed, and they are now grown on about 190 million hectares in more than twenty countries. Supporters call them a vital tool for feeding a growing population. Opponents fear risks to health and the environment, and in many countries, especially in Europe, GM crops are restricted or banned.
paras.B: Supporters begin with yields and costs. Some GM crops contain a gene from a soil bacterium that produces a protein which is poisonous to certain insect pests. Farmers who plant these crops need to spray fewer insecticides, and in India, studies found that cotton with this gene increased yields and reduced poisoning among farm workers. Others are tolerant of a weedkiller, allowing farmers to control weeds without ploughing, which saves fuel and reduces soil erosion.
paras.C: GM can also improve nutrition. 'Golden Rice', modified to contain beta-carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A, was developed to help children in places where rice is the main food and vitamin A deficiency causes blindness and death. Approval for growing it has been slow, and it has been used little so far, but supporters see it as an example of what GM can do for the poor. Other researchers are working on crops that can survive drought and salty soil, which will become more important as the climate changes.
paras.D: Scientific bodies, including national academies of sciences and the World Health Organization, have reviewed hundreds of studies and concluded that approved GM foods are as safe to eat as conventional foods. In more than twenty years of use, no confirmed case of illness caused by eating an approved GM food has been recorded. Supporters argue that some of the opposition is based on fear of the unnatural, not on evidence, and that conventional breeding, which mixes thousands of genes at random, can also produce surprises.
paras.E: Opponents, however, raise concerns that go beyond the safety of food. One fear is that modified genes could spread to wild relatives of the crop, making weeds more difficult to control. Insects have become resistant to some of the toxins, and weeds have evolved to survive the weedkillers, which has led farmers to use more chemicals in some regions. Critics also worry about the effect on wildlife and on the soil.
paras.F: A second set of objections concerns economics and control. A few large companies hold patents on most GM seeds, and farmers who plant them usually cannot save seed for the next season, and must buy new seed every year. Critics see this as a way of making farmers dependent on corporations. Supporters respond that farmers choose GM seeds freely because they find them profitable, and that hybrid seeds also have to be bought every year.
paras.G: In my view, each GM crop should be judged individually, on the basis of evidence, and not accepted or rejected as a whole. The technology itself is not dangerous, but it can be used well or badly. Governments should fund independent research, enforce clear labelling and ensure that smallholder farmers can benefit from it. At a time of climate change and rising populations, it would be unwise to reject a tool that could help provide food, but equally unwise to ignore the real risks.

paras.A: In the far north of Canada, Alaska and Greenland, in lands where winter temperatures can fall below minus forty degrees Celsius and the sun does not rise for weeks, live the Inuit. The word 'Inuit' means 'the people' in their language, Inuktitut, and the older word 'Eskimo' is regarded as offensive by many Inuit in Canada. The Inuit are the descendants of the Thule people, who spread eastwards from Alaska across the Arctic about a thousand years ago, bringing with them dogs, sledges, boats made of skin and tools of bone and stone.
paras.B: Surviving in such a climate demanded great skill. Since almost nothing can be farmed in the Arctic, the Inuit lived mainly by hunting. Seals were the most important animal; people waited patiently by breathing holes in the ice, or stalked seals lying beside their holes. In summer, they hunted caribou and fished in rivers. The largest prey were whales, which were pursued in groups from skin boats called umiaks, and a single whale could feed a community for months.
paras.C: Everything from an animal was used. Meat and blubber provided food and fuel for lamps. Skins were made into clothing, tents and boat covers; bones and antlers became tools, needles and harpoon points. Clothing was a matter of life and death. Women sewed layers of caribou and sealskin, with the fur turned inward, trimmed with strips of fur to keep out drifting snow. A traveller dressed in a well-made parka could stay warm in temperatures that would quickly endanger someone in ordinary winter clothing.
paras.D: The best-known Inuit building is the igloo, a dome of snow blocks. The word 'iglu' in fact means 'house' and refers to any kind of home. Snow houses were used mainly by the Inuit of central Canada in winter hunting camps, and they were built in an hour or so with a long knife. Snow is a good insulator, because it contains a lot of trapped air, and a lamp burning seal oil can raise the temperature inside to above freezing while it is far colder outdoors. Other families lived in tents of skin in summer and in houses of stone, whalebone and turf in winter.
paras.E: In a landscape that looks the same in all directions, people navigated without maps by reading the wind, the stars and the pattern of snowdrifts, which are formed in a constant direction by the prevailing winds. They also built stone figures called inuksuit as landmarks, to point to good hunting grounds or fishing places or to mark a safe route. An inuksuk is now a symbol of Inuit culture and appears on the flag of Nunavut.
paras.F: In the twentieth century, life changed rapidly. Traders, missionaries and government officials arrived; many families were moved to permanent settlements, and children were sent to boarding schools where they were forbidden to speak their own language. In 2008, the Canadian government formally apologised for this policy. In 1999, the territory of Nunavut, which means 'our land' in Inuktitut, was created from part of the Northwest Territories. It covers about two million square kilometres, almost twenty per cent of Canada, but has fewer than 45,000 inhabitants, most of them Inuit.
paras.G: Today's Inuit live in modern towns, use snowmobiles and satellite phones, and work in government, mining and tourism, but hunting remains important for food and for identity. Climate change is a threat: the Arctic is warming about three or four times faster than the global average, sea ice forms later and melts sooner, and thawing ground damages houses and roads. Many scientists now work with Inuit elders, whose knowledge of ice and animals, called Inuit Qaujimajatuqangit, helps to understand these changes.

qs.title: Questions 9–13

paras.A: The adult human brain weighs about 1.4 kilograms and contains roughly 86 billion nerve cells, called neurons. Each neuron can connect with thousands of others at junctions called synapses, giving a total of perhaps a hundred trillion connections. For much of the twentieth century, scientists believed that this network was fixed after childhood. We now know that the brain is constantly changing in response to experience, a property known as neuroplasticity.
paras.B: The basic idea was proposed by the Canadian psychologist Donald Hebb in 1949. He suggested that when two neurons are active at the same time, the connection between them becomes stronger. His principle is often summarised in the phrase 'neurons that fire together wire together'. Each time we practise a skill or recall a fact, the same pathway is used, and the connections along it are reinforced; pathways that are not used gradually weaken.
paras.C: Some of the most striking evidence comes from taxi drivers in London. To obtain a licence, they must memorise the layout of about 25,000 streets, a process that takes three or four years. In 2000, scientists scanned their brains and found that a part of the hippocampus, a region important for memory and navigation, was larger than in other people, and that the longer someone had worked as a taxi driver, the larger this part was. Later, the same team showed that the region grew in people who passed the test, but not in those who failed.
paras.D: Other studies show that new skills can change the brain within weeks. In one experiment, volunteers with no experience of juggling were taught to juggle with three balls. After three months, brain scans showed an increase in grey matter in areas that process visual motion. When the volunteers stopped practising, the areas shrank again. Learning a language, playing music and even learning to read as an adult have been shown to cause similar changes.
paras.E: Plasticity is strongest in childhood. In the first years of life, the brain forms connections far faster than at any other time, and then it prunes the ones that are not used. There are 'sensitive periods' when particular abilities are learned most easily: children who hear a language from an early age usually speak it without an accent, while adults rarely lose their accent completely. Nevertheless, scientists emphasise that learning continues throughout life, although it may need more effort.
paras.F: Understanding plasticity has practical value. After a stroke, which can destroy part of the brain, patients can sometimes regain lost abilities because other areas take over, especially if they receive intensive therapy soon afterwards. Healthy people can also support their brains. Regular physical exercise appears to promote the growth of new connections, while chronic stress and lack of sleep make it harder to learn. Good sleep helps to transfer new memories into long-term storage.
paras.G: What is the best way to learn? Research points to a few reliable methods. Testing yourself is more effective than rereading. Spreading practice over several days works better than cramming the night before, because the brain needs time to consolidate what it has learned. Mixing different kinds of problems helps more than practising one kind repeatedly. By contrast, the popular idea that people have fixed 'learning styles', such as visual or auditory, has little support. Commercial 'brain training' games improve performance on the games themselves, but there is little evidence that skills transfer to other tasks.

ps.title: Should Young People Do National Service?

paras.A: In several countries, young people must spend a period of time in national service after school. In South Korea and Israel, military service is compulsory for most men and, in Israel, for most women; in Switzerland and Singapore, men are required to serve. Some countries, including Sweden, have reintroduced conscription in recent years after abolishing it. Elsewhere, the idea of compulsory service, military or civilian, is regularly proposed. Is it a good idea?
paras.B: Supporters argue that national service builds a sense of community. Young people from different regions, classes and backgrounds would work and live together for months, and these shared experiences might reduce prejudice and create friendships that would otherwise never exist. In societies that are becoming more divided, they say, a common experience is valuable. National service can also develop useful qualities such as discipline, teamwork and responsibility.
paras.C: A second argument is practical. A civilian programme could provide workers for projects that the labour market neglects: caring for elderly people, assisting in hospitals and schools, helping after floods and fires or restoring parks. Military service gives a country a trained reserve that can be called upon in an emergency. In states close to potential enemies, conscription is seen as a necessary insurance.
paras.D: Opponents begin with freedom. Compelling people to give a year or two of their lives to the state, they argue, is a serious restriction of individual liberty, which is justified only in extreme circumstances, such as war. Young people also have other plans: study, training or a career. A delay of one or two years may reduce their lifetime income, and the lost time may be harder to recover for the poor than for the rich, who can often find ways to avoid service.
paras.E: There are doubts about quality. Volunteers who have chosen to serve are usually more motivated than conscripts, and many modern armies need specialised technical skills that cannot be learned in a short period. Many countries, including the United Kingdom and the United States, abandoned conscription in the 1960s and 1970s for this reason and found that professional forces performed better. Compulsory civilian service could also take work away from paid employees.
paras.F: The costs are considerable. Housing, feeding, training and supervising a whole age group, which in a country like the United Kingdom would be perhaps 700,000 people each year, would require enormous investment. Critics suggest that the money could be spent on schools, youth centres and professional services with better results. Supporters respond that the benefits, in citizens who are healthier, better educated and more committed, would justify the price, though evidence for this is limited.
paras.G: I am not persuaded that universal compulsory service is the right answer for most democracies. The benefits, such as social mixing and civic spirit, are valuable but can also be achieved by voluntary programmes, which attract motivated participants and do not compel anyone. Governments could make such programmes attractive with grants, educational credits and recognition from employers. The exception may be a country facing a real military threat, where compulsion may be reasonable. Even there, exemptions and alternative civilian options should be available for conscientious objectors.

paras.A: Rising from the jungle in north-west Cambodia, Angkor Wat is the largest religious monument in the world. It covers an area of about 162 hectares, and its five lotus-shaped towers have become the symbol of Cambodia, appearing on the national flag. The temple was built in the early twelfth century by King Suryavarman II, ruler of the Khmer Empire, which at that time controlled much of what is now Cambodia, Thailand, Laos and southern Vietnam.
paras.B: Angkor Wat was originally a Hindu temple dedicated to the god Vishnu, but by the end of the twelfth century, the kings had adopted Buddhism, and the temple gradually became a Buddhist site. Its design represents the cosmos as Hindus imagine it. The central tower stands for Mount Meru, the home of the gods, the outer walls for the mountains at the edge of the world, and the surrounding moat, nearly 200 metres wide, for the cosmic ocean.
paras.C: The scale of construction was extraordinary. The temple was built of millions of blocks of sandstone, quarried in the Kulen hills about forty kilometres to the north-east and probably transported on rafts along canals and rivers. The stone was cut and fitted without mortar, and the surface was decorated with carvings. Historians estimate that the project took perhaps thirty-seven years, and employed thousands of labourers, craftsmen and elephants.
paras.D: The walls of the lowest level carry a continuous gallery of carvings, nearly 800 metres long. They show scenes from the Hindu epics, the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, as well as historical battles and the Churning of the Sea of Milk, in which gods and demons pull a great serpent to produce the elixir of immortality. Nearly two thousand carved celestial dancers, known as apsaras, decorate the walls, and no two are quite alike.
paras.E: Angkor Wat was only a part of a vast city. The capital of the Khmer kings, Angkor, was spread over hundreds of square kilometres and, at its height in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, may have been one of the largest cities in the world, with perhaps 750,000 inhabitants. Laser scanning from aircraft, begun in 2012, revealed streets, canals, ponds and mounds hidden in the forest, and showed that the urban area was even bigger than archaeologists had believed. The city depended on a remarkable system of reservoirs, canals and dikes to store the monsoon rain and irrigate rice fields.
paras.F: Why was Angkor abandoned? There is no single answer. In the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, the region experienced alternating periods of severe drought and heavy monsoon rains, which tree-ring evidence has confirmed, and these may have damaged the water system on which the city depended. Wars with neighbours, especially the kingdom of Ayutthaya in Thailand, which attacked the city in 1431, drained its strength. The kings moved the capital south, towards the Mekong, where trade by sea was easier.
paras.G: Angkor Wat itself was never completely lost. Buddhist monks continued to care for it, and Khmer people never forgot it. Western attention was drawn to the temple in 1860, when the French naturalist Henri Mouhot published drawings and descriptions. It was designated a World Heritage Site in 1992, and more than two million tourists now visit each year, which brings money but also damages the stone and the water supply. Conservators from many countries are working with Cambodians to repair the monument and to control the number of visitors.

paras.A: Every hour, the Earth receives more energy from the sun than humanity uses in an entire year. Solar panels offer a way to capture a small part of this flow and convert it directly into electricity, without moving parts, noise or smoke. The technology they use, the photovoltaic effect, was discovered in 1839 by the French physicist Edmond Becquerel, who noticed that a voltage appeared when light fell on certain materials immersed in liquid.
paras.B: The first practical solar cell was made in 1954 at Bell Laboratories in the United States. Made of silicon, it converted about six per cent of the sunlight into electricity, enough to power a small toy and a radio. Silicon is an ideal material because it is one of the most abundant elements in the Earth's crust, being the main ingredient of sand, and it belongs to a group of materials called semiconductors, which can be controlled to conduct electricity in useful ways.
paras.C: A solar cell is a sandwich of two layers of silicon. To make the layers, tiny amounts of other elements are added, a process called doping. The top layer is doped with phosphorus, which gives it extra electrons, and the bottom layer with boron, which leaves it short of electrons. Where the two layers meet, some electrons cross the boundary, creating an electric field, rather like a one-way slope, which only allows electrons to move in one direction.
paras.D: Light consists of particles of energy called photons. When a photon of sufficient energy strikes the cell, it knocks an electron loose from an atom. The electric field pushes the free electron to the top layer. Metal contacts on the cell collect the electrons, and when a wire connects the top and bottom, the electrons flow through it as an electric current, before returning to the bottom layer. Electricity continues to flow for as long as light keeps arriving.
paras.E: A single cell produces only about half a volt, so manufacturers connect dozens of cells together in a panel, protected by glass and a metal frame. Panels produce direct current, but homes and the electricity grid use alternating current, so a device called an inverter changes one form into the other. A typical modern panel converts about twenty per cent of the sunlight that strikes it, and the best laboratory cells exceed thirty per cent when different materials are combined in layers.
paras.F: Solar power has become much cheaper. Since 2010, the price of solar panels has fallen by around ninety per cent, and in many sunny countries, new solar plants now produce electricity at a lower cost than coal or gas. Uzbekistan has been building large solar plants in desert areas, such as the one near Navoi, which opened in 2021, and plans many more. Panels last for twenty-five to thirty years or more, and the energy used to make a panel is repaid within one or two years of operation.
paras.G: Solar energy has limits. It stops at night and drops in cloudy weather, so electricity networks need other sources or large batteries to supply power when the sun is down. Panels also require land, and recycling the glass, metals and silicon in old panels is still developing. Researchers are working on thin, flexible materials, such as perovskites, which could be printed on rolls and used on windows or clothing. If these obstacles are overcome, solar power could become the world's largest source of electricity within a few decades.

paras.A: Every time we search the web, use a map, buy something online or post a photograph, we leave a trail of data. Companies collect this information to understand what we want, to show us advertisements and to improve their products. Governments collect it to fight crime and terrorism. Many people shrug and say that they have nothing to hide. Others argue that privacy is a basic right that is fast disappearing. Is it worth protecting?
paras.B: Defenders of privacy begin with the observation that the 'nothing to hide' argument misunderstands the point. Privacy is not about hiding wrongdoing, but about control: deciding who knows what about us. Most people close the bathroom door or keep their medical information private, not because they are criminals but because some things are personal. The same principle applies to data about our location, health, friendships and political opinions.
paras.C: The risks are real. Information collected for one purpose can be misused for another. Data can be stolen: major breaches have exposed hundreds of millions of passwords, addresses and card numbers, which criminals use for fraud and identity theft. Companies can use data to set prices, to decide who receives a loan or a job interview, or to influence the news we see, often without telling us how the decisions are made. Researchers have shown that even 'anonymous' data can often be linked back to individuals.
paras.D: There is also a danger to freedom. When people believe they are being watched, they tend to censor themselves, avoiding sensitive subjects, controversial opinions or contact with certain people. Critics fear that mass surveillance, even if introduced for good reasons, could one day be used by a less trustworthy government against journalists, opponents or minorities. Safeguards, such as independent courts and clear limits on how long data may be kept, are therefore necessary.
paras.E: On the other side, many users value the benefits. Free services such as search engines, maps and email are paid for by advertising, and advertising works better if it is relevant. Medical researchers argue that combining health data from millions of people could lead to faster discoveries and earlier diagnosis of diseases. Police say that access to phone and internet records helps them to solve serious crimes and prevent attacks. Total privacy, they argue, would have costs for safety and convenience.
paras.F: Studies suggest that people care about privacy in theory but often behave differently in practice. Most do not read long privacy policies, accept cookies without a second thought and trade personal information for small rewards. Economists call this the 'privacy paradox'. Some interpret it as a sign that people do not really mind. Others reply that it shows how hard it is for individuals to make informed choices when the rules are complicated and the alternatives are limited.
paras.G: My view is that privacy is worth protecting, and that individuals should not be left to do so alone. Governments should require companies to collect only the data they need, to explain clearly how it is used and to let people see and delete it. The European Union's General Data Protection Regulation, which took effect in 2018, is an imperfect but important step. At the same time, individuals can help themselves by using strong passwords, updating software and thinking before they share. Trust in the digital world must be earned, not assumed.
