paras.A: Lying in the Indian Ocean, about four hundred kilometres east of Africa across the Mozambique Channel, Madagascar is the fourth-largest island in the world. With an area of roughly 587,000 square kilometres, it is larger than France, and is home to about thirty million people. Its landscape ranges from tropical rainforest on the east coast to dry spiny forest in the south, and its central highlands are covered with terraced rice fields. Scientists often call Madagascar a 'mini-continent' because of its variety of habitats and its extraordinary wildlife.
paras.B: The island's uniqueness is a result of isolation. Madagascar broke away from the African mainland about 160 million years ago, and separated from India roughly 88 million years ago. Since then, the animals and plants that were stranded there have evolved on their own, with no contact with other continents. Over millions of years, they have developed into new species that exist nowhere else. As a result, about ninety per cent of Madagascar's wildlife is endemic, which means that it is found only on the island.
paras.C: The best-known endemic animals are the lemurs, a group of primates that includes more than one hundred species, ranging from the mouse lemur, which weighs only about thirty grams, to the indri, which is about the size of a small dog and whose loud calls can be heard several kilometres away. The ring-tailed lemur, with its black-and-white striped tail, is the species most often seen by visitors. Lemurs once lived in many parts of the world, but on the African mainland they were largely replaced by monkeys, which competed with them for food. On Madagascar there were no monkeys, so lemurs were able to flourish.
paras.D: Many other creatures are also unique. Around half of the world's species of chameleon live on Madagascar, including the tiny Brookesia nana, one of the smallest reptiles known, which is less than three centimetres long. The fossa, a cat-like predator related to the mongoose, is the island's largest meat-eating mammal. Among the plants, six of the world's eight species of baobab tree are found only on Madagascar, and the avenue of baobabs near Morondava is one of the island's most photographed sights.
paras.E: Humans arrived surprisingly late. The first settlers, who came by boat probably from south-east Asia, reached the island roughly two thousand years ago, and were later joined by people from Africa. This mixed heritage is still seen in Malagasy, the national language, which belongs to the same family as languages spoken in Indonesia and Borneo. Soon after the arrival of people, a number of large animals disappeared, among them the elephant bird, a flightless creature that stood about three metres tall and laid the largest eggs of any known bird, and several giant lemurs.
paras.F: Today, Madagascar's wildlife is in serious danger. It is estimated that the island has lost roughly ninety per cent of its original forest. Many farmers practise tavy, a traditional form of slash-and-burn agriculture in which forest is cleared and burned to grow rice for a few years before the soil is exhausted and people move on. Other pressures include illegal logging of rosewood, charcoal production and mining. Because so many species live in small areas, the loss of even a small patch of forest can drive an animal to extinction.
paras.G: Conservationists are trying to protect what remains. National parks and reserves now cover a significant part of the island, and programmes encourage villagers to benefit from the forest, for example through ecotourism, or by growing vanilla, an orchid that Madagascar produces in larger quantities than any other country. Experts agree, however, that the long-term survival of the island's wildlife depends on reducing poverty, since people who cannot afford food or fuel have little choice but to cut trees.

paras.A: A telescope is, in essence, a device for collecting light. The human eye has a pupil that is only a few millimetres wide when it is open as far as it will go, so it gathers very little light from faint, distant objects. A telescope uses a much larger lens or mirror to collect more light and bring it to a focus, producing an image that is both brighter and, with the help of an eyepiece, larger. The amount of light gathered depends on the area of the main lens or mirror, so a telescope with a diameter twice as great collects four times as much light.
paras.B: The first telescopes appeared in the Netherlands in 1608, when the spectacle-maker Hans Lippershey applied for a patent for an instrument that made distant objects seem nearer. News of the invention spread quickly. In 1609, the Italian scientist Galileo Galilei built his own version, improved it, and turned it towards the sky. Within a year he had seen mountains on the Moon, countless stars invisible to the naked eye, and four moons orbiting Jupiter, observations which provided strong evidence that not everything in the heavens circled the Earth.
paras.C: Galileo's telescope was a refractor, which uses lenses to bend, or refract, light. Refractors have a weakness: a simple lens bends different colours by different amounts, so images are surrounded by coloured fringes, a defect called chromatic aberration. Large lenses are also heavy and can only be supported around their edges, so they sag under their own weight. In 1668, Isaac Newton solved the first problem by building a reflecting telescope, which uses a curved mirror instead of a main lens. A mirror reflects all colours equally, and it can be supported from behind.
paras.D: Almost all of the large telescopes used by professional astronomers are reflectors. However, observing from the ground has a drawback, because the atmosphere is constantly moving, which makes stars twinkle and blurs the image. To reduce the problem, observatories are built on high, dry mountains, such as Mauna Kea in Hawaii and the Atacama Desert in Chile, where the air is thin and clear. Some modern telescopes also use adaptive optics, in which a flexible mirror changes its shape hundreds of times a second to cancel out the distortion caused by the air.
paras.E: The ultimate solution is to put a telescope in space. The Hubble Space Telescope, launched in 1990, orbits about 540 kilometres above the Earth. Its mirror was found to be slightly the wrong shape, giving blurred pictures, but in 1993 astronauts fitted corrective optics during a space-shuttle mission. Hubble has since made more than a million observations, helped to measure the age of the universe, and produced images such as the Hubble Deep Field, which showed thousands of galaxies in a tiny patch of sky.
paras.F: Light is only one kind of electromagnetic radiation, and other kinds can reveal things that visible light cannot. Radio telescopes use large dishes to detect radio waves from objects such as pulsars and distant galaxies. Infrared telescopes can see through clouds of dust where stars are forming. The James Webb Space Telescope, launched on 25 December 2021, observes mainly in infrared. Its main mirror, 6.5 metres across, is made up of eighteen hexagonal segments coated with gold, and it operates about 1.5 million kilometres from Earth, where a huge sunshield keeps it extremely cold.
paras.G: Even larger instruments are on the way. The Extremely Large Telescope, under construction in the Atacama Desert by the European Southern Observatory, will have a main mirror 39 metres wide, made of almost 800 segments. Astronomers hope it will be able to study the atmospheres of planets orbiting other stars, looking for chemical signs of life. Each new generation of telescopes has revealed an unexpectedly rich universe, and there is every reason to think that this will happen again.

paras.A: In 2008, a French-born American woman named Bea Johnson began to attract attention with a startling claim: her family of four produced so little rubbish that a year's worth would fit in a single jar. She wrote a book and started a blog explaining how, and the 'zero-waste' movement grew rapidly. Its followers buy food in bulk with their own containers, refuse plastic bags and straws, repair rather than replace, and compost what is left. Supporters see this as the answer to the mountains of waste that modern societies produce. Critics think it is an unrealistic distraction.
paras.B: The scale of the problem is not in doubt. The World Bank has estimated that the world generates more than two billion tonnes of municipal solid waste each year and that, without action, the figure could rise by about seventy per cent by 2050. Much of this waste ends up in landfills or is burned, and some is dumped in rivers and oceans. Plastic is a special concern, because it breaks down very slowly. One widely cited study calculated that only about nine per cent of all the plastic ever made has been recycled.
paras.C: Supporters argue that individual choices matter. Recycling, they say, is not enough, because it is often expensive, many materials cannot be recycled, and recycled products are often of lower quality. It is better to avoid creating waste at all. They also point out that people who change their habits often save money, since they buy fewer things, and that visible examples encourage others. Shops that sell loose goods and refill stations for detergent, which hardly existed a decade ago, are now found in many cities, showing that consumer demand can change what businesses offer.
paras.D: Critics respond that household waste is only a small part of the story. In many countries, the waste from construction, mining, industry and farming is many times greater than the rubbish put out by families, so even a perfect zero-waste household would reduce the total only slightly. Some also argue that the movement lets companies off the hook: the idea that the individual is responsible for pollution, they say, shifts attention from the manufacturers who design products that are hard to reuse or repair, and from governments that could regulate them.
paras.E: There are also practical objections. Zero-waste living takes time and planning: shopping at several specialist stores, making products such as toothpaste at home, and cooking everything from scratch. Bulk shops are often more expensive and are not available in rural areas or in poorer neighbourhoods. People with limited incomes, disabilities, or demanding jobs and small children may find it impossible. Some medical items, such as syringes, must be single-use for reasons of hygiene, and packaging can actually reduce food waste by keeping products fresh for longer.
paras.F: Many experts therefore suggest a middle path, and it is a sensible one. Rather than aiming for perfection, households can concentrate on the changes with the greatest effect: wasting less food, which is the largest category of rubbish in many homes; buying fewer, more durable goods; and using what they own for longer. At the same time, governments can introduce deposit schemes for bottles, ban the most wasteful kinds of packaging, and require producers to pay for the cost of dealing with the products they sell. Several countries have already adopted such policies with encouraging results.
paras.G: In the end, perhaps the importance of the zero-waste movement lies less in the jar than in the questions it raises. It reminds us that waste is the result of decisions, made by designers, companies, governments and ordinary shoppers, and that those decisions can be changed. Whether or not any one family can truly send nothing to landfill, a society that thought harder about what it throws away would almost certainly be a cleaner one.

paras.A: For nearly a thousand years, Hagia Sophia in Istanbul was the largest cathedral in the world, and today it remains one of the great buildings of history. Its name is Greek for 'Holy Wisdom'. The structure that stands today was built in an astonishing five years, between 532 and 537, on the orders of the Byzantine emperor Justinian I. It was the third church on the site; the second had been destroyed by fire during the Nika riots of 532, a violent uprising in which a large part of the city was burned.
paras.B: Justinian chose two scholars rather than traditional builders as his architects: Anthemius of Tralles, a mathematician, and Isidore of Miletus, a physicist. About ten thousand workers are said to have taken part. The best materials were gathered from across the empire: marble in many colours from quarries around the Mediterranean, and columns taken from ancient temples. According to a later story, when the building was finished, Justinian entered it and exclaimed, 'Solomon, I have outdone you.'
paras.C: The greatest achievement was the dome, which is about 31 metres across and rises some 55 metres above the floor. It appears to float above the interior because a ring of forty windows runs around its base, so that light seems to hold it up. The architects solved a difficult problem by using pendentives, curved triangular sections of masonry that carry the weight of a circular dome down onto a square base. This technique, which had never been used on such a scale, strongly influenced later churches and mosques.
paras.D: Even so, the first dome was too shallow, and exerted so much sideways force that it was damaged by earthquakes. In 558, part of it collapsed. It was rebuilt by Isidore the Younger, the nephew of one of the original architects, who raised it by about six metres. Since then, further earthquakes have caused damage, and the building has had to be strengthened many times, with massive buttresses added on the outside.
paras.E: For more than nine hundred years, Hagia Sophia was the principal church of the Eastern Orthodox world, and the place where emperors were crowned. In 1204 it was looted by soldiers of the Fourth Crusade, and in 1453, when the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II captured the city, it was converted into a mosque. Minarets were added, and the Christian mosaics were covered with plaster, as Islamic tradition discourages the display of figures. Over the centuries, Ottoman architects, including the great Sinan, who strengthened the structure, took the building as a model for their own mosques.
paras.F: After the Ottoman Empire collapsed and the Republic of Turkey was founded, Mustafa Kemal Ataturk ordered in 1934 that Hagia Sophia be turned into a museum, and it opened to visitors in 1935. Restorers uncovered the mosaics, including a famous one of the Virgin Mary and the infant Jesus. In 1985, the building was included in the UNESCO World Heritage listing for the historic areas of Istanbul. It became one of Turkey's most visited monuments, attracting millions of people every year.
paras.G: In July 2020, a Turkish court cancelled the museum's status, and the building became a mosque once more. The decision was welcomed by many Turkish people, but criticised by some governments and religious leaders abroad. The authorities have said that the building remains open to visitors of all faiths, and that the Christian images are covered during prayer times with curtains or lights. Whatever its function, Hagia Sophia continues to stand as a symbol of the long and layered history of the city on the Bosphorus.

paras.A: Before the twentieth century, a small cut or a case of pneumonia could kill. Infections caused by bacteria were among the leading causes of death in every country, and doctors had few effective weapons against them. This changed with the discovery of antibiotics, medicines that kill bacteria or stop them from multiplying. Antibiotics are sometimes described as the greatest advance in the history of medicine, and they made possible not only the treatment of infections but also modern surgery, cancer treatment and organ transplants, all of which depend on controlling infection.
paras.B: The story is usually said to begin in 1928, when the Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming returned from holiday to his laboratory at St Mary's Hospital in London. He noticed that a dish on which he had been growing bacteria had been contaminated by a mould, and that around the mould, the bacteria had been killed. The mould was of the genus Penicillium, and Fleming named the substance it produced penicillin. However, he found it hard to produce in a pure form, and it was not until the late 1930s that Howard Florey and Ernst Chain, working in Oxford, turned it into a usable drug.
paras.C: The Second World War gave new urgency to the work. American companies learned to produce penicillin in huge tanks, and by 1944 there was enough to treat the Allied soldiers wounded in the D-Day landings. Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the Nobel Prize in 1945. Many other antibiotics followed, including streptomycin, the first effective treatment for tuberculosis, in the 1940s. Drug companies searched soil samples from around the world for microbes that might produce more of them, and the period from the 1940s to the 1960s is sometimes called the golden age of antibiotic discovery.
paras.D: How do antibiotics work? Each kind attacks a feature of bacteria that human cells do not have. Penicillin, for example, stops bacteria from building their cell walls, so that they burst. Others interfere with the ribosomes, the tiny structures where bacteria make proteins, or with the way they copy their genetic material. Because human cells are built differently, these drugs can kill bacteria without harming the patient. For the same reason, antibiotics have no effect on viruses, which is why they are useless against colds and influenza.
paras.E: The greatest threat to antibiotics is resistance. Whenever a population of bacteria is exposed to a drug, most are killed, but a few may have a random mutation that allows them to survive. These survivors multiply, and soon the whole population is resistant, a clear example of natural selection. Bacteria can also pass resistance genes to one another, even between different species, in small rings of DNA called plasmids. Because bacteria can reproduce in as little as twenty minutes, resistance can spread with surprising speed.
paras.F: Human behaviour makes the problem worse. Doctors sometimes prescribe antibiotics for viral infections, and patients often stop taking them as soon as they feel better, leaving the strongest bacteria alive. In many countries, large quantities are also given to farm animals, to prevent disease and in some cases to make them grow faster. The result is the appearance of 'superbugs', such as MRSA, a form of Staphylococcus aureus that is resistant to many drugs. A major study published in 2022 estimated that drug-resistant infections were directly responsible for more than a million deaths in 2019.
paras.G: Researchers are searching for solutions. Few new classes of antibiotic have reached the market in recent decades, partly because they are not very profitable, since they are taken for a short time and doctors try to use them as little as possible. Teixobactin, discovered in 2015 in bacteria grown from soil, and halicin, identified by an artificial-intelligence programme in a study published in 2020, are among the promising candidates. Others are studying bacteriophages, viruses that attack bacteria. In the meantime, the simplest measures are the most important: using antibiotics only when they are needed, and following the doctor's instructions about how long to take them.

paras.A: Gambling is one of the oldest human activities. Dice have been found in ancient tombs, and betting on games, races and fights has existed in almost every society. Today, however, it is changing quickly. Online casinos and betting apps allow people to place a wager from their phone at any hour of the day, and in 2018 the United States Supreme Court struck down a federal law that had restricted sports betting to a few states, which was followed by a rapid spread of legal betting across the country. This growth has revived an old question: how far should governments regulate gambling?
paras.B: Those who favour tough regulation point first to the harm. Most people who gamble do so occasionally and without problems, but estimates suggest that somewhere between one and three per cent of adults in many countries develop a serious gambling problem. The consequences can include debt, broken families and serious mental-health problems. Games are designed to be difficult to stop: slot machines use bright lights and sounds, 'near misses' that feel almost like wins, and unpredictable rewards, a pattern that psychologists have found to be especially habit-forming. Because losses are concentrated among a minority of heavy gamblers, critics argue that the industry depends on people who can least afford to play.
paras.C: Advertising is another concern. In countries where betting companies sponsor football clubs, children can grow up seeing gambling logos on their favourite team's shirt. Researchers worry that this makes betting seem a normal part of sport. Some governments have responded: Italy banned most gambling advertising in 2018, and Spain introduced strict restrictions in 2020. There are similar worries about video games with 'loot boxes', virtual items bought with real money for a chance to win something rare, which Belgium banned in 2018 on the grounds that they were a form of gambling aimed at children.
paras.D: Opponents of heavy regulation reply that gambling is a legal pleasure for adults, like alcohol, and that people should be free to spend their own money. Taxes on betting raise large sums for governments, which are often spent on schools, hospitals and sport. The industry also provides jobs. Above all, they argue that prohibition does not work. When gambling is banned or heavily restricted, demand does not disappear; it moves to illegal operators, who pay no tax, have no duty to protect customers and are often linked to organised crime.
paras.E: Between these positions, many regulators have tried a middle course based on protecting the vulnerable while leaving others free. In Britain, the Gambling Commission requires operators to check customers' identity and age, and a scheme called GAMSTOP, launched in 2018, allows people to exclude themselves from all licensed online sites at once. Other countries have introduced limits on the amount that can be bet, compulsory pauses in play, and warnings showing how much time and money a player has spent. Early evidence suggests that such tools help, though they are only effective if people actually use them.
paras.F: Critics of these measures say that they are easily avoided. A person who has excluded himself from British sites can still use unlicensed ones overseas, and companies may be reluctant to restrict their most profitable customers, since a small group of heavy players can generate a large part of revenue. Some campaigners therefore want a more radical approach, such as a ban on all online slot-style games, a statutory levy on the industry to fund treatment, or a single national limit on losses for each customer.
paras.G: In my view, the evidence supports firm regulation rather than prohibition, but with an important condition: the rules must be enforced, and the money raised must pay for research and treatment. Gambling will not disappear, and pretending otherwise only hands the market to criminals. But treating it as an ordinary product ignores the fact that it is built to encourage people to lose more than they intended. A sensible law should accept both of these facts.

paras.A: In the 1960s the Aral Sea, between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan in Central Asia, was the fourth-largest lake in the world, covering about 68,000 square kilometres, an area roughly the size of Ireland. Today, most of it has gone. The shrinking of the Aral Sea is often described as one of the worst environmental disasters of the twentieth century, and it shows how quickly human activity can transform a landscape.
paras.B: The lake was fed by two great rivers, the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya, which carry meltwater from the mountains of the Pamirs and the Tien Shan across the desert. Because the lake has no outlet to the ocean, water leaves it only by evaporation, and the inflow from the rivers had been just enough to balance this loss. For centuries, fishing communities lived along the shores. In the 1950s, the fishing industry employed tens of thousands of people, and canneries in towns such as Moynaq processed the catch.
paras.C: In the 1960s the Soviet government decided to turn the dry plains of Central Asia into a major cotton-growing region. Huge canals, some of them hundreds of kilometres long, took water from the two rivers to irrigate the fields. Many of these canals were unlined, so a large part of the water seeped into the ground before it reached the crops. Cotton, a thirsty plant, was grown in great quantities, and Uzbekistan became one of the world's largest producers. The plan achieved its goal, but the rivers were drained, and very little water was left to reach the sea.
paras.D: The consequences were dramatic. From the 1960s the level fell year after year; by 1987 the lake had split into two parts, the small North Aral and the larger South Aral, and by 2007 the surface area had fallen to about ten per cent of its original size. As the water retreated, the salt content increased several times over, killing most of the fish. The fishing industry collapsed, thousands of people lost their jobs, and boats lay rusting on sand many kilometres from the nearest water. The ship graveyard near Moynaq, now a strange tourist attraction, is a haunting reminder.
paras.E: The dry lake bed also caused health problems. Much of it was left covered with salt and the chemical residues of pesticides and fertilisers washed in from the cotton fields. Strong winds lift this dust into the air, and carry it over villages. Local people have suffered high rates of respiratory illnesses, throat cancers and other diseases, though the exact causes are still debated by scientists. The climate of the region has also changed: with no large body of water to moderate the temperature, summers have become hotter and winters colder, and the new desert, called the Aralkum, is now one of the world's youngest.
paras.F: Yet the story has one encouraging chapter. In the 2000s, with the help of the World Bank, Kazakhstan built a dam, completed in 2005, across the channel linking the North Aral to the South. The water level of the northern part rose rapidly, its salt content fell, and fish returned. Within a few years, catches had increased enough for the fishing industry to revive, and the shoreline moved back towards the town of Aralsk. The success shows that even severe damage can sometimes be partly reversed.
paras.G: The South Aral, however, in Uzbekistan, has not been so fortunate. Its eastern basin dried up completely in the 2010s, and the western basin continues to shrink. Efforts there have concentrated on planting salt-tolerant shrubs, such as saxaul, across the exposed seabed to hold down the dust. Meanwhile, the countries of the region are trying to use water more efficiently by lining canals, changing to crops that need less water and improving irrigation. The Aral Sea has become a warning to the world about the high price of ignoring the limits of natural resources.

paras.A: Sound is all around us, yet it is invisible. Every sound, from a whisper to a thunderclap, begins with something vibrating. When a guitar string is plucked, a drum is struck or a person speaks, the vibrating object pushes on the air next to it, which pushes on the air next to that, and so on. In this way a disturbance travels outwards as a wave. The air itself does not travel from the source to your ear; its particles simply move back and forth a small distance, passing the energy along, rather like a crowd doing a 'Mexican wave' in a stadium.
paras.B: Sound waves are called longitudinal waves, because the particles move in the same direction as the wave is travelling. They create alternating regions of compression, where particles are squeezed together, and rarefaction, where they are spread apart. Because sound needs particles to carry it, it cannot travel through a vacuum. In space, where there is almost no matter, the loudest explosion would be completely silent. This was demonstrated in the seventeenth century by experiments in which a ringing bell was placed in a jar and the air was gradually pumped out; the sound faded away, although the bell could still be seen vibrating.
paras.C: The speed of sound depends on the material. In air at 20 degrees Celsius, sound travels at about 343 metres per second, or roughly 1,235 kilometres per hour. It moves faster in liquids and solids, where the particles are closer together: about 1,480 metres per second in water, and around 5,000 metres per second in steel. Temperature also matters, because sound travels faster in warm air than in cold. The speed is why we see lightning before we hear thunder, and a rough way to estimate the distance of a storm is to count the seconds between the flash and the thunderclap and divide by three to find the distance in kilometres.
paras.D: Two properties describe what we hear. The first is frequency, the number of vibrations per second, which is measured in hertz (Hz) and which we hear as pitch. A young person with healthy hearing can detect frequencies from about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Sounds above this range are known as ultrasound, which is used by bats to find insects in the dark, and by doctors to produce images of unborn babies. The second property is amplitude, the size of the vibration, which determines loudness and is measured in decibels (dB). A whisper is about 30 dB, normal conversation about 60, and a rock concert about 110.
paras.E: Our ears are remarkably sensitive. Sound waves are collected by the outer ear and make the eardrum vibrate. Behind the eardrum, three tiny bones, the hammer, the anvil and the stirrup, amplify the vibrations and pass them to the cochlea, a spiral-shaped organ filled with fluid. Inside the cochlea, thousands of microscopic hair cells convert the vibrations into electrical signals, which the brain interprets as sound. Hair cells do not regrow in humans, so damage to them is permanent. Listening to sounds above about 85 dB for long periods can destroy them, which is why experts advise using ear protection at loud events and keeping the volume down on headphones.
paras.F: When sound waves meet an obstacle, several things can happen. They may be absorbed, as they are by soft materials such as curtains and carpets, or they may be reflected. A reflected sound that is heard separately from the original is called an echo. Since sound travels about 343 metres per second and the ear needs a gap of around a tenth of a second to separate two sounds, the reflecting surface must be at least seventeen metres away for a clear echo. Bats and dolphins use echoes to navigate and hunt, and ships use sonar to map the seabed in the same way.
paras.G: The pitch of a sound can also change when its source is moving. As an ambulance approaches, its siren sounds higher than when it is stationary, because the waves are squeezed together; as it moves away, the waves are stretched and the pitch drops. This is the Doppler effect, named after the Austrian physicist Christian Doppler, who described it in 1842. When an aircraft travels faster than sound, it outruns its own pressure waves, which build up into a shock wave heard on the ground as a sonic boom. In 1947, the American pilot Chuck Yeager became the first pilot officially recognised as breaking the sound barrier.

paras.A: In many of the world's most popular cities, finding an affordable home to rent is becoming harder. In New York, London, Berlin and Sydney, rents have risen faster than wages in recent years, and many young people spend more than a third of their income on housing. Faced with angry tenants, politicians are often tempted by a simple solution: limit how much landlords can charge. This policy, known as rent control, is one of the most debated policies in economics, and it divides opinion more sharply than almost any other.
paras.B: Supporters begin with the human argument. A home is not like other goods, they say; it is the base from which people work, raise children and build friendships. When rents suddenly increase, families can be forced to leave a neighbourhood where they have lived for decades, and children may have to change schools. Rent control gives tenants security and predictability, and it helps older residents and low-paid workers, such as nurses and bus drivers, to stay in the communities they serve. They also argue that, in a city with a shortage of homes, landlords hold the power in the market, and need to be restrained.
paras.C: Most economists, however, are sceptical. In a standard market, they say, a price below the market level raises the demand for housing while reducing the supply. Landlords who cannot earn enough from a controlled flat may stop maintaining it, convert it into flats for sale, or leave the rental market altogether. Developers may decide not to build new rental housing. One well-known study of San Francisco, published in 2019, found that landlords of properties subject to rent control reduced the supply of rental housing by around fifteen per cent, which helped to push up rents across the city.
paras.D: The benefits of control also tend to be unevenly spread. Tenants who already have a controlled flat gain, even if they are wealthy, and have a strong reason to stay put even when the flat no longer suits them: a family with spare rooms may not move, while a young couple seeks a place in vain. Newcomers, meanwhile, face higher rents in the uncontrolled part of the market. In Stockholm, where rents in the regulated sector are low, the average wait for a flat can be many years; some people queue for a decade or more.
paras.E: Defenders reply that modern rent regulation is not the crude freeze of the past. Many current schemes allow rents to rise each year in line with inflation, permit larger increases between tenants, or exempt new buildings, so that developers are not discouraged. In 2019, for example, Oregon became the first American state to introduce statewide rent control; it limited annual increases but exempted buildings less than fifteen years old. Supporters say such 'second-generation' policies protect tenants while leaving room for investment.
paras.F: The experience of Berlin shows how difficult the issue can be. In 2020 the city introduced a five-year cap on rents. Tenants welcomed it, but the number of flats advertised for rent dropped sharply, and many owners put their properties up for sale. In 2021 Germany's Federal Constitutional Court ruled that the city did not have the authority to pass the law, as rents were a matter for the national government, and the cap was cancelled. Some tenants then faced demands to repay the savings they had made.
paras.G: Housing is, in the end, a problem of supply. Most experts agree that the real answer to high rents is to build more homes, by relaxing planning rules, releasing land and financing social housing. But building takes years, and tenants who face a rent increase today cannot wait. For this reason, a carefully designed form of rent regulation, one which limits sudden increases without freezing prices and which exempts new buildings, may be a reasonable short-term measure, as long as it is accompanied by a serious plan to build more homes.

paras.A: Hidden among the desert mountains of southern Jordan lies Petra, a city carved into cliffs of rose-coloured sandstone. For this reason it is often called the 'Rose City'. It was the capital of the Nabataeans, an Arab people who were originally nomads of the desert, but who, from about the fourth century BC, became wealthy by controlling trade. Caravans carrying incense and spices from Arabia and India to the Mediterranean passed through Petra, and the Nabataeans taxed them and provided water and protection.
paras.B: Petra's builders faced a serious problem: very little rain falls in this part of the desert, and when it does, it tends to arrive in sudden, violent floods. The Nabataeans solved both problems at the same time. They cut channels into the rock to carry rainwater into huge underground tanks called cisterns, built dams to control floods, and laid pipes made of clay to bring spring water into the city. This system allowed Petra to support tens of thousands of people in a place where few others could have survived.
paras.C: Most visitors enter the city through the Siq, a narrow gorge about 1.2 kilometres long, whose walls in places rise to eighty metres. The path winds between the cliffs, sometimes so narrow that it is almost possible to touch both sides. Then, suddenly, the gorge opens, and the visitor sees the Treasury, known in Arabic as Al-Khazneh. About forty metres high, its columns and statues are cut directly out of the rock face. It was probably built as the tomb of a king in the first century BC or the first century AD.
paras.D: The name 'Treasury' comes from a local legend, which said that pirates or an Egyptian pharaoh had hidden treasure in the stone urn at the top of the building. Over the centuries, Bedouin passers-by fired guns at the urn, hoping to break it open, and the marks of the bullets can still be seen. In fact, the interior is only a plain room, and no treasure has ever been found. Higher up the valley are other monuments, such as the Monastery, called Ad Deir, which is reached by climbing about eight hundred rock-cut steps.
paras.E: Petra had a Greek-style theatre, with seats for about three thousand people, cut from the rock, and hundreds of tombs. In 106 AD, the Romans took control of the Nabataean kingdom, and the city continued to prosper for some time. But new sea routes reduced the importance of the caravan trade, and an earthquake in 363 AD destroyed many buildings. Over the following centuries, Petra was gradually abandoned, and by the Middle Ages it was known only to the local Bedouin.
paras.F: The outside world rediscovered the city in 1812, when the Swiss explorer Johann Ludwig Burckhardt, who had disguised himself as a Muslim scholar, persuaded a guide to take him there. Petra was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1985, and in 2007 it was named one of the New Seven Wonders of the World. Today, about a million people visit in a good year. This brings valuable income, but also problems of erosion and damage, and archaeologists point out that large parts of the city have still not been excavated.

paras.A: Many people believe that a refrigerator makes cold. In reality, there is no such thing as 'making cold'; there is only the removal of heat. Heat always flows from a warmer place to a cooler one, just as water runs downhill. A refrigerator is a machine that does the opposite: it takes heat from the inside of the cabinet, where the food is, and pumps it out into the kitchen. The heat you can feel at the back of a fridge is the heat that has been removed from your food.
paras.B: To do this, the machine uses a special liquid called a refrigerant, which circulates in a closed loop of pipes. Inside the cabinet, the pipes are part of the evaporator. Here, the liquid is at low pressure and turns into a gas, a process that absorbs a lot of heat, in the same way that water on your skin makes you feel cold as it evaporates. The gas then goes to the compressor, which squeezes it, so that its pressure and temperature rise sharply.
paras.C: The hot gas flows through the condenser, the coiled pipes at the back or underneath the fridge. Because the gas is now hotter than the room, it loses its heat to the air, and as it cools, it condenses back into a liquid. The liquid is then forced through a very narrow opening, called an expansion valve, where its pressure drops suddenly and it becomes extremely cold. It returns to the evaporator, and the cycle starts again. A thermostat switches the compressor on and off to keep the inside at a steady temperature.
paras.D: Artificial cooling developed slowly. For thousands of years, people stored food in cellars or used ice cut from frozen lakes in winter. In 1748, the Scottish professor William Cullen demonstrated, in Glasgow, that liquid evaporating in a partial vacuum could produce cooling. In 1834, the American inventor Jacob Perkins patented a machine using the vapour-compression cycle that is still used today. Domestic refrigerators became common in the United States in the 1920s and 1930s, and in Europe and Asia, mainly after the Second World War.
paras.E: The early machines used poisonous gases such as ammonia. In the 1930s, they were replaced by chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs, which were safe to handle. However, in the 1970s, scientists discovered that CFCs were destroying the ozone layer that protects the Earth from harmful ultraviolet light. In 1987, countries signed the Montreal Protocol, which phased them out. Their replacements, called HFCs, did not harm the ozone but were powerful greenhouse gases, so in 2016 an international agreement, the Kigali Amendment, set out a plan to reduce them as well.
paras.F: The refrigerator has changed how people eat. Bacteria multiply slowly at temperatures below five degrees Celsius, so food kept in a fridge, normally at about four degrees, stays fresh for days longer. A freezer, at around minus eighteen degrees, stops bacterial growth almost completely. Fridges, together with refrigerated lorries and supermarket freezers, form a 'cold chain' that allows fresh food to be transported over long distances. In countries where the cold chain is weak, a considerable proportion of food is lost before it reaches the consumer.

paras.A: In March 2020, Luxembourg became the first country in the world to make all public transport free for everyone, residents and visitors alike. The city of Tallinn, the capital of Estonia, had already introduced free travel for its residents in 2013, and a few smaller cities, such as Dunkirk in France, have followed. In the summer of 2022, Germany sold a nine-euro monthly ticket valid on regional transport across the entire country, and tens of millions of tickets were bought. The idea that fares might be abolished altogether, once seen as unrealistic, is now being discussed seriously.
paras.B: Supporters present three main arguments. The first is environmental: if buses and trains cost nothing, more people will leave their cars at home, reducing traffic jams, noise and air pollution. The second is social: transport fares are a heavy burden for the poor, and free travel would give everybody access to jobs, schools and hospitals. The third is practical: collecting fares costs money, because of machines, ticket inspectors and administration, and in cities where fares cover only a small part of the budget, collection may cost nearly as much as it earns.
paras.C: Opponents answer that nothing is really free. Public transport has to be paid for, and if passengers do not pay, taxpayers must, including those who never use buses. In many cities, fares provide a large proportion of the money needed to run the system, and removing them would require either higher taxes or cuts in other services. There are also doubts about the environmental benefits. Studies of free-fare schemes suggest that many of the new passengers are people who used to walk or cycle, rather than drivers, so the effect on car traffic is much smaller than supporters hope.
paras.D: The evidence from Germany supports this view. During the three months of the cheap ticket, the number of journeys by public transport rose sharply, but surveys indicated that car use fell only slightly. Many of the extra journeys were leisure trips, and some trains became so crowded that travellers complained about the lack of space. This highlights another problem: if a service is free, demand may increase faster than the supply of buses and trains, and the quality of the service may fall.
paras.E: Free transport can work well in small cities with low traffic, where the cost is modest and the buses are not full. In larger cities, there are alternative ways to reach the same goals. Reduced fares or free passes can be targeted at students, pensioners and people on low incomes. Money saved by not cutting fares can instead pay for more frequent services, new routes and safer stations. Surveys in many countries show that when people choose not to use public transport, the most common reasons are not the price but the waiting time, the lack of a direct route and the unreliability of the service.
paras.F: In my view, free public transport is an attractive slogan but rarely the best use of limited funds. A bus that arrives every five minutes and takes passengers where they want to go will persuade more drivers to leave their cars than a bus that is free but comes once an hour. Cities should therefore invest first in frequency and reliability, keep fares low for those who need help, and consider free travel only where the system already has spare capacity.

paras.A: The Bayeux Tapestry is one of the most famous works of medieval art, and one of the most remarkable historical documents ever made. Although it is called a tapestry, it is in fact an embroidery: the pictures were stitched with coloured wool on a long strip of linen cloth. It is about seventy metres long but only about half a metre high, and it tells the story of the events that led to the Norman conquest of England in 1066.
paras.B: The story begins with the English king, Edward the Confessor, who had no children. The tapestry shows Harold, the most powerful English nobleman, travelling to Normandy, where he swears an oath, apparently promising to support William, the Duke of Normandy, as Edward's successor. When Edward dies, Harold is crowned king himself. William, angry at this betrayal, builds a fleet and sails across the Channel with an army. The final scenes show the Battle of Hastings, fought on 14 October 1066, in which Harold is killed and the English are defeated.
paras.C: The embroidery is full of lively details. Hundreds of people, horses, ships and buildings appear in the main scenes, and the Latin words stitched above them explain what is happening. Above and below the main story run narrow borders, which contain animals, birds and scenes from fables, and in the later parts, show the bodies of dead soldiers. In one famous scene, a comet appears in the sky as people point at it in fear. Modern astronomers believe it was Halley's Comet, which passed close to the Earth in 1066.
paras.D: The most famous scene shows a figure with an arrow in his face, and for centuries it has been assumed to be King Harold killed by an arrow in the eye. Historians, however, are not sure. The figure beside him is being struck down by a sword, and either could be the king. Some have also noticed that the stitching in this part of the tapestry was altered by restorers in later times, so it is hard to know what the original embroiderers intended.
paras.E: Who made the tapestry? Most historians think it was commissioned by Bishop Odo of Bayeux, William's half-brother, who appears in the story and who fought at Hastings. The wool was dyed in only a few colours, using plants, and the style resembles that of English manuscripts from Canterbury, so it was probably embroidered by skilled English needlewomen. Because the right-hand end is missing, the story ends abruptly, and some experts think the original showed William being crowned king.
paras.F: For centuries, the work was displayed once a year in Bayeux Cathedral, and it narrowly escaped destruction during the French Revolution, when it was almost cut up to cover military wagons. In 1803, Napoleon had it brought to Paris to inspire an invasion of England, and in the Second World War it was studied with great interest by German officials. Today it is kept in a museum in Bayeux, in a specially darkened gallery, because light and humidity would damage the fragile threads.

qs.title: Question 13

paras.A: A hurricane is one of the most destructive forces in nature. At its peak, it is a rotating storm hundreds of kilometres wide, with winds that can exceed 250 kilometres per hour and rain that can flood entire regions. The same type of storm is called a hurricane in the Atlantic and north-eastern Pacific, a typhoon in the north-western Pacific, and a cyclone in the Indian Ocean and around Australia. All are known to scientists as tropical cyclones.
paras.B: Hurricanes begin over warm tropical oceans. They need sea water that is at least about 26.5 degrees Celsius to a depth of some fifty metres, which is why they form mainly in late summer and autumn. Warm water evaporates, and the moist air rises. As the air rises, it cools, and the water vapour condenses into clouds and rain. This releases large amounts of heat, which warms the air further and makes it rise even faster. The rising air leaves low pressure near the surface, so more air flows in to replace it.
paras.C: If this were all, the air would simply flow straight into the centre. However, the Earth's rotation deflects moving air, an effect called the Coriolis force, and as a result, the air spirals inwards. In the northern hemisphere, a hurricane rotates anticlockwise; in the southern hemisphere, clockwise. Because the Coriolis force is weak close to the equator, hurricanes almost never form within about five degrees of it. As the storm strengthens, the spiral develops a clear structure, with long bands of cloud and rain curving around a central core.
paras.D: At the centre of a mature hurricane is the eye, usually thirty to sixty kilometres across, where the air is surprisingly calm and the sky may be clear. Surrounding it is the eyewall, a ring of towering thunderclouds, where the winds are strongest and the rain heaviest. The danger does not end when the eye passes, because the winds then return from the opposite direction. Meteorologists classify hurricanes on the Saffir-Simpson scale, which runs from Category 1, with winds of at least 119 kilometres per hour, to Category 5, with winds of 252 kilometres per hour or more.
paras.E: Strong winds cause great damage, but most deaths are caused by water. The low pressure and the force of the wind push the sea up in a dome, called a storm surge, which can flood coastal areas with several metres of water. In 2005, Hurricane Katrina's surge overwhelmed the defences of New Orleans, and flooding killed well over a thousand people. Heavy rain falling over several days can also cause rivers to overflow and trigger landslides, sometimes hundreds of kilometres inland.
paras.F: When a hurricane moves over land or cooler water, it loses its supply of warm, moist air and weakens quickly. Scientists expect that global warming will affect these storms, though they are still studying exactly how. Warmer oceans provide more energy, and warmer air holds more water vapour, so the strongest hurricanes are likely to become more intense and rainier. It is less clear whether the total number of hurricanes will change. Meanwhile, satellites and computer models now allow forecasters to predict the path of a storm several days in advance, which has saved many lives.

qs.title: Questions 23–26

paras.A: The average person now looks at a smartphone dozens of times a day. Many of us reach for the phone as soon as we wake up and check it while we eat, travel and watch television. This habit has led to a widespread belief that smartphones are damaging our ability to concentrate, particularly among the young. But is this true, or is it the latest in a long line of moral panics about new technology? The evidence is more mixed than headlines suggest.
paras.B: The case against smartphones starts with interruptions. Each notification, whether a message, a news alert or a social-media 'like', pulls attention away from the task in hand. Researchers who study workplaces have found that after an interruption, it can take a long time to return fully to the original task: some have estimated that it can take more than twenty minutes. Because we also tend to switch from one app to another, the brain is repeatedly forced to start again, a habit which psychologists call 'task switching' and which tends to make people slower and more error-prone.
paras.C: A well-known experiment, published in 2017, suggested that the mere presence of a phone on the desk, even switched off, reduced performance on tests of memory and problem solving. The authors argued that part of the brain's resources was being used to resist the temptation to check it. However, later attempts to repeat this experiment have produced mixed results, and some researchers believe the effect, if it exists, is much smaller than first claimed. The science is therefore not as settled as some commentators claim.
paras.D: Defenders of smartphones make several points. Concerns about a new technology harming the mind are very old: the philosopher Socrates worried that writing would weaken memory, and in the nineteenth century, some doctors warned that reading novels was dangerous. Phones also help concentration in many ways, for example through timers, notes, dictionaries and apps that block distractions. And the real problem, they say, may be not the device but how it is used, since a person who turns off notifications can use a phone with no more distraction than a book.
paras.E: Schools are at the centre of the debate. France banned phones in primary and middle schools from 2018, and the Netherlands introduced a ban in classrooms in 2024. Teachers in many countries report that lessons are calmer and that pupils talk to each other more at break time when phones are put away. But critics respond that a ban alone does not teach children to manage technology themselves, and that sooner or later they will have to learn to do so.
paras.F: On balance, the claim that smartphones are destroying our concentration is exaggerated, but the evidence that they can interrupt it is strong. Practical steps help: turning off non-essential notifications, keeping the phone out of the bedroom, and setting aside periods of the day for uninterrupted work or study. The goal should be neither to condemn the technology nor to ignore its dangers, but to use it deliberately instead of being used by it.

ps.title: The Delta Works: Holding Back the Sea

paras.A: About a quarter of the Netherlands lies below sea level, and much of the rest is only a few metres above it. The country's name, which means 'low countries', is therefore very appropriate. For a thousand years, the Dutch have lived with the threat of floods, and have fought it by building dikes, draining lakes and constructing windmills to pump out water. Land reclaimed from the sea is called a polder, and a large proportion of the country's population lives and works on such land.
paras.B: The worst disaster of modern times occurred on the night of 31 January 1953. A powerful storm drove the North Sea against the south-western coast, and in many places the sea walls broke. More than 1,800 people were killed, tens of thousands of animals drowned, and about 70,000 people had to be evacuated from their homes. Most of the victims were asleep when the water arrived, and many lived in the province of Zeeland, where a maze of islands and estuaries made the land especially vulnerable.
paras.C: The Dutch government responded by launching the Delta Works, a series of dams, sluices, locks, dikes and storm-surge barriers, built between 1950 and 1997 in the south-west of the country. The original plan was to close off nearly all the sea inlets with solid dams, which would shorten the coastline by hundreds of kilometres and make it much easier to defend. Several of the dams were completed in the 1960s and 1970s, and they transformed the region's geography by turning sea inlets into freshwater lakes.
paras.D: But environmental concerns changed the plan. The Eastern Scheldt estuary was home to rich beds of mussels and oysters, and fishermen and scientists protested that a solid dam would kill the salt-water ecosystem. After years of debate, the government decided to build a barrier with huge steel gates, which would normally stay open to allow the tide to flow in and out, but could be closed when a storm threatened. Completed in 1986, the Eastern Scheldt barrier is about nine kilometres long, and was among the most expensive projects in Dutch history.
paras.E: The last major work was the Maeslant barrier, finished in 1997, which protects the port of Rotterdam. It has two giant arms, each about 210 metres long, which normally rest on the banks of the waterway. When a storm surge threatens, they float out and meet in the middle, then sink to the bottom to close the channel. The barrier is controlled by a computer rather than by a person. Engineers regard the Delta Works as one of the greatest achievements of modern engineering, and in 1994 the American Society of Civil Engineers listed it as one of the seven wonders of the modern world.
paras.F: The Dutch know that the job is never finished. Sea levels are rising because of climate change, and the land in some places is slowly sinking. Today the country spends large sums on safety, using a system of standards which requires the most protected areas to withstand a flood that has only a very small chance of happening in any year. Dutch engineers also work with nature rather than against it: a programme called 'Room for the River' lowered flood plains and widened channels, to give rivers space to rise safely. Many countries now look to the Netherlands for advice.

qs.title: Questions 10–13

paras.A: A bridge has to do a simple job: carry a load across a gap. But the way it does so depends on how it deals with two basic forces. Compression is a pushing force that squeezes a material, and tension is a pulling force that stretches it. Every part of a bridge is under one or the other. Stone and concrete are strong under compression but weak in tension, while steel and cables are very strong when pulled. Good design puts each material where it is best suited.
paras.B: The simplest type is the beam bridge, which is a horizontal beam resting on supports at each end, such as a plank across a stream. When a load presses down on the middle, the top of the beam is squeezed and the bottom is stretched. A beam can only span short distances, because a longer beam would bend or break under its own weight. For longer crossings, engineers add piers, or they use trusses, frameworks of triangles, which are rigid and use material efficiently.
paras.C: Arch bridges, used since ancient times, turn the downward weight into compression. The load pushes along the curve of the arch to the ends, where it is carried into the ground by strong abutments. The Romans built arches of stone, and some, such as the Pont du Gard in France, have lasted two thousand years. Because stone does not need to resist tension, builders could use it without any metal. Modern arches are often made of steel or reinforced concrete.
paras.D: Suspension bridges can cross the longest gaps. Two tall towers support massive cables that hang in a curve, and thinner vertical cables hang from them to hold up the deck. The load is carried by the main cables, which are in tension, and by the towers, which are in compression. The Golden Gate Bridge in San Francisco, opened in 1937, has a main span of about 1,280 metres. The longest bridge span in the world belongs to the 1915 Canakkale Bridge in Turkey, which opened in 2022 and stretches over 2,000 metres.
paras.E: In a cable-stayed bridge, the cables run straight from the towers to the deck in a fan or harp pattern, instead of hanging from a curve. This design is economical for medium spans. The Millau Viaduct in southern France, opened in 2004, is a cable-stayed bridge whose tallest tower is about 343 metres from base to tip, making it higher than the Eiffel Tower's structure. Engineers value it because it is both strong and elegant, and it hardly disturbs the valley of the River Tarn below.
paras.F: Bridge designers also face dangers that are not obvious. In 1940, the Tacoma Narrows Bridge in the United States twisted violently in a moderate wind and collapsed only four months after opening. The cause was flutter, a self-reinforcing vibration, and the disaster taught engineers to test models of their designs in wind tunnels. Today, bridges are also built to withstand earthquakes, floods, heavy lorries and the effects of rust. A well-built modern bridge may last well over a hundred years, but only if it is regularly inspected and maintained.

ps.title: Should Governments Pay for the Arts?

paras.A: Every year, governments around the world spend billions on theatres, orchestras, museums and galleries. In some countries, such as France and Germany, public support for the arts is generous; in others, such as the United States, the state contributes comparatively little and most funding comes from private donors and ticket sales. The question of whether public money should be used to support the arts at all is often debated, especially when budgets are tight and hospitals and schools are in need.
paras.B: Supporters of public funding begin with an argument about value. The arts, they say, enrich life in ways that cannot be measured by prices. Great works of music, literature and painting are part of a nation's heritage, and everybody should have the chance to enjoy them, not only the wealthy. If theatres and museums had to survive on ticket sales alone, they would have to set prices so high that ordinary families could not go, or choose only the popular shows that are sure to sell.
paras.C: There is also an economic argument. Cultural activity attracts tourists, who spend money in hotels, restaurants and shops. A large gallery or festival can transform a declining city: the Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao, which opened in 1997, is often cited as an example of a building that helped revive a former industrial port. Supporters add that artists often work for low pay, and without subsidies, many talented people would give up, depriving the country of future creativity.
paras.D: Critics reply that it is unfair to force all taxpayers to pay for activities that only a minority enjoy. Surveys in several countries show that audiences for opera and classical music tend to be older, richer and better educated than the population as a whole, so subsidies may amount to a transfer of money from poorer people to richer ones. Some also argue that subsidised art becomes safe and dull, because artists write to please the committees that decide on funding rather than the public.
paras.E: Opponents add that private support can do the job. In the United States, wealthy donors, companies and foundations give huge sums to museums and orchestras, and new methods, such as crowdfunding, allow thousands of small donors to support a project they like. Furthermore, some of the most popular art of the last century, such as pop music and film, flourished without subsidies. Perhaps the market, they suggest, is a better judge of what people want than a committee of experts.
paras.F: The writer's view is that a middle position is the most sensible. Governments should support the things that markets are likely to neglect, such as young artists, local theatres, school music programmes and the care of historic collections. These bring benefits to the whole community, in the same way as parks and libraries. At the same time, subsidies should come with conditions: cheap tickets for those on low incomes, touring programmes to reach small towns, and regular checks that public money is used well. Such a policy would respect both the value of art and the taxpayer.

qs.title: Questions 39–40

paras.A: For many Europeans in the nineteenth century, Timbuktu was a name that stood for the end of the earth. In reality, this city in the West African country of Mali was for centuries one of the most important centres of trade and learning in Africa. It lies just north of the Niger River on the southern edge of the Sahara, at a point where the desert routes met the river. Tuareg nomads founded a settlement here around the twelfth century, and its position soon made it prosperous.
paras.B: Timbuktu's wealth came from the exchange of goods between two very different regions. Caravans of camels crossed the desert carrying salt from mines in the Sahara, which was scarce and valuable in the forests of the south. They returned with gold, ivory and enslaved people from the south, and the goods were also moved by boat along the river. The city's markets were also full of cloth, copper and books. A saying quoted in Africa claimed that salt came from the north, gold from the south and silver from the country of the white men, but that the word of God and the treasures of wisdom were found only in Timbuktu.
paras.C: The city's most famous ruler was not its own. Mansa Musa, the emperor of Mali, travelled to Mecca on pilgrimage in 1324 and 1325 with a huge retinue and so much gold that he is said to have lowered its price in Cairo for years. On his return, he brought back scholars and architects, among them the poet Abu Ishaq al-Sahili, who designed the Djinguereber Mosque in Timbuktu, built in 1327. The mosque, made of mud and wood, still stands today.
paras.D: The city reached its height in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Its mosque schools, the best known of which was at Sankore, attracted students from across the Muslim world, who studied the Quran, law, mathematics, astronomy and medicine. Libraries were established by families, and the copying and trading of manuscripts became a respected profession. Estimates suggest that several hundred thousand manuscripts survive in the region, written in Arabic and in local African languages, many of them still in private hands.
paras.E: The decline began in 1591, when a Moroccan army crossed the Sahara and defeated the Songhai Empire, which then ruled the city. Many scholars were exiled, and Timbuktu lost its independence. Later, sea routes along the African coast diverted trade away from the desert. Europeans meanwhile were hearing rumours of a city of gold. Alexander Gordon Laing, a Scot, reached it in 1826, but he was killed soon afterwards. The Frenchman René Caillié, who arrived in 1828 disguised as a Muslim traveller, was the first European to reach the city and return to describe it.
paras.F: UNESCO listed Timbuktu as a World Heritage Site in 1988. In 2012, armed groups occupied the city and destroyed several tombs of Muslim saints, which they considered idolatrous. Before they arrived, librarians and local people secretly removed many manuscripts from the libraries and smuggled them to the capital, Bamako, in trunks and boats, saving much of the collection. The mausoleums have since been rebuilt, and efforts continue to preserve and catalogue the manuscripts, which have so much to tell us about African history.

paras.A: Glass is so common that we hardly notice it. We look through it in windows, drink from it, and read the screens of phones protected by it. Yet it is a very unusual material. Most solids are crystals, with their atoms arranged in a regular pattern. Glass is an amorphous solid: its atoms are arranged randomly, like those of a liquid, but fixed in place. For this reason, glass is transparent, as light passes through without being scattered by crystal boundaries.
paras.B: Glass can occur naturally. When lightning strikes sand, or when a volcano erupts, the intense heat can melt sand into natural glass. One example is obsidian, a black volcanic glass, which prehistoric people chipped into razor-sharp blades and arrowheads. People learned to make glass themselves around 3,500 years ago in the Middle East, but the invention of glassblowing, probably in the first century BC in the Roman Empire, was the great breakthrough, because it made it possible to produce containers cheaply and in large numbers.
paras.C: The main ingredient of modern glass is silica, normally in the form of sand, which makes up about seventy per cent of ordinary glass. Pure silica melts only at extremely high temperatures, so manufacturers add soda ash, a form of sodium carbonate, which lowers the melting point. However, soda ash makes glass dissolve in water, so limestone is also added to make it durable. The mixture, called the batch, is heated in a furnace at around 1,500 degrees Celsius until it forms a thick, glowing liquid.
paras.D: Recycled glass, called cullet, is usually added to the batch. Cullet melts at a lower temperature than the raw materials, so every tonne used saves energy, and it reduces the quantity of raw materials that must be dug up. Glass can be recycled again and again without losing its quality. Different colours come from small additions: iron makes bottles green, and a trace of cobalt makes them blue. Manufacturers must separate clear, green and brown glass before recycling it, because even a small amount of the wrong colour can spoil a batch.
paras.E: Most window glass is now made by the float process, invented by the British engineer Alastair Pilkington in the 1950s. Molten glass flows out of the furnace onto a bath of molten tin. Because tin is heavier than glass, the glass floats on it and spreads out to form a perfectly flat ribbon with smooth surfaces. The ribbon is then cooled slowly in a long oven called a lehr, a step known as annealing, which prevents internal stresses that would make the glass crack. Finally, it is cut into sheets.
paras.F: Further treatment can give glass special properties. Toughened glass, used in car windows, is heated and then cooled very quickly, which makes it several times stronger, and if it breaks, it shatters into small blunt pieces. Borosilicate glass, which contains boron, expands very little when heated, and is therefore used for laboratory equipment and cooking dishes. A popular myth says that old windows are thicker at the bottom because glass flows slowly over centuries, but in fact, early glassmakers produced uneven sheets, and builders usually placed the heavy edge downwards.

paras.A: We are surrounded by advertising. In a typical day, a person in a modern city may see thousands of messages: on billboards and buses, on websites, in apps and on social media, before videos and between television programmes. The advertising industry argues that this is harmless, and that it informs consumers and supports free services and the media. Critics argue that the amount of advertising has become excessive and that some of it is harmful. The question is how far the state should go in restricting it.
paras.B: Some restrictions are already widely accepted. Most countries ban or severely limit advertising of tobacco, a policy encouraged by an international health treaty signed in 2003 and in force since 2005. Many have rules to prevent false claims, and in several countries, advertisements aimed at young children are controlled. These measures are seen as protection against products that cause serious harm, or against deception. Few people argue that anything at all should be allowed to be advertised.
paras.C: Some places have gone further. In 2006, the Brazilian city of São Paulo passed the Clean City Law, which banned billboards and most outdoor advertising. Hundreds of signs were removed, and the city's buildings, long hidden behind them, suddenly came into view. Surveys suggested that most residents approved. The French city of Grenoble also decided, in 2014, to remove hundreds of advertising panels from its streets and to use the space for trees and community notices instead.
paras.D: Supporters of tighter controls claim that advertising does more than provide information. Its aim is to persuade, often by creating a sense of dissatisfaction, so that people feel they need things they did not want before. This encourages consumption, with costs for the environment, and it can lead people, especially the young, to compare themselves with unrealistic images. Some argue that food advertising contributes to unhealthy eating habits, and that promotion of junk food to children should be restricted in the same way as tobacco.
paras.E: Opponents respond that advertising is a form of free speech, and that restrictions can be a slippery slope: once the state decides which messages are acceptable, there is no clear place to stop. Advertising also pays for much of the media and the internet, so cutting it could lead to higher prices for consumers or the closure of newspapers. Small businesses rely on it to compete with big firms, and consumers need information in order to make choices. In their view, the best response to bad advertising is education, not prohibition.
paras.F: In my view, there is a case for focusing on the cases where the evidence of harm is strongest. Products such as tobacco and gambling, and marketing aimed at children, deserve firm limits, and the public spaces of a city should not be treated as places that anyone with money can fill. On the other hand, a general ban on advertising would be a blunt tool with unpredictable consequences. A balanced policy would protect the vulnerable and keep streets pleasant, while leaving honest advertisers free to describe their goods.

paras.A: The Komodo dragon is the largest lizard alive today. Adults commonly reach about two and a half metres in length and weigh around seventy kilograms, although captive animals can be heavier. It is found only on a handful of Indonesian islands: Komodo, Rinca, Gili Motang and Gili Dasami, and parts of the larger island of Flores. Outside the world of local fishermen, it was unknown until 1910, when a Dutch officer, hearing stories of 'land crocodiles', went to look and returned with a skin and a report that interested scientists.
paras.B: Komodo dragons are formidable hunters. They can run at short bursts of speed, climb trees when young, and swim from island to island. Their prey includes deer, wild pigs and, occasionally, water buffalo, which can weigh many times more than the lizard. A dragon usually lies in ambush beside a trail, then rushes out and bites. It has sharp, curved teeth with serrated edges, like those of a shark, and swallows large lumps of meat whole, stretching its jaws wide, and can eat up to eighty per cent of its body weight in a single meal.
paras.C: For many years, it was believed that the dragon's mouth contained so many bacteria that a bite would cause fatal infection. In 2009, however, researchers found that Komodo dragons possess venom glands in their lower jaws. Their venom contains substances that lower blood pressure and prevent blood from clotting, so that the victim goes into shock and bleeds heavily. The scientists suggested that the dragon bites its prey and then simply follows it until it weakens. The question of how much is due to venom and how much to bacteria is still debated.
paras.D: The senses of the Komodo dragon are well adapted to finding food. Its forked yellow tongue flicks in and out, collecting scent particles in the air and passing them to a special organ in the roof of the mouth. In this way a dragon can detect a carcass several kilometres away, if the wind is in the right direction. Its eyesight and hearing are less impressive. Adult dragons are solitary animals and, when many gather at a kill, fights break out, with the largest males eating first.
paras.E: Female dragons lay about twenty eggs in a hole in the ground, or in the nests of other birds, and guard them for several months. The young are small, about 40 centimetres long, and very vulnerable, even to adult dragons, which sometimes eat them. For this reason, they spend their first years in trees, feeding on insects and small lizards. In 2006, scientists in Britain discovered that a female in a zoo, which had never been with a male, had produced fertile eggs, an event called parthenogenesis. The young were all male.
paras.F: The Komodo dragon is classified as Endangered, with only a few thousand individuals left in the wild. The animals' range is small, and they are threatened by loss of habitat, poaching of their prey and, in the long run, by climate change, because rising seas may flood the low-lying areas where they live. Komodo National Park was created in 1980 to protect them, and it became a World Heritage Site in 1991. Visitors are accompanied by trained rangers, and the number of tourists is controlled to reduce disturbance.
