qs.title: Questions 9–13

paras.A: Every time you watch a video on a streaming site, make a video call or send a message to another continent, there is a good chance that your data is travelling as pulses of light through a thin strand of glass. These strands, called optical fibres, are the backbone of the modern internet. A single fibre is thinner than a human hair, yet it can carry vast amounts of information at nearly the speed of light, over very long distances, with very little loss of signal.
paras.B: The idea behind optical fibres is total internal reflection. When light travels from one transparent material to another, for example from glass to air, it bends. If it strikes the boundary at a shallow angle, it does not escape at all but is reflected back, just as if the boundary were a mirror. A fibre uses this effect. It has a central core of very pure glass, surrounded by a layer of cladding, which is glass with a slightly lower refractive index. Light entering the core keeps bouncing off the boundary, and is guided along the fibre even if it bends.
paras.C: Light pulses are produced by lasers or light-emitting diodes, switched on and off millions or billions of times a second. A pulse stands for a one, and its absence for a zero, so that any digital information can be transmitted. At the far end, a detector converts the pulses back into electrical signals. Engineers can send many signals through the same fibre at the same time by using different colours of light, a technique known as wavelength-division multiplexing, which multiplies the capacity of a cable many times over.
paras.D: The technology was made possible by the work of Charles Kao, a Chinese-born engineer at Standard Telecommunication Laboratories in England. In 1966, he and a colleague showed that, if glass could be made much purer, fibres could carry signals over long distances. At that time, light faded within a few metres in the best glass available. In 1970, researchers at the American company Corning produced a fibre with low enough loss to be practical. Kao received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2009 for his work.
paras.E: Optical fibres have several advantages over copper wires. They can carry far more information, the signal weakens much less over distance, so fewer amplifiers are needed along a cable, and they are not affected by electrical interference. They are also light, and made from glass, which is abundant. The first transatlantic fibre-optic cable, TAT-8, began operating in 1988. Today, a network of undersea fibre cables carries the great majority of intercontinental data traffic, far more than satellites.
paras.F: Beyond communications, fibres have other uses. In medicine, a bundle of fibres in an endoscope lets doctors see inside the body through a small opening without major surgery. Industries use fibres as sensors, since stretching or heating changes the way light passes through them, and engineers have embedded them in bridges and pipelines to detect stresses. As demand for data grows, researchers are developing new types of fibre with multiple cores and even hollow centres, in which light travels through air and may travel even faster than in glass.

ps.title: Is a Universal Basic Income a Good Idea?

paras.A: Imagine that every citizen received a regular payment from the government, enough to cover basic needs, whether they worked or not, and without any conditions. This is the idea of a universal basic income, or UBI. Once thought to be an eccentric dream, it has been taken up by economists, technology entrepreneurs and politicians of both the left and the right. The growth of automation, the insecurity of many jobs and the experience of the pandemic have made it seem less impractical than it once did.
paras.B: Its supporters offer several arguments. The first is poverty: a basic income would guarantee that nobody falls below a minimum standard of living. The second concerns administration. Existing benefits are complicated, and many people who need help do not receive it, because they do not understand the rules or are ashamed to apply. A universal payment would be simple and would not need officials to check whether people qualify. The third is freedom: with a secure income, people could study, care for relatives, start businesses or leave poor jobs.
paras.C: Opponents have two main objections. The first is cost. If every adult received an amount sufficient to live on, the sum would be enormous, and the money would have to come from higher taxes or cuts in other services, such as health or education. The second is the fear that people would stop working. Why take a boring job, critics ask, if you are paid anyway? If many people withdrew from the labour market, the economy would suffer, and there would be fewer taxes to pay for the scheme.
paras.D: Evidence from experiments is still limited, but it offers some answers. In Finland, in 2017 and 2018, two thousand unemployed people received 560 euros a month without conditions. The results showed that they were slightly more likely to be in work than a control group, and they reported better wellbeing and less stress. In Stockton, California, 125 residents received 500 dollars a month for two years, and the proportion of them in full-time work rose faster than among a comparison group. Neither of these projects found that people stopped working.
paras.E: Critics respond that such experiments are small, short and not truly universal. Because the participants knew the payments would end, they may have behaved differently from people who would receive money for life. Moreover, a national scheme would require taxes, and taxes themselves can change behaviour. Another long-running example is the Alaska Permanent Fund, which has paid every resident a yearly dividend from oil revenues since 1982. It is popular and has not been found to reduce employment, but the sums are fairly small, and are not enough to live on.
paras.F: The writer concludes that the evidence is not yet strong enough to support a full national scheme, but it is strong enough to justify further experiments. Larger and longer trials, in different kinds of places, would show how basic incomes affect work, health and children, and how much they would really cost. Meanwhile, governments could simplify existing benefits and extend help where it is most needed. A basic income may or may not be the future, but the question deserves to be tested, not simply argued about.

ps.title: Chocolate: From Sacred Drink to Sweet Treat

paras.A: Chocolate begins with the seeds of the cacao tree, a small evergreen that grows in the warm, wet regions near the equator. Its scientific name, Theobroma cacao, means 'food of the gods' in Greek. The tree is native to the upper Amazon region, but people in Central America were the first to turn its seeds into a drink, more than three thousand years ago. The Olmec, and later the Maya, prepared a bitter, frothy mixture of ground cacao, water and spices, and served it at ceremonies.
paras.B: The Aztecs valued cacao so highly that they used the beans as money. According to Spanish accounts, a turkey could be bought for a few hundred beans. Their drink, called xocolatl, was often flavoured with chilli and was consumed mainly by warriors, priests and nobles. When Spanish explorers reached Mexico in the sixteenth century, they found the taste bitter, but they discovered that adding sugar and honey made it pleasant, and they took the drink back to Spain, where it became fashionable at court.
paras.C: For about two hundred years, chocolate was a luxury drink for the rich across Europe. It was made at home by grinding roasted beans, and the result was usually gritty and greasy. A big change came in 1828, when the Dutch chemist Coenraad van Houten invented a press that squeezed most of the fat, called cocoa butter, from the ground beans. The remaining cake could be turned into a fine powder that mixed easily with water. Van Houten's process also made the cocoa less bitter.
paras.D: The solid bar followed. In 1847, the British firm J. S. Fry and Sons mixed cocoa powder with sugar and melted cocoa butter to produce the first chocolate that could be moulded and eaten. In 1875, the Swiss manufacturer Daniel Peter created milk chocolate, using condensed milk developed by his neighbour, Henri Nestlé. A few years later, in 1879, another Swiss, Rodolphe Lindt, invented the conche, a machine that stirs the chocolate for many hours, giving it a smooth, melting texture.
paras.E: Making chocolate today is still a long process. Farmers harvest the large pods by hand, split them open and scoop out the seeds with their sweet white pulp. The seeds are piled in heaps and left to ferment for several days, which develops the flavour, and then they are dried in the sun. At the factory, the beans are roasted, cracked, ground into a paste and refined. Dark chocolate contains a high percentage of cocoa, while milk chocolate has less cocoa and added milk powder.
paras.F: The industry now faces serious challenges. More than half of the world's cocoa comes from just two countries in West Africa, Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana, where most of it is grown by millions of small farmers who earn very little. There are well-documented cases of child labour on some farms, and the clearing of forest for new plantations has damaged wildlife. Certification schemes such as Fairtrade try to improve conditions, but critics say that real change will require higher prices and more transparent supply chains.

ps.title: How the Immune System Protects Us

paras.A: Every day, we are surrounded by bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites that could make us ill. Most of the time we do not notice, because the body has a defence system of cells, tissues and organs that detects and destroys invaders. This is the immune system. It must perform two difficult tasks: recognise a very wide range of threats, and avoid attacking the body's own healthy cells. When it works well, we hardly notice it; when it fails, the consequences can be serious.
paras.B: The first line of defence is physical. The skin forms a tough barrier that most germs cannot cross, and the openings of the body are protected by sticky mucus, which traps particles, and by tiny hairs, called cilia, which sweep them out. Stomach acid destroys many of the germs that we swallow, and tears and saliva contain chemicals that kill bacteria. These defences are known as innate immunity, since they work against all kinds of germs in the same way, and we are born with them.
paras.C: If a germ gets through, the innate immune system responds quickly. White blood cells called phagocytes surround and swallow the invader. At the same time, damaged tissue releases chemicals that make blood vessels wider, so that more blood and more defenders reach the area. This causes the redness, heat and swelling that we call inflammation. Sometimes the body also raises its temperature. A fever makes it harder for many bacteria to multiply, and speeds up the activity of immune cells.
paras.D: The second line of defence, adaptive immunity, is slower but far more precise. It depends on lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell. B cells produce antibodies, proteins shaped to fit a particular invader, which stick to it and mark it for destruction. T cells either destroy infected cells directly or help to organise the attack. Because each lymphocyte recognises only one specific target, the body needs to produce enough of the right ones, and this is why it can take several days to fight a new infection.
paras.E: The most remarkable feature of adaptive immunity is memory. After an infection is defeated, some of the B and T cells remain in the body as memory cells, sometimes for decades. If the same germ returns, they recognise it immediately and respond much faster and more strongly, often before any symptoms appear. This is why people rarely get diseases such as measles twice. Vaccines exploit this feature by showing the immune system a harmless piece or a weakened form of a germ, so that memory cells are ready for the real thing.
paras.F: Sometimes the system makes mistakes. In an allergy, the immune system overreacts to a harmless substance such as pollen or peanuts. In autoimmune diseases, such as type 1 diabetes, it attacks the body's own cells. In other cases, it is too weak: people with HIV, which destroys a type of T cell, become vulnerable to infections that healthy people can fight off. Research into how to control the immune system, up or down, is one of the most active areas in medicine.

paras.A: In the United States, a customer who eats in a restaurant is expected to add a tip of between fifteen and twenty per cent to the bill. In many other countries, including Japan, tipping is rare or even considered rude, and in Europe, it is usually a small extra. Tipping is, however, spreading. Card machines in coffee shops and takeaway counters now ask customers to choose a percentage, and many people say that they feel pressured to tip for services that once did not require it. This has led to a growing debate about whether the practice should be abolished.
paras.B: Supporters of tipping argue that it rewards good service. A waiter who is friendly and efficient is likely to earn more, so there is a financial reason to try hard. They also point out that tips allow restaurants to keep menu prices lower, because the cost of paying staff is shared with the customers. For many workers, particularly in places where wages are low, tips make up the greater part of their income, and some servers say that they earn more under the tipping system than they would with a fixed salary.
paras.C: Critics reply that the connection between tips and service is much weaker than people believe. Researchers who have studied restaurant bills find that the size of the tip is only slightly related to the quality of the service. Instead, it is influenced by other factors, such as the appearance of the server, the size of the party and even the weather. Some studies in the United States have also found that servers from minority groups, on average, receive lower tips for the same service, which suggests that the system can reflect prejudice.
paras.D: Another objection is that tipping makes income unpredictable. A server's earnings can vary widely from one evening to the next, and workers who are not on the floor, such as cooks and cleaners, may be paid much less. In some places, employers are allowed to pay staff below the usual minimum wage on the assumption that tips will make up the difference. The result is that the customer, not the employer, decides what a worker is paid, which many people find unfair.
paras.E: Some restaurants have experimented with abolishing tips and paying a higher wage, with a service charge included in the price. In 2015, a well-known restaurant group in New York announced that it would phase out tipping in its restaurants, but it reversed the policy a few years later, after some of its best-paid staff left, because their earnings under the new system were lower. Elsewhere, however, a number of independent restaurants have kept a no-tip policy successfully, and customers often say they prefer knowing the full price in advance.
paras.F: In my view, the best system is one in which every worker receives a fair wage from the employer, and the price on the menu shows the true cost of the meal. Tipping would then become what it is in much of the world: an occasional gesture of thanks for exceptional service, not a necessary part of anyone's pay. The change would have to be gradual, with prices adjusted so that customers are not surprised, but it would remove a source of inequality and uncertainty from a large number of jobs.

qs.title: Questions 39–40

paras.A: The Colosseum, in the centre of Rome, is the largest amphitheatre ever built in the ancient world, and it still dominates the city nearly two thousand years later. Construction began around 70 or 72 AD under the emperor Vespasian, who belonged to the Flavian dynasty, which is why it was originally called the Flavian Amphitheatre. It was officially opened in 80 AD by his son Titus, with games that are said to have lasted a hundred days. The name 'Colosseum' probably came later, from a huge statue of the emperor Nero that stood nearby.
paras.B: The scale of the building is impressive. It is an oval, about 189 metres long and 156 metres wide, and the outer wall rises to about 48 metres. According to ancient sources, it could seat around fifty thousand spectators, who entered through eighty numbered arches and found their seats by following passages and staircases. The crowds could enter and leave quickly, and many modern stadiums still follow the same principle. Seats were assigned by rank: senators sat nearest the arena, ordinary citizens above, and women and the poor at the top.
paras.C: Roman engineers used a combination of materials. The outer walls were built of travertine, a hard, pale limestone from nearby quarries, held together with iron clamps. Lighter volcanic stone and brick were used in the inner walls, and concrete, a Roman speciality, formed the foundations and the vaults that carried the seating. The arches on the outside are decorated with columns of three different styles, Doric on the bottom level, Ionic in the middle and Corinthian on the third, a pattern copied by many later architects.
paras.D: The shows were the main attraction. Gladiators, mostly slaves, prisoners or volunteers, fought one another in combat to entertain the crowd, and some became famous. In the mornings, there were hunts in which exotic animals such as lions, bears and elephants, brought from distant provinces, were killed. The arena floor was covered with sand, in Latin 'harena', which gave us the English word 'arena'. A huge awning, called the velarium, could be pulled over the seats to provide shade, and it was operated by sailors from the Roman fleet.
paras.E: Beneath the wooden floor was a network of tunnels and rooms, known as the hypogeum, which was added slightly later. Animals were kept in cages here, and gladiators waited to enter. Lifts and ramps worked by ropes and pulleys, hauled by teams of men, raised animals and scenery to the arena, so that a lion or a tree might suddenly appear in the middle of the stage. Some historians think that the arena could even be flooded, but this is much debated by scholars.
paras.F: After the fall of the western Roman Empire, the fights gradually ended, and the building fell into disuse. Earthquakes in 847 and 1349 brought down part of the outer wall, and in the Middle Ages, the stone was taken away to build palaces and churches in Rome. For this reason, only about a third of the outer ring is still standing. The Colosseum survived, and today it is one of the most visited monuments in the world, and was named one of the New Seven Wonders of the World in 2007.

paras.A: Anyone who has spent a day by the sea knows that the water level rises and falls twice a day. At high tide, waves reach far up the beach, and at low tide, they may retreat hundreds of metres, leaving rocks and pools exposed. These regular movements, called tides, have been noticed since ancient times, and sailors, fishermen and farmers have long used them. The explanation, however, was found only in the seventeenth century, when Isaac Newton showed that tides are caused by gravity.
paras.B: The Moon is the main cause. Gravity becomes weaker with distance, so the Moon pulls most strongly on the side of the Earth nearest to it, less strongly on the middle, and least on the far side. The water on the near side is therefore pulled towards the Moon, and forms a bulge. On the opposite side, the Earth itself is pulled away from the water more than the water is, which leaves a second bulge. As the Earth turns, a place on the coast passes through both bulges every day, which explains two high tides.
paras.C: The time between two high tides is not exactly twelve hours, but about twelve hours and twenty-five minutes. This is because the Moon is also moving in its orbit around the Earth, so that the Earth has to turn a little more than once a day to catch up with it. For this reason, high tide occurs about fifty minutes later each day. Tide tables, which give the predicted times for each port, are therefore an essential tool for sailors.
paras.D: The Sun also influences the tides, although its pull is less than half as strong as the Moon's, since it is so much farther away. When the Sun, the Moon and the Earth are in a line, at new moon and full moon, their pulls combine and produce especially large tides, called spring tides. The name has nothing to do with the season. When the Sun and the Moon are at right angles to each other, at the quarter phases, their effects partly cancel out, and the tides are smaller. These are called neap tides.
paras.E: The height of tides varies greatly from place to place, depending on the shape of the coast and the sea floor. In the Mediterranean, which is almost enclosed, tides are only a few centimetres. In the Bay of Fundy, in eastern Canada, the funnel shape of the bay concentrates the water, and the difference between high and low tide can reach sixteen metres, among the highest in the world. Along some coasts, a tide entering a river can produce a wave, called a tidal bore, that travels upstream.
paras.F: Tides have practical uses. Tidal power stations use the movement of water to generate electricity; the first large one, at La Rance in France, has operated since 1966. Unlike wind or sunshine, tides are completely predictable. Tides also have a slow effect on the planet itself: friction between the moving water and the sea floor is gradually slowing the Earth's rotation, making each day a tiny fraction of a second longer every century, and pushing the Moon slightly further away.

qs.title: Questions 23–26

paras.A: Most school subjects, such as mathematics, history or science, are about learning facts and skills. Philosophy is different: it asks questions to which there may be no single right answer. What is fairness? Is it ever right to lie? Can we be sure that the world around us is real? In several countries, including Britain, Australia and France, there are programmes that introduce children as young as five to such questions. Supporters believe they are of great value; sceptics think the time could be better spent.
paras.B: The modern movement began in the 1970s with the American philosopher Matthew Lipman, who was concerned that university students could not reason well. He believed that it was better to start much earlier, and wrote stories for children, which raised philosophical problems. Pupils read the story together, choose a question that interests them, and then discuss it, with the teacher acting as a guide rather than as an expert. This approach is now known as 'Philosophy for Children', or P4C.
paras.C: Supporters list several benefits. The first is thinking skills: children learn to give reasons for their views, to listen to opposing arguments, and to change their minds when the evidence demands it. The second is language: discussing abstract ideas encourages pupils to use more precise words and longer sentences. The third is confidence and respect. In a philosophical discussion, there are no stupid questions, and shy children discover that their ideas are taken seriously, while confident ones learn to wait their turn.
paras.D: There is some evidence to support these claims. In England, a large trial in schools, published in 2015, followed more than three thousand pupils aged nine and ten. Those who took part in weekly philosophy sessions for a year made about two months' more progress in reading and mathematics than similar pupils who did not. The gains were greatest among children from poorer families. Researchers cautioned, though, that the results came from one study, and that they depended heavily on the quality of the teachers.
paras.E: Critics raise several objections. The school curriculum is already crowded, and teachers are under pressure to improve results in literacy and numeracy, so a new subject would mean less time for something else. Some parents worry that discussion of questions about religion, death or morality might be unsuitable for young children, or that teachers might promote their own opinions. Others doubt that young minds can deal with abstract ideas at all, since according to the psychologist Jean Piaget, children develop the ability to think abstractly only at about eleven or twelve.
paras.F: On the whole, the objections seem weaker than the arguments in favour. Piaget's stages are now regarded as too rigid, and children's questions show that they think about fairness, truth and death from an early age. A short weekly session need not take time away from other subjects, because the skills it develops, such as listening, explaining and reasoning, are useful in all of them. With well-trained teachers and sensible guidelines on sensitive topics, philosophy deserves a regular place in the primary classroom.

paras.A: In the early hours of Sunday, 2 September 1666, a fire broke out in a bakery in Pudding Lane, in the heart of London. The baker, Thomas Farriner, had gone to bed after checking that his oven was out, but sparks set fire to a pile of wood, and by the time the family woke up, the house was full of smoke. Farriner and his family escaped, but a maid was too frightened to climb out of an upper window and became the first victim. In four days, the fire would destroy most of the medieval city.
paras.B: London was extremely vulnerable. Most houses were built of timber, many were coated with pitch to keep out the rain, and the upper floors of neighbouring houses leaned so close across the narrow streets that people could almost shake hands from the windows. The summer had been dry, and a strong east wind blew the flames westwards. Warehouses beside the river were full of flammable goods such as oil, tallow, coal and spirits, and the fire jumped from building to building faster than anyone could stop it.
paras.C: The authorities responded slowly. The Lord Mayor, Sir Thomas Bloodworth, was woken and, according to one account, said that a woman could put the fire out by urinating on it, and went back to bed. The usual method of fighting a fire was to pull down nearby houses to make a firebreak, but the mayor was reluctant to give the order because the owners would have to be paid. By the time King Charles II ordered the destruction of buildings with gunpowder, the fire was out of control. The king and his brother, James, personally helped to pass buckets of water.
paras.D: We know a great deal about the event from the diary of Samuel Pepys, a government official who watched it from a boat on the Thames and from a church tower. He wrote of 'a most horrid, malicious, bloody flame', and of people carrying their belongings to the river in terror. He buried his valuable cheese and a bottle of wine in a pit in his garden, to save them from the flames, a detail that has made his account very famous. The fire finally stopped on Wednesday, when the wind dropped.
paras.E: The scale of the destruction was enormous. About 13,000 houses were destroyed, along with 87 parish churches and the old St Paul's Cathedral. An estimated 70,000 of the city's 80,000 inhabitants lost their homes. Only a handful of deaths were officially recorded, but modern historians believe the true figure was higher, because the poor were not always counted, and some bodies may have been burned beyond recognition. Many people camped in fields to the north of the city, and the king ordered that food be brought to them.
paras.F: Rebuilding began almost at once. Plans for a completely new city with wide avenues were rejected, since property owners wanted to rebuild on their old plots, but the new law required houses to be made of brick or stone, and streets were widened. Sir Christopher Wren designed 51 new churches, and his masterpiece, St Paul's Cathedral, was completed in 1710. Close to the site of the bakery, he built a stone column, the Monument, 202 feet high, which is exactly the distance between it and the place where the fire began. The first fire insurance company was founded in London in 1680.

paras.A: A map is a flat picture of a curved world, and that simple fact lies behind many of the problems of making one. The Earth is almost a sphere, and a sphere cannot be flattened without being stretched, torn or squashed, just as an orange peel cannot be pressed flat without breaking. Mapmakers have to decide which kind of distortion they are prepared to accept, and the method they use to transfer the globe on to paper is called a projection.
paras.B: Every projection distorts something: shape, area, distance or direction. The most famous is the Mercator projection, published in 1569 by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator. On it, lines of constant compass direction appear as straight lines, which made it extremely useful for sailors. The price is that areas near the poles appear far too large. On a Mercator map, Greenland looks as big as Africa, although Africa is in fact about fourteen times bigger.
paras.C: Other projections reduce this problem. The Gall-Peters projection shows areas accurately but stretches shapes, so that countries near the equator look long and thin. The Robinson projection, used for many wall maps, is a compromise that is neither fully accurate nor too distorted anywhere. Each projection is therefore suitable for a particular purpose: navigation, comparison of area, or general reference. There is no perfect flat map, only the best map for the job.
paras.D: Before a map can be drawn, someone must measure the world. As early as 240 BC, the Greek scholar Eratosthenes estimated the circumference of the Earth by comparing the lengths of the shadows cast by the Sun in two Egyptian cities, and his result was impressively close to the modern value. Later, surveyors measured distances by chains and angles using instruments called theodolites, creating networks of points whose positions were known exactly. Heights were shown by contour lines, which join places of equal height.
paras.E: Today, most maps begin with data from the sky. Aircraft carrying cameras take overlapping photographs of the ground, and from them, computers can calculate the shape of the land. Satellites orbiting hundreds of kilometres above the Earth capture images of the whole planet, and some use radar or lasers to measure heights, even through clouds. The positions of roads, rivers and buildings are then drawn on the images, either by people or increasingly by software that can recognise them automatically.
paras.F: Digital maps are now stored in geographic information systems, or GIS, which keep information in layers: one for roads, another for rivers, another for population, and so on. Users can switch layers on and off or combine them to answer questions, such as where to build a hospital so that the most people live within half an hour. Navigation apps use the Global Positioning System, a network of satellites that tells a phone its position to within a few metres, and constantly update the maps with data from millions of users.

paras.A: In 1885, an insurance company in Chicago completed a building ten storeys high, supported by an iron and steel frame instead of thick stone walls. It is generally regarded as the first skyscraper. Since then, buildings have grown steadily taller, helped by safer lifts, invented by Elisha Otis in the 1850s, and by stronger steel and concrete. Today, the world's tallest tower, the Burj Khalifa in Dubai, is 828 metres high. As cities grow, planners must decide whether to build upwards or outwards.
paras.B: Supporters of tall buildings argue that they are the best way to house and employ more people on a limited amount of land. Dense cities need less land than sprawling ones, so more countryside is left untouched. When people live and work close together, they can walk, cycle or use public transport, instead of driving, which reduces traffic and carbon emissions. A tower in a city centre may also bring many businesses together, which helps them to share ideas and attract customers.
paras.C: Opponents point to the drawbacks. Skyscrapers are expensive to build and to maintain: the lifts, the pumps that lift water to the top and the systems that protect against fire use large amounts of energy. Glass towers can be hot in summer, requiring heavy use of air conditioning, and they are a danger to migrating birds. A tall building also casts a long shadow and can create strong winds at street level, making the surrounding area unpleasant. Some residents say the towers also destroy the character of historic districts.
paras.D: Safety concerns have also grown. The attacks on the World Trade Center in New York in 2001 showed how difficult it is to evacuate thousands of people from a very tall building, and led to changes in design, such as stronger stairwells and extra emergency staircases. Engineers say that modern skyscrapers are among the safest buildings in earthquakes and storms, as they are designed to sway without breaking. However, a serious fire high above the reach of fire engines remains a very difficult problem.
paras.E: There is also a social argument. Critics claim that luxury towers are often bought by wealthy investors as an asset, and left empty, while ordinary families cannot afford to live in the city. Tall buildings can make a neighbourhood more exclusive rather than more affordable. Defenders reply that adding any new housing, even at the high end, eases pressure on the rest of the market, and that cities can require developers to include a share of affordable apartments in each project.
paras.F: The writer's view is that skyscrapers have a place, but not everywhere. They make sense near major transport stations in the centres of big cities, where the infrastructure to support many people already exists. Elsewhere, mid-rise buildings of six to ten storeys can provide similar density, with less cost and less impact on the neighbourhood. Wherever towers are approved, they should meet strict standards for energy use, safety and public benefit, and should contribute to housing that ordinary people can afford.

paras.A: For nearly fourteen hundred years, nobody could read the writing of ancient Egypt. The hieroglyphs carved on temples and tombs, with their pictures of birds, eyes and snakes, were a mystery, and scholars suspected that they were purely symbolic. This changed with the discovery of a broken slab of dark stone, the Rosetta Stone, which is now one of the most visited objects in the British Museum.
paras.B: The stone was found in July 1799 by French soldiers who were repairing a fort near the town of Rashid, which Europeans called Rosetta, in the Nile Delta. They were part of Napoleon's army, which had invaded Egypt the year before, and had been accompanied by scholars. An officer realised that the stone carried writing in several scripts, and it was taken to Cairo for study. It is about 112 centimetres high, and weighs about 760 kilograms.
paras.C: The text is a decree issued in 196 BC by a council of priests, in honour of the young king Ptolemy V. It lists the good things that the king had done for the temples, and orders that copies of the decree be placed in every temple. It is not an exciting text, but its importance lies in the fact that it is written three times, in three different scripts: ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs, a cursive form of Egyptian called Demotic, and ancient Greek. Because scholars could still read Greek, the stone offered a key.
paras.D: After the French were defeated in Egypt, the stone passed into British hands under the Treaty of Alexandria in 1801, and it has been on display in London since 1802. Copies were made so that scholars all over Europe could study it. The first breakthrough was made by the English scientist Thomas Young, who suggested that the hieroglyphs enclosed in oval rings, called cartouches, were royal names, such as Ptolemy, and who worked out the meaning of some signs.
paras.E: The decisive work was done by the French scholar Jean-François Champollion. A gifted linguist, he had learned Coptic, the last form of the Egyptian language, which was still used in the Christian church in Egypt. He realised that hieroglyphs were not just pictures or ideas but also stood for sounds, and that they could be used like an alphabet as well as a code of word-signs. In 1822, he announced his results, and within a few years, he was able to read many Egyptian texts.
paras.F: The Rosetta Stone had made it possible to read thousands of inscriptions, papyri and tomb walls, and opened up three thousand years of Egyptian history. The expression 'Rosetta Stone' is now used for any key that unlocks a mystery. The stone remains controversial, as Egypt has repeatedly asked for its return, arguing that it was taken in the course of a war. The British Museum replies that the stone has been legally acquired and has been seen by millions of people in London.

paras.A: Every photograph, whether taken with an old film camera or a modern phone, is a record of light. The basic principle is very old. If you make a tiny hole in one wall of a dark room, an upside-down image of the outside scene appears on the opposite wall. This is the camera obscura, a Latin name meaning 'dark chamber', described by scholars more than a thousand years ago. A camera is essentially a small, portable dark room with a way of recording the image.
paras.B: A pinhole produces a sharp but very dim image, because it lets in only a tiny amount of light. To make the picture brighter, cameras use a lens, a curved piece of glass that gathers light from each point of the scene and focuses it on the same point at the back of the camera. To focus on objects at different distances, the lens is moved closer to, or farther from, the recording surface. The same principle works in the human eye.
paras.C: Three settings control how much light reaches the recording surface and how the picture looks. The aperture is an adjustable opening in the lens: a wide aperture lets in more light and blurs the background, while a narrow one lets in less light and keeps more of the scene sharp. The shutter speed is the time for which light is allowed in. A fast shutter, such as one-thousandth of a second, freezes motion, while a slow one makes moving objects blur. The third setting, ISO, controls how sensitive the surface is to light.
paras.D: For most of the twentieth century, the recording surface was film, coated with chemicals that change when struck by light. The film then had to be developed in a darkroom before the picture appeared. In a digital camera, film is replaced by a sensor, a chip covered by millions of tiny light-sensitive points called pixels. Each pixel produces an electrical signal proportional to the light falling on it, and the camera's processor converts the signals into an image file. Colour is recorded by placing red, green and blue filters over the pixels.
paras.E: The first digital camera was built in 1975 by Steven Sasson, an engineer at Kodak. It weighed about four kilograms, recorded black-and-white images of only 0.01 megapixels, and took twenty-three seconds to store a single picture on a cassette tape. Kodak did not develop the idea, fearing that it would damage its film business, and it was other companies that brought digital cameras to the mass market in the 1990s. By the early 2000s, digital cameras were outselling film cameras.
paras.F: Today most photographs are taken with phones. Their lenses and sensors are tiny, so they would produce poor pictures if used alone. Instead, they use computational photography: the phone takes several pictures in a fraction of a second, then merges them to reduce noise, increase detail and balance bright and dark areas. Software can also blur the background artificially. As a result, a modern phone can produce results that once required large and expensive equipment, although it cannot yet match the optical quality of a big lens.

ps.title: Is Organic Food Worth the Extra Cost?

paras.A: Walk into any supermarket, and you will see 'organic' labels on everything from apples to breakfast cereal. The market has grown rapidly, and in some countries, organic products now account for around ten per cent of food sales. Organic food usually costs a good deal more than the ordinary kind, sometimes by half. Many consumers are willing to pay for it because they believe it is healthier, safer and better for the environment. But how well do these beliefs stand up to scientific evidence?
paras.B: First, it helps to know what 'organic' means. Organic farmers do not use synthetic fertilisers or most synthetic pesticides, and they avoid genetically modified crops. Animals must have access to the outdoors and are given fewer medicines. Organic farms are inspected and certified. It is a common misunderstanding that organic farming uses no pesticides at all: it permits certain substances of natural origin, and some of these, in large amounts, can be harmful too.
paras.C: On health, the evidence is not strong. A well-known review of studies, published at Stanford University in 2012, found little proof that organic food is more nutritious than ordinary food. Organic produce did have lower levels of pesticide residues, but those in conventional food were nearly always within safety limits. Some studies suggest that organic fruit and vegetables may contain slightly more of certain antioxidants, while organic milk may contain more of a particular type of fatty acid, but it is not clear that these differences matter for health.
paras.D: The environmental case is more complicated. Organic farms often have richer wildlife, with more insects, birds and plants, and they usually put less pollution into rivers and keep more carbon in the soil. However, they tend to produce lower yields, on average, perhaps a fifth lower than conventional farms. This means that more land is needed to grow the same amount of food. If more forest or grassland were ploughed to make up the difference, the environmental gains could be cancelled, so some scientists question whether a world fed entirely by organic farming would be better for the planet.
paras.E: Cost is the most obvious drawback. Organic farms need more labour, and have lower yields, and their products are often sold in smaller quantities, so prices are higher. For families on a limited budget, spending more on organic items may mean buying less fresh fruit and vegetables overall, which would be bad for health. Nutritionists say that the most important thing is to eat plenty of fruit and vegetables, whether organic or not, and that washing them well removes most residues.
paras.F: The writer's conclusion is that organic food is not necessarily a bad choice, but it is not the clear winner that its supporters claim. Those who can afford it may choose it for reasons of animal welfare or wildlife, which are real benefits. Anyone who buys it only in the hope of better health should be aware that the evidence is weak. For the planet, the choices that matter most are probably what we eat, such as less meat, and how much food we throw away, not whether the label says organic.

paras.A: In the western Pacific Ocean, east of the Philippines and near the island of Guam, the sea floor drops away into the deepest place on Earth. This is the Mariana Trench, a curved valley about 2,500 kilometres long. Its deepest known point, a small basin called the Challenger Deep, lies roughly 10,900 metres below the surface. If Mount Everest, which is 8,849 metres high, were placed at the bottom, its summit would still be more than two kilometres under water.
paras.B: The trench exists because of the movement of the plates that make up the Earth's crust. Here, the huge Pacific plate is moving slowly towards the smaller Philippine plate, and because the Pacific plate is older, colder and denser, it slides beneath the other in a process called subduction. As it bends downwards, it forms the deep trench. The same process causes earthquakes and builds the chain of volcanic islands, including the Marianas themselves, along the edge of the trench.
paras.C: Conditions in the Challenger Deep are extreme. No sunlight reaches such a depth, so it is completely dark. The temperature is just above freezing, at between one and four degrees Celsius. The most striking feature is the pressure: the weight of the water above is more than a thousand times the pressure at the surface, which is equivalent to having about a hundred jumbo jets pressing on a person. Humans can only survive there in vehicles with extremely strong walls.
paras.D: Only a few people have ever visited. In January 1960, the Swiss engineer Jacques Piccard and the American naval officer Don Walsh descended in a bathyscaphe, the Trieste, and spent about twenty minutes at the bottom, noticing what they believed to be a flatfish. More than fifty years passed before the next human visit. In 2012 the film director James Cameron made a solo dive in a submarine, and in 2019 the American explorer Victor Vescovo, who has dived there several times, reached the bottom as well, and found plastic waste.
paras.E: It was once believed that nothing could live in such conditions, but scientific expeditions have shown otherwise. Tiny shrimp-like animals called amphipods swarm in the deepest parts, and large single-celled organisms live on the sediment. A type of small, translucent fish called a snailfish has been filmed at a depth of about eight thousand metres, which may be close to the limit at which fish can survive. Microbes feed on chemicals that rain down from above or seep out of the rocks.
paras.F: The trench also tells a worrying story about human activity. In recent years, scientists have found microplastics in the bodies of amphipods collected in the Mariana Trench, and other pollutants, such as chemicals once used in electrical equipment, have been found in the tissues of deep-sea animals. The trench acts as a trap for material that sinks from the surface. Studies of this remote environment help scientists to understand how life adapts to extremes, and also how far human influence has reached.

paras.A: On the wall of almost every chemistry classroom hangs a chart of the elements. This is the periodic table, and it is one of the most useful tools in science. It lists all the known chemical elements, the pure substances from which everything is made, and arranges them in such a way that their chemical behaviour can be predicted from their position. To a chemist, it is a map of the material world. Each box tells a story about one element: how heavy its atoms are, how it combines with others, and whether it is a solid, a liquid or a gas at room temperature.
paras.B: By the middle of the nineteenth century, scientists had discovered about sixty elements, and they had noticed that some behaved in similar ways. Lithium, sodium and potassium, for example, are all soft metals that react violently with water. Several chemists tried to find a pattern. The Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev succeeded in 1869. He arranged the known elements in order of increasing atomic mass and noticed that properties repeated at regular intervals, which is why the table is called 'periodic'.
paras.C: Mendeleev's genius lay in his courage. When the pattern did not fit, he did not change it. Instead, he left gaps, convinced that elements still to be discovered would fill them. He even predicted the properties of three of them, which he called eka-aluminium, eka-boron and eka-silicon. Within about fifteen years, they were found, and named gallium, scandium and germanium. Their properties closely matched Mendeleev's predictions, and this success convinced the scientific community.
paras.D: The table was improved in 1913 by the English physicist Henry Moseley, who discovered that the true basis for the order was not the mass of an atom but the number of protons in its nucleus, called the atomic number. This solved a few places where Mendeleev's order had been slightly wrong. It also showed exactly how many elements were missing between hydrogen, which has an atomic number of one, and uranium, which has ninety-two.
paras.E: In the modern table, the rows are called periods and the columns are called groups. Elements in the same group have the same number of electrons in their outer shell, which explains why their behaviour is similar. Group 1, the alkali metals, are all highly reactive. On the far right, the noble gases such as helium, neon and argon hardly react with anything because their outer shells are full. The block in the middle contains the transition metals, such as iron, copper and gold.
paras.F: The table is still growing. Scientists create new elements in laboratories by smashing nuclei together; these elements are heavy and unstable, and disappear within seconds or even fractions of a second. In 2016, four new elements were officially named, nihonium, moscovium, tennessine and oganesson, completing the seventh row and bringing the total to 118. Some researchers are trying to make element 119 and beyond, hoping to find an 'island of stability' where heavy atoms would last longer.

qs.title: Questions 23–26

ps.title: Do We Still Need Public Libraries?

paras.A: For centuries, a library was a building full of books. Today, we can read newspapers, look up facts and even borrow books on our phones, so it is reasonable to ask whether public libraries are still necessary. In many countries, the answer given by local governments in recent years has been no: in Britain, for example, hundreds of libraries have closed since 2010 as councils have tried to save money. Defenders of libraries respond that the building is more important than ever, but for different reasons.
paras.B: The first reason is access. Not everyone has a computer, a fast internet connection or the money to buy books. A public library provides all three, free of charge. People use library computers to apply for jobs, fill in government forms, search for housing and study. For children from poor families, the library may be the only quiet place with a table and a lamp where they can do their homework. Supporters argue that a society cannot claim to offer equal opportunities if such facilities disappear.
paras.C: Another reason is that libraries have changed. Modern libraries lend e-books and audiobooks as well as paper ones, and many also offer classes in languages, computing and job skills, as well as reading groups for children and older people. Some lend tools, musical instruments or even seeds. The Oodi library in Helsinki, opened in 2018, has a cinema, a recording studio, 3D printers and sewing machines, and attracts thousands of visitors a day. Such places show that a library can be a community centre, as well as a store of books.
paras.D: Critics say that these changes show how little demand there is for the library's original purpose. Book loans have fallen in many places, and information is now available on the internet, usually for nothing. Running a library is costly: buildings must be heated, staff paid and collections updated. At a time when councils face difficult choices between libraries and services such as social care, roads and schools, they argue that a large number of libraries should be closed or replaced by cheaper options such as a mobile van or a small collection in a community centre.
paras.E: Defenders reply that these arguments underestimate the value of a library. Information on the internet is not free of problems: it can be inaccurate, and finding reliable sources takes skill, which librarians can teach. Libraries also provide something that the internet cannot: a shared public space where people of different ages and backgrounds meet, with no obligation to buy anything. In an age when many people feel isolated, such places can be important for mental health and social life. Their benefits are real but hard to measure in money.
paras.F: The writer believes that libraries should be kept, but also continue to adapt. Local authorities should resist the temptation to close them, because once a building and its staff are gone, they are very difficult to replace. At the same time, libraries should listen to their communities, adjust their opening hours and services to local needs, and make use of volunteers and partnerships with schools, charities and businesses. A library that serves its neighbourhood well is likely to be defended by that neighbourhood when budgets are cut.

paras.A: Pearls are the only gems made by living creatures. Diamonds, rubies and emeralds are minerals formed deep in the earth, but a pearl grows inside a soft-bodied animal, usually an oyster or a mussel, in the sea or in a river. For thousands of years, pearls have been valued as ornaments, and in ancient Rome, they were so highly prized that wealthy women wore them as a sign of status. According to the writer Pliny, the queen Cleopatra once dissolved a priceless pearl in vinegar and drank it to win a bet.
paras.B: A pearl forms as a defence. When a tiny irritant, such as a grain of sand or a parasite, becomes trapped inside the shell, the animal cannot remove it. To protect itself, it covers the object with thin layers of a smooth substance called nacre, which is the same material that lines the inside of the shell and is known as mother-of-pearl. Over months or years, hundreds of layers build up. The way that light is reflected and refracted by these layers gives a pearl its soft glow, called lustre.
paras.C: The value of a pearl depends on several qualities. The most important is lustre: a pearl with a bright, mirror-like shine is worth far more than one that looks dull. Others are shape, size, surface and colour. The most prized shape is a perfect sphere, but many natural pearls are irregular or oval. Pearls come in many colours, from white and cream to pink, gold and grey. Black pearls, which are in fact dark grey, green or blue, come mostly from a large oyster found around the islands of Tahiti.
paras.D: Natural pearls are very rare. Before the twentieth century, the pearl industry depended on divers, who held their breath and plunged to the bottom of the sea to collect oysters. For centuries, the Persian Gulf was the centre of this trade, and a typical ship's crew might open thousands of oysters to find only a few pearls. Diving was dangerous, and many divers suffered from injuries or illness. In the 1930s, the discovery of oil in the Gulf region, along with competition from cultured pearls, ended most of the trade.
paras.E: Cultured pearls are made on farms. The principle is simple: a technician places a small bead of shell, together with a piece of tissue from another oyster, inside a living oyster, which then covers it with nacre. In 1893, the Japanese entrepreneur Kokichi Mikimoto produced the first cultured pearls, and by the early 1900s, he had found a way to grow round ones. Cultured pearls are real pearls, made of the same material as natural ones, and they brought pearl jewellery within the reach of millions of people.
paras.F: Today, most pearls sold are cultured. Freshwater pearls, produced mainly in China in mussels, are the cheapest, while saltwater pearls from Japan, Australia and French Polynesia are more valuable. Pearl farming depends on clean water, so it can be harmed by pollution and by changes in the temperature or acidity of the sea. Farmers in some regions have therefore become active in protecting coastal waters, because their livelihoods depend on healthy oysters. In this way, the industry has an interest in protecting the environment.

paras.A: To leave the Earth and reach space, a spacecraft must overcome two obstacles: gravity and the atmosphere. To remain in a low orbit, it must travel at about 7.8 kilometres per second, which is more than twenty times the speed of sound. Only one kind of engine can achieve this and also work in the vacuum of space: the rocket. Its operation depends on one of the basic laws of physics, discovered by Isaac Newton more than three hundred years ago.
paras.B: Newton's third law of motion states that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. A rocket works by throwing mass in one direction at great speed, and is pushed in the opposite direction. You can see the same effect when you let go of an inflated balloon: the air rushes out of the back, and the balloon shoots forward. A common mistake is to think that a rocket pushes against the air. In fact it works best in space, where there is no air to slow it down.
paras.C: In a rocket engine, fuel is burned in a combustion chamber, producing hot gases that expand and rush out of a nozzle at very high speed. Because there is no oxygen in space, a rocket must carry its own oxidiser, a substance that allows the fuel to burn. Some rockets use liquid fuel and liquid oxygen, stored in separate tanks and pumped into the engine. Others, such as the boosters on some launch vehicles, use solid fuel, a mixture that burns steadily once it is lit and cannot be switched off.
paras.D: The main difficulty is that most of the weight of a rocket is fuel. The Russian teacher Konstantin Tsiolkovsky showed in 1903 that to reach a high speed, the rocket must carry a large amount of fuel, but the extra fuel itself adds weight that must be carried. The solution is to build the rocket in stages. When the first stage has used up its fuel, it falls away, so that the engines of the next stage need not carry the empty tanks. A rocket that reaches orbit may be ninety per cent fuel.
paras.E: Modern rocketry grew from the experiments of pioneers. In 1926, the American physicist Robert Goddard launched the first liquid-fuelled rocket, which flew for only a couple of seconds. During the Second World War, German engineers developed the V-2, the first long-range ballistic missile, and after the war, its designers worked for both the United States and the Soviet Union. In 1957, a Soviet rocket put the first artificial satellite, Sputnik, into orbit, and in 1969, the enormous Saturn V carried astronauts to the Moon.
paras.F: For most of the space age, rockets were thrown away after one use, which made launches extremely expensive. A recent change has been reusable rockets. In 2015, a company called SpaceX landed the first stage of a Falcon 9 rocket upright on a landing pad after launching a satellite, and since then, the same boosters have been flown many times. If launches become much cheaper, they may open space to new uses, such as satellite networks and perhaps one day, regular journeys beyond the Earth.

qs.title: Questions 23–26

paras.A: Fish are one of the main sources of protein for humans. According to the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization, about three billion people get at least a fifth of their animal protein from fish, and in many poor coastal countries, the dependence is far greater. Yet the oceans are under pressure. The same organisation estimates that more than a third of the world's fish stocks are being caught faster than they can reproduce, a situation called overfishing, and the proportion has risen over the past fifty years.
paras.B: The most famous example is the collapse of the cod fishery off Newfoundland, in Canada. For centuries, the waters there were so rich that early explorers wrote that the fish could be caught in baskets lowered from the side of the boat. After the Second World War, large factory ships with powerful nets began to fish there, and catches reached a peak in the 1960s. By the early 1990s, the cod had almost vanished. In 1992, the government stopped fishing altogether, putting about 30,000 people out of work. Even after thirty years, the stocks have not fully recovered.
paras.C: Why do fishermen continue to catch too many fish? One answer is that the sea is a shared resource, and nobody owns the fish until they are caught. Each captain knows that a fish left in the water will probably be caught by someone else, so each has a reason to take as many as possible, even though this is harmful for everybody in the end. Governments make matters worse by giving subsidies, such as cheap fuel, which allow boats to go farther and fish for longer than would be profitable otherwise.
paras.D: Several solutions have been tried. Quotas limit the total amount of a species that may be caught each year, and in some countries, each fisherman receives a share of the quota, which can be traded. Where this has been done properly, as in Iceland and New Zealand, fish stocks have generally stayed healthy. Marine protected areas, in which fishing is banned or limited, give fish a place to breed, and studies show that they can lead to bigger and more numerous fish, which then spread to nearby waters.
paras.E: Another answer is fish farming, or aquaculture, which now supplies about half of the fish eaten by people. Farms can reduce the pressure on wild populations, but they bring problems of their own. Farmed salmon, for example, are often fed on smaller wild fish, so that several kilos of wild fish are needed to produce one kilo of farmed fish. Waste and disease can spread from crowded pens to wild fish, and in some tropical regions, coastal forests have been destroyed to make space for shrimp ponds.
paras.F: The writer believes that overfishing can be stopped, but only if rules are enforced. Science-based quotas, the removal of harmful subsidies, and well-managed protected areas have all worked in some places. The difficulty is that oceans are huge, fishing boats are hard to monitor and some countries do not cooperate. Satellite tracking of ships and stricter rules on imports of illegally caught fish are making enforcement easier, and consumers can help by choosing seafood that carries a trustworthy label.

ps.title: The Dodo: A Bird Lost to History

paras.A: The phrase 'as dead as a dodo' is used to describe something that has disappeared for good. The dodo was a real bird that lived on the island of Mauritius, in the Indian Ocean, about 900 kilometres east of Madagascar. It could not fly and, as far as we know, was found nowhere else. When the first Dutch sailors arrived there in 1598, they met a bird about a metre tall, with a large hooked beak, small wings and a tuft of curly feathers on its tail.
paras.B: The dodo was a relative of pigeons. Its ancestors probably flew to Mauritius millions of years ago, and since the island had no large land predators, there was no need for them to flee. Over time, the birds grew larger and lost the ability to fly, which saved energy. They nested on the ground, and fed on fallen fruit, seeds and roots. Early drawings show a very fat bird, but scientists now think these pictures were based on overfed animals in captivity, and that wild dodos were probably slimmer.
paras.C: The birds showed little fear of humans, which made them easy to catch, but they were probably not very popular as food. Sailors described the meat as tough, though they killed them anyway when other food was scarce. The greatest damage was done by the animals that came with people. Rats, pigs and monkeys, introduced by ships, ate dodo eggs, which lay unprotected on the ground, and competed for fruit. Forests, where dodos lived, were also cleared. Within less than a hundred years, the species had disappeared.
paras.D: The last widely accepted sighting was in 1662, though the bird was probably already extremely rare by then. By 1700, no one could say for certain whether any survived. Because few people had studied the dodo while it was alive, little reliable information remained. Only a few paintings, written descriptions and parts of specimens survived. The best-preserved remains, a head and a foot, are in Oxford, and the bones were found later in a swamp in Mauritius.
paras.E: The dodo gained fame in the nineteenth century, when the author Lewis Carroll included a Dodo as a character in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, published in 1865. Since then it has become a symbol of extinction. In 2016, scientists published the first full DNA sequence for a dodo, taken from a museum specimen. It confirmed that its closest living relative is the Nicobar pigeon, a bird with iridescent feathers from islands in south-east Asia.
paras.F: Why does the dodo matter today? It was one of the first animals whose extinction was clearly caused by humans, and it showed that species could vanish from the Earth. Islands remain particularly dangerous for wildlife, as animals there often have no defences against newcomers. Conservationists have since saved a number of island birds by removing rats and cats, protecting nests and breeding birds in captivity. Mauritius itself has been successful with the Mauritius kestrel, whose population rose from four birds in 1974 to several hundred.

paras.A: A flash of lightning is one of the most dramatic sights in nature. In a fraction of a second, a bolt can heat the air around it to about 30,000 degrees Celsius, which is roughly five times hotter than the surface of the Sun. Yet for most of human history, people believed that lightning was the weapon of the gods. It was not until the eighteenth century that scientists began to understand that it is a form of electricity.
paras.B: Lightning begins in a tall, dark storm cloud called a cumulonimbus. Inside, strong currents of air carry water droplets up to heights where they freeze, forming ice crystals and soft pellets of ice called graupel. As these particles collide, they exchange electric charge, in a way similar to that of a balloon rubbed against hair. The lighter crystals, which are mostly positively charged, are carried to the top of the cloud, while the heavier pellets, mostly negative, sink to the bottom.
paras.C: The charge difference grows until the air, which normally does not conduct electricity, can no longer resist it. A faint channel of electrical charge, called a stepped leader, then moves down from the cloud in a series of jumps, each about fifty metres long. When it nears the ground, a similar channel reaches up from objects on the surface, such as trees and buildings. As soon as the two connect, a huge current surges up the path from the ground to the cloud. This return stroke produces the bright flash we see.
paras.D: Thunder is the sound of the lightning. The extreme heat makes the air in the channel expand violently, producing a shock wave that spreads outwards as sound. Light travels almost a million times faster than sound, so we see the flash first. Sound moves about a kilometre in three seconds, so by counting the seconds between the flash and the thunder, we can estimate how far away the storm is. The rumbling of thunder happens because the sound comes from different parts of a long channel, and arrives at different times.
paras.E: Lightning is far more common than most people think. Scientists using satellites estimate that there are more than forty flashes of lightning every second around the world, mostly over land in tropical regions. Some of the most active places are in central Africa, and around Lake Maracaibo in Venezuela, where storms are almost nightly events. Lightning is also dangerous: it kills thousands of people each year, and starts many forest fires. At the same time, it plays a role in nature by helping to convert nitrogen in the air into a form that plants can use.
paras.F: The best protection is to be sensible. The safest place during a storm is inside a large building or a car with a metal roof, which carries the current around the people inside. Standing under an isolated tree, or in an open field, or on a hilltop, is dangerous, because lightning tends to strike the tallest objects. In 1752, the American Benjamin Franklin proposed the lightning rod, a pointed metal rod on the top of a building, connected to the ground by a wire, which provides a safe path for the current.

ps.title: Should We Edit the Genes of Human Embryos?

paras.A: In 2012, scientists developed a tool called CRISPR, which allows them to cut and change DNA with an accuracy that was not possible before. Often described as 'molecular scissors', it is cheaper and quicker than earlier methods, and is used by laboratories all over the world. It has been used to grow crops that resist disease, to create animals for research, and, increasingly, to treat patients. But when the changes are made to human embryos, they would be passed on to future generations, and this raises some of the most difficult questions in modern ethics.
paras.B: It helps to distinguish two kinds of editing. Somatic editing changes the cells of a patient who already exists, for example, the blood cells of someone with a genetic disease. The changes affect only that person and are not inherited. This type of treatment is already in use: in 2023, regulators in Britain and the United States approved the first CRISPR-based therapy, for sickle-cell disease. Germline editing, on the other hand, changes an egg, sperm or embryo, so that every cell of the resulting child, and all of that child's descendants, will carry the alteration.
paras.C: Supporters of germline editing point to the suffering caused by inherited diseases such as cystic fibrosis and Huntington's disease. If the faulty gene could be corrected in the embryo, they argue, the child would be spared a life of illness, and so would their children. They add that parents already make choices about the health of their children, for example, by screening embryos before a pregnancy, and that editing is simply a more precise technique. To refuse a safe cure, they say, would itself be a moral failure.
paras.D: The opponents have several objections. The first is safety. Editing sometimes changes the wrong part of the DNA, or creates mosaic embryos in which only some cells are altered, and the long-term effects of changes that are passed on for generations are unknown. A second concern is the 'slippery slope': once editing is accepted to prevent disease, it will be hard to stop parents from asking to choose intelligence, height or appearance. A third is fairness: if only wealthy families could afford enhancements, existing inequalities could become biological ones.
paras.E: These fears became real in 2018, when a Chinese scientist, He Jiankui, announced that he had created twin girls whose DNA had been edited to resist infection with HIV. The announcement was condemned around the world. Scientists pointed out that the experiment was unnecessary, since HIV can be prevented and treated by other means, and that the safety of the procedure had not been proven. In 2019, a Chinese court sentenced him to three years in prison. The case led many countries to reaffirm bans on editing embryos for pregnancy.
paras.F: The writer's view is that the present rules are about right. Somatic therapies should be developed as quickly as safety allows, because they offer real hope to patients. Germline editing for reproduction should not be permitted for now, since the risks are not understood and since alternatives, such as screening embryos, are available in most cases. However, research on embryos in the laboratory, under strict control and without implantation, should continue, so that future generations can make informed decisions on the basis of knowledge rather than fear.

ps.title: Lake Baikal: The Deepest Lake on Earth

paras.A: In the heart of Siberia, not far from the border with Mongolia, lies a lake unlike any other. Lake Baikal is 636 kilometres long, about the distance from London to Edinburgh, and in places 80 kilometres wide. It is the deepest lake in the world, reaching 1,642 metres, and the oldest, at about twenty-five million years. It also contains about a fifth of all the unfrozen fresh water on the planet, more than all five Great Lakes of North America combined.
paras.B: Baikal exists because of a rift in the Earth's crust, where two parts of the continent are slowly moving apart. The crack has widened by a few centimetres a year, and the valley has deepened. This is why the lake is so deep, and why earthquakes are frequent in the region. Scientists believe that, in millions of years, Baikal could grow into a new ocean, as the Red Sea did. Hot springs along the shores are another sign of the Earth's heat below.
paras.C: More than 330 rivers and streams flow into Baikal, but only one, the Angara, flows out. The water is exceptionally clear, partly because of tiny crustaceans called Epischura, which filter the water and eat algae and bacteria. In some places, visitors can see objects through forty metres of water. The water is also rich in oxygen, even at the greatest depths, since the lake is mixed by currents. This allows animals to live at the bottom, unlike in most deep lakes.
paras.D: Baikal is also a treasure house of wildlife. More than 1,700 species of animals and plants have been recorded, and about two-thirds of them are found nowhere else. The most famous is the Baikal seal, or nerpa, the only freshwater seal in the world. Nobody knows for certain how its ancestors reached this lake, which is far from the sea, but they may have travelled along rivers from the Arctic Ocean during the Ice Age. Another native is the omul, a fish that is caught by local people and eaten smoked.
paras.E: In winter, the lake changes completely. From January to May, the surface freezes to a thickness of up to a metre or more, and the ice is so strong that trucks drive across it, and it is used as a road. The ice is transparent, and sometimes cracked into patterns, and divers can swim beneath it to explore. In the spring, the seals give birth in lairs built in the snow on the ice, and when it melts, the water temperature rises only slightly, even in summer.
paras.F: Baikal faces threats. For decades, a paper mill on the southern shore discharged waste into the lake, and many scientists protested; the mill finally closed in 2013. Pollution from rivers, tourism, and the shrinking of water levels because of dams on the Angara are other concerns. The lake was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996, and the surrounding region has become a destination for hikers, cyclists and visitors in search of one of the world's most remarkable natural places.

paras.A: A modern phone can hold thousands of photographs, hours of music, and a large number of apps, all in a case thinner than a finger. Yet inside, there are no pictures, songs or words, only patterns of ones and zeros. To understand how computers store information, it helps to begin with the simplest unit, the bit. A bit is a single piece of information that has only two possible values, usually written as 0 or 1.
paras.B: Everything a computer handles is turned into bits. A letter of the alphabet, for example, is represented by a code of eight bits, called a byte. The letter 'A' is 01000001 in the commonly used system. A photograph is stored as a grid of tiny coloured dots, and the colour of each is recorded as a number. A song is stored as a series of measurements of the sound wave, taken thousands of times a second. Storing information in this way is called digital, as opposed to analogue, and its main advantage is that it can be copied perfectly.
paras.C: Inside a computer, bits are represented by electricity. The processor is made of billions of microscopic switches called transistors, each of which can be on or off, standing for 1 or 0. Short-term memory, known as RAM, holds the data that the computer is using at the moment, and it is very fast. But it is volatile, which means it forgets everything when the power is turned off. For permanent storage, a different kind of device is needed.
paras.D: For decades, the usual choice was the hard disk drive. It contains one or more metal discs coated with a magnetic material, which spin thousands of times a minute. A tiny head floats just above the surface and magnetises minute areas, in one direction for a 1 and in the other for a 0. The first hard drive, built by IBM in 1956, held about five million characters and weighed more than a tonne. Today, a drive that fits in a pocket can hold several million times that amount.
paras.E: Most new devices now use solid-state drives, which have no moving parts. They rely on flash memory, which stores bits by trapping tiny quantities of electric charge in cells made of silicon. The charge remains for years even when the power is off. Solid-state drives are faster, quieter and more resistant to shocks than hard disks, though they have been more expensive per unit of storage. Optical discs, such as DVDs, are different again: a laser reads microscopic pits in a reflective surface.
paras.F: What about 'the cloud'? The word suggests something floating in the sky, but it simply means data stored on other people's computers, in huge buildings called data centres, which are connected to the internet. When you upload a photo to a cloud service, the data is copied to several machines, often in different cities, to protect it from failure. Engineers also add extra bits, called error-correcting codes, which allow damaged information to be repaired. Despite this, nothing lasts for ever, and important files should be backed up in more than one place.
