ps.title: Should Taxpayers Pay for Sports Stadiums?

paras.A: Professional sport is big business, and teams often ask for new stadiums, which can cost hundreds of millions of pounds or dollars. In many cases, the money comes at least partly from the public. City governments offer cheap land, tax breaks or direct grants, and in some countries, the national government does the same when a country hosts the Olympic Games or the football World Cup. Supporters say the investment brings great benefits to the host city. Critics say that taxpayers are paying for the profits of rich owners.
paras.B: The case for funding rests mainly on economics. A new stadium, supporters say, creates jobs, both in construction and afterwards, and attracts visitors who spend money in nearby hotels, restaurants and shops. It can help to revitalise a run-down area, and put the city on the map. Politicians also point to non-financial benefits: pride in the home team, the pleasure of watching live sport, and a sense of community that cannot easily be measured in money.
paras.C: Most economists, however, are not convinced. When researchers have looked at the evidence, they have found little sign that stadiums produce much growth in the local economy. The main reason is that people only have a limited amount to spend on entertainment. Money spent on tickets and food at a match is money not spent at the cinema, restaurant or theatre in the same city. Many of the jobs created are seasonal and low-paid, and much of the profit goes to the team owners and the star players, who may live elsewhere.
paras.D: The experience of large events is often even worse. The Olympic stadium built for the 1976 Games in Montreal was so expensive that the city took thirty years to pay off the debt, which it did in 2006. Some stadiums built for major tournaments have become 'white elephants', huge buildings that are hardly used after the event, but cost large sums to maintain. Estimates before such events tend to be too optimistic about costs and visitor numbers.
paras.E: Defenders of public funding give some answers. They point out that teams could move to another city if they do not receive a deal, and that cities compete with each other. A few stadiums have succeeded because they were built in the right place and used for many purposes, such as concerts, conferences and community events. Some argue that a stadium is a public good, like a park or museum, which should be judged by the pleasure it brings, not by its financial return.
paras.F: On balance, the writer believes that taxpayers should be cautious. If a stadium really is a good investment, private investors will be willing to pay for it. When public money is used, there should be clear conditions: a cap on the cost, a share of the profits, guaranteed access for community groups and schools, and a firm plan for how the building will be used after a major event. Without such conditions, a stadium may be an expensive gift to a few wealthy people.

ps.title: Samarkand: Jewel of the Silk Road

paras.A: Samarkand, in eastern Uzbekistan, is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world. Archaeologists have found evidence of settlement at the site of Afrosiab, on the northern edge of the modern city, from about the seventh century BC, which makes it roughly as old as Rome. The city lies in a fertile valley watered by the Zeravshan River, on the routes that linked China, India, Persia and the Mediterranean, and its position made it a natural meeting place for merchants and travellers.
paras.B: The history of Samarkand is a history of conquerors. Alexander the Great captured the city, then called Maracanda, in 329 BC. Arab armies arrived in the eighth century and brought Islam, and according to tradition, the technique of making paper reached the city from China after a battle in 751 and then spread westwards. In 1220, the Mongol army of Genghis Khan destroyed much of the city, and its inhabitants were killed or enslaved. For a time, Samarkand lay in ruins.
paras.C: Its greatest period began in 1370, when Timur, known in the West as Tamerlane, made it the capital of his empire. Timur conquered lands from India to the Mediterranean, and brought skilled craftsmen, architects and artists from the cities he captured to Samarkand. Under his rule, the city was filled with mosques, palaces, gardens and tombs, decorated with the brilliant blue tiles that are still its trademark. He named villages near the city after the great cities of the world, such as Baghdad and Damascus, to show that Samarkand was the centre of the world.
paras.D: The most famous monument is the Registan, a great square surrounded by three madrasas, or religious schools, with tall arched entrances and walls covered in blue, turquoise and gold tiles. The oldest, built in the 1420s, belongs to Ulugh Beg; the others, the Sher-Dor and the Tilya-Kori, were added in the seventeenth century. Nearby stands the huge Bibi-Khanym Mosque, which Timur ordered built after returning from India, and the Gur-e-Amir, the mausoleum where he was buried in 1405.
paras.E: Timur's grandson, Ulugh Beg, ruled Samarkand from 1409 to 1449, and was more interested in science than war. He built a great observatory, with a giant sextant whose arc was set in a trench in the ground, and spent years observing the stars. The star catalogue produced by his team, published in the 1430s, listed more than a thousand stars with exceptional accuracy, and was used by astronomers for two centuries. Ulugh Beg was murdered in 1449, reportedly on the orders of his own son.
paras.F: Later, new sea routes reduced the importance of the overland trade, and Samarkand declined. It was captured by Russia in 1868, and after the arrival of the railway in 1888, a new European-style town was built beside the old city. After Uzbekistan became independent in 1991, many monuments were restored. UNESCO included Samarkand on its World Heritage list in 2001, under the title 'Crossroads of Cultures'. Today, it is a lively city of more than half a million people and one of the most visited places in Central Asia.

paras.A: A river does not simply flow across the land; it constantly changes it. Over thousands and millions of years, rivers cut valleys, carry away rock and soil, and deposit them somewhere else. Three processes are at work: erosion, which wears away the land, transportation, which carries the material along, and deposition, which drops it when the water slows down. The balance between these processes changes along the length of the river, which is why the same river looks completely different near its source and at its mouth.
paras.B: In the upper course, near the source, the river is usually in the mountains. The slope is steep, the water moves fast, and the main work is vertical erosion, as the river cuts down into its bed. It carries boulders and stones, which grind against the rock like sandpaper and deepen the channel. The result is a narrow, V-shaped valley. Where a band of hard rock lies above softer rock, the softer rock is worn away more quickly, and a waterfall forms, which slowly moves upstream.
paras.C: In the middle course, the slope is gentler and the river is wider. Erosion is now mostly sideways, and the river begins to bend in loops called meanders. On the outside of each bend, the water flows faster and wears away the bank, while on the inside, it slows down and deposits sand and gravel. Over time, the loops become more and more pronounced. Eventually, a river can cut through the narrow neck of a loop, leaving the old bend as a curved lake, known as an oxbow lake.
paras.D: In the lower course, the river flows across a wide, flat floodplain. Here it carries mostly fine sediment, such as silt and clay. When the river floods, the water spreads over the plain, slows down and drops this material, which is why floodplains have rich, fertile soil. This is one reason why some of the world's earliest civilisations, in Egypt, Mesopotamia and China, grew up beside great rivers. Some rivers build raised banks, called levees, from sediment, which help to contain floods.
paras.E: At the mouth of a river, where it meets the sea or a lake, the current slows down and the load it carries is dropped. If waves and tides are weak, the sediment builds up into a delta, a fan-shaped area of new land with many branching channels. The Nile and the Mississippi are famous examples. Deltas are among the most fertile and densely populated places on Earth, but they are low and vulnerable, and many are now sinking or being eroded because of dams that trap sediment upstream.
paras.F: Some of the greatest landscapes are the work of rivers. The Grand Canyon in Arizona was cut by the Colorado River over millions of years, as the land was slowly uplifted. It is about 446 kilometres long and in places more than a mile deep, and the rocks on its walls record almost two billion years of Earth's history. A river's power is not obvious on a human time scale, but over geological time, flowing water is one of the most effective sculptors of the Earth's surface.

ps.title: Should Cities Charge Drivers to Enter the Centre?

paras.A: In 1975, Singapore introduced a system in which drivers had to pay to enter its central area. It was the first scheme of its kind in the world. Since then, London, Stockholm, Milan and other cities have followed, and in January 2025, New York became the first American city to charge drivers entering the busiest part of Manhattan. The idea behind congestion charging is simple: if roads are crowded because they are free, then putting a price on them should reduce the number of vehicles.
paras.B: Supporters can point to results. When London introduced a charge of five pounds in 2003, the number of vehicles entering the zone fell by about fifteen per cent, and traffic moved faster. In Stockholm, a trial in 2006 cut traffic across the inner city by around a fifth. The public, which had been opposed to it at first, voted to keep the scheme in a referendum after seeing the benefit. Air pollution in the zone declined, and money from the charge was spent on buses, which improved the alternatives to the car.
paras.C: There is also a fairness argument for the charge. Driving into a congested centre imposes costs on others: delays for buses and delivery vans, noise, and pollution that harms the health of pedestrians. Economists call these external costs, and argue that those who cause them should pay. Many of those who drive into city centres are relatively wealthy, while poorer residents are more likely to take public transport. A charge, supporters say, is therefore a fairer way of funding transport than increasing general taxes.
paras.D: Opponents have several objections. The first is that the charge hits people on lower incomes, who may live far from the centre and have no convenient bus or train, and who have to drive for work. A nurse working night shifts, or a plumber with tools, may be unable to use public transport. The second is that businesses in the zone may lose customers if people prefer to shop elsewhere. The third is a concern about privacy, since the systems depend on cameras that record the movements of vehicles.
paras.E: Designers of the schemes have developed answers. Discounts or exemptions can be offered to residents, disabled people, emergency workers and those on low incomes. Charges can vary by time of day, vehicle size and pollution levels, so that cleaner cars pay less. Camera data can be deleted soon after payment is checked. Studies of shops in London and Stockholm found that retail sales in the zone did not fall in the way that critics feared, perhaps because many shoppers arrive by public transport and on foot.
paras.F: In my view, congestion charging works best when three conditions are met. There must be good alternatives, so that people have a real choice. The revenue should be seen to be spent on transport, which builds public support. And the scheme should be introduced with fair exemptions and clear information. With these conditions, a charge can reduce traffic, clean the air and improve public transport together; without them, it risks becoming just another tax on those who have no alternative.

paras.A: Bamboo looks like a tree, but it is actually a grass, a distant relative of wheat, rice and the lawn in a garden. There are more than a thousand species, ranging from tiny plants a few centimetres tall to giants that reach thirty metres. Bamboo grows on every continent except Europe and Antarctica, from tropical rainforests to cold mountain slopes, and it is most abundant in Asia, where it has been used for thousands of years.
paras.B: The most remarkable thing about bamboo is its speed. Some species can grow almost a metre in a single day, which makes them among the fastest-growing plants in the world. A new shoot emerges from the ground already at its full width, and then extends upwards like a telescope, while the segments are separated by solid joints called nodes. Within a few months, it has reached its full height, though the wood continues to harden for several years. Unlike trees, bamboo does not need to be replanted after harvesting, since it regrows from its roots.
paras.C: The plant has an unusual life cycle. Many species flower very rarely: some only once in sixty or even a hundred and twenty years, and then all the plants of the same kind flower at the same time, wherever they are in the world, and then die. This is known as gregarious flowering. The mass of seeds produced attracts rats, which multiply, and in the past, the following famine has caused hardship for people in some parts of India. Scientists still do not fully understand how the plants synchronise their flowering.
paras.D: Bamboo is also essential to wildlife. The giant panda, which lives in the mountains of central China, eats almost nothing else; an adult may eat between twelve and thirty-eight kilograms a day, and it spends most of its waking hours feeding. Pandas have a digestive system more suited to meat, and extract little nourishment from the plant, which is one reason why they must eat so much. When bamboo forests flower and die, or are cut down, the pandas must move to other areas, and fragmentation of forest is a major threat.
paras.E: For people, bamboo is one of the most versatile materials. It is very strong for its weight, in some ways comparable to steel, and cheap. In Hong Kong, builders still use bamboo scaffolding on skyscrapers, tied with nylon straps. Bamboo is used to make furniture, floors, bridges, paper, baskets and musical instruments. Its young shoots are a common food in Asian cooking. In 1880, the American inventor Thomas Edison used carbonised bamboo fibres as the filaments in his early electric light bulbs, because they lasted longer than other materials he tried.
paras.F: Because it grows quickly, bamboo is often promoted as an environmentally friendly material. A bamboo forest absorbs large amounts of carbon dioxide from the air, and its roots hold soil together, preventing erosion on slopes. Fabrics made from bamboo are often described as natural, but the process of turning the plant into soft cloth usually involves strong chemicals, so such claims should be treated with caution. Used sensibly, however, bamboo can replace wood and plastic in many products, and reduce pressure on forests.

paras.A: Every day, millions of people check the weather forecast on their phones. Most do not realise that the figures they see are the result of one of the largest scientific operations in the world, involving satellites, aircraft, ships, thousands of weather stations, and some of the most powerful computers ever built. A modern forecast is not a guess based on experience but the solution of a huge set of mathematical equations that describe the atmosphere.
paras.B: The first step is to find out what the atmosphere is doing now. Weather stations on land and buoys at sea measure temperature, pressure, wind and humidity. Twice a day, at the same time all around the world, balloons carrying instruments, called radiosondes, are released to measure conditions as they rise through the atmosphere to a height of about thirty kilometres. Radar shows where rain is falling, and satellites provide pictures of clouds and measure the temperature of the oceans and the air from space.
paras.C: All these observations are fed into a computer model. The model divides the atmosphere into millions of cells in a three-dimensional grid, each covering a few kilometres, and calculates how the air in each one will change over the next minutes using the laws of physics. The results are used to calculate the next step, and so on, for days ahead. The idea was first proposed in the 1900s, and the British scientist Lewis Fry Richardson tried it by hand in 1922; his calculation for one six-hour forecast took him months, and the result was wrong. The first successful computer forecast was made in 1950.
paras.D: Why, then, are forecasts sometimes wrong? One reason is that the atmosphere is chaotic. In the 1960s, the American meteorologist Edward Lorenz discovered that tiny differences at the start of a calculation can grow into very large differences later, an effect popularly known as the butterfly effect. Because our measurements are never perfect, errors grow with time, and beyond about two weeks, detailed forecasts have no skill. Another reason is that cells in a model are too large to capture small features, such as individual thunderstorms.
paras.E: To deal with uncertainty, forecasters run the model many times, each with slightly different starting conditions. This is called an ensemble forecast. If all the runs produce rain, the forecaster can be confident; if only a few do, the chance is lower. This is what lies behind a statement like 'a 30 per cent chance of rain'. Contrary to what many people believe, it does not mean that it will rain on 30 per cent of the area, but that in three of ten similar situations, rain would be expected at a given location.
paras.F: Forecasts have improved enormously. Studies show that, on average, the accuracy of forecasts improves by about a day every decade: a five-day forecast today is about as reliable as a three-day forecast was in the 1990s. The gains came from better satellites, faster computers and better models. They save lives and money, by giving warning of hurricanes, floods and heatwaves, and helping farmers, airlines and energy companies to plan. Researchers are now using artificial intelligence to speed up the calculations further.

ps.title: Should the Retirement Age Be Raised?

paras.A: When Germany introduced the world's first national old-age pensions in 1889, workers qualified at seventy, an age that few of them reached. Today, the usual retirement age in many countries is between 60 and 67, and people can expect to live well into their eighties. In 2023, the French government raised the age at which most people could receive a full pension from 62 to 64, and the move led to months of strikes and demonstrations. Similar arguments are under way in many other countries.
paras.B: The case for raising the age starts with arithmetic. Pension systems in most countries are paid for largely by the taxes of people currently working. As life expectancy has risen and birth rates have fallen, there are fewer workers for each retiree. In the early 1960s, there were about five people of working age for each person over 65 in the developed world; by 2050, the ratio is expected to be around two. Governments say the choice is between raising taxes, cutting pensions and asking people to work longer.
paras.C: Supporters also argue that work is good for people. Many older workers want to remain active, and studies suggest that staying in work, at least part-time, helps people stay healthy and connected to others. Employers benefit from the experience and skills of older staff, and the economy gains from the taxes they pay. In a time of labour shortages, they argue, it would be wasteful to retire millions of capable people in their early sixties.
paras.D: Opponents point out that the average hides large differences. Life expectancy is lower for those who have done hard physical work, such as builders, miners and cleaners, and for people who have lived on low incomes. In some countries, the poorest men live many years fewer than the richest. A single higher age therefore means that those who paid into the system for forty years might receive far fewer years of pension than others. Their jobs are also often tiring, and it is harder for them to carry on into their late sixties.
paras.E: There are other concerns. Older people often have difficulty finding work if they are made redundant, as employers may prefer younger staff, a form of discrimination known as ageism. Raising the retirement age without addressing this would force many to live on unemployment benefits or savings. Some also say that older workers who stay in jobs prevent young people from getting them, although economists mostly reject this idea, noting that the number of jobs is not fixed.
paras.F: Overall, the writer thinks a rise in the retirement age is justified, but only with safeguards. The change should be gradual, announced many years in advance, and linked to life expectancy so that it does not need to be negotiated each time. People in physically demanding jobs or with poor health should be allowed to retire earlier. Governments should also help older workers by funding training and by tackling age discrimination. With such measures, longer working lives could be both affordable and fair.

paras.A: Most plants make their food from sunlight, water and minerals, but a small number have found a remarkable additional source of nutrition: animals. Carnivorous plants trap insects and, occasionally, larger creatures, and digest them with special juices. There are about eight hundred known species, and they are found on every continent except Antarctica. Their strange habits fascinated Charles Darwin, who spent years studying them and published a book on the subject, Insectivorous Plants, in 1875.
paras.B: Why do these plants hunt? The answer lies in where they live. Most carnivorous plants grow in bogs, swamps and other places where the soil is very poor in nutrients, especially nitrogen. Ordinary plants cannot flourish there, but a plant that can supplement its diet with insects can. The animals are not the plant's main source of energy, which still comes from photosynthesis, but they supply the minerals that the soil lacks, in the same way that a gardener adds fertiliser.
paras.C: The best-known species is the Venus flytrap, which grows naturally only in a small area of North and South Carolina in the United States. Its leaves form a trap with two halves, edged with stiff bristles. Inside each half are tiny trigger hairs. If an insect touches two of them within about twenty seconds, or touches one hair twice, the trap snaps shut in a fraction of a second. This double test prevents the plant from wasting energy on raindrops or falling debris. The trap then seals completely and digests its prey over several days.
paras.D: Other plants use different tactics. Pitcher plants have leaves shaped like deep jugs, containing a pool of liquid. Insects are attracted by nectar around the rim, which is slippery, so they fall inside and cannot climb out. One tropical species, Nepenthes rajah, from the island of Borneo, has pitchers large enough to hold two litres of water, and has been found to have trapped small rats. Sundews have leaves covered with hairs tipped with sticky droplets, like dew, which hold small insects while the leaf slowly curls around them.
paras.E: The fastest trap belongs to bladderworts, a group of water plants. Each has numerous tiny bladders under water, with a door that is held closed by a pressure that is lower than the water outside. When a small animal such as a water flea touches the trigger hairs, the door opens, and the prey is sucked in within a few thousandths of a second, and the door closes again. This is one of the fastest movements known in the plant kingdom.
paras.F: Many carnivorous plants are now under threat. Drainage of wetlands for farming and building has destroyed much of their habitat. Pollution can enrich the soil with nutrients, so that other plants outgrow them. The Venus flytrap has also been poached from the wild in large numbers, which is now a crime in the United States. Conservationists protect bogs, and many carnivorous plants are now sold legally from nurseries, which reduces the pressure on wild populations.

paras.A: On rare occasions, in the middle of the day, the sky grows dark, the temperature drops, birds fall silent and the Sun appears to vanish. Throughout history, such events have frightened people, and many ancient cultures believed that a monster was devouring the Sun. Today, we know that a total solar eclipse is a result of simple geometry: the Moon passes exactly between the Earth and the Sun, and blocks the light.
paras.B: The coincidence that makes an eclipse possible is astonishing. The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon, but it is also about 400 times farther away. As a result, the two bodies appear to be almost exactly the same size in the sky. When the Moon passes directly in front of the Sun, it can just cover the bright disc and leave the outer atmosphere visible. No other planet in our solar system has a moon that fits so exactly, and in the far future, the match will not last.
paras.C: If this happened every month at new moon, eclipses would be common. They are not, because the Moon's orbit is tilted by about five degrees compared with the path of the Earth around the Sun. Most months, the Moon passes above or below the Sun in the sky. Only when the new moon happens to be close to the points where the two orbits cross does an eclipse occur. Somewhere on Earth, a total eclipse occurs about once every eighteen months, but at any one place, it is very rare, often once in several centuries.
paras.D: The Moon casts a shadow with two parts. The darker centre, the umbra, is a narrow cone, and anyone standing inside it sees a total eclipse. The outer part, the penumbra, is much wider, and people there see only a partial eclipse, with the Sun partly covered. Because the Moon moves quickly, the umbra sweeps across the Earth in a path that is often about 160 kilometres wide, and the maximum time of totality at any one place is just over seven minutes, although most last only two or three.
paras.E: During totality, spectacular things can be seen. Just before and after, sunlight shines through valleys on the edge of the Moon, forming bright spots called Baily's beads, and a last flash creates the 'diamond ring' effect. When the Sun is completely covered, the corona, the Sun's faint outer atmosphere, appears as a glowing white halo, and bright stars and planets become visible. It is safe to look at the Sun without protection only during totality; at all other times, it is essential to use special eclipse glasses.
paras.F: Eclipses have also advanced science. In 1919, the British astronomer Arthur Eddington travelled to the island of Príncipe, off Africa, to photograph stars near the eclipsed Sun. The positions of the stars appeared to have shifted slightly, just as Albert Einstein's theory of general relativity predicted, because the Sun's gravity bends light. The result made Einstein world-famous. Today, scientists use eclipses to study the corona. In about 600 million years, the Moon will have moved too far away to cover the Sun completely.

paras.A: Since chatbots that can write essays, solve equations and explain difficult ideas became freely available, schools around the world have struggled to decide how to respond. Some have banned the tools outright. Others have encouraged pupils to use them, and many have no clear policy at all. Teachers worry that pupils will simply copy what the software writes. Supporters say that AI, like the calculator or the internet before it, is going to be part of life, so pupils need to learn to use it well.
paras.B: The main argument against allowing AI in school is that it could weaken learning. Writing an essay is not only a way of producing text; it is a way of thinking, and struggling with a problem is how skills develop. If a pupil asks a program to write the answer, he or she may get a good grade without learning anything. There are also worries about accuracy, because chatbots sometimes state false things with complete confidence, and about fairness, because some pupils have access to better tools than others.
paras.C: Teachers also face a practical problem: how to tell whether work is the pupil's own. Software designed to detect machine-written text has proved unreliable, sometimes accusing honest pupils, and easy to fool. Some schools have returned to handwritten exams and spoken assessments, in which pupils must explain their ideas in person. Critics say these methods favour pupils who are good at talking or who write quickly, and take more of the teachers' time, but they do show what a pupil understands.
paras.D: On the other side, supporters list opportunities. A chatbot can act as a patient tutor, available at any hour, which can explain a concept in several ways and give a pupil instant feedback. It may be especially valuable for children whose families cannot afford private lessons. Teachers can use AI to prepare materials, adapt tasks for pupils with different needs, and save time on routine work, such as marking quizzes. Learning to question and check the output of a machine could become an important skill in itself.
paras.E: Some early research suggests that the way in which pupils use the tools is crucial. A pupil who asks for the answer learns little, but one who asks for hints, or for an explanation of a mistake, can learn faster. Several experiments have found that tutoring programs which are designed to guide pupils rather than give answers produced better results than ordinary software. This suggests that the question is not whether AI should be in schools, but what kind of AI and in what circumstances.
paras.F: The writer's opinion is that a blanket ban is unrealistic and unwise. Pupils will use these tools at home whatever the school says, so it is better to teach them how to do so honestly and critically. Schools should make clear which tasks may use AI and which may not, set more assessment in class, and train teachers. Basic skills such as reading, writing and arithmetic must still be taught without help, since a person who cannot do them cannot judge what the machine produces.

paras.A: Rising to 3,776 metres, about a hundred kilometres south-west of Tokyo, Mount Fuji is the highest mountain in Japan, and one of the most recognisable in the world. Its almost perfectly symmetrical cone, topped with snow for much of the year, has been a subject of Japanese art and poetry for centuries. On a clear day, it can be seen from Tokyo and even from the windows of the bullet trains that run between the capital and Osaka.
paras.B: Fuji is a volcano, and it is classified as active, although it has been quiet for a long time. It was formed over hundreds of thousands of years by repeated eruptions that piled up layers of lava and ash, which is why it has such a regular shape. Its last eruption began on 16 December 1707 and lasted about two weeks. The ash blew as far as Edo, today's Tokyo, about a hundred kilometres away, and covered the city. Scientists monitor the mountain constantly, and the government has plans in case it erupts again.
paras.C: Fuji has always been sacred. In the Shinto religion, it is the home of a goddess, Konohanasakuya-hime, who is associated with blossom and with volcanoes, and shrines have stood at its base and summit for centuries. In the Edo period, from the seventeenth century, religious groups made pilgrimages to climb it, and until the nineteenth century, women were forbidden to climb above a certain level. Buddhist monks also meditated on its slopes, and it became a symbol of the whole nation.
paras.D: The mountain has inspired countless artists. The most famous is Katsushika Hokusai, whose series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, made around 1830, includes The Great Wave off Kanagawa, in which the peak appears small in the distance beneath a gigantic wave. Hokusai's prints influenced European painters such as Monet and Van Gogh. In 2013, UNESCO listed Fuji as a World Heritage Site, not as a natural site but as a cultural landscape, in recognition of its role in religion and art.
paras.E: Each year, hundreds of thousands of people climb the mountain. The official climbing season is short, from early July to early September, when the snow has melted and the huts on the slopes are open. Most hikers start at night and aim to reach the summit for sunrise, a tradition known as goraiko. The climb takes between five and eight hours, and the weather at the top can be cold and windy even in summer. Climbing at other times is dangerous because of ice, snow and storms.
paras.F: The popularity of Fuji has brought problems. In the peak season, there are traffic jams of walkers on the trails, and rubbish and damage to the paths have been constant difficulties. Some people try to climb through the night without rest and become ill from the altitude. The authorities have introduced measures, including an entry fee for the most popular trail, a limit on the number of climbers per day and guidance to discourage 'bullet climbing'. The aim is to protect both the mountain and the people who climb it.

paras.A: A glacier looks like a frozen river, and it behaves like one. Although the ice appears solid and motionless, it flows slowly downhill under the force of its own weight. Glaciers form in places where more snow falls in winter than melts in summer, so that over the years it accumulates. Today, glaciers cover about ten per cent of the Earth's land, mainly in the polar regions and in high mountains, and they contain roughly three-quarters of the planet's fresh water.
paras.B: The process begins with snow. Newly fallen snow is light and full of air. As more snow piles on top, the weight squeezes out the air and the flakes are compressed into a granular material called firn. After many years, firn turns into dense, blue glacier ice. In a place like the Alps, this may take a few decades, while in Antarctica, where snowfall is very small, it may take thousands of years. Ice from deep inside an ice sheet can therefore be hundreds of thousands of years old.
paras.C: Once the ice is thick enough, perhaps thirty metres or more, it begins to move. There are two main mechanisms. In internal deformation, the ice crystals slowly slide past one another, like a pack of cards being pushed. In basal sliding, a thin film of meltwater at the bottom of the glacier acts as a lubricant, allowing the whole mass to slide over the bedrock. Speeds vary greatly, from a few centimetres per day to many metres a day in the fastest glaciers, such as those of Greenland.
paras.D: Movement causes cracks. The surface of a glacier is brittle, and where the ice flows over a bump or round a bend, deep cracks called crevasses open, sometimes concealed by snow, which makes glacier travel hazardous. In the lower part of the glacier, where the ice melts faster than it is replaced, the front, or snout, is found. Where the glacier reaches the sea, pieces break off and fall into the water as icebergs, a process called calving.
paras.E: Glaciers are powerful sculptors of the landscape. As the ice moves, it picks up rocks and drags them along the valley floor, scraping and polishing the surface. A river valley, which is V-shaped, is thus widened and deepened into a U-shaped valley. Glaciers also carve bowl-shaped hollows called cirques, leave sharp ridges, and carry debris that they deposit when the ice melts, forming ridges known as moraines. Many lakes in Canada, Scandinavia and Scotland sit in hollows scooped out by ice.
paras.F: Today, most glaciers are shrinking. Rising temperatures cause the ice to melt faster than snow replaces it. Swiss glaciers lost about ten per cent of their remaining volume in just two years, 2022 and 2023. The effects are serious. The meltwater adds to the rise in sea level, and the Greenland ice sheet alone holds enough ice to raise the oceans by about seven metres if it all melted. Many communities rely on glaciers to supply water for drinking and farming during the dry season, and these supplies are at risk.

paras.A: In 1917, the French artist Marcel Duchamp bought a porcelain urinal from a shop, signed it with a false name, and sent it to an exhibition in New York under the title Fountain. The organisers rejected it, but it has since become one of the most influential works of the twentieth century. More recently, in 2019, a banana taped to a wall by the Italian artist Maurizio Cattelan sold for 120,000 dollars at an art fair. Many visitors to galleries ask the same question: is this really art?
paras.B: Critics of modern art make several points. The first is skill. In the past, great artists such as Leonardo or Rembrandt spent years mastering their craft, and the beauty of their work reflects this effort. By contrast, some modern works, such as a blank canvas, a pile of bricks or an unmade bed, seem to require no ability at all. The second point is that the public cannot understand the work without lengthy explanations, which suggests that it has failed to communicate. The third is money: huge prices make people suspect that the art world is a fashion game for the wealthy.
paras.C: Defenders reply that art has never been only about skill or beauty. In earlier centuries, painters did not always aim to copy nature exactly; the invention of photography in the nineteenth century freed artists from the job of recording faces and landscapes, and they began to explore feelings, ideas and new ways of seeing. Duchamp's urinal, they say, made people ask what makes something art, and it did so very effectively. A work does not have to be pleasant to look at in order to make us think.
paras.D: Another argument is that much modern art does require great skill, although not always the kind that critics expect. The abstract paintings of Mark Rothko, which consist of large blocks of colour, look simple, but many viewers report that they are deeply moving, and they depend on delicate decisions about colour and proportion. Some works involve complex planning and teamwork, such as large installations that need engineers. Other works, such as those of the street artist Banksy, are enjoyed by people who never go to galleries.
paras.E: It is also true that opinions about art change. The Impressionists were mocked by critics in the 1870s, who thought their loose brushwork looked unfinished. Today, their paintings are among the most popular in the world. Defenders of modern art say that people should be cautious about dismissing what they do not understand, because history shows that today's shock can become tomorrow's classic. Nevertheless, not everything new is good, and it is perfectly reasonable to say that some pieces are poor.
paras.F: The writer's view is that the question 'Is it art?' is less useful than 'Is it good?'. Almost anything can be called art if the creator intends it, but not every work deserves attention. A reasonable approach is to spend a little time with a work, read what the artist says about it, and see whether it gives you a new idea or feeling. If not, you are entitled to move on. A gallery should be a place for curiosity, not for pretending to admire what one does not like.

ps.title: Marie Curie: A Life in Science

paras.A: Marie Curie is the only person to have won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences, and she remains one of the most admired scientists in history. She was born Maria Sklodowska in Warsaw in 1867, at a time when Poland was ruled by the Russian Empire. Her parents were teachers, and she was a brilliant pupil, but women were not allowed to attend university in Warsaw. She worked as a governess to help to pay for her sister's medical studies in Paris, and in 1891, she was at last able to follow her.
paras.B: In Paris, she studied physics and mathematics at the Sorbonne, living in a tiny attic room, and sometimes going hungry. She graduated at the top of her class. In 1895, she married Pierre Curie, a French physicist who shared her passion for research. Soon after, the discovery of X-rays, followed in 1896 by that of Henri Becquerel, who found that uranium gave off mysterious rays, caught Marie's attention. She decided to make this the subject of her doctoral research.
paras.C: Working in a cold, damp shed, she measured the rays from different substances, and found that the amount of radiation depended only on the quantity of uranium, not on its chemical form. She concluded that the rays came from the atoms themselves. She gave the phenomenon a name, radioactivity. She also noticed that some uranium ore was far more radioactive than could be explained by the uranium in it, and so it must contain some other, unknown elements.
paras.D: In 1898, the Curies announced the discovery of two new elements. The first they named polonium, after Marie's native country, and the second radium, from the Latin word for 'ray'. Separating radium took years of heavy, dangerous work, as they processed tonnes of ore by hand. In 1902, she succeeded in producing a tiny amount of pure radium salt. It glowed faintly in the dark. In 1903, Marie, Pierre and Becquerel shared the Nobel Prize in Physics, and Marie became the first woman to win the award.
paras.E: In 1906, Pierre was killed when he slipped in a street and was run over by a horse-drawn cart. Marie, left with two young daughters, took his place as a professor at the Sorbonne, becoming the first woman to teach there. In 1911, she was awarded a second Nobel Prize, this time in Chemistry, for the discovery of polonium and radium, and she won it alone. She faced hostility in the press because of her gender and her foreign origin, but she continued to work.
paras.F: During the First World War, she realised that X-ray machines could help surgeons to find bullets and broken bones in wounded soldiers. She organised a fleet of about twenty mobile X-ray vehicles, which became known as 'little Curies', and trained women to operate them. She even drove one herself. After the war, she raised money for a research institute in Paris, which still bears her name. She died in 1934 of a blood disease, probably caused by years of exposure to radiation. Her notebooks are still radioactive today and kept in lead-lined boxes.

paras.A: Place a steel coin in water, and it sinks immediately. Yet the largest container ships weigh hundreds of thousands of tonnes, are made mostly of steel, and still float easily. The explanation lies in a principle discovered about 2,200 years ago by the Greek mathematician Archimedes, and it depends not on the material of the ship, but on its shape.
paras.B: When an object is placed in water, it pushes some of the water out of the way. This is called displacement. The water pushes back on the object with an upward force called buoyancy. Archimedes realised that the buoyant force is exactly equal to the weight of the water that has been displaced. This is known as Archimedes' principle. If the buoyant force is large enough to equal the weight of the object, the object floats; if it is smaller, the object sinks.
paras.C: A solid steel block is about eight times denser than water. It displaces only a small amount of water, whose weight is much less than its own, and so it sinks. But if the same steel is shaped into a hollow bowl, the shape changes everything. The bowl sinks lower into the water, and displaces a much greater volume. As it sinks deeper, the buoyant force increases, until it matches the weight of the bowl. The hull of a ship works in the same way, and because most of its interior is filled with air, its overall density is much lower than that of water.
paras.D: The amount of cargo that a ship can safely carry is limited by how deep it sinks. In the nineteenth century, many ships were overloaded and lost at sea. The British politician Samuel Plimsoll campaigned for a law to prevent this, and in 1876, it became compulsory for merchant ships to carry a mark on the hull showing the maximum safe loading level. The 'Plimsoll line' still appears on ships today, with several marks to allow for different types of water, because salt water is denser than fresh, so a ship rides higher in the sea than in a river.
paras.E: Floating is not enough; a ship must also be stable. Stability depends on the relation between the ship's centre of gravity, the point where its weight is concentrated, and the centre of buoyancy, the centre of the displaced water. When a ship tilts, the centre of buoyancy moves, and if the ship is designed correctly, this creates a force that pushes the ship upright again. Designers lower the centre of gravity by placing heavy items, such as engines and fuel, low in the hull. If cargo shifts or is loaded badly, a ship can capsize.
paras.F: Submarines make use of the same principle in a different way. They have special tanks called ballast tanks. To dive, the crew lets in seawater, which increases the weight of the vessel until it sinks. To rise, they force compressed air into the tanks, which pushes out the water and makes the submarine lighter. By balancing the water and air carefully, the crew can make the submarine hover at any chosen depth. This shows that floating, sinking and hovering are all a matter of the balance between weight and buoyancy.

paras.A: Electronic cigarettes, or vapes, are devices that heat a liquid, usually containing nicotine and flavourings, into a vapour that the user inhales. They first appeared in China in the early 2000s, and are now used by tens of millions of people worldwide. Governments are divided about how to treat them. Some, such as India and Singapore, have banned them. Others, such as Britain, actively encourage smokers to switch to vaping. The disagreement reflects a real conflict between two important aims: helping adult smokers to quit, and protecting young people.
paras.B: Supporters of vaping begin with the harm caused by cigarettes. Smoking tobacco is one of the leading causes of preventable death in the world, killing around eight million people every year. The worst damage is caused not by nicotine itself but by the thousands of chemicals produced when tobacco is burned. Vapes do not burn anything, and so they produce far fewer harmful substances. In 2015, a review by Public Health England concluded that vaping was likely to be much less harmful than smoking, a figure often quoted as '95 per cent', although that estimate has been criticised.
paras.C: There is also evidence that vapes can help people to quit. A large trial in Britain, published in 2019, found that smokers given an e-cigarette were nearly twice as likely to be smoke-free after a year as those given nicotine patches or gum. For millions of smokers who have tried to quit and failed, supporters argue, banning vapes would remove one of the few options that works, and could push people back to cigarettes or to an illegal market.
paras.D: Opponents have serious concerns. First, vapes are not harmless. Nicotine is highly addictive and can affect the developing brain, and the long-term effects of inhaling the vapour are still unknown, because the products are so new. Second, there is a worry about young people. In several countries, the number of teenagers who vape has risen sharply, helped by sweet flavours, bright packaging and social media marketing. Some research suggests that teenagers who vape are more likely to take up smoking later, although it is difficult to prove cause and effect.
paras.E: Countries that have banned vapes face their own problems. In India, a ban introduced in 2019 reduced legal sales, but a black market has been reported, and cigarettes remain widely available. Critics say it is illogical for governments to allow a product that kills people, while forbidding one that is probably less dangerous. A ban may also encourage disposable vapes sold by criminals, which are not subject to any safety rules. These arguments suggest that a total ban would create new difficulties without solving the old ones.
paras.F: The writer believes that strict regulation is a better answer than a ban. Selling vapes to anyone under eighteen should be illegal and strictly enforced, and advertising and flavours that attract children should be restricted. Vapes should be taxed less than cigarettes, so that smokers have a financial reason to switch, but not so cheap that they tempt non-smokers. Governments should fund independent research and explain clearly that vaping is a way to quit smoking, not a harmless hobby for people who have never smoked.

paras.A: Chess is probably the most widely played board game in the world, with hundreds of millions of players. Two players move sixteen pieces each across a board of sixty-four squares, and the aim is to trap the opponent's king. The rules seem simple, but the game is so rich that no one has ever mastered it completely. Mathematicians estimate that the number of possible games is far greater than the number of atoms in the observable universe.
paras.B: The game began in India, around the sixth century AD, as a game called chaturanga, a Sanskrit word meaning 'four divisions'. These were the four parts of an Indian army: infantry, cavalry, elephants and chariots, which became the ancestors of the pawn, knight, bishop and rook. The game spread to Persia, where it was known as shatranj, and the Persians introduced the call of 'shah mat', meaning 'the king is helpless', which is the origin of the word 'checkmate'.
paras.C: After the Arab conquest of Persia in the seventh century, chess spread across the Islamic world, and from there to Europe, probably through Spain and Italy, by around the year 1000. Pieces changed shape in the Middle Ages. Since Islamic tradition avoids representing living beings, Arab sets used abstract shapes, and when the game reached Europe, new pieces were modelled on the figures of medieval society, such as kings, queens, bishops and knights. The 'vizier' beside the king became a queen.
paras.D: The modern game was created in Europe in the late fifteenth century, probably in Spain or Italy. At this time, the queen, which could previously move only one square diagonally, became the most powerful piece on the board, able to move any distance in any direction, and the bishop also became much more powerful. The new rules made the game faster and more exciting, and it was called 'the madness of the queen' in some places. The rules have changed very little since.
paras.E: Chess entered a new period in the nineteenth century, with the first international tournament in London in 1851, and the growth of clubs and professional players. In 1886, the first official World Championship was played. For most of the twentieth century, the best players came from the Soviet Union, where chess was supported by the state and taught in schools. The contest between the American Bobby Fischer and the Soviet Boris Spassky in Reykjavik in 1972 attracted worldwide attention, and Fischer won.
paras.F: Computers have changed chess completely. In 1997, an IBM computer called Deep Blue defeated the world champion, Garry Kasparov, in a match, the first time a machine had beaten a reigning champion under tournament conditions. Today, even a phone program can beat the best human players. Rather than ending interest in the game, computers have become a tool for training, and the popularity of chess has risen, especially online, helped by streaming and by the success of a television series in 2020. Many schools now teach chess because it is believed to improve concentration.

paras.A: For thousands of years, farmers have grown crops in soil, so it comes as a surprise to learn that soil is not essential. Plants need light, water, air and minerals, and the soil is simply the place from which most plants obtain the last two. If the same minerals are dissolved in water and delivered to the roots, a plant can grow perfectly well without any soil at all. This method is called hydroponics, from Greek words meaning 'working water'.
paras.B: The idea is not new. In the seventeenth century, scientists showed that plants could grow in water, and in the nineteenth century, researchers identified which minerals, including nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, plants need. The term hydroponics was introduced in the 1930s by the American scientist William Gericke, who grew tomato plants taller than a person in tanks of nutrient solution. During the Second World War, the American army used hydroponics to produce fresh vegetables on islands in the Pacific where the soil was poor.
paras.C: There are several kinds of hydroponic system. In the simplest, the roots hang in a tank of nutrient-rich water, which is bubbled with air so that the roots can breathe. In another, called the nutrient film technique, a thin stream of solution flows continuously along a channel past the roots. Some systems hold plants in an inert material, such as clay pebbles or fibres from coconuts, and the solution is pumped through at intervals. All use pumps, timers and sensors to monitor acidity and mineral levels.
paras.D: The main advantage is efficiency. Since the water is recycled, hydroponic farms can use up to ninety per cent less water than field farming, which is vital in dry regions. Plants are often fed exactly what they need, so they grow faster and give a higher yield. Without soil, there is no need for weeding, and few soil-borne pests. Farms can be set up anywhere, even in cities, deserts or the basements of buildings, and the crops can be grown all year round in a controlled climate.
paras.E: These benefits have led to the idea of 'vertical farms', where trays of plants are stacked in layers inside a building, lit with LED lamps. Growing food close to the people who eat it reduces transport and spoilage. Singapore, a small country that imports most of its food, has set a goal of producing thirty per cent of its nutritional needs locally by 2030, and is investing in such farms. Space agencies are also interested, since hydroponics may provide fresh food for astronauts on long missions.
paras.F: There are drawbacks. Setting up a hydroponic system is expensive, and it needs electricity for pumps and lights, which can be costly and, if the electricity comes from fossil fuels, harmful to the climate. If the system fails, plants can die within hours. At present, the method works best for leafy vegetables, herbs, tomatoes and strawberries, but not for staple crops such as wheat, rice and maize, which feed most of the world. Hydroponics will probably complement traditional farming, not replace it.

paras.A: A phone sold in London may have been designed in California, assembled in China from parts made in a dozen countries, and powered by minerals mined in Africa. This is globalisation: the growth of trade, investment, communication and travel across borders, which has linked the economies of the world as never before. Since the Second World War, the value of goods traded between countries has multiplied many times. The question that now divides economists and voters alike is who has gained and who has lost.
paras.B: Supporters point first to the reduction of poverty. According to the World Bank, the proportion of people in the world living in extreme poverty fell from around a third in 1990 to under a tenth by 2019. Much of the progress took place in China and India, which opened their economies to trade and attracted foreign investment. Consumers in rich countries also gained, because imports are cheaper. Supporters add that trade spreads technology and ideas, and makes wars between trading partners less likely.
paras.C: Critics reply that the benefits have been unequally shared. In rich countries, factory workers lost their jobs when production moved to places with lower wages. Whole towns in the American Midwest and in northern England suffered long periods of decline, and new jobs in services often paid less. Even in poorer countries, gains have gone mainly to cities and to those with education, while some rural areas have been left behind. Globalisation may raise the overall income of a country, but it creates winners and losers.
paras.D: There are also environmental objections. Transporting goods around the world burns fuel, and competition between countries to attract business can lead to weaker environmental rules. Forests are cleared to grow export crops such as soya and palm oil. Defenders respond that trade can also spread cleaner technology, and that the carbon emitted in shipping is often smaller than people expect, since the main emissions come from production. Others argue that the real problem is not trade, but the lack of international agreements on the environment.
paras.E: The pandemic that began in 2020 exposed another weakness. When factories closed and shipping was disrupted, countries found that they depended on distant suppliers for essential goods such as medical masks and microchips. As a result, many governments have started to talk of bringing production closer to home, or of using suppliers in friendly countries. Critics warn that such policies would raise prices and slow growth, and that self-sufficiency would be costly. Others say that a degree of resilience is worth paying for.
paras.F: The writer believes that globalisation has brought great benefits, but that these were not fairly shared, and that the solution is better management, not retreat. Governments should help workers who lose their jobs through retraining and support, spend more on regions that decline, and agree on rules that protect the environment and prevent unfair competition. Withdrawing from world trade would harm poorer people most, because they gain most from cheaper goods and from markets abroad. The task is to make globalisation work for more of those it touches.

paras.A: High in the mountains of Central and South Asia, among cliffs and snowfields at heights between three and four and a half thousand metres, lives one of the most elusive animals on Earth. The snow leopard is so rarely seen, even by the people who live in its territory, that it has been nicknamed the 'ghost of the mountains'. Its range stretches across twelve countries, from the Himalayas and the Tien Shan to the Altai, and covers about two million square kilometres.
paras.B: Everything about the snow leopard is adapted to life in the cold. Its thick, smoky-grey coat, marked with dark rosettes, blends perfectly with rock and snow. Its fur can be as long as five centimetres on the back and even longer on the belly. Its broad paws act like snowshoes, spreading its weight on soft snow, and have fur on the soles for insulation. Its nose is wide, to warm the freezing air before it enters the lungs. When resting, it wraps its tail around its body like a scarf.
paras.C: The tail, which is almost as long as the body, is also the animal's balance. Snow leopards move across steep and broken ground with astonishing agility, and are able to leap long distances: they can cross gaps of ten metres or more in a single jump. Unlike lions, tigers and jaguars, they cannot roar, because the structure of their throat is different. Instead, they communicate with a range of sounds, including hisses, growls and a soft call called a 'chuff', and they mark their territory with scratches and scent.
paras.D: Snow leopards are solitary hunters, usually active at dawn and dusk. Their main prey are wild sheep and goats, such as the blue sheep and the Siberian ibex, which may weigh as much as the leopard itself. They stalk their prey from above, creep close and attack in a rush. Having made a kill, a snow leopard may feed on it for several days. When wild prey is scarce, however, it may turn to domestic animals such as sheep, goats and yaks, which causes conflict with herders.
paras.E: Mothers give birth in a den among the rocks, usually to two or three cubs. The cubs, which are blind at first, stay with their mother for about eighteen months to two years, learning to hunt. An adult needs a very large territory, sometimes several hundred square kilometres, because prey is thinly spread in these barren mountains. This is one reason why the snow leopard is so rare, and why the exact number is uncertain. Estimates suggest that between four thousand and seven thousand remain in the wild.
paras.F: The snow leopard was listed as Endangered until 2017, when the international conservation organisation IUCN changed its status to Vulnerable. This was due partly to better surveys, which found more animals than expected. However, serious threats remain: killing by herders to protect their livestock, poaching for fur and bones, loss of prey and the effects of climate change, which may shift the tree line upwards and reduce the animal's habitat. Conservationists are working with local people, offering livestock insurance and building predator-proof pens, so that communities see the leopard as a benefit rather than a threat.

ps.title: Auroras: The Northern and Southern Lights

paras.A: On clear winter nights in places such as northern Norway, Iceland, Canada and Alaska, the sky sometimes fills with ribbons of green, pink and violet light that ripple and shift like curtains in a breeze. These are auroras, among the most beautiful of natural sights. In the north, they are called the aurora borealis, a name given by Galileo in 1619, and in the south, the aurora australis. For centuries, people explained them with myths, but science has now shown how they work.
paras.B: The story begins at the Sun. The Sun constantly throws out a stream of electrically charged particles, mainly electrons and protons, called the solar wind. It travels through space at around 400 kilometres per second, and reaches the Earth in about two or three days. Fortunately for us, the Earth is protected by its magnetic field, which acts like an invisible shield and deflects most of the particles. The field is generated deep inside the planet, where movement of molten iron in the outer core produces electric currents.
paras.C: The magnetic field does not block the particles completely. It is shaped like a funnel near the poles, where the field lines plunge into the Earth. Some of the charged particles are guided down these lines into the upper atmosphere, and they strike atoms and molecules of gas at heights of 100 to 300 kilometres. The collisions give the atoms extra energy, which they release as light. This is similar to the way that electricity makes the gas in a neon sign glow.
paras.D: The colour of an aurora depends on which gas is struck and at what height. The most common colour, a pale green, is produced by oxygen atoms at about 100 to 150 kilometres up. At greater heights, around 200 to 300 kilometres, oxygen glows a rarer deep red. Nitrogen produces blue and purple, usually at the lower edge of the display. Because our eyes are less sensitive to colour in the dark, faint auroras often look grey or white to the eye, but cameras with long exposures reveal their colours.
paras.E: The strength of the solar wind varies with the Sun's activity, which follows a cycle of about eleven years. Occasionally, the Sun releases a huge burst of material called a coronal mass ejection, which can cause a geomagnetic storm. During these storms, auroras can appear far from the poles. The strongest storm on record, the Carrington Event of 1859, produced auroras that were seen in the Caribbean, and disrupted telegraph systems. In May 2024, an intense storm brought auroras to places in Europe and North America where they are rarely seen.
paras.F: Besides their beauty, auroras are a reminder of the Sun's influence on the Earth. Powerful storms can damage satellites, disturb radio and navigation signals, and in extreme cases overload power grids. Space-weather forecasters therefore monitor the Sun to give warnings. Tourists now travel thousands of kilometres to see auroras, and the best time is between September and April, away from the light of cities, around midnight. A good aurora forecast, a clear sky, and some patience are all that is needed.

ps.title: Should Rich Countries Give More Foreign Aid?

paras.A: In 1970, the United Nations set a target: rich countries should give 0.7 per cent of their national income as aid to developing countries. More than fifty years later, only a handful of countries, such as Sweden, Norway, Luxembourg and Germany, have reached this level in recent years. Most give far less, and in some wealthy countries, politicians are calling for cuts. The debate over foreign aid raises basic questions about duty, effectiveness and self-interest.
paras.B: Supporters of aid begin with moral arguments. Hundreds of millions of people still live in extreme poverty, without clean water, adequate food or basic healthcare, and rich countries can help at a cost that is small for them. Aid has also achieved clear successes. The eradication of smallpox, declared in 1980, was possible because of international cooperation. Vaccination programmes, funded partly by donors, have prevented millions of children from dying, and the number of children who die before the age of five has fallen by more than half since 1990.
paras.C: There is also a self-interest argument. Disease does not stop at borders: helping poor countries to control epidemics protects everybody. Poverty and instability can lead to conflict and migration, and spending on development may be cheaper than spending on military responses to crises. Aid can also build trade, because countries that become richer become better customers. Many of today's strongest economies, such as South Korea, received substantial aid in the past.
paras.D: Critics offer several objections. The first is that aid does not work. Some economists argue that, over fifty years, large flows of money have not produced the growth that was hoped for in many countries, and that other factors, such as good government and trade, matter more. They say aid can be wasted on poorly planned projects, or lost to corruption, because money given to governments can end up in the hands of officials and not those who need it.
paras.E: A second criticism is that aid may do harm. It can make governments accountable to donors rather than to their own citizens, weaken local industries when free food or goods undercut local producers, and create dependence. A third is that charity should begin at home: citizens in rich countries have their own problems, from housing to healthcare, and many feel that their taxes should be spent on them first. Surveys show that people typically overestimate how much of the national budget goes on foreign aid, which in most countries is below one per cent.
paras.F: The writer believes that aid is worth giving, but that how it is given matters more than how much. Aid works best when it is targeted at things with a strong record of success, such as vaccines, clean water, school meals and basic health services, and when results are measured honestly. Giving cash directly to poor families has also performed well in studies. Donors should also support local organisations and not impose their own plans, and should reduce trade barriers, which can harm poor countries more than aid helps them.

paras.A: On a small island in New York Harbor stands a copper figure of a woman, 46 metres high, holding a torch in her raised right hand and a tablet in her left. The Statue of Liberty, whose official name is 'Liberty Enlightening the World', has welcomed millions of visitors and immigrants to the United States. It was a gift from the people of France, intended to celebrate the friendship between the two countries and the ideals of freedom and democracy that they shared.
paras.B: The idea came from a French historian and anti-slavery campaigner, Édouard de Laboulaye, in 1865, soon after the end of the American Civil War. The sculptor chosen to design the statue was Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi. It was agreed that France would pay for the statue, and the Americans would provide the pedestal on which it would stand. For years, both sides struggled to raise the money, using lotteries, theatre performances and exhibitions.
paras.C: Building the statue was a huge engineering task. Bartholdi first made small models, then enlarged them in plaster, section by section, until he had full-size forms. Thin sheets of copper, only about 2.4 millimetres thick, were hammered over wooden moulds to produce the skin. Because such a thin skin could not support itself, the engineer Gustave Eiffel, who later built the Eiffel Tower, designed an iron framework inside, which allows the figure to flex slightly in strong winds without breaking.
paras.D: The statue was completed in France in 1884, then taken apart into 350 pieces and packed in more than 200 crates, and shipped across the Atlantic. In the meantime, the American effort to pay for the pedestal had almost stopped. The newspaper publisher Joseph Pulitzer launched a campaign in his paper appealing to ordinary citizens, and more than 120,000 people, most of them giving less than a dollar, contributed. The pedestal was finished in 1886, and the statue was reassembled in four months.
paras.E: President Grover Cleveland dedicated the statue on 28 October 1886, in front of a large crowd, in heavy rain. The figure carries symbols of freedom: a crown with seven rays, representing the seas and continents; a tablet inscribed with the date of the Declaration of Independence, 4 July 1776, in Roman numerals; and a broken chain and shackle at her feet, showing the end of oppression. Originally, the statue was the colour of new copper, but over about twenty years, the metal reacted with air and rain and gradually turned green.
paras.F: The statue acquired a new meaning for immigrants. From 1892, newcomers arriving by ship were processed at nearby Ellis Island, and for many, the statue was the first sight of America. In 1903, a bronze plaque was placed inside the pedestal bearing the poem 'The New Colossus', written by Emma Lazarus in 1883, which includes the lines about welcoming 'huddled masses yearning to breathe free'. The statue has been restored several times, most notably for its centenary in 1986, when the torch was replaced, and it was listed by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site in 1984.

paras.A: Lasers are found in supermarket checkouts, DVD players, hospitals, factories and the optical fibres that carry the internet. The beam of a laser is unlike ordinary light, such as that from a lamp or the Sun. It is extremely narrow, and can travel a long way without spreading out, and it has just one colour. In 1969, astronauts left mirrors on the Moon, and scientists on Earth still bounce laser beams off them to measure the distance to the Moon to within a few centimetres.
paras.B: The word laser is an abbreviation of 'light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation'. The key idea comes from Albert Einstein, who proposed in 1917 that an atom that has been given extra energy can be made to release this energy as light if it is struck by a particle of light of the right kind. The light released is identical to the light that triggered it, in colour, direction and timing. One photon goes in; two identical photons come out.
paras.C: A laser makes use of this effect in a chain reaction. Inside is a material called the gain medium, which can be a crystal, a gas or a semiconductor. Energy is supplied to it, by a flash lamp, an electric current or another light source, in a process called pumping, which raises many of its atoms into an excited state. When one of these atoms emits a photon, the photon stimulates others to emit identical photons, and these in turn stimulate more, so that the light is amplified.
paras.D: To make the beam strong and straight, the gain medium is placed between two mirrors, one fully reflecting and the other partially reflecting. The light travels back and forth between them, stimulating more emission each time. Light that is not travelling exactly along the axis escapes from the sides and is lost, while light that is aligned continues to build up. Eventually, a small fraction passes through the partially reflecting mirror as the laser beam. The result is light that is monochromatic, meaning of a single colour, coherent, meaning that all the waves are in step, and highly directional.
paras.E: The first working laser was built in 1960 by the American physicist Theodore Maiman, who used a rod of synthetic ruby. When he fired it, it produced a pulse of red light. Many scientists had doubted that such a device would work, and at first, it was described as 'a solution looking for a problem'. Within a few years, however, lasers made of gas and of semiconductors had been developed, and uses began to multiply.
paras.F: Today, lasers are used for an enormous range of tasks. Weak ones scan barcodes and read discs. Medical lasers can correct eyesight by reshaping the cornea, remove tattoos, or repair damage inside the eye. Powerful ones can cut steel, drill diamonds and weld the body of a car. In communications, lasers send pulses of light through optical fibres. They are also used in surveying, in measuring pollution, and in research, where scientists use them to cool atoms to temperatures close to absolute zero.

qs.title: Questions 23–26

paras.A: Every adult has to make financial decisions: how to save, when to borrow, how to choose a pension, whether to invest. Yet many of us leave school without any formal teaching about money. International surveys suggest that only about one in three adults around the world can answer basic questions about interest, inflation and risk. As financial products become more complex, with credit cards, online loans, 'buy now, pay later' schemes and cryptocurrencies, a growing number of people believe that schools should teach personal finance.
paras.B: Supporters begin with the cost of ignorance. People who do not understand compound interest may not realise how quickly a debt can grow, or how much a small, regular saving can increase over decades. Many borrow at very high rates, or do not save for retirement. Young people are targeted by advertising for credit, and are often unaware of the risks. Teaching them in school, supporters argue, gives them tools before they make costly mistakes, in the same way that lessons about health help them to avoid illness.
paras.C: They also stress fairness. Children from wealthier families often learn about money from parents who discuss budgets, savings and investments at home. Those from poorer families have fewer chances to learn, and may have parents who are themselves under financial stress. School lessons offer every child the same basic knowledge, and may help to break the cycle of debt. In England, financial education became part of the secondary curriculum in 2014 for this reason.
paras.D: Sceptics raise several points. The school day is already full, and adding another subject means taking time from something else. There is also a question about whether the lessons work. Some studies have found that financial education in school leads to a small improvement in knowledge and behaviour, but others have found little effect, particularly when the lessons are short and are taught by teachers who have not been trained in finance. Knowing what to do is not the same as doing it.
paras.E: Another objection is that financial decisions are not simply a question of knowledge. Behavioural economists have shown that people often act against their own interest, even when they know better, because they prefer immediate pleasure to long-term benefits. A teenager has little money and few decisions to make, so lessons may be forgotten by the time they are needed. Some critics add that the problem lies with the financial products themselves, which are often too complicated, and that stricter regulation would protect people more reliably than education.
paras.F: The writer believes that schools should teach financial skills, but in a practical way. Lessons are most effective when they are linked to real situations, such as planning a budget, comparing loans, and understanding payslips and taxes, and when they are given close to the time at which students will need them, for example in the final years of school. Teachers need proper training, and the lessons should be supported by regulation, which prevents companies from exploiting the very young. Education will not solve every problem, but it is a necessary part of the answer.
