paras.A: Amber is a gemstone of an unusual kind: it is not a rock or a mineral, but the hardened resin of ancient trees. About 40 to 50 million years ago, huge forests of pine-like trees grew in northern Europe. They oozed sticky resin to seal wounds and keep out insects. Over millions of years, buried in sediment, the resin hardened and turned into the golden, translucent material we call amber. The richest deposits in the world are along the shores of the Baltic Sea, and the finest pieces come from the region around Kaliningrad.
paras.B: People have valued amber since prehistoric times. Beads and carvings have been found in graves more than ten thousand years old. The Ancient Greeks noticed that when amber is rubbed with cloth, it attracts light objects such as feathers, an effect of static electricity. Their word for amber, 'elektron', gave us the word 'electricity'. In the Roman Empire, amber was prized as a luxury, and trade routes known as the Amber Road carried it from the Baltic to the Mediterranean.
paras.C: Amber is also a valuable window on the past. When insects, spiders, plant fragments or even small lizards were trapped in the sticky resin, they were preserved in perfect detail, sometimes for tens of millions of years. Scientists use these 'inclusions' to study ancient ecosystems, and discoveries have included flowers, feathers of early birds and the oldest known examples of some insects. A work of fiction suggested that dinosaur DNA might be taken from insects in amber, but in reality, DNA does not survive for such periods.
paras.D: The most famous use of amber was in the Amber Room. In 1701, the king of Prussia, Frederick I, commissioned a room panelled with amber, decorated with gold leaf and mirrors. In 1716, his son gave it to Tsar Peter the Great of Russia as a gift to seal an alliance. It was later moved to the Catherine Palace near St Petersburg, where it covered about 55 square metres and contained around six tonnes of amber, and became known as 'the Eighth Wonder of the World'.
paras.E: In 1941, German troops invaded the Soviet Union and captured the palace. They dismantled the Amber Room in a matter of days and took it to Königsberg, where it was displayed in a museum. After 1945, it disappeared. Some people believe it was destroyed in the bombing of the city, others that it was hidden, and searches have been carried out for decades without success. The mystery has inspired many books and treasure hunts, though most historians think it was probably lost in a fire.
paras.F: In 1979, the Soviet government began to rebuild the room using old photographs, and a team of craftsmen worked for more than twenty years. The new room was opened in 2003, during the celebration of the 300th anniversary of St Petersburg, with funds partly provided by a German company. Today, amber remains popular in jewellery. It is light, warm to the touch, and floats in salt water, which helps to tell it from fakes made of plastic or glass. Some buyers test for authenticity with a hot needle or with salt water.

paras.A: A wind turbine looks like a giant propeller on a tall tower, but it works in the opposite way to an aeroplane's propeller. A propeller uses electricity or fuel to push air; a turbine uses moving air to produce electricity. A modern turbine converts the energy of the wind into electrical power with no fuel, no smoke and almost no pollution, and wind has become one of the fastest-growing sources of electricity in the world.
paras.B: The blades are shaped like the wings of an aeroplane. When wind flows past them, the air moves faster over the curved side than over the flat side, creating a difference in pressure that produces lift, a force at right angles to the wind. Because the blades are fixed to a hub, the lift makes them turn. Most large turbines have three blades, which provides a good compromise between efficiency, cost and smoothness of operation, and the blades are made of light, strong materials such as fibreglass.
paras.C: The rotor turns slowly, about ten to twenty times per minute, which is too slow for a generator. Inside the nacelle, the housing at the top of the tower, a gearbox increases the speed of rotation to more than a thousand revolutions per minute. The fast shaft turns the generator, in which magnets move past coils of wire, creating an electric current, according to the principle of electromagnetic induction discovered by Michael Faraday in 1831. The current is carried down the tower in cables and sent to the grid.
paras.D: Turbines must also adapt to the wind. Sensors measure the wind direction, and motors turn the whole nacelle to face the wind, a movement known as yaw. The angle of the blades can be altered, in a process called pitching, to catch more wind when it is light and to spill wind when it is too strong. At wind speeds of about 25 metres per second, the turbine is shut down to protect it from damage. Even the best turbine cannot capture all the energy of the wind; the theoretical limit, known as the Betz limit, is about 59 per cent.
paras.E: Turbines have grown enormously. The first machine designed to produce electricity was built in 1887 in Ohio by the American inventor Charles Brush. The early turbines had a power of a few kilowatts. A typical modern turbine on land has a capacity of three to five megawatts, enough for several thousand homes, and the largest offshore machines, with blades over a hundred metres long, may reach fifteen megawatts. Offshore turbines are more expensive, but the wind at sea is stronger and steadier.
paras.F: Wind power has some drawbacks. The wind does not blow all the time, so electricity from turbines varies, and must be balanced by other sources or by storage. Some people dislike the appearance of turbines and the noise, and turbines can harm birds and bats if they are placed in migration routes. Even so, wind is increasingly popular. In Denmark, wind supplies about half of the electricity, and many countries now regard wind as one of the cheapest ways to generate new power.

ps.title: Is Renewable Energy Ready to Replace Fossil Fuels?

paras.A: Over the last decade, renewable energy has changed from a hopeful idea into a mainstream industry. The cost of solar panels has fallen by around ninety per cent since 2010, and wind power has also become much cheaper. In 2023, renewable sources supplied around thirty per cent of the world's electricity, and in many places, new solar and wind plants are now cheaper to build than new coal or gas plants. Yet fossil fuels still provide most of the world's total energy, including transport, heating and industry. Can renewables take over completely?
paras.B: Optimists begin with the pace of change. Solar power has grown faster than almost anyone predicted, and the cost of batteries has also fallen sharply, making it possible to store electricity from sunny or windy periods for use at night or when the wind is calm. Several small countries and regions already run almost entirely on renewable electricity for much of the year, such as Iceland, which uses hydropower and geothermal energy. Supporters say that with enough investment, other countries can follow, and that the benefits include cleaner air and energy independence.
paras.C: Sceptics point to the main weakness: intermittency. The sun does not shine at night, and the wind sometimes drops for days. A grid that relies mainly on these sources needs large amounts of storage, long-distance cables to move power from where it is produced to where it is needed, and backup plants for the worst weeks of the year. Today's batteries are good at storing power for a few hours but not for weeks, and storing electricity for a whole season remains very expensive.
paras.D: Another difficulty is that electricity is only part of the picture. Steel, cement, shipping and aviation are hard to power with batteries, and they need new technologies such as green hydrogen, which is produced using electricity to split water. These are still expensive. Heating homes with electric heat pumps and driving electric vehicles are possible, but they need big investments and will add to the demand for electricity. Building the new infrastructure also requires large quantities of minerals such as lithium, copper and cobalt, and mining them brings its own environmental and social problems.
paras.E: Politics and speed add to the difficulty. Connecting new plants to the grid can take years in many countries, because of slow permits and local opposition. Existing industries and workers depend on coal, oil and gas, and communities will need help to change. Poorer countries may find it harder to pay for the up-front cost of renewable plants, although they can be cheaper in the long run. Experts say that the problem is no longer technology but how quickly societies can build, finance and agree on what is needed.
paras.F: The writer's view is that renewables will provide most electricity within a generation, but that a complete replacement of fossil fuels will take longer than enthusiasts hope and needs more than solar panels and wind farms. A realistic plan combines rapid expansion of renewables with better grids, more storage, energy efficiency and, for the time being, other low-carbon sources such as nuclear power. Governments should stop subsidising fossil fuels, and support research in the areas that are hardest to clean. The transition is both possible and urgent, but it will not be quick or simple.

paras.A: Hummingbirds are among the smallest and most remarkable birds in the world. There are about 360 species, and all of them live in the Americas, from Alaska to the southern tip of South America, with the greatest variety in the tropical forests of Ecuador and Colombia. The smallest, the bee hummingbird of Cuba, is only about five centimetres long and weighs around two grams, less than a small coin, and is the smallest bird on Earth.
paras.B: Their name comes from the humming sound produced by their wings, which beat very fast. In most species, the wings beat between fifty and eighty times per second, and during courtship displays, some can reach much higher speeds. Hummingbirds can do things that no other bird can. They can hover in one place, fly sideways and even fly backwards. The secret lies in their shoulder joints, which allow the wings to rotate and sweep in a figure-of-eight pattern, so that they produce lift on both the forward and backward strokes.
paras.C: Such flying demands an enormous amount of energy. A hummingbird has the highest metabolism of any vertebrate animal. Its heart can beat more than 1,000 times a minute during flight, and it breathes several hundred times a minute. To fuel this activity, it must feed constantly, visiting hundreds of flowers a day to drink nectar, a sugary liquid. A hummingbird may consume more than its own body weight in nectar every day, and it also catches small insects and spiders to obtain protein.
paras.D: Its body is well designed for feeding. The bill is long and thin, and the tongue is split at the tip and fringed, so that it works like a pair of tiny pumps, flicking in and out of the flower up to twenty times a second. Different species have bills of different shapes, matched to the flowers they visit. The sword-billed hummingbird of the Andes has a bill longer than its body, and it can reach into the deepest flowers. In return for food, the birds pollinate the plants as they move from flower to flower.
paras.E: Because they burn energy so fast, hummingbirds face a risk of starvation at night, when they cannot feed. To survive, they enter a state called torpor, in which the body temperature and the heart rate drop dramatically. A hummingbird in torpor looks almost dead and does not react to a touch. At dawn, it warms up and becomes active again. This saves a large amount of energy, which would otherwise be needed to keep the body warm in cool conditions.
paras.F: Despite their size, some hummingbirds make remarkable journeys. The ruby-throated hummingbird, which weighs about as much as a coin, breeds in eastern North America and migrates to Central America for the winter. Many individuals cross the Gulf of Mexico in a single flight of about 800 kilometres without stopping, which can take around twenty hours. To prepare, they nearly double their weight by feeding intensively. Hummingbirds are now threatened by habitat loss and climate change, which may disturb the timing of flowers and migrations.

paras.A: When you hear on the news that 'the market rose today', the reporter is usually talking about the stock market. It is a place, mostly electronic today, where people buy and sell shares in companies. A share is a small piece of ownership in a business. If you buy a share in a company, you become a part-owner, and you may profit if the company does well. The stock market therefore allows firms to raise money from many investors, and gives investors a chance to share in the profits.
paras.B: The first modern stock market is generally considered to be the Amsterdam exchange, which began in the early 1600s. The Dutch East India Company, founded in 1602, needed large sums to finance its trading ships, which were expensive and risky. It sold shares to the public, and the shareholders could sell their shares to others. Today, there are exchanges in almost every major country, such as the New York Stock Exchange, the London Stock Exchange and the Tokyo Stock Exchange.
paras.C: A company usually first sells its shares to the public in an event called an initial public offering, or IPO. After that, the shares are traded between investors on the exchange. Prices are set by supply and demand. If more people want to buy a share than sell it, the price rises; if more want to sell, it falls. Investors' views of the future matter more than a company's past performance, so news about profits, new products or competitors can change a price within seconds.
paras.D: Many shareholders receive part of the company's profits as a payment called a dividend. Others hope to make money when the price of the share goes up, which is called capital gain. To follow the market as a whole, people use an index, which tracks a group of shares. The S&P 500, for example, follows the shares of 500 large American companies. When people say that the market is 'up', they usually mean that an index has risen. A rising market is called a bull market; a falling market, a bear market.
paras.E: Investing in shares is risky. Prices can fall as well as rise, and an investor can lose some or all of the money invested. There have been spectacular falls: in 1929, the American market lost almost 90 per cent of its value over the following years, leading to the Great Depression; in October 1987, the market fell by more than twenty per cent in a single day; and in 2008, a financial crisis caused global prices to fall sharply. On the other hand, over very long periods, shares have usually produced higher returns than savings accounts or bonds.
paras.F: Experts advise ordinary investors not to try to pick winners or to guess when to buy and sell, because even professionals find that difficult. A safer approach is diversification: spreading money across many companies, industries and countries, so that the failure of one does not ruin the investor. Many people now buy index funds, which hold a small amount of every share in an index at low cost. They should only invest money that they will not need for several years, and should be wary of anyone promising quick, guaranteed profits.

paras.A: In 2009, a person or group using the name Satoshi Nakamoto launched Bitcoin, a digital currency that works without banks or governments. Transactions are recorded in a public ledger called a blockchain, which is maintained by thousands of computers across the world. Since then, thousands of other 'cryptocurrencies' have appeared, and trillions of dollars in value have been created and lost. The market is very volatile, and attracts both enthusiastic investors and serious concern. Governments are now deciding how far to regulate it.
paras.B: The case for regulation starts with the protection of ordinary investors. Many people who put money into cryptocurrencies have little idea of the risks. Prices can fall by half in weeks, and the market has seen a stream of frauds and collapses. In November 2022, the large exchange FTX went bankrupt, and its customers lost billions of dollars; its founder was later convicted of fraud. Without rules, critics argue, there is nothing to stop companies from misleading buyers or from taking their money.
paras.C: Regulators have other worries. Because transactions can be made anonymously and across borders, cryptocurrencies are attractive to criminals, who use them for ransomware attacks, drug dealing and avoiding sanctions. Mining new coins uses huge amounts of electricity, which has environmental costs. There is also a concern that, if cryptocurrencies become part of the mainstream, a crash could spread to banks and pension funds, and endanger the wider economy.
paras.D: Some governments have chosen to ban cryptocurrencies. China prohibited trading and mining in 2021, and several other countries have imposed restrictions. Others have taken a different approach: in 2021, El Salvador became the first country to make Bitcoin legal tender, though the experiment proved unpopular, and the government later moved to make its use optional. The European Union has agreed a comprehensive set of rules, known as MiCA, which require firms to be licensed, to hold reserves and to give clear information to customers.
paras.E: Opponents of heavy regulation make several arguments. Strict rules, they say, might drive innovation and jobs to other countries and stifle useful new technologies. They believe that blockchain could make payments cheaper and faster, particularly for migrants who send money home, who often pay high fees to banks. Some argue that the freedom from central control is the whole point of cryptocurrencies, and that regulation would destroy what makes them valuable. Others say that the existing laws against fraud and money-laundering are enough.
paras.F: The writer believes that sensible regulation is necessary and need not destroy innovation. Companies that look after customers' money should be licensed, audited and required to keep customers' assets separate from their own, as banks do. Advertising should be honest about the risks. Rules against money-laundering should apply equally to crypto and traditional finance. At the same time, regulators should avoid banning the technology outright, and should keep watching how it develops. Buyers should remember that no rule can guarantee profits, and should never invest more than they can afford to lose.

paras.A: Yellowstone, in the north-west of the United States, was established in 1872 as the world's first national park. It is famous for its geysers and hot springs, and for its wildlife, which includes bison, elk, bears and, since the 1990s, wolves. The return of the wolves, after seventy years of absence, is one of the most closely studied experiments in conservation, and it has changed the way scientists think about the relationship between predators and their environment.
paras.B: When the park was founded, wolves were regarded as dangerous pests. Ranchers and hunters in the surrounding areas feared for their livestock, and the government, which held the same view, ran campaigns to eliminate wolves throughout the country. By the 1920s, the last wolf packs had been killed in the park, and by the 1940s wolves had disappeared from nearly all of the western United States outside Alaska. Without their natural predator, elk numbers rose rapidly.
paras.C: The effects of this change were gradual but serious. The large herds of elk ate young willow, aspen and cottonwood trees along the rivers, so that few of them could grow into adult trees. Without trees, the riverbanks became weaker, birds and beavers lost their habitat, and the park's ecosystem became simpler. By the 1990s, scientists and the public increasingly believed that wolves played an important part in nature, and in 1973, wolves were protected by the Endangered Species Act.
paras.D: In 1995 and 1996, after years of argument and legal battles, thirty-one wolves were captured in Canada and released in Yellowstone. Ranchers opposed the plan, and compensation was offered for any livestock killed. The wolves flourished. Within a few years, the number rose to more than a hundred, and packs established territories across the park. Elk, now hunted, became more watchful and moved around more, instead of staying in one place and eating the same plants.
paras.E: Biologists have documented a chain of effects, sometimes called a 'trophic cascade'. In places where elk had grazed heavily, willows and aspens began to recover, providing food and building material for beavers, whose numbers increased. Songbirds returned to the thicker vegetation. Wolves also left carcasses, which fed scavengers such as ravens, eagles and bears. Coyotes, which had spread without wolves, were reduced, and populations of the animals they hunted, such as foxes and small rodents, recovered.
paras.F: Not everything is simple, though. Some scientists argue that the claim that wolves 'changed the course of rivers', made in a popular video, is exaggerated, since other factors, such as drought, the return of bears and the numbers of hunters outside the park, also affect elk and trees. Elk herds have declined, to the concern of some hunters. Nevertheless, the project is widely regarded as a success, and has encouraged other countries to consider bringing back lost predators such as the lynx and the wolf in Europe.

paras.A: Every medicine you buy in a pharmacy has gone through years of testing before it was allowed on the market. The rules are strict because the consequences of mistakes can be tragic. In the late 1950s, a drug called thalidomide was sold in many countries as a treatment for morning sickness in pregnancy. It had not been tested properly for its effect on unborn children, and thousands of babies were born with serious malformations. The disaster led governments to introduce much tougher requirements.
paras.B: The testing process begins in the laboratory. Scientists first study the new compound in cells and in computer models to see whether it has the desired effect and whether it is toxic. Promising candidates are then tested on animals, which allows researchers to see how the substance behaves in a whole living body, how it is absorbed and removed, and what dose is safe. Only a small fraction of compounds pass these first tests, and they must satisfy regulators before they can be given to people.
paras.C: Testing in humans takes place in four stages, called phases. In Phase I, a small group of volunteers, usually between twenty and a hundred, receive the drug, often starting with a very small dose, and doctors check for side effects. In Phase II, the drug is given to a few hundred patients who have the disease, to see whether it works and to find the best dose. In Phase III, thousands of patients take part in a large comparison with existing treatments or with a placebo, over a long time.
paras.D: A placebo is a dummy treatment that contains no active ingredient, such as a sugar pill. It is used because the mere belief that one is being treated can make people feel better, and the effect must be separated from the real effect of the drug. In the best trials, patients are assigned at random to the new drug or the placebo, and neither the patients nor the doctors know who is receiving what, until the end. This is called a randomised, double-blind trial, and is regarded as the most reliable way to test a treatment.
paras.E: The idea of a controlled trial is much older than modern medicine. In 1747, the Scottish naval surgeon James Lind divided twelve sailors with scurvy into six pairs and gave each pair a different treatment, including cider, vinegar and sea water. The two who received oranges and lemons recovered quickly. Lind's experiment showed that careful comparison, not opinion, is the best way of finding out what works.
paras.F: If Phase III shows that a drug is safe and effective, the company applies to a regulator, such as the US Food and Drug Administration or the European Medicines Agency, which examines all the data before deciding. Even after approval, the drug is monitored for rare side effects in Phase IV. The whole process often takes ten to fifteen years and costs hundreds of millions of dollars or more. Most candidates fail along the way; only about one in ten that enter human trials is eventually approved.

ps.title: Should Parents Monitor Their Children Online?

paras.A: Children today spend a large part of their lives online. They chat with friends, watch videos, play games and do homework on computers and phones, often out of sight of their parents. This brings opportunities, but also risks: contact with strangers, bullying, harmful content and addiction. Many parents therefore use software to monitor what their children do online, by checking messages, limiting screen time or tracking their location. Others believe that such surveillance does more harm than good.
paras.B: Parents who favour monitoring start with safety. The internet contains material that is unsuitable for young children, such as violence and pornography, and criminals can use social media and games to contact and deceive them. Younger children cannot always judge what is dangerous. Parental controls can block harmful sites, filter inappropriate content and warn parents if their child receives worrying messages. Parents are responsible for their children's wellbeing, supporters say, and it would be negligent to give a ten-year-old unrestricted access to the whole internet.
paras.C: Monitoring may also protect against less obvious risks. Excessive screen time can harm sleep, concentration and physical activity, and many children find it difficult to stop on their own. Software that limits the hours of use or switches off devices at bedtime helps parents to enforce rules without constant arguments. Some parents say that knowing where their children are, through location sharing, gives them peace of mind and allows them to give more freedom to go out.
paras.D: Critics reply that excessive monitoring damages trust. Teenagers, in particular, need privacy as part of growing up, and a child who discovers that a parent has been reading their messages in secret may feel betrayed. Research suggests that heavy surveillance can lead to secrecy rather than safety: children find ways around the controls, such as using friends' devices or hidden accounts, and are less likely to tell their parents when something frightening happens, for fear of losing their phone.
paras.E: There is also the question of developing independence. Children need chances to make decisions and mistakes, and to learn how to deal with problems. If parents control everything, children may have little chance to practise self-control and judgment. Experts note that no software can detect every danger, and that the best protection is a child who knows what to do when something goes wrong. Open conversations about what children see online appear more effective, in many studies, than technical controls alone.
paras.F: The writer believes that the right level of monitoring depends on the age of the child. Young children should use only devices that have strong filters, and always in shared places. As they grow, parents should gradually withdraw the controls and replace them with discussion and trust, agreeing rules together and explaining the reasons for them. Secret surveillance should be avoided except in cases of real danger. The aim is to prepare children to be responsible online, not to keep them in a protective bubble.

paras.A: Stretching across the north of England from the North Sea to the Irish Sea, Hadrian's Wall was the northern frontier of the Roman Empire in Britain for nearly three hundred years. Today it is the largest Roman monument in the country, and a popular path for walkers. Its construction began in the year 122 AD, after the emperor Hadrian visited Britain. By this time, the Romans had held much of the island for eighty years, but they had never managed to conquer the tribes of the far north.
paras.B: Hadrian was an emperor who preferred consolidating the empire to expanding it. He ordered a continuous barrier to mark the limit of Roman territory, to control movement across the frontier and to protect the province from raids. The wall ran for 80 Roman miles, about 117 kilometres, from Wallsend on the River Tyne in the east to Bowness-on-Solway in the west. It was built mainly by soldiers of three legions, who also made the bricks, quarried the stone and burned the lime for the mortar.
paras.C: The wall was a complex system and not just a wall. In the east, it was built of stone, about three metres thick and perhaps four to five metres high, while in the west, where there was less stone, it was first made of turf. Every Roman mile along the wall stood a small fort, called a milecastle, with a gate through the wall, and between each pair of milecastles were two watchtowers, or turrets. To the north lay a wide ditch, and to the south ran a second ditch and banks, known as the vallum.
paras.D: Larger forts, with room for several hundred soldiers, were built along the wall or just behind it. The troops stationed in them were mostly auxiliaries, recruited from the provinces of the empire, such as Gaul, Spain and the region of the Danube. Some were archers from Syria. Housesteads, one of the best-preserved forts, had barracks, a hospital, granaries and latrines, and a civilian settlement grew up outside it, with shops, bars and families.
paras.E: Remarkable discoveries have been made at Vindolanda, a fort just south of the wall. Archaeologists found hundreds of thin wooden writing tablets, preserved in the damp soil, with messages written in ink. They include a request for more beer, a note about socks and underpants sent to a soldier, and an invitation to a birthday party sent by a woman called Claudia Severa, which is among the oldest known examples of writing in Latin by a woman. These documents show everyday life on the frontier with unusual intimacy.
paras.F: The wall was not entirely a barrier, since the soldiers could control and tax the movement of people and goods through its gates. In the 140s, the Romans moved north and built a new wall, the Antonine Wall, in Scotland, but within about twenty years, they withdrew to Hadrian's line. By about 410, when Roman rule in Britain ended, the wall was abandoned. In later centuries, much of its stone was taken for farms, roads and churches. It was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987.

paras.A: The surface of the Earth looks solid and unchanging, but it is in constant, slow motion. The continents drift across the globe at about the speed that a fingernail grows, and over millions of years, they have rearranged themselves completely. The theory that explains this is called plate tectonics, and it is one of the most important ideas in the history of science, because it links together earthquakes, volcanoes, mountains and ocean trenches.
paras.B: The idea began with a German scientist, Alfred Wegener. In 1912, he proposed that the continents had once been joined in a single supercontinent, which he called Pangaea, and had since drifted apart. He noted that the coastlines of South America and Africa fit together like pieces of a jigsaw, and that identical fossils, such as those of a small freshwater reptile called Mesosaurus, had been found on both sides of the Atlantic. Other scientists rejected the idea, because Wegener could not explain what force could move continents.
paras.C: The answer came in the 1950s and 1960s, when new technology allowed scientists to map the ocean floor. They discovered a vast chain of underwater mountains, the mid-ocean ridge, running through the oceans. The American geologist Harry Hess suggested that molten rock rises at the ridge, forming new sea floor, which then spreads out on either side. Magnetic patterns in the rocks, which record the reversals of the Earth's magnetic field, confirmed this 'sea-floor spreading', and by the late 1960s, the theory of plate tectonics was accepted.
paras.D: According to the theory, the outer shell of the Earth, the lithosphere, is broken into about fifteen large plates and several smaller ones. They move because they rest on a layer of hot, partly molten rock, called the asthenosphere. Heat from the Earth's interior causes slow currents in this layer, and the plates are also pulled by their own weight where one sinks into the interior. They move at between two and ten centimetres a year, and most geological activity occurs at their boundaries.
paras.E: There are three kinds of boundary. At a divergent boundary, plates move apart and new crust is formed, as along the mid-Atlantic ridge, where Iceland is being slowly split in two. At a convergent boundary, plates move together. If one plate is oceanic, it is pushed under the other in a process called subduction, creating deep ocean trenches and chains of volcanoes, as around the Pacific 'Ring of Fire'. When two continents collide, neither sinks, and they crumple to form mountains. The Himalayas were formed in this way, when India crashed into Asia about fifty million years ago.
paras.F: At the third type, a transform boundary, plates slide past each other. The movement is not smooth: the rocks stick, stress builds up for decades, and then it is suddenly released as an earthquake. The San Andreas Fault in California is a famous example. Plate tectonics also explains why volcanoes and earthquakes are concentrated in certain zones, and it helps scientists to assess where hazards are greatest. It will also shape the future: in about 250 million years, the continents may form another supercontinent.

ps.title: Should We Abolish Daylight Saving Time?

paras.A: Twice a year, millions of people around the world change their clocks. In spring, they move them forward by an hour, to give longer evenings in summer, and in autumn, they move them back. The practice, called daylight saving time, was first adopted on a large scale by Germany in 1916, during the First World War, in an attempt to save fuel. Many other countries followed. Today, around seventy countries use it, but a growing number of people ask whether it is still worth the trouble.
paras.B: Supporters of the system claim that it saves energy. The original reasoning was that by shifting the working day closer to daylight hours, people would use less artificial lighting in the evening. They also say that lighter evenings encourage people to spend more time outdoors, to shop, and to play sport, which benefits business and health. Some studies have found that road accidents involving pedestrians decrease in the lighter evenings, since drivers can see better.
paras.C: Critics reply that the energy savings have almost disappeared. Modern lighting is much more efficient than in 1916, while other forms of energy use, such as heating and air conditioning, may increase, depending on the climate. Studies in several countries have found small savings, no savings, or even increases. In addition, the changes themselves are costly: computers and equipment need to be updated, transport timetables adjusted, and many people feel tired and irritable for days.
paras.D: Health is the greatest concern. Scientists point out that our body clocks, called circadian rhythms, follow the daily cycle of light. A one-hour shift in spring, which costs an hour of sleep, is similar to a mild form of jet lag. Studies have found that in the days after the spring change, the number of heart attacks, strokes and road accidents increases slightly. Many sleep specialists argue that the best choice for health would be to stay on standard time all year, which keeps our schedule closest to the natural day.
paras.E: In practice, abolition is not easy. If a country decides to stop changing its clocks, it must choose which time to keep: permanent 'summer' time, with long evenings and dark winter mornings, or permanent 'winter' time, with earlier sunsets in summer. Neither satisfies everybody. Russia tried the first in 2011, found winter mornings too dark, and changed to permanent winter time in 2014. In 2019, the European Parliament voted to end clock changes, but the plan has never been put into effect because member states disagreed on which time to choose.
paras.F: The writer believes that the twice-yearly clock change should end. The evidence of benefits is weak, and the evidence of harm, though modest, is clear. Countries should then choose permanent standard time, which is best for sleep and health, and allow businesses and schools to adjust their opening hours if they want more evening light. Neighbouring countries should coordinate, to avoid confusion in trade and travel. A change as simple as leaving the clocks alone could improve millions of people's lives a little.

paras.A: The emperor penguin is the largest of all penguins, standing about 1.1 metres tall and weighing between 22 and 45 kilograms. It lives only in Antarctica, the coldest place on Earth, and it is the one animal that chooses to breed there in the depths of winter, when temperatures can fall below minus forty degrees Celsius and winds blow at up to 200 kilometres per hour. The story of its breeding cycle is one of the most extraordinary in the natural world.
paras.B: In March and April, as the Antarctic autumn begins, emperor penguins leave the sea and walk or slide on their bellies, sometimes more than a hundred kilometres, to breeding colonies on the sea ice. After courtship, each female lays a single egg in May or June. She then passes the egg carefully to the male, who balances it on his feet and covers it with a warm fold of skin called a brood pouch. The female, exhausted after weeks of fasting, walks back to the sea to feed.
paras.C: For the next two months, the males remain on the ice through the worst of the polar winter. They do not eat, living on stored fat, and they lose up to a third or even half of their body weight. To keep warm, thousands of males crowd together in huddles. The birds on the outside, which face the wind, slowly move towards the centre, while those inside move out, so that everyone takes a turn in the warmer places. The temperature in the middle of a huddle can be much higher than outside.
paras.D: The chicks hatch in July or August, at about the time that the females return, carrying food in their stomachs. They feed the chick by bringing up a rich, milky liquid, while the starving male can finally go to sea to feed. For the rest of the season, the parents take turns to look after the chick and to fetch food. By December, when the sea ice breaks up and the open water comes nearer, the chicks have grown their waterproof adult feathers and can swim.
paras.E: Emperor penguins are expert divers. They hunt fish, squid and krill, and can dive to more than 500 metres, deeper than any other bird, holding their breath for over twenty minutes. Their bodies are adapted for this: their bones are solid and not hollow like those of flying birds, they can slow their heartbeat, and their blood stores oxygen very efficiently. Underwater, they are fast and agile, and can leap out of the water on to the ice.
paras.F: The greatest danger today is climate change. The birds depend on stable sea ice for breeding, and the ice must last from April until the chicks are ready to swim. In 2022, in the Bellingshausen Sea, ice broke up early in four out of five colonies being studied, and almost all of the chicks drowned or froze. Scientists predict that, if warming continues, a large share of emperor colonies could be lost by the end of the century. In 2022, the United States listed the species as threatened.

paras.A: Soap is so familiar that few people stop to wonder how it works. Yet the question is not trivial: oil and water do not mix, so why does a bar of soap remove greasy dirt from our hands when water alone cannot? The answer lies in the structure of soap molecules, which have two very different ends, and it is why regular washing with soap is one of the most effective ways of preventing disease.
paras.B: Soap is among the oldest chemical products. Clay tablets from Babylon, dating from about 2800 BC, describe a mixture of fats and ashes that was used for washing. The Egyptians and Romans also made soap-like substances, though they were mostly used for medicine and for cleaning cloth, and not for the body. In the Middle Ages, soap was made in Italy, Spain and France, using olive oil, and soap-making became a major industry. By the nineteenth century, cheap soap was available to most people in Europe.
paras.C: Soap is made by a reaction called saponification. Fat or oil, from animals or plants such as olive, palm or coconut, is heated with a strong alkali, traditionally lye made from wood ash, and nowadays sodium hydroxide. The reaction splits the fat into glycerine and the salts of fatty acids, which are the soap molecules. Because the reaction needs care, since the alkali is dangerous, makers usually add more fat than needed so that no alkali is left in the finished soap.
paras.D: Each soap molecule has a long tail made of carbon and hydrogen and a head that carries an electric charge. The head is hydrophilic, meaning 'water-loving', and dissolves readily in water. The tail is hydrophobic, meaning 'water-hating', and is attracted to oil and grease. When soap is mixed with water, the molecules surround particles of grease, with their tails pointing into the grease and their heads pointing out into the water. The grease is thus enclosed in a tiny ball called a micelle, which can be rinsed away.
paras.E: Soap also lowers the surface tension of water. Pure water has a strong tendency to form droplets and to stay on the surface of the skin, rather than enter the tiny spaces of cloth or dirt. Soap molecules gather at the surface and weaken the attraction between water molecules, so that the water spreads out and wets the surface much better. This is why soapy water forms bubbles: a thin film of water is held between layers of soap molecules. The bubbles themselves are not what cleans, however.
paras.F: Soap also destroys some germs. Many viruses, including coronaviruses and influenza, are surrounded by an outer layer of fat. Soap molecules push into this layer and tear it apart, and the virus breaks and cannot infect. For this reason, health experts recommend rubbing the hands with soap for at least twenty seconds, which gives it time to work. Soap has a disadvantage in hard water, which contains calcium and magnesium: these combine with soap to form a scum. Detergents, first developed in Germany during the First World War, avoid this problem.

ps.title: Should Students Take a Gap Year?

paras.A: A gap year is a period, usually a year, that a young person takes between school and university or between university and work. Students may spend the time travelling, volunteering, working or learning a skill. The practice is well established in countries such as Britain and Australia, and is growing in others, including the United States, where some universities actively encourage it. But is it a valuable experience or a risky delay?
paras.B: Supporters offer several benefits. A gap year allows students to mature, to become independent, and to find out what they really want to study. Many eighteen-year-olds choose a course without knowing much about it, and some drop out after a year. After a break, students tend to be more motivated and focused. Studies in several countries have found that students who took a gap year performed slightly better in their university courses than those who did not, although it is hard to be sure that the year itself was the cause.
paras.C: A gap year can also build skills that classrooms do not teach. Working in a shop or on a farm teaches responsibility and teamwork; volunteering abroad can develop communication skills and an understanding of other cultures; learning a language by living in another country is often more effective than studying it at school. Employers say that they value this kind of experience, and a student who has managed a budget and solved practical problems may be better prepared for the workplace than one who has only been in education.
paras.D: Critics raise several worries. The first is cost. A year of travelling can cost thousands of pounds, and the students who gain most are often those whose families can afford it, so that gap years may widen inequality. The second is the risk of losing momentum. Some students find it hard to return to studying after a year of freedom, and others never do. A third criticism is that some gap-year projects, especially short volunteering trips, may do little good for the communities they claim to help.
paras.E: Another worry concerns time and money. A gap year delays earning, and by the time a person graduates, he or she is a year older than the others. For students who need to repay loans or who must support their families, the delay can be significant. Some also argue that the benefits depend on how the year is spent, and that a year of doing nothing in particular is unlikely to help anyone. Without a plan, a gap year can easily turn into a holiday at someone else's expense.
paras.F: The writer believes that a gap year is valuable for many students, provided it is planned. Students should have a clear idea of what they want to achieve, such as earning money, learning a language or gaining work experience, and they should arrange a place at university in advance, so that they have something to return to. Schools and universities should provide advice, and support those from poorer backgrounds with grants, so that the opportunity is not limited to the wealthy. With these safeguards, a year out can be a year well spent.

paras.A: Florence Nightingale is remembered as the founder of modern nursing, 'the Lady with the Lamp'. She was born in 1820 in the Italian city of Florence, after which she was named, to a wealthy English family. Her parents expected her to marry well and live as a lady. Florence had other ideas. From her teens, she felt a calling to serve others, and she shocked her family by announcing that she wanted to become a nurse, a job that was then considered low and disreputable, often done by untrained women.
paras.B: After years of struggle against her parents' wishes, she trained for a few months in 1851 at a hospital in Kaiserswerth, in Germany, run by a religious community. In 1853, she became superintendent of a small hospital for women in London. Her chance came with the Crimean War, which began in 1854 when Britain and France fought Russia. Reports in the newspapers described terrible conditions in the army hospitals, where wounded soldiers lay in filth. The secretary of war, who knew her, asked her to lead a group of nurses to the military hospital at Scutari, in Turkey.
paras.C: She arrived in November 1854 with thirty-eight nurses and found a scene of horror. The hospital was overcrowded and dirty, with no clean bandages, and rats ran through the wards. More men were dying from infections such as typhus and cholera than from wounds. Nightingale ordered scrubbing brushes, organised the washing of linen, improved the diet, and set up a kitchen. She worked long hours, and at night she walked through the wards with a lamp to check on the patients, which made the soldiers call her 'the Lady with the Lamp'.
paras.D: The death rate fell dramatically, although historians now say that the main improvement came after a government commission in 1855 forced a clean-up of the sewers and ventilation. Nightingale herself later concluded that most of the deaths had been caused by poor sanitation, not by the war itself. She returned to England in 1856 as a national heroine, but she was in poor health, probably as a result of an illness caught in Crimea, and she spent much of the rest of her life working from her bed.
paras.E: Her greatest influence came from her work as a reformer and statistician. She was a gifted mathematician and collected data on deaths in the army. To persuade politicians, who would not read long tables, she invented a diagram, similar to a pie chart, in which coloured wedges showed the causes of death in each month. In 1858, she became the first woman elected a Fellow of the Royal Statistical Society. Her figures showed that sanitary reform could save thousands of lives, and they led to changes in army hospitals and in public health in India.
paras.F: In 1860, she used a fund raised in her honour to found the Nightingale Training School for nurses at St Thomas' Hospital in London. Her book Notes on Nursing, published in 1859, became a classic. Nursing became a respectable profession for women, based on training and discipline. She died in 1910 at the age of ninety, having been the first woman to receive the Order of Merit. Her birthday, 12 May, is celebrated as International Nurses Day.

paras.A: Every movement we make, from a blink to a sprint, depends on muscles. The human body has more than 600 of them, which together make up about forty per cent of its weight. Muscles are the only tissues that can contract, that is, become shorter and pull. They can only pull, never push, and so they have to work in pairs or groups, with one muscle pulling in one direction and another pulling back.
paras.B: The body contains three kinds of muscle. Skeletal muscles are attached to bones and are under voluntary control; they move the arms, legs, face and trunk. Smooth muscle forms the walls of internal organs such as the stomach, intestines and blood vessels, and works automatically, without our decision. Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart, and contracts rhythmically throughout life without tiring. This text deals mostly with the skeletal type, which is the one we use to move.
paras.C: Skeletal muscles are attached to bones by strong, cord-like tendons. When a muscle contracts, it pulls on the tendon, which pulls on the bone, and the joint moves. The biceps and triceps in the upper arm are a good example. When the biceps contracts, it bends the elbow and raises the forearm, while the triceps relaxes. To straighten the arm, the triceps contracts and the biceps relaxes. Such pairs of muscles are called antagonists. The largest muscle in the body is the gluteus maximus in the buttock, and the smallest is the stapedius, a tiny muscle in the ear.
paras.D: To see how a muscle contracts, we must look inside. A muscle is made of bundles of long cells called fibres, and each fibre is packed with thread-like structures called myofibrils. These consist of two kinds of protein filaments, thin ones made of actin and thicker ones made of myosin, arranged in repeating units. When the brain sends a signal along a nerve, the myosin filaments grab the actin filaments and pull them past, like hands pulling a rope. Each unit becomes shorter, and so does the whole muscle.
paras.E: All this takes energy, which comes from a molecule called ATP, produced from the food we eat and the oxygen we breathe. During intense exercise, the muscles may run short of oxygen and begin to produce energy without it, a process that creates lactic acid. Muscles contain two main kinds of fibre. Slow-twitch fibres contract slowly but can keep going for a long time, and are used for endurance activities such as marathon running. Fast-twitch fibres contract quickly and powerfully, but tire quickly, and are used in sprinting and lifting.
paras.F: Muscles respond to use. When they are regularly stretched against resistance, as in weight-training, the fibres grow thicker and stronger, and when they are not used, as when a limb is in plaster or a person is bedridden, they shrink. This is why exercise is important at every age: after about thirty, people gradually lose muscle unless they keep active. Regular activity also helps the heart, bones and brain. The old saying 'use it or lose it' is in this case literally true.

ps.title: Should Teachers Be Paid According to Results?

paras.A: Teachers are among the most important professionals in any society, but there is much disagreement about how they should be paid. In most countries, pay is based on qualifications and years of service: a teacher with ten years' experience earns more than one with two, regardless of how well their pupils perform. A number of governments and school systems have experimented with 'performance-related pay', in which part of a teacher's salary depends on pupils' test results or on assessments of teaching quality. Is this a sensible way to improve schools?
paras.B: Supporters argue that pay should reflect performance, as it does in many other jobs. Teachers who work hard and help their pupils to make good progress deserve extra reward, and the prospect of a bonus may encourage others to improve. Under a system based on seniority, they say, the best teachers receive the same as the weakest, which can be discouraging and may drive talented people out of the profession. It may also attract ambitious graduates, who would like the chance to be rewarded for success.
paras.C: Critics reply that measuring a teacher's performance is extremely difficult. If pay depends on test scores, the results are affected by many factors beyond the teacher's control, including the pupils' home backgrounds, prior knowledge and even their health on the day of the test. A teacher in a poor area may do an excellent job and still have lower scores than one in a rich area. Methods that try to measure how much pupils improve, called 'value-added' models, are more fair, but they are complicated and can be unreliable from year to year.
paras.D: There is also the danger of unintended consequences. When rewards depend on test results, teachers have an incentive to teach only what is tested, to spend lessons on exam practice, and in extreme cases to cheat. Subjects that are not tested, such as art, music and physical education, may be neglected. Performance pay may also damage cooperation among teachers, who may keep good ideas to themselves rather than share them with colleagues who are competing for the same bonuses.
paras.E: The evidence is mixed. In a carefully designed experiment in Nashville, Tennessee, between 2006 and 2009, teachers were offered bonuses of up to 15,000 dollars if their pupils' scores rose; on average, the pupils did no better than those of teachers who were not offered bonuses. Other trials, particularly in developing countries, have found some improvements, for example in India, where bonuses led to modest gains in test scores. The results seem to depend on how the scheme is designed and on how teachers are paid at the start.
paras.F: The writer concludes that individual bonuses based on test scores are not the answer, but this does not mean that pay should be fixed for ever. Better ideas include rewarding teams of teachers for the progress of a whole school, paying more to those who take on difficult schools or subjects with shortages, and creating a career ladder in which excellent teachers gain responsibility and higher pay by mentoring colleagues. Above all, teachers should be paid enough to attract good graduates in the first place, since no system of bonuses can make up for a poorly paid profession.

ps.title: Cappadocia: A Land Carved from Rock

paras.A: In central Turkey, the landscape looks like another planet. Tall cones of pale rock, some of them topped with a flat cap, stand in valleys of smooth, curving hills. This is Cappadocia, a region famous for its 'fairy chimneys', for homes and churches carved into stone, and for the hot-air balloons that rise over the valleys at dawn. Every year, millions of visitors come to see one of the most unusual landscapes on Earth.
paras.B: The landscape was created by volcanoes and by erosion. Between nine and three million years ago, the volcanoes of the region, including Mount Erciyes and Mount Hasan, erupted repeatedly, covering the plateau with thick layers of ash. Over time, the ash hardened into a soft rock called tuff. Rain, wind and frost then wore away the surface, cutting deep valleys. Where a harder piece of rock lay on top of softer tuff, the soft rock beneath was worn away more slowly, leaving a column with a cap, the fairy chimney.
paras.C: The soft tuff was easy to dig, but it hardens when it is exposed to air, and this made it an ideal building material. For thousands of years, people carved houses, stables, storerooms and even entire villages out of the rock. These dwellings were cool in summer and warm in winter, which is valuable in a region with hot summers and cold winters. In some villages, people still live and keep animals in cave homes, and a number have been turned into hotels.
paras.D: Early Christians settled the region from the first centuries AD, and especially after the fourth century, when monks came to live in remote valleys. They carved hundreds of churches and monasteries, and decorated the walls with paintings of saints and scenes from the Bible. The best-known group is at Göreme, now an open-air museum, where churches such as the Dark Church preserve brilliant frescoes in blue, red and gold. The colours survived because the inner rooms were sheltered from light.
paras.E: Beneath the surface lie even more remarkable structures: underground cities. The largest known, at Derinkuyu, goes down some 60 metres and has about eighteen levels, containing living rooms, stables, wells, kitchens, chapels and ventilation shafts. It could shelter thousands of people, and perhaps as many as twenty thousand, together with their animals and food. Huge round stones could be rolled across the passages to block them. The cities were probably used as hiding places during periods of invasion, though some may have been started in much earlier times.
paras.F: In 1985, UNESCO listed Göreme National Park and the rock sites of Cappadocia as a World Heritage Site. Tourism has brought wealth to a region that was once poor, but also problems, such as damage to fragile rock, traffic and the pressure of many visitors. Balloon flights, which began in the 1980s, have become the symbol of the region; on a good morning, over a hundred balloons float over the valleys. Authorities now regulate them and limit visitor numbers in some places, in order to protect the landscape that visitors have come to see.

ps.title: How Radio Carries Sound Through the Air

paras.A: A radio station broadcasts music from a studio in one city, and within a fraction of a second, a small plastic box thousands of kilometres away plays it. There are no wires between them. The signal travels through the air, or even through empty space, in the form of radio waves. These are a kind of electromagnetic wave, the same family as visible light, but with much longer wavelengths, and they move at the speed of light, about 300,000 kilometres per second.
paras.B: The existence of radio waves was predicted by the Scottish physicist James Clerk Maxwell in the 1860s, and shown by the German physicist Heinrich Hertz in 1887, who generated waves in his laboratory and detected them across the room. The unit of frequency, the hertz, is named after him. Hertz himself did not see any use for his discovery, but a young Italian, Guglielmo Marconi, did. In 1901, Marconi sent a signal across the Atlantic Ocean, from Cornwall to Newfoundland, proving that wireless communication over long distances was possible.
paras.C: Sound cannot be sent directly by radio waves. The vibrations of sound have a low frequency, and a wave of that sort would not travel far. Instead, the radio uses a high-frequency 'carrier wave', and the sound is added to it by a process called modulation. In amplitude modulation, or AM, the strength of the carrier wave is varied in time with the sound. In frequency modulation, or FM, the strength stays the same but the frequency rises and falls slightly.
paras.D: At the receiver, the process is reversed. The antenna picks up thousands of radio signals, from many stations, at once. A tuning circuit selects the one at the frequency that the listener wants, ignoring the others, in the same way that a guitar string vibrates only when notes of the right pitch are played. The receiver then separates the sound from the carrier wave, a step known as demodulation, amplifies the signal and sends it to a loudspeaker, which turns it back into sound.
paras.E: AM and FM have different strengths. AM waves can bounce off a layer of the upper atmosphere called the ionosphere, particularly at night, so AM stations can be heard hundreds of kilometres away. However, AM is easily disturbed by interference from electrical equipment and thunderstorms, and the sound quality is limited. FM provides much clearer sound and is less affected by interference, but its waves travel in straight lines and are blocked by hills, so reception is limited to about 50 to 100 kilometres.
paras.F: Radio waves are now used for much more than broadcasting. Mobile phones, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, GPS, garage-door openers, aircraft navigation and radar all rely on them, each using its own range of frequencies, which governments allocate to avoid interference. Digital radio, which converts sound to numbers before sending it, offers better quality and more stations. Even though people have predicted for decades that radio would be replaced by newer media, it remains one of the most widespread forms of communication in the world.

ps.title: Should the Sale of Fur Be Banned?

paras.A: Fur has been worn for as long as people have had to protect themselves from the cold. Today, however, it is mostly a fashion product, and the question of whether it is acceptable to kill animals for it has become one of the most controversial in the clothing industry. Britain banned fur farming in 2000, and several other European countries have done the same. In 2017, the Italian fashion house Gucci announced that it would stop using fur, and many others have followed. Some cities and states, such as California, have gone further and banned the sale of new fur products.
paras.B: Those who want to ban fur point first to animal welfare. Most fur today comes from farms, where animals such as mink, foxes and rabbits are kept in small wire cages, often for their whole lives. These animals are wild, not domesticated, and campaigners say that confinement causes great stress and unnatural behaviour. They are killed for their pelts when they are a few months old. Opponents argue that, in a world where synthetic materials can keep us warm and look good, it is not justifiable to cause such suffering for the sake of fashion.
paras.C: There are also health and environmental arguments. During the pandemic, outbreaks of coronavirus on mink farms in Denmark and the Netherlands led to the killing of millions of animals, and the Netherlands has since ended mink farming. Critics say that fur farms also produce large amounts of waste, which pollutes water and soil, and that the processing of pelts uses toxic chemicals to prevent them from rotting.
paras.D: The fur industry disagrees. It says that modern farms are regulated and that standards of care have improved. It also argues that fur is a natural, long-lasting material that can be repaired and reused for decades, while fake fur is made from plastic derived from oil, which does not break down and sheds microplastics into the environment. For these reasons, supporters claim, a coat made of real fur may be less harmful to the environment than a cheap synthetic coat that is thrown away after a season.
paras.E: Another argument concerns jobs and traditions. In some northern regions, such as parts of Canada, trapping has been a way of life for indigenous people for thousands of years, and they depend on it for income. A total ban, the industry says, would destroy livelihoods, and would be unfair when other industries that use animals, such as leather and meat, are allowed. Critics respond that farmed fur is a different matter from traditional subsistence trapping, and that exemptions can be made for indigenous communities.
paras.F: The writer's view is that the sale of fur from intensive farms should be phased out. Unlike food, fur is not necessary, and alternatives exist. Governments should first ban the farming of animals that suffer most in captivity, and set a date by which the sale of new fur products ends, giving workers time and help to change jobs. Meanwhile, they should require honest labels and fund research on better synthetic materials, so that people can look for warmth and style without causing needless suffering.

ps.title: Jane Goodall and the Chimpanzees of Gombe

paras.A: In July 1960, a twenty-six-year-old Englishwoman with no university degree arrived on the shore of Lake Tanganyika, in what is now Tanzania, to study wild chimpanzees. Her name was Jane Goodall, and her work, which would last for decades, would change our understanding of animals and of ourselves. She had been sent by the Kenyan palaeontologist Louis Leakey, who believed that studying the great apes might shed light on the behaviour of early humans.
paras.B: Goodall was born in London in 1934, and she had loved animals since childhood. As a girl, she read the Tarzan books and dreamed of living in Africa. She worked as a secretary and waitress to save the fare, and travelled to Kenya in 1957, where she met Leakey. He was impressed by her patience and her passion, and he gave her the chance to start a study at the Gombe Stream reserve. The authorities at first refused to let a young woman go into the forest alone, so her mother came with her for the first months.
paras.C: At first, the chimpanzees fled whenever she came near. It took months of patient waiting before they accepted her. Gradually, she was able to watch them from a short distance, and she began to recognise individuals. She broke the rules of science at the time by giving them names, such as David Greybeard, Flo and Fifi, instead of numbers, and by describing their personalities and emotions. Some scientists criticised her for being unscientific, but her approach showed that each chimpanzee is an individual, with a character and a history.
paras.D: Her most famous discovery was made in the autumn of 1960. She saw David Greybeard push a blade of grass into a termite mound and pull it out covered with termites, which he ate. He was making and using a tool. Until then, scientists had believed that only humans made tools, and the definition of 'man' was based on this. When Leakey heard the news, he is said to have replied: 'Now we must redefine tool, redefine man, or accept chimpanzees as humans.'
paras.E: Over the following years, she and her team recorded many other behaviours: chimpanzees hunting and eating meat, which had been thought to be unusual, forming close bonds between mother and child, and showing affection with hugs and kisses. They also saw darker behaviour, including aggression, and in the 1970s, a prolonged conflict between two groups of chimpanzees. This showed that these animals can be violent as well as gentle. In 1965, Goodall received a doctorate from Cambridge University, one of very few people to be admitted without a first degree.
paras.F: By the 1980s, Goodall realised that chimpanzees were in danger. Forests were being cut down, animals were being hunted for meat and captured for sale, and their numbers had fallen from perhaps a million a century earlier to a few hundred thousand. She left her research and became a campaigner. She founded the Jane Goodall Institute in 1977 and, in 1991, a youth programme, Roots & Shoots, which now operates in many countries. She was made a Dame of the British Empire in 2004, and she spent most of her later life travelling and giving talks.

paras.A: An ant on its own is not very clever. Its brain has only about 250,000 cells, compared with the 86 billion in a human brain. Yet together, ants can build complex nests, farm fungus, wage wars and find the shortest route to food. A colony behaves like a single organism, and scientists call it a 'superorganism'. There are more than 12,000 known species of ant, living on every continent except Antarctica, and their combined weight is estimated to be comparable to that of all humans.
paras.B: A typical colony has three kinds of ant. The queen is a large female whose job is to lay eggs. A queen may live for many years, with some reaching twenty or even thirty years, and produce millions of eggs in her lifetime. Workers, which are all sterile females, do almost all the other jobs: they find food, care for the young, build and defend the nest. Males, which have wings, exist only to mate with new queens and die soon afterwards.
paras.C: Workers divide labour according to age and need. Young workers tend to stay inside the nest, caring for eggs and larvae; older ones become builders and guards; the oldest ones go out to look for food, which is the most dangerous job. The colony changes the proportions as conditions change. If food becomes scarce, more workers become foragers. There is no boss giving orders: the queen does not command the colony. Instead, each ant follows simple rules, responding to signals from other ants and to the work that needs doing.
paras.D: The main form of communication is chemical. Ants release substances called pheromones, which others detect with their antennae. When a forager finds food, it lays a trail of pheromone on its way back to the nest. Other ants follow the trail, and reinforce it with their own pheromone on the return trip, so the trail becomes stronger. Over time, shorter paths get stronger scent, because ants complete the trip more quickly and lay down more pheromone, and the colony finds the best route without any ant having a map.
paras.E: Some ants have developed remarkable lifestyles. Leafcutter ants of Central and South America cut pieces of leaves and carry them to their nest, where they use them to grow a fungus, which they eat. The colony may contain millions of ants and an underground fungus garden the size of a room. Army ants have no permanent nest. They march in huge columns, up to millions of individuals, and eat insects and other small animals in their path. Weaver ants build nests in trees by joining leaves with silk produced by their larvae.
paras.F: Ants can also be very successful at invading new places. The Argentine ant, introduced to Europe, formed a vast 'supercolony' that stretches for about 6,000 kilometres along the Mediterranean coast, in which ants from different nests do not fight. Elsewhere, introduced ants such as the red fire ant have harmed native wildlife and crops. Despite this, ants are generally very beneficial: they move soil, spread seeds and control pests. Computer scientists have also copied their behaviour in programs that solve routing problems.

ps.title: Should People Be Able to Vote Online?

paras.A: In most countries, voters still go to a polling station on election day, mark a paper ballot and put it in a box. The system is old, but it is simple, and people can see how it works. In the digital age, many ask why we cannot vote on our phones, in the same way that we bank and shop. Estonia, a small country in northern Europe, has done just that. It first allowed online voting in 2005, and in the 2023 parliamentary election, about half of all votes were cast over the internet.
paras.B: Supporters of internet voting begin with convenience and participation. Voters would not have to queue or travel to a polling station, which would be especially useful for people who are disabled, ill, living abroad or working long hours. It might raise turnout, particularly among young people, who tend to vote less than other groups. Counting would be faster and cheaper, with fewer mistakes than manual counting, and the results could be known within minutes. The paper ballots used today also cost large sums to print, transport and store.
paras.C: Opponents begin with security. Every computer system can be attacked by hackers, and an election is an especially tempting target. A foreign government or criminal group could try to change votes, disable the system on election day or spread doubt about the result. Computer scientists note that a secure vote requires a system that is both secret and verifiable, and that it is very difficult to achieve both on the internet, because voters' own devices may be infected with viruses of which they are unaware.
paras.D: There are other concerns. At a polling station, each person enters a booth alone, so that nobody can see how they vote. This protects against pressure and vote-buying. If people vote at home, a family member or employer could stand beside them, or demand proof of their vote. Trust is also important: with paper, observers from all parties can watch the counting and understand it. With electronic voting, few citizens understand the technology, and if there is a problem, they may find it harder to believe that the result is genuine.
paras.E: Estonia shows what is possible, but also what is needed. Its system relies on a national digital identity card, which every citizen has and uses for many services, on a long period of voting in advance, and on the right to change one's vote, or to cancel it by voting in person. Experts have still questioned its security. Other countries have been more careful: Switzerland, after trials in several cantons, stopped some of them in 2019 when security problems were found, and restarted with stricter testing.
paras.F: The writer believes that online voting is a risk that most countries should not yet take for national elections. Convenience is valuable, but the integrity of elections is more so. A better course would be to make existing voting easier, through advance voting, postal ballots and more polling stations, while testing online systems carefully in smaller, less critical votes. If one day secure and verifiable technology is developed, it can be reconsidered, but trust takes years to build and moments to destroy.

paras.A: In the dry centre of Australia, some 450 kilometres from the nearest large town, a huge block of red rock rises suddenly from the flat desert. This is Uluru, formerly known as Ayers Rock, one of the most famous natural landmarks in the world. It stands 348 metres high, taller than the Eiffel Tower, and measures about 9.4 kilometres around its base. Yet what is seen is only the tip: most of the rock lies underground, extending perhaps several kilometres beneath the surface.
paras.B: Uluru is made of a coarse sandstone called arkose, which was formed from sand and gravel laid down in a vast shallow sea or river system more than 500 million years ago. Over time, the sediments were buried, hardened into rock, and then tilted until the layers were almost vertical. Later erosion wore away the softer rock around it, leaving Uluru standing alone. The rock looks smooth from a distance, but close up, it is marked with caves, ridges, holes and water channels.
paras.C: The rock is famous for its changing colours. At midday, it looks a dull orange-brown, but at dawn and sunset, it glows deep red, then purple, as the angle of the Sun changes. The red colour is caused by a thin layer of rust on the surface: iron minerals in the rock have reacted with oxygen in the air. The surface of a freshly broken piece of rock is in fact grey. Rainfall is rare, but when it does fall, thin waterfalls pour down the sides, and the rock is transformed.
paras.D: For the Anangu, the traditional owners of the land, Uluru is far more than a geological wonder. They have lived in the area for at least 30,000 years. In their culture, the landscape was created by ancestral beings in a period called Tjukurpa, which is both a creation story and a code of law, and every cave, crack and waterhole has a meaning. Some places are sacred, and certain information may be shared only with initiated men or women. The Anangu have a deep responsibility to look after the land, which they call Country.
paras.E: European explorers reached the area in the 1870s. The surveyor William Gosse saw the rock in 1873 and named it Ayers Rock after Sir Henry Ayers, a politician in South Australia. Over the next century, the area was taken from its owners, who were pushed away from their land. In 1985, after a long campaign, the Australian government returned the title of Uluru–Kata Tjuta National Park to the Anangu, who immediately leased it back to the government, so that it could be managed jointly. In 1993, the rock was given its dual name, Uluru / Ayers Rock.
paras.F: For many years, tourists were allowed to climb the rock, although the Anangu asked them not to, because the climb crosses a sacred path, and because several visitors had died. After much discussion, the climb was permanently closed on 26 October 2019. Visitors can now walk around the base, join guided tours led by Anangu guides, and learn about the stories, plants and animals. The park was listed by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site in 1987, for its natural features, and again in 1994 for its cultural value.
