ps.title: Inside the Cell: The Unit of Life

paras.A: All living things, from bacteria to blue whales, are made of cells. A cell is the smallest unit that can be considered alive. It can take in food, release waste, grow and reproduce. Some organisms, such as bacteria and amoebas, consist of only one cell; others, such as humans, are made of trillions. The adult human body contains an estimated thirty to forty trillion cells of about 200 different types, from nerve cells to muscle cells and red blood cells.
paras.B: Cells were discovered with the help of the microscope. In 1665, the English scientist Robert Hooke looked at a thin slice of cork under a microscope and saw tiny box-like compartments that reminded him of the small rooms, or cells, in which monks lived. The name stuck, even though what he saw were the walls of dead plant cells. In the 1670s, the Dutch merchant Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, using lenses that he had made himself, saw living cells for the first time, including bacteria in pond water.
paras.C: It took almost two centuries for scientists to realise the importance of the discovery. In 1838 and 1839, the German scientists Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann proposed that all plants and animals are made of cells. In 1855, Rudolf Virchow added that new cells arise only from existing cells. Together, these ideas form the cell theory, one of the foundations of biology. They replaced older beliefs, such as the idea that living things could arise spontaneously from mud or rotting meat.
paras.D: There are two main kinds of cell. Prokaryotic cells, such as those of bacteria, are small and simple, with no nucleus; their genetic material floats freely in the cell. Eukaryotic cells, found in plants, animals, fungi and other organisms, are bigger and more complex. They contain a nucleus, which holds the DNA, and many specialised structures called organelles. Each organelle does a particular job, just as the organs in the body do.
paras.E: The main organelles include the nucleus, which controls the cell's activities; the mitochondria, which release energy from food and are often called the power stations of the cell; and the ribosomes, which make proteins. The whole cell is surrounded by a thin membrane that controls what enters and leaves. Plant cells have two additional features: a rigid cell wall, which gives support, and chloroplasts, which capture the energy of sunlight for photosynthesis.
paras.F: Cells reproduce by dividing. Before dividing, a cell copies all of its DNA, so that each daughter cell receives a full set of instructions. In the process of mitosis, the copied chromosomes are separated and pulled to opposite ends of the cell, which then splits into two. Our bodies use mitosis to grow and to repair damage. Skin cells, for instance, divide continuously to replace those that are lost. When the controls on division fail, cells may multiply without restraint, forming a tumour, which is how cancer begins.

ps.title: Should Animals Be Used in Circuses?

paras.A: For more than two hundred years, the circus has been a form of popular entertainment, and for much of that time, animals have been among its stars: lions jumping through hoops of fire, elephants standing on stools, and horses performing tricks. Today, however, attitudes are changing. Many people feel that it is wrong to keep wild animals in travelling shows, and a growing number of countries have banned or restricted them. In 2016, the American circus Ringling Bros announced that it would stop using elephants, and the following year, it closed.
paras.B: Opponents of animal acts start with welfare. Wild animals such as elephants, big cats and bears evolved to roam over huge areas, to live in complex social groups and to hunt or forage. In a circus, they spend most of their time in small cages or wagons, travelling long distances, and they are taught tricks by methods which, campaigners say, often involve fear or pain. Animals may show signs of distress, such as swaying from side to side or walking up and down repeatedly, which are rare in the wild.
paras.C: Defenders of circus animals reply that modern circuses have improved. Many animals are born in captivity, they say, and the performers care for them as members of the family; since the animals are valuable, it makes no sense to treat them badly. They argue that training uses rewards, not punishment, and that performing keeps animals active and mentally stimulated. Circuses also say that they help to educate the public about animals and to maintain rare skills, such as horse riding and training.
paras.D: Critics counter that the argument about education is weak. What audiences learn from watching an elephant stand on its back legs is not natural behaviour, but an artificial trick, and it may give a false impression of the animal. Scientists who have studied the welfare of travelling circus animals have generally found that the conditions cannot meet the needs of species like elephants and big cats. Furthermore, the public is increasingly uncomfortable with watching them, and many circuses, such as Cirque du Soleil, have been successful without any animal acts.
paras.E: Governments have responded in different ways. Around forty countries have restricted the use of wild animals in circuses, among them Austria, Greece, India and Mexico. In 2020, England banned the use of wild animals in travelling circuses, after years of discussion. Some places have made exceptions for domestic animals such as horses and dogs, on the grounds that they are used to life with humans. Others have also asked what to do with animals that cannot be released into the wild, since many have spent their entire lives in captivity.
paras.F: The writer believes that wild animals should no longer perform in travelling circuses, because the conditions of life on the road cannot meet their needs. Existing animals should be moved to sanctuaries, where they can live out their lives in better surroundings, and the cost should be shared between the government and the circuses. Horses and other domestic animals, treated well, may continue to be part of shows. Circuses do not need wild animals to survive, as the success of those that rely on human acrobats, clowns and musicians has shown.

paras.A: On the night of 12 to 13 August 1961, the people of Berlin went to sleep in one city and woke up in two. Soldiers and workers of East Germany had unrolled barbed wire and closed the streets between the eastern and western parts of the city. Within days, the wire was replaced with concrete blocks. The Berlin Wall, as it became known, would divide the city for twenty-eight years, and it became the most famous symbol of the Cold War.
paras.B: To understand why the wall was built, it is necessary to go back to 1945. After the defeat of Nazi Germany, the country was divided into four zones controlled by the United States, Britain, France and the Soviet Union. The capital, Berlin, which lay deep within the Soviet zone, was also divided into four sectors. In 1949, the western zones became West Germany, a democracy with a market economy, while the Soviet zone became East Germany, a communist state. The three western sectors of Berlin formed an island of freedom inside East Germany.
paras.C: By the late 1950s, West Germany was prospering, while East Germany faced shortages and strict control. Berlin, where the border was open, offered an easy escape. Between 1949 and 1961, about 2.7 million East Germans left for the West, many of them young, well-educated people such as doctors, engineers and teachers. The East German government feared that the country would be left without workers. The wall was built to stop the flow, although the government called it an 'anti-fascist protection barrier'.
paras.D: Over the years, the barrier became a complex system. It consisted of two walls with a wide 'death strip' between them, which contained raked sand, floodlights, watchtowers, dogs, trip wires and anti-vehicle trenches. Guards were ordered to shoot people trying to cross. The wall surrounded West Berlin for about 155 kilometres. At least 140 people are known to have died trying to cross it or at the border. Ordinary Berliners were separated from friends and relatives, and many families did not meet for decades.
paras.E: In the 1980s, communism began to weaken. In 1987, US President Ronald Reagan stood before the Brandenburg Gate and challenged the Soviet leader, Mikhail Gorbachev: 'Mr Gorbachev, tear down this wall.' In 1989, reforms in Poland and Hungary opened new routes to the West, and thousands of East Germans left through Hungary and Czechoslovakia. At home, mass demonstrations demanded freedom. The government, in a crisis, announced new travel rules on 9 November, but a spokesman, Günter Schabowski, mistakenly said that they took effect immediately.
paras.F: That evening, crowds gathered at the border crossings and demanded to be let through. The guards, who had no clear orders, eventually opened the gates, and thousands of people streamed across, many in tears. Ordinary people began to chip pieces from the wall with hammers. Germany was reunified on 3 October 1990. Today, only a few sections of the wall remain, including the East Side Gallery, a stretch of 1.3 kilometres decorated with paintings, and a line of cobblestones in the pavement marks where the wall once stood.

paras.A: Honey is the only food made by insects that humans eat. A jar of honey is the result of the work of tens of thousands of bees, who between them have visited millions of flowers. It seems simple, but the process is a complicated one, involving chemistry, teamwork and a remarkable ability to engineer a perfect food that can last for years without refrigeration.
paras.B: The story begins with nectar, the sweet liquid produced by flowers to attract insects. A forager bee sucks the nectar through her long tongue and stores it in a special stomach, called the honey stomach, which is separate from her ordinary stomach. She may visit between fifty and a hundred flowers before the stomach is full. In it, enzymes begin to change the nectar. One of them, invertase, breaks down the sugar sucrose into two simpler sugars, glucose and fructose.
paras.C: Back at the hive, the forager passes the nectar to a house bee, mouth to mouth. The nectar is passed from bee to bee several times, with more enzymes added each time. The nectar contains about 70 per cent water, which is too much for it to keep. To remove the water, the bees spread the droplets in thin layers across the honeycomb cells and fan them with their wings, creating currents of warm air. After a day or so, the water content has fallen to about 18 per cent.
paras.D: Once the honey is ready, the bees store it in the hexagonal cells of the honeycomb, which they build from wax secreted by their own bodies. The hexagon is the most efficient shape, since it uses the smallest amount of wax to build cells that fit together without gaps. When a cell is full, the bees seal it with a cap of wax. Thus a colony stores food for the winter, when there are no flowers. A single worker bee makes only about one-twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in her whole life, so a jar represents an enormous amount of work.
paras.E: Honey is almost unique in not going bad. It contains very little water, so the bacteria and moulds that spoil other foods cannot grow in it. It is also quite acidic, and the bees' enzymes produce small amounts of hydrogen peroxide, a mild antiseptic. Because of these properties, honey has been used for thousands of years to treat wounds, and jars of it found in ancient Egyptian tombs are said to have been still edible. One caution is that honey should not be given to babies under a year old, because it can contain bacteria that may cause a rare, serious illness.
paras.F: Humans have collected honey since prehistoric times, as shown by cave paintings in Spain that depict people harvesting it from wild nests. Modern beekeeping took a leap forward in 1851, when the American Lorenzo Langstroth invented a hive with movable frames, so that honey could be removed without destroying the colony. Today, honey is produced in almost every country, but bees face serious problems from pesticides, disease and the loss of wild flowers. Protecting them matters not only for honey, but for the pollination of many of the crops we eat.

paras.A: A curfew is a rule that requires people to be at home between certain hours. A few cities in the United States, Britain and elsewhere have imposed curfews on young people, usually forbidding those under sixteen or seventeen to be out in public in the late evening unless accompanied by an adult. The idea is attractive to many parents and politicians, who see it as a simple way to protect young people and reduce crime. But does it work, and is it fair?
paras.B: Supporters point out that crime, particularly by young people and against them, tends to peak in the late evening. If teenagers are at home, they cannot be involved in vandalism, theft or fights, nor can they become victims. A curfew also gives the police a clear rule: officers can take any young person who is out late home without having to prove that anything wrong has been done. Some residents who live in areas with problems of noise and anti-social behaviour say that curfews have made their streets calmer.
paras.C: Supporters also stress that parents benefit. Many parents find it hard to set limits when their child's friends are free to go out. A rule applied to everyone helps those parents to refuse requests without being the only 'strict' one. There are health aspects too. Teenagers need around nine hours of sleep, and many do not get it. Time at home in the late evening gives more chance to rest before school the next day.
paras.D: The evidence for crime reduction is weak, however. A major review of studies from the United States, published in 2016, found that juvenile curfews had no significant effect on crime or on victimisation. One reason is that much youth crime takes place in the afternoon, immediately after school, rather than at night. Another is that curfews are hard to enforce, and the police spend time on young people who have done nothing wrong, time that could be used for more serious matters.
paras.E: Critics also worry about fairness and freedom. A curfew treats all young people as potential offenders because of the behaviour of a few. It can prevent teenagers from legitimate activities, such as getting home from a part-time job, going to a late class, or attending a sports event. There are concerns that curfews are applied unequally, with the police stopping young people from minority groups more often. Teenagers need chances to practise independence and judgment, and critics say that rigid rules prevent that.
paras.F: Some places have tried a different approach. In Iceland, a law since the 1990s has stated that children aged twelve and under must be home by eight in the evening in winter and ten in summer, and those aged thirteen to sixteen must be home by ten in winter and midnight in summer. But the rule was part of a wider programme that provided free sports and arts activities and encouraged parents to be involved in their children's lives, and rates of teenage drinking and drug use fell sharply. The writer concludes that curfews, if they have any role, are most useful as one part of broader support for young people and not as a stand-alone cure for crime.

ps.title: The Maldives: Paradise at Sea Level

paras.A: Scattered across the Indian Ocean, south-west of India and Sri Lanka, the Maldives is a nation of about 1,190 small coral islands, grouped into twenty-six natural rings of coral called atolls. Only about 200 of them are inhabited. Together, they cover a vast area of ocean, but their total land area is only around 300 square kilometres, making the Maldives one of the smallest countries in Asia. It is also the lowest-lying country on Earth: the average height of the land is only about 1.5 metres above sea level.
paras.B: The islands were formed in a remarkable way. Charles Darwin suggested in the 1830s that atolls start as volcanic islands surrounded by coral reefs. As the volcano slowly sinks, the coral continues to grow upwards towards the sunlight, until only a ring of reef is left around a central lagoon. This explanation has been largely confirmed by drilling. The islands consist of coral rock, sand and the remains of marine animals, and they sit on top of the submerged peaks of an ancient volcanic ridge.
paras.C: For centuries, the people of the Maldives lived by fishing, trading in cowrie shells, which were used as money in parts of Asia and Africa, and making rope from coconut fibre. They were converted to Islam in the twelfth century, and today almost all Maldivians are Muslim. The country was ruled by sultans, came under British protection in 1887, and became independent in 1965. It is now a republic, with a population of about 520,000, of whom roughly a third live in the capital, Malé, one of the most crowded cities in the world.
paras.D: Tourism has transformed the economy. Beginning in the early 1970s, when the first resort opened, the Maldives became famous for its white beaches, clear lagoons and rich marine life. The government made a policy that each resort should occupy a separate island, so visitors can enjoy privacy, and so that local communities are not disturbed. Tourism now accounts for a large part of the country's income, and fishing, once the main industry, has become secondary. Many Maldivians work in hotels and boats.
paras.E: The greatest challenge is climate change. Since most of the land is less than two metres above the sea, a rise in sea level of even half a metre could flood large areas, and storms and high tides already cause damage. Rising ocean temperatures also threaten the coral reefs, which protect the islands from waves and are essential for tourism and fishing. In 2009, to draw the world's attention, the president held a cabinet meeting underwater, with ministers wearing diving equipment, who signed a call for cuts in carbon emissions.
paras.F: The government is taking practical steps. It has built sea walls around Malé and an entire artificial island, Hulhumalé, raised several metres above the sea, to house a growing population. Plans for floating buildings and for protecting coral reefs have been explored. At the same time, the country has set targets to reduce its own emissions, although these are tiny compared with those of larger nations. Some experts believe that, with careful adaptation, many islands can survive far longer than predicted. Others fear that the Maldives may eventually become unlivable.

paras.A: For a century, the car meant a petrol or diesel engine. Today, electric vehicles are changing that. In 2023, around one in five new cars sold worldwide was electric or a plug-in hybrid, and sales are rising in many countries. An electric car works in a very different way from a conventional one, and it has far fewer moving parts. There is no engine, no exhaust, no gearbox with many gears, and no oil to change.
paras.B: The main components are the battery, the electric motor and the control electronics. The battery stores the energy in the form of chemical energy, and almost all modern electric cars use lithium-ion batteries, similar to those in phones but much larger. A typical pack consists of thousands of small cells and weighs several hundred kilograms, and is placed under the floor to keep the car stable. The energy is stored as direct current, but the motors normally run on alternating current.
paras.C: A device called an inverter changes the direct current from the battery into alternating current for the motor, and also controls its frequency and strength, which determines the speed. In the motor, alternating current creates a rotating magnetic field in a fixed outer part, which drags a rotating inner part around with it. The motor turns the wheels through a simple gear. When the driver presses the pedal, the controller sends more power, and the car accelerates smoothly, without the delay of changing gears.
paras.D: Electric motors have two great advantages. One is efficiency. An electric motor converts about 85 to 90 per cent of the energy it receives into movement, while a petrol engine turns only about 20 to 30 per cent of the energy in fuel into motion, with the rest lost as heat. The other is torque, the turning force. A motor delivers its full torque from zero speed, so electric cars accelerate quickly, even though they are heavy.
paras.E: Electric cars also recover energy. When the driver lifts a foot from the pedal or presses the brake, the motor works in reverse and acts as a generator, converting the car's movement back into electricity that is fed into the battery. This is called regenerative braking. It increases the range, particularly in city driving, and reduces wear on the brake pads. Some cars allow 'one-pedal driving', in which lifting the foot slows the vehicle noticeably.
paras.F: The idea is much older than people think. Electric carriages were built in the 1830s, and around 1900, about a third of the cars on American roads were electric. They lost out to petrol cars, which could go further and were cheaper after the discovery of large oil fields. Now, the main obstacles are cost, the time needed for charging and the availability of charging points. Environmental benefits depend on how the electricity is made, and on the mining of materials like lithium and cobalt for batteries, but studies generally find that, over their lifetime, electric cars produce lower emissions than conventional cars.

ps.title: Should Schools Teach Children to Cook?

paras.A: In 2014, England made cooking and nutrition a compulsory part of the school curriculum for children up to the age of fourteen. The decision followed campaigns by chefs and health experts who warned that a generation was growing up without knowing how to prepare a simple meal. Many other countries are debating the same question. Is cooking a skill that schools ought to teach, or is it the job of parents, and does the lesson have any effect on what children eat?
paras.B: Supporters begin with health. In many countries, rates of obesity, diabetes and heart disease are rising, and diets based on ready meals, takeaways and snacks are part of the cause. People who cook from fresh ingredients tend to eat more vegetables and less sugar, salt and fat. Learning to cook, supporters argue, gives children the knowledge and confidence to make healthier choices for life. The earlier the habit is formed, the more likely it is to last.
paras.C: A second argument is about equality. Children whose parents cook at home often learn by watching and helping, but a growing number of families rely on convenience food because both parents work long hours, or because they lack the money or space to cook properly. If schools do not teach cooking, those children may reach adulthood without the skills. School lessons give every child the same chance. Cooking can also be a good way to teach other subjects, such as maths through measuring, science through heat and chemistry, and culture through traditional dishes.
paras.D: There are also practical benefits. Cooking at home is usually cheaper than buying ready meals or eating out, so those who know how to do it can save money. It also reduces food waste, as people learn to use leftovers and to plan meals. In Japan, school lunches are prepared with an emphasis on 'shokuiku', or food education, and children help to serve and clean up; many experts believe that this has helped to keep childhood obesity rates among the lowest in the developed world.
paras.E: Critics raise some objections. Schools are already under pressure to teach a crowded curriculum and to improve exam results, and cooking lessons require special rooms, equipment and ingredients, which are costly. Some schools in poorer areas have not been able to afford them. Others point out that the responsibility for teaching children to eat well belongs to families, not teachers. A further criticism is that knowing how to cook does not guarantee that people will do so; many adults who can cook choose not to because they are tired or busy.
paras.F: The writer believes that cooking should be taught in schools, but that it should be done practically and sensibly. Lessons should concentrate on simple, affordable meals that children can make at home, and not only on elaborate dishes. Schools should receive the funding for equipment and trained staff, and should involve families, for example by sending recipes home. Cooking alone will not solve problems of diet, which also depend on prices, advertising and time, but it gives young people a basic skill that they will use for the rest of their lives.

ps.title: Isaac Newton: The Man Who Explained the Heavens

paras.A: Isaac Newton is regarded as one of the greatest scientists who ever lived. He was born on Christmas Day 1642 in the village of Woolsthorpe, in Lincolnshire, England, three months after the death of his father. His mother soon remarried and left him in the care of his grandmother. He was an unhappy child, and as a boy he was more interested in building models, such as sundials and a water clock, than in farming, which his family expected him to do.
paras.B: An uncle recognised his talent and persuaded the family to send him to Trinity College, Cambridge, which he entered in 1661. In 1665, when the university closed because of an outbreak of plague, Newton returned to Woolsthorpe, and during the next eighteen months, he made discoveries in mathematics, optics and gravitation that would change science. He later called this his 'year of wonders'. It was during this period that he saw an apple fall in the garden, and began to wonder whether the force that pulled it to the ground might also keep the Moon in its orbit.
paras.C: The story that the apple hit Newton on the head is almost certainly a myth, but he told it himself in a milder form, and it contains the heart of an important idea. He realised that gravity is universal: the same force acts on an apple, the Moon and the planets. In 1687, after years of work encouraged by the astronomer Edmond Halley, he published Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica, usually known as the Principia. It set out three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation, and showed that they could explain the orbits of the planets and the tides.
paras.D: Newton made great discoveries in optics too. Using a glass prism, he showed that white light is not pure but a mixture of all the colours of the rainbow, and that each colour bends by a different amount. He built the first practical reflecting telescope, in 1668, which used a mirror instead of a lens and avoided the coloured fringes of earlier instruments. His book Opticks, published in 1704, became a classic. He also developed a form of calculus, a mathematical way of describing change, though the German scholar Gottfried Leibniz independently invented it, and the two men became involved in a bitter quarrel about who deserved the credit.
paras.E: Newton was a difficult man. He was secretive, sensitive to criticism and sometimes vengeful toward rivals. He suffered at least one period of mental breakdown, in 1693. He spent far more time on alchemy, the attempt to turn metals into gold, and on the study of the Bible than on physics. After 1696, he moved to London, where he became Warden and, in 1699, Master of the Royal Mint, and used his scientific skill to reform the coinage and pursue counterfeiters. In 1703, he became President of the Royal Society, a post he held until his death.
paras.F: In 1705, Queen Anne knighted him, the first scientist to receive this honour. He died in 1727 at the age of eighty-four, and was buried in Westminster Abbey, among kings and poets. The French writer Voltaire, who attended the funeral, was impressed that a nation could honour a scientist in this way. Newton himself remained modest. Towards the end of his life, he is said to have remarked that he felt like a boy playing on the seashore, finding a smoother pebble or prettier shell, while the great ocean of truth lay undiscovered before him.

paras.A: Oil is so familiar that it seems almost like a natural feature of the planet. We burn it in cars and planes, and make it into plastics, medicines, fertilisers and countless other products. But oil is not something that was created with the Earth. It is the end result of a long chain of events that began with tiny living things, millions of years ago, and conditions that had to be just right for the chain to work.
paras.B: The story starts in ancient seas and lakes. Most of the oil we use today began as plankton, microscopic plants and animals that drifted in the water. When they died, their remains sank to the bottom, mixing with mud and sand. In most places, such material is eaten by bacteria or rots in the presence of oxygen. But in some basins, the water at the bottom was deprived of oxygen, so the organic matter was preserved. Over millions of years, layers of mud accumulated above it, burying it ever deeper.
paras.C: As the layers piled up, the organic matter was subjected to growing heat and pressure. The mud hardened into rock, called source rock, usually shale. At depths of around two to four kilometres, where temperatures are between about 60 and 120 degrees Celsius, the organic matter slowly changed into oil. This temperature band is called the 'oil window'. Deeper still, where it is hotter, the oil breaks down into natural gas, and at even greater depths, the organic matter is destroyed.
paras.D: Oil formed in source rock is not yet ready to be drilled. The oil is lighter than water and rock, and it is squeezed out and slowly rises through tiny cracks and pores. If nothing stops it, it reaches the surface and escapes, as in natural seeps such as the tar pits of Los Angeles. But in some places, the oil encounters a layer of rock which it cannot pass, called a cap rock, usually made of clay or salt. The oil collects below it in a reservoir rock, such as sandstone, which is full of tiny holes, like a hard sponge.
paras.E: For oil to be found, a particular combination must be present: a source rock, a reservoir rock, a cap rock and a trap, which is a shape such as a dome in which the oil is held. Geologists search for such structures by studying maps, measuring tiny differences in gravity and magnetism, and sending sound waves into the ground to build images of the layers beneath. Even then, the only way to be certain is to drill. Many exploratory wells find nothing.
paras.F: The modern oil industry began in 1859, when Edwin Drake drilled the first commercial well in Pennsylvania, striking oil at about 21 metres. Crude oil is a mixture of hundreds of compounds, so it is sent to a refinery, where it is heated and separated into fractions according to their boiling points: gases, petrol, kerosene, diesel and heavy oils. Because oil takes millions of years to form, it is a non-renewable resource. Burning it releases carbon dioxide, which is one reason why many countries are looking for alternative sources of energy.

paras.A: Mars has fascinated people for centuries. It is the most Earth-like of the other planets, with a day only slightly longer than ours, seasons, polar ice caps and signs that rivers once flowed over its surface. In recent years, private companies and space agencies have talked seriously of sending humans to the planet, and some entrepreneurs have spoken of building a city there. Supporters see this as the next great step in human history; critics see it as a dangerous and wasteful fantasy.
paras.B: Supporters give several reasons. The first is survival. Earth is the only home we know, but a disaster, such as an asteroid impact or a global war, could destroy civilisation. A settlement on another planet would be a kind of insurance for the human species. The second is discovery: exploring Mars could tell us whether life ever existed there, and help us understand how planets develop. The third is inspiration and innovation. The Apollo programme led to many technological advances and inspired a generation of scientists.
paras.C: Critics respond that Mars is extremely hostile. The atmosphere is thin, only about one per cent of the pressure on Earth's surface, and consists mostly of carbon dioxide, so people could not breathe it. The average temperature is around minus 60 degrees Celsius. With almost no magnetic field and a thin atmosphere, the surface is exposed to dangerous radiation, and the soil contains toxic chemicals. The planet would be a far less pleasant place than Antarctica, which we do not regard as suitable for large settlements.
paras.D: The journey itself is a challenge. At its closest, Mars is about 55 million kilometres from Earth, and a trip takes six to nine months, during which the crew would be exposed to radiation and the harmful effects of weightlessness on bones and muscles. Help would be months away, and a return would be possible only when the planets were again in the right position, which happens about every two years. Medical emergencies, equipment failures or psychological problems in a small group could be deadly.
paras.E: Progress has been made, however. Robots have landed on Mars many times, and in 2021, the Perseverance rover touched down, carrying an experiment, called MOXIE, that produced oxygen from the carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. Engineers are developing rockets large enough to carry people and cargo. Supporters say that many of the difficulties can be overcome by technology, and that the right comparison is not with a comfortable holiday but with the first voyages across the oceans.
paras.F: Then there is the question of cost and priorities. Estimates for a human mission run to hundreds of billions of dollars. Many people argue that this money would be better used to deal with problems on Earth, such as climate change, disease and poverty, and that it is easier to protect our own planet than to make another habitable. The writer's view is that robotic exploration should continue, and that sending a small number of astronauts for research may eventually be justified, but that a permanent settlement is not a sensible goal for this century. The first duty is to look after the world we already have.

paras.A: No animal is more closely associated with Australia than the kangaroo. It appears on the country's coat of arms, on coins and on the tail of the national airline. The word 'kangaroo' is often said to come from an Aboriginal word, though the exact origin is disputed. There are four large species: the red kangaroo, the eastern grey, the western grey and the antilopine kangaroo. They belong to a group of animals called marsupials, whose young are born at an early stage of development and are carried in a pouch.
paras.B: The red kangaroo is the largest marsupial in the world. A big male can stand 1.8 metres tall and weigh up to 90 kilograms, and has a reddish-brown coat. The females, which are smaller, are often bluish-grey, which has earned them the name 'blue fliers'. Red kangaroos live in the dry interior of the continent, where they feed on grasses at dawn and dusk, and rest in the shade during the heat of the day. They can survive for long periods without drinking, getting most of their water from their food.
paras.C: Kangaroos move by hopping, which is a very efficient way of travelling. Their powerful back legs and long feet, combined with large tendons which act like springs, store energy with each hop and return it with the next, so that a kangaroo uses little extra energy when it goes faster. A red kangaroo can cruise at 20 to 25 kilometres per hour, reach about 70 kilometres per hour over short distances, and leap as far as nine metres in a single bound. The long, thick tail acts as a balancing aid and as a support when the animal stands or fights.
paras.D: Kangaroos cannot walk backwards, because of the shape of their feet and the large tail. This is one reason, according to a popular story, why the kangaroo and the emu appear on the national coat of arms: they symbolise a nation that moves forward and does not go back. When moving slowly, a kangaroo uses its tail as a fifth leg, putting its weight on the tail and front legs while swinging its back legs forward.
paras.E: The breeding of kangaroos is remarkable. A newborn joey is about two centimetres long and weighs less than a gram, about the size of a jelly bean. It is blind and hairless, but it crawls unaided through its mother's fur into the pouch, where it attaches to a teat. It stays inside for around six to eight months, growing, until it begins to put its head out. Even after leaving the pouch, it continues to return for milk for several more months. A female may have a joey in the pouch, another at foot, and an embryo waiting to develop.
paras.F: There are many millions of kangaroos in Australia, and in some regions their numbers are high enough to damage crops and compete with sheep and cattle for grass. Some of them are culled each year under government licence, and their meat and skins are sold. This is controversial: animal welfare groups object to the killing, while farmers and some scientists argue that management is necessary. At the same time, kangaroos face threats from drought, bushfires and cars. Maintaining a balance between protecting them and living alongside them is a continuing challenge.

paras.A: The human voice is among the most versatile instruments in nature. With it, we can whisper, shout, sing, laugh and speak thousands of different words. Yet it is produced by a small group of structures in the neck and head, and is controlled by the brain with extraordinary precision. Understanding how the voice works helps to explain why people sound different from one another, and how to look after it.
paras.B: Sound begins in the larynx, the voice box, a structure of cartilage at the top of the windpipe. Inside are two folds of flexible tissue called the vocal folds, or vocal cords. When we breathe quietly, they are apart, and air passes freely between them. To make a sound, muscles bring the folds together, and air pushed up from the lungs forces them apart repeatedly, so that they vibrate rapidly, chopping the airflow into a series of tiny puffs. These puffs are the raw sound, a buzzing tone.
paras.C: The pitch of the voice depends on the number of times per second that the folds open and close, called the fundamental frequency. Shorter, thinner folds vibrate faster and produce higher notes; longer, thicker folds vibrate more slowly. The folds of an adult man are about 17 to 25 millimetres long, and those of a woman 12 to 17 millimetres, which is why men's voices are generally lower: the average frequency is about 110 hertz for men and 210 for women. We change pitch by altering the tension of the folds, as a guitarist does by tightening a string.
paras.D: The buzzing sound from the larynx is then shaped by the throat, mouth and nose, which act as resonating chambers, like the body of a violin. Their size and shape strengthen some frequencies and weaken others, giving each person a characteristic quality, or timbre. This is why we can recognise a friend on the telephone, even when they are singing or whispering. When we have a cold, the nasal passages are blocked and the sound of the voice changes.
paras.E: Speech requires one more step: articulation. By moving the tongue, lips, jaw and soft palate, we change the shape of the mouth and block or release the airflow, producing the vowels and consonants of a language. A vowel such as 'ee' or 'ah' is made by changing the shape of the mouth while air flows freely; a consonant such as 'p' or 't' is made by stopping or narrowing the flow. When we whisper, the vocal folds do not vibrate at all; the sound comes from air rushing through a narrow gap.
paras.F: The voice changes with age. At puberty, a boy's larynx grows rapidly, and the vocal folds lengthen by about a centimetre, so the voice drops by around an octave. In old age, the folds may become thinner and stiffer, changing the sound. To protect the voice, doctors advise drinking plenty of water, avoiding shouting for long periods, and resting when it is hoarse. Professional singers and teachers, who use their voices heavily, often train to use their breath and muscles efficiently so as to avoid damage.

ps.title: Is Online Shopping Harming the High Street?

paras.A: Walk down the main shopping street of almost any town, and you will probably see empty shops with 'to let' signs in the windows. Over the last twenty years, the number of people buying goods on the internet has grown dramatically. In Britain, about a quarter of all retail sales are now made online, and in some categories, such as books and electronics, the share is much higher. Amazon, founded in 1994 as an online bookshop, has become one of the biggest companies in the world. Many people blame such companies for the decline of the high street.
paras.B: Supporters of online shopping point to its advantages. It is convenient: you can buy at any hour, without travelling, and have goods delivered to your door. It offers a far wider choice than any shop could stock, and comparing prices is easy, which tends to keep costs down. For people who are elderly, disabled, ill or live in remote areas, it is often the only practical way to buy what they need. Online retail has also created jobs in warehouses, delivery and technology, and has helped small businesses to reach customers around the world.
paras.C: Critics reply that the loss of shops has costs that are not seen on a price tag. High streets are not just places to buy things; they are meeting places, which give a town its character and sense of community. When shops close, local jobs are lost, and empty buildings can attract crime and drag down nearby businesses. Many online retailers pay less tax in proportion to their sales than shops, which pay rent and local business taxes, and some warehouse workers face demanding conditions.
paras.D: There are environmental arguments on both sides. Defenders of online shopping say that one van delivering to many homes can replace many separate car journeys, and may produce less pollution. Critics reply that the evidence is mixed, because fast delivery often means vans travelling half-empty, and customers return a large share of items, particularly clothes, which then travel again. The packaging of parcels also generates plastic and cardboard waste. Which kind of shopping is better for the climate depends on how people travel to the shops and on how deliveries are organised.
paras.E: It would be wrong, however, to say that the internet is solely responsible. The high street was already under pressure from out-of-town shopping centres and supermarkets, high rents and business taxes, and changes in the way people spend their time. The pandemic accelerated the shift online, but some shops have bounced back, and many successful retailers now combine both: they offer 'click and collect' and use their shops as places where customers can see and try goods. Towns that have adapted by adding cafes, services, housing and cultural activities have often fared better than those that have relied only on shopping.
paras.F: The writer believes that the high street will not return to what it was, but that it need not die. Governments should make the tax system fairer by reducing the burden on shops with premises and by ensuring that large online companies pay their share. Councils should make it easier to turn empty shops into homes, workshops and community spaces, and to bring people into town centres with markets, events and public transport. Shoppers also have a role: if they want to have a lively centre, they must use it, instead of treating it only as a place to look before buying online.

paras.A: Mongolia is a country of vast open grassland, high mountains and desert, squeezed between Russia and China. It has fewer than four million people, but it is almost twice the size of Texas, and is one of the most thinly populated countries on Earth. For thousands of years, the people of the Mongolian steppe have lived as nomads, moving with their animals in search of pasture. Even today, about a quarter of the population lives in this traditional way.
paras.B: The wealth of a Mongolian herder is counted in animals. Families keep what they call the 'five snouts': horses, camels, cattle, sheep and goats. Each has a purpose. Horses are used for riding and herding, and their milk is made into a mildly alcoholic drink called airag. Camels carry loads across the desert. Sheep and goats provide meat, milk and wool, and cattle and yaks give milk and transport. Mongolian children learn to ride almost as soon as they can walk, and some take part in horse races at the age of five or six.
paras.C: Herders move several times a year, following the seasons. In summer, they go to river valleys where the grass is fresh and water is plentiful; in winter, they move to sheltered places in the hills, where the cold is less severe. The temperature in Mongolia can fall below minus forty degrees in winter and rise above thirty degrees in summer. A family may travel only a few kilometres or hundreds, depending on the region, and the whole household can pack up and move within a day.
paras.D: Their home, the ger, called a yurt in other languages, is designed for this life. It is a round tent with a frame of folding wooden lattice walls and a roof of thin poles that meet at a central ring. The frame is covered with thick layers of felt, made from sheep's wool, which keep out the wind and cold, and tied with ropes. A stove stands in the centre, with a chimney through the roof. The door always faces south, and the interior is arranged according to a traditional pattern, with a place for guests, family and the altar. A ger can be taken down or put up in about an hour.
paras.E: Hospitality is a core value. A traveller arriving at a ger will be welcomed, given tea and food, and often offered a place to sleep, because in this harsh land, help can be a matter of survival. Mongolian culture is also proud of its sporting tradition, shown at the Naadam festival in July, which features the 'three manly games': wrestling, horse racing and archery. The festival goes back centuries, and its roots lie in the military training of the armies of Genghis Khan, who united the Mongol tribes in 1206.
paras.F: Nomadic life is under pressure. In recent decades, severe winters called dzud, in which deep snow and extreme cold stop animals from reaching grass, have killed millions of livestock and ruined many families. Climate change and overgrazing are damaging pastures. As a result, many herders have given up and moved to the capital, Ulaanbaatar, where almost half of the country's population now lives, often in ger districts without proper water or sewage. Yet the traditions endure, and many young Mongolians take pride in their nomadic heritage and try to keep it alive.

paras.A: Wi-Fi is so common that many people use it without a thought. Phones, laptops, televisions, speakers, doorbells and even refrigerators connect to the internet without a wire. Behind this convenience lies a clever use of radio waves, the same kind of waves that carry radio and television broadcasts, but arranged so that devices can both send and receive large amounts of data in a small area.
paras.B: A Wi-Fi network begins with a router, which is connected to the internet by a cable, through a telephone line, fibre or a television cable. The router has a small radio transmitter and receiver. When you ask your laptop to load a web page, the laptop turns your request into a series of numbers, sends them as radio waves to the router, and the router forwards the request over the cable. The reply returns the same way: the router converts the data into radio waves, and the laptop's antenna picks them up.
paras.C: Wi-Fi radio waves use two main frequency bands, around 2.4 gigahertz and 5 gigahertz, which is billions of oscillations per second. These bands are 'unlicensed', which means that anyone can use them without a permit, provided the equipment meets technical rules. The 2.4 gigahertz band travels farther and passes through walls more easily, but it is crowded, because microwave ovens, Bluetooth devices and cordless phones also use it. The 5 gigahertz band offers higher speeds but has a shorter range.
paras.D: To send information, the radio wave must be modified in a way that represents the data, as in AM and FM radio, but in a much more complex manner. Wi-Fi splits the information into many streams on neighbouring frequencies and changes tiny properties of each wave thousands of times a second. The more precisely the receiver can tell the changes apart, the more data it can capture in a second. If there is interference or the signal is weak, the devices automatically switch to a slower but more reliable mode.
paras.E: Many devices share the same router, so the system needs rules to avoid chaos. Devices 'listen' before they transmit and wait for a quiet moment, and if two devices speak at the same time, they both stop and try again after a short random delay. Newer standards allow a router to talk to several devices at once. The technology is defined by a set of international standards, known as IEEE 802.11, first published in 1997. The name 'Wi-Fi', adopted in 1999 by an industry group, was chosen because it sounded good, and is not an abbreviation of anything.
paras.F: Wi-Fi has limits. Walls, floors, metal objects and even water absorb or reflect the radio waves, so the signal weakens quickly and may not reach all parts of a house. Because the waves travel through the air, they can be picked up by anyone nearby, so networks encrypt the data with a password, using protocols such as WPA3. Public networks without a password are not secure, and users should avoid sending sensitive information on them. The newest standards, such as Wi-Fi 6, aim to give faster and more reliable connections where many devices share a network.

ps.title: Should Students Choose Their Own School Subjects?

paras.A: In some countries, students must specialise early. In England, for example, pupils usually choose just three subjects to study at age sixteen for their final two years of school, and may never study science, or languages, or art again. In other countries, such as the United States and those following the International Baccalaureate, students continue to study a broad range of subjects, including maths, a language, a science and the arts, until the end of school. Which approach better prepares young people for life?
paras.B: Supporters of early choice say that it motivates students. Teenagers who can follow their interests are likely to work harder and enjoy school more. A student who loves history but struggles with chemistry will usually do better if allowed to drop chemistry and concentrate on history. Specialisation also allows deeper study, which prepares students for university courses, where they study a single subject in depth. It can reduce the time needed for a degree, because the students arrive with advanced knowledge.
paras.C: Supporters also stress that choice teaches responsibility. Deciding what to study is one of the first important decisions that young people make about their own lives, and being trusted to make it can build maturity. Giving freedom, they say, treats students as responsible individuals who know best what suits their talents, and it helps to avoid the boredom of being forced to study subjects they dislike or find useless.
paras.D: Critics reply that sixteen is too early to make such decisions. Young people change their minds, and a student who drops mathematics or a science at sixteen may find that doors are closed later. Teenagers may be influenced by friends, by teachers who are popular, or by the belief that a subject is 'easy', instead of thinking about their future. There is also a risk that girls, for example, are less likely to choose physics or computing, which can reinforce unequal career patterns.
paras.E: Another argument for a broad education is that modern life requires many kinds of knowledge. Scientists need to be able to write clearly and understand history and ethics; writers and lawyers need to understand data and statistics; everyone needs some knowledge of how technology works. Employers often say that they look for adaptability and communication skills as much as specialist knowledge. Many jobs of the future do not exist yet, so a wide base may be a better preparation than a narrow one.
paras.F: The writer believes that students should have a say in their education, but that choice should come later and be limited. Until sixteen, all students should study a core of subjects, including language, mathematics, science, humanities and the arts, in which they develop a good general foundation. After that, they should be able to specialise, but required to keep up at least one subject from the arts and one from the sciences or mathematics. In this way, schools can respect young people's interests and still prepare them for a changing world.

paras.A: On the border between Canada and the United States, the Niagara River drops over a cliff and crashes into a deep gorge below. Niagara Falls is not the highest waterfall in the world, nor the widest, but it is one of the most powerful, and it draws about twenty million visitors a year. There are in fact three falls: the Horseshoe Falls, mostly on the Canadian side, which is about 57 metres high and 790 metres wide; the American Falls; and the small Bridal Veil Falls, which is separated from the others by islands.
paras.B: The falls were created at the end of the last Ice Age. About twelve thousand years ago, the huge ice sheets that covered North America began to melt and retreat. The melting water filled the Great Lakes, and the overflow from Lake Erie found its way to Lake Ontario by a new route: the Niagara River. The river flows across a hard layer of rock, called dolostone, which lies above softer layers of shale. The softer rock is worn away faster by the spray and churning water, and the hard cap is left overhanging until it breaks off.
paras.C: This process means that the falls have been moving. Over thousands of years, they have retreated about eleven kilometres upstream, cutting the Niagara Gorge as they went. Historically, they moved back at an average of about a metre a year, but in the twentieth century, engineers diverted water to generate electricity, and the erosion has slowed to about thirty centimetres a year. In the far future, the falls will reach Lake Erie, and the lake will drain, although this is tens of thousands of years away.
paras.D: The power of the falls has long been put to use. In 1895, one of the first large hydroelectric power plants in the world began operating at Niagara, using the alternating current system developed by Nikola Tesla and promoted by George Westinghouse. It sent electricity to the city of Buffalo, about thirty kilometres away. Today, power stations on both sides of the border can generate enough electricity for millions of homes. A treaty signed in 1950 requires that at least half of the river's flow must pass over the falls during the daytime in the tourist season.
paras.E: The falls have always attracted daredevils. In 1859, the French acrobat Charles Blondin walked across the gorge on a tightrope, and later repeated the feat blindfolded, pushing a wheelbarrow and even carrying a man on his back. In 1901, a 63-year-old schoolteacher, Annie Taylor, became the first person to go over the Horseshoe Falls in a barrel and survive. Many who tried afterwards were not so lucky, and the practice is now illegal, with heavy fines.
paras.F: Tourism has been a mainstay of the region for nearly two centuries. The boat Maid of the Mist has taken visitors close to the base of the falls since 1846, and at night, coloured lights illuminate the water. The surrounding area has been developed with hotels, casinos and attractions that critics say spoil the natural setting. On the American side, however, a state park designed by Frederick Law Olmsted, the architect of Central Park, protects the land near the falls, and it was the first state park in the United States, opened in 1885.

paras.A: The Sun is so central to life on Earth that it is easy to forget that it is a star, a gigantic ball of hot gas about 1.4 million kilometres across. More than a million Earths could fit inside it. It contains 99.86 per cent of all the mass in the solar system, and its gravity holds the planets in their orbits. For thousands of years, people wondered what makes it burn, and the correct answer was found only in the twentieth century.
paras.B: In the nineteenth century, scientists thought that the Sun might be burning like a giant lump of coal. Calculations showed that this would last only a few thousand years, far less than the age suggested by geology. A more refined idea, that the Sun was slowly shrinking under its own gravity, which would release heat, would allow it to shine for tens of millions of years, but this was still too short, as evidence from fossils showed that the Earth was much older.
paras.C: The solution came from Albert Einstein's equation, E equals mc squared, which shows that mass can be converted into a very large amount of energy. In the 1920s and 1930s, physicists realised that the source of the Sun's energy is nuclear fusion. In the core of the Sun, the temperature is about 15 million degrees Celsius, and the pressure is enormous. Under these conditions, the nuclei of hydrogen atoms, which normally repel each other, collide with such force that they join together, forming helium.
paras.D: The helium nucleus has slightly less mass than the four hydrogen nuclei that made it. The missing mass is turned into energy. Every second, the Sun turns about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium, and in the process, about four million tonnes of matter are converted into energy. This sounds like a great deal, but the Sun is so large that it has lost only a tiny fraction of its mass since it formed. It has been shining for about 4.6 billion years, and it is about halfway through its life.
paras.E: The energy created in the core takes a surprisingly long time to reach us. The core is surrounded by a dense layer in which the light is absorbed and re-emitted countless times, so a particle of light takes between tens of thousands and a hundred thousand years to struggle outwards. Once it breaks free, it takes only about eight minutes and twenty seconds to cross the 150 million kilometres to Earth. The surface of the Sun, which we see, is much cooler than the core, at about 5,500 degrees Celsius.
paras.F: The Sun is not unchanging. Dark patches called sunspots appear on its surface, and the number rises and falls over a cycle of about eleven years. Occasionally, great eruptions throw charged particles into space, causing storms that disturb radio communications and create auroras on Earth. In about five billion years, the Sun will run out of hydrogen in its core. It will swell into a red giant, probably swallowing Mercury and Venus, and perhaps the Earth, before shrinking at last into a small, dim star called a white dwarf.

paras.A: In many schools, music is a subject that is easily squeezed out of the timetable. When budgets are tight and exam results matter, headteachers may decide to spend time on mathematics and reading instead of singing and instruments. Yet many teachers and parents argue that music is a core subject, not a luxury. Should every child have the chance, or even the duty, to learn music at school?
paras.B: Supporters begin with the claim that music makes children cleverer. Several studies have found that children who learn an instrument do better in tests of memory, language and reading. Playing music uses many parts of the brain at once, they argue, and involves listening, coordination, reading symbols and practising over a long period. However, it is important to be cautious. Most of the research shows an association, not proof of cause: children from richer families, who tend to do well at school, are also more likely to have music lessons.
paras.C: A stronger argument is that music has value of its own. It is a basic part of human culture, found in every society, and it gives pleasure, a way of expressing emotions and a sense of belonging. Singing in a choir or playing in an orchestra teaches teamwork, discipline and patience, and gives children the pride of achieving something difficult. A venture like El Sistema, a programme begun in Venezuela in 1975, has used orchestras to give thousands of children from poor neighbourhoods a purpose and a community.
paras.D: Opponents of compulsion respond that not all children enjoy music. Forcing a reluctant child to play the recorder or sing in front of others can produce embarrassment and dislike, and may put them off for life. Schools face real constraints: the day is full, and instruments, rooms and specialist teachers are costly. In some countries, many primary teachers have little training in music. Others say that children can learn music outside school, in lessons or youth groups, as many do.
paras.E: This reply, however, is part of the supporters' case. Lessons outside school are expensive, and so only children from comfortable families are likely to receive them. If music is not taught in school, a significant cultural and educational experience becomes a privilege of the rich. In England, a number of surveys have shown a sharp difference in the proportion of children learning an instrument according to family income, and hundreds of music teaching posts have been cut.
paras.F: The writer believes that all children should have regular music lessons in the early years of school, as they do for reading and mathematics. In this period, the emphasis should be on singing, rhythm and playing simple instruments together, with the aim of enjoyment and of discovering talents. Later, music should be optional, and students should have a chance to continue with instruments if they wish, supported by grants for those who cannot afford them. The case for music does not depend on whether it raises exam scores: it is worth teaching because it is part of a full education.

paras.A: Greenland is the largest island in the world that is not a continent. With an area of about 2.17 million square kilometres, it is roughly as big as Mexico, yet it is home to only around 56,000 people, which makes it the least densely populated territory on Earth. It lies mostly within the Arctic Circle, between the Atlantic and Arctic Oceans, and although it is geographically part of North America, it has been linked politically with Europe for centuries.
paras.B: Its most striking feature is the ice. About eighty per cent of the island is covered by an ice sheet, which in places is over three kilometres thick. If it all melted, the global sea level would rise by about seven metres. People live only on the ice-free coastal fringe, mostly on the west coast, and the settlements are linked by air and by sea, because there are almost no roads between towns. The capital, Nuuk, with about 19,000 people, is the largest town.
paras.C: The first people arrived from Arctic Canada around 4,500 years ago, and successive waves of Inuit hunters crossed over the following millennia. The Norse, or Vikings, came in about 985, led by Erik the Red, who had been exiled from Iceland. According to the sagas, he gave the land an attractive name, Greenland, to persuade others to settle there. The Norse farmed and traded for around four hundred years, but their settlements vanished in the fifteenth century, possibly because of a colder climate and the loss of trade.
paras.D: Denmark claimed the island in the eighteenth century and later made it a colony. In 1953, Greenland became part of the Danish kingdom, and in 1979, it received home rule, with its own parliament. In 2009, it was given a wider form of self-government, and responsibility for matters such as justice and natural resources. Greenlanders have the right to decide on independence, though they depend on an annual grant from Denmark for much of their public spending, and the debate continues.
paras.E: The economy is based mainly on fishing; shrimp and halibut are the main exports. Tourism is growing, as visitors come to see the glaciers, icebergs and the northern lights. The island also has great mineral wealth, including rare earth elements, which are used in electronics and wind turbines, as well as gold, zinc and possibly oil. But there is disagreement about whether mining should be allowed, because of the risk of pollution and damage to the fragile environment, and because some Greenlanders see it as a path to independence.
paras.F: Greenland is at the centre of the debate about climate change. Satellite measurements show that the ice sheet has been losing, on average, hundreds of billions of tonnes of ice a year in recent decades, which is adding to the rise in sea levels. The island is warming faster than the global average. At the same time, the melting ice has opened up new shipping routes and attracted the interest of great powers, who regard the island as strategically important; the United States, for example, operates an air base there, Pituffik Space Base.

paras.A: Sharks have lived in the oceans for more than 400 million years, long before dinosaurs, and they have survived several mass extinctions. There are about five hundred species, from the whale shark, which grows to over twelve metres but eats only plankton, to the dwarf lantern shark, which can fit in a human hand. Their success owes much to a set of senses and body features that make them superb hunters.
paras.B: A shark's skeleton is not made of bone but of cartilage, the same flexible material that forms the human ear and nose. Cartilage is lighter than bone, which helps the shark to float, and its flexibility allows quick turns. Many sharks also have a large liver full of oil, which is lighter than water and acts as a kind of buoyancy tank. Unlike bony fish, sharks have no swim bladder, and some species must keep swimming to push water over their gills and breathe.
paras.C: Sharks possess an amazing set of senses. Their sense of smell is extremely sensitive: a significant part of the brain is devoted to it, and some species can detect tiny amounts of blood from a long way off in the water. A line of sensitive cells along the body, called the lateral line, picks up vibrations and movements made by animals. Their eyes are adapted to dim light, with a reflective layer that helps them see in murky water. Nobody doubts that sharks hear well, especially low-frequency sounds like those made by struggling fish.
paras.D: The most unusual sense is electroreception. Around a shark's snout are small pores, called the ampullae of Lorenzini, filled with a jelly and connected to nerves. They can detect the faint electric fields produced by the muscles of other animals, even those hidden in the sand. This is why hammerhead sharks sweep their wide heads over the sea floor, searching for stingrays. Sharks can also sense the Earth's magnetic field, which may help them to navigate across the oceans.
paras.E: A shark's teeth are its weapons, and they are continually replaced. Behind the front row is a series of rows in waiting, and when a tooth is lost, another moves forward like a conveyor belt. A shark may use thousands of teeth in a lifetime. The shape depends on diet: the great white has triangular, serrated teeth for tearing flesh, the tiger shark has teeth for cutting through turtle shells, and the nurse shark has flat teeth for crushing shellfish. The skin is covered with tiny tooth-like scales that reduce drag and make swimming more efficient.
paras.F: Sharks have a bad reputation, but attacks on humans are very rare. Worldwide, sharks kill fewer than ten people in a typical year, a tiny number compared with the deaths caused by dogs, snakes or mosquitoes. By contrast, humans kill an estimated 70 to 100 million sharks every year, many for their fins, which are used in soup, or accidentally in fishing nets. Many species are now endangered. Because sharks are top predators that keep other populations healthy, their decline could affect the entire ocean ecosystem.

ps.title: Should Schools Teach About Climate Change?

paras.A: Climate change is one of the defining issues of our time, and young people will live with its consequences for longest. In 2019, Italy announced that it would be the first country to make climate education compulsory in schools, and others have followed with plans of their own. But in many countries, the topic receives little attention, and what is taught differs widely from school to school. Should climate change be a required part of the curriculum, and if so, how should it be taught?
paras.B: Supporters argue that the facts are clear. The overwhelming majority of scientists agree that the climate is warming because of human activity, and young people should learn about this in the same way that they learn about biology or history. They will need the knowledge in their future lives, as voters, consumers and workers: many new jobs will be in renewable energy, building efficiency and environmental management. Understanding the causes and possible responses will help them to make informed decisions and to judge the claims of politicians and advertisers.
paras.C: Supporters also say that education changes behaviour. Surveys suggest that people with more education about the climate are more concerned about it and more willing to act. Young people often influence their families: children who learn about recycling or energy use at school take the message home. By teaching about solutions, such as renewable energy, protection of forests and sustainable farming, schools can also give pupils a sense that they can do something, and not merely face a distant disaster.
paras.D: Critics raise several objections. Some fear that lessons could become political, with teachers promoting their own opinions or particular policies as if they were facts. Others are worried about anxiety: surveys of young people in many countries show high levels of worry about the future, and some children feel helpless when they learn about the scale of the problem. There is also the matter of time. Since the curriculum is already full, adding a new subject would have to replace something else.
paras.E: Educators have answers to these points. Teaching should distinguish between scientific findings, which are well established, and political choices about what to do, which are legitimate subjects for debate and should be presented fairly. To reduce anxiety, lessons should be age-appropriate, hopeful in tone, and include action, such as projects to cut waste at school or plant trees. And climate change does not require a new subject: it can be woven into science, geography, mathematics, economics and literature, which makes lessons richer and more relevant.
paras.F: The writer believes that climate change should be taught in all schools as part of existing subjects. The science should be accurate and up-to-date, teachers should be trained, and pupils should be encouraged to discuss different solutions and to think critically about them. Lessons should help children to understand the problem without frightening them, and show that practical responses are possible. A generation that knows the facts is better placed to decide what to do about them.

paras.A: Few objects in the world of music are as famous as a violin made by Antonio Stradivari. Born in northern Italy around 1644, he spent almost all of his long working life in the small city of Cremona, and he lived to the age of about ninety. During those decades he produced an extraordinary number of instruments, and today the best of them are treated almost as sacred objects, guarded in vaults, insured for huge sums and played only by the most gifted performers.
paras.B: Cremona had been a centre of string-instrument making since the sixteenth century, and Stradivari learned his craft there. He is generally believed to have been trained in the workshop of the Amati family, whose violins were already admired across Europe. Eventually he opened his own workshop, where his sons helped him. He did not make only violins. His workshop also produced violas, cellos, guitars, harps and mandolins, and it is thought that he made around 1,100 instruments in total, although the precise figure is uncertain.
paras.C: His finest work is usually dated to a 'golden period' from about 1700 to 1720, when his designs became slightly longer and flatter, with a bold, powerful tone. About 500 violins survive today from his workshop, together with a smaller number of cellos and violas. Many have been given names, taken from the people who owned them or from some striking feature. Among the best known are the 'Messiah', which is almost unplayed and kept in a museum in England, and the 'Lady Blunt', which was named after the granddaughter of the poet Lord Byron.
paras.D: Since the nineteenth century, scientists and violin-makers have tried to discover why these instruments sound so beautiful. One theory is that the wood is special. Stradivari worked during a period of unusually cold weather in Europe, often called the Little Ice Age, when trees grew slowly and produced dense, even wood that may have vibrated better. Another proposal is that he treated the wood with chemicals to protect it from woodworm, which altered its properties. Others point to the varnish, though analysis has shown nothing mysterious in it. So far, there is no agreement.
paras.E: A different line of research has questioned whether the Stradivari sound is really better. In several well-known experiments, violinists played old Italian instruments and modern copies while wearing dark glasses, so that they could not see which violin they held. In these blind tests, the players often could not reliably tell which was which, and a majority sometimes preferred a modern violin. Audiences listening in concert halls had the same difficulty. Defenders of the old violins reply that such tests cannot capture the subtle qualities that a great soloist hears in a fine instrument.
paras.F: Whatever the truth, the market has made its judgment. The Lady Blunt was sold at auction in 2011 for about ten million pounds, which was then a record for any musical instrument. Because the prices are beyond the reach of nearly all musicians, wealthy collectors and foundations lend the violins to talented performers, often for several years at a time. Meanwhile, today's makers in Cremona and elsewhere continue to produce instruments in the same tradition, and many of them argue that the best new violins already equal the old masters.

paras.A: Every day, billions of journeys are made in elevators, and most passengers give them no thought at all. Yet without the elevator the modern city could not exist. Buildings taller than five or six storeys would be impractical if everyone had to climb the stairs, and the skyscrapers that define the skylines of Shanghai, Dubai and New York would have been impossible to inhabit. The story of the elevator is therefore, in a sense, the story of how cities learned to grow upwards.
paras.B: Lifting devices are very old. The ancient Greek scientist Archimedes is said to have built a lifting machine around 236 BC, using ropes and pulleys, and Roman amphitheatres used hoists to bring wild animals up from underground rooms into the arena. For many centuries, such machines were powered by people, animals or flowing water. They were slow, they were used mostly for goods, and they were dangerous, because if the rope broke, the platform fell. Few people were willing to trust their lives to a rope.
paras.C: The turning point came in 1853, when an American mechanic, Elisha Otis, invented a safety brake. At a public exhibition in New York in 1854, he stood on a platform high above a crowd and ordered the rope to be cut. The platform dropped only a few centimetres before the brake caught it. This dramatic demonstration convinced the public, and in 1857 the first passenger elevator was installed in a department store in New York. Orders for the safety device soon followed from factories and hotels.
paras.D: Early elevators were driven by steam engines, and later by water pressure, in a system known as hydraulics. The next step was electricity. The German engineer Werner von Siemens built an electric elevator in 1880, and by the end of the century, electric motors had replaced steam in most new buildings. They were faster and cleaner, and, more importantly, they could lift cars much higher. In 1885, the ten-storey Home Insurance Building in Chicago, usually regarded as the first skyscraper, was built, and taller buildings soon followed.
paras.E: The modern elevator uses a steel cable that passes over a wheel at the top of the shaft. At one end is the car, and at the other a heavy counterweight, which is roughly equal to the car's weight plus about half of a full load. Because the weights nearly balance, the motor needs to lift only the difference, which saves energy. Several independent safety systems are fitted, and statistics show that travelling in an elevator is much safer, per journey, than using the stairs or an escalator.
paras.F: Today's engineers are working to make elevators smarter and faster. In 'destination dispatch' systems, passengers enter their floor on a keypad before boarding, and a computer groups people who are going to the same place, reducing waiting and the number of stops. The fastest elevators, such as those in the Shanghai Tower, travel at about 20 metres per second. A longer-term challenge is the cable itself, which becomes too heavy in very tall buildings, and one company has designed a cable-free system that moves cars sideways as well as up and down.
