qs.title: Questions 23–26

paras.A: Every year, publishers sell hundreds of millions of novels, and yet there is a persistent feeling that reading fiction is a luxury, something we do when the important work is finished. In schools, students are often urged to read non-fiction for their studies, and in a time of limited attention, many adults say they have no time for long novels. Is there a good reason to protect the habit of reading stories, or is it merely one entertainment among many?
paras.B: Defenders of fiction argue that stories are a unique training in empathy. When we read a novel, we spend hours inside the mind of another person, often one who is very different from us in age, culture or background, and we follow that person's thoughts and feelings as they face difficulties. Some psychological studies suggest that readers of literary fiction perform slightly better on tests of understanding other people's emotions, although researchers disagree about how large and lasting this effect really is.
paras.C: There are also benefits for language. Readers of novels meet a far wider vocabulary than that of ordinary conversation or television, and they see complex sentences used skilfully. Children who read for pleasure tend to do better in vocabulary and writing, even after allowing for the wealth of their families, and adults who read widely often find it easier to express themselves. Fiction, in this view, is a quiet and enjoyable way of building skills that matter in almost every profession.
paras.D: Sceptics make several points. First, they note that most of the evidence is only a correlation: people who are already thoughtful and curious may choose to read novels, rather than novels making them thoughtful. Second, they argue that non-fiction can teach empathy and knowledge just as well, through biography, history and journalism, and often with more accuracy. Third, they say that a belief in the moral value of literature has a long history of being disproved, since some of the cruellest people in history were avid readers.
paras.E: A further point concerns time. Reading a long novel may take ten or fifteen hours, and in that time a person might learn a new language, a musical instrument or a practical skill. For people with busy lives, the argument goes, choosing a novel is an expensive decision, and it is hard to justify as an essential activity. Some critics also suggest that the idea of fiction as 'improving' is a way of making a pleasure feel respectable, which is unnecessary, since enjoyment is a sufficient reason by itself.
paras.F: The writer concludes that both sides contain some truth. The research on empathy is promising but far from conclusive, and nobody should be made to feel guilty about not reading novels. However, the evidence about vocabulary and the pleasure that fiction gives are real benefits, and schools should therefore protect time for children to read stories for enjoyment, not only for tests. For adults, a book that they truly want to read is almost certainly a better choice than one they feel they ought to read.

paras.A: In the south-east of the African country that now bears its name, the ruins of Great Zimbabwe rise from a green valley. They are the largest ancient stone structures in sub-Saharan Africa south of the Sahara's great monuments, and the word 'zimbabwe' is generally understood to come from a Shona phrase meaning 'houses of stone'. When European explorers first described the site in the nineteenth century, many refused to believe that Africans had built it, and invented stories of foreign builders. Modern archaeology has shown beyond doubt that they were wrong.
paras.B: The city flourished between about the eleventh and the fifteenth centuries, and at its height it may have housed as many as 18,000 people. It was the capital of a Shona-speaking kingdom whose rulers grew wealthy by controlling trade. Cattle were the main measure of wealth, and the surrounding grasslands supported large herds. Gold, mined in the interior, and ivory were carried to the coast and exchanged for cloth, glass beads and porcelain, and archaeologists have found fragments of Chinese and Persian pottery among the ruins.
paras.C: The site is divided into three main areas. The Hill Complex, on a granite hill, is the oldest part and is thought to have been the home of the spiritual leaders. Below it, the Valley Complex contains the remains of many smaller houses. The best-known part is the Great Enclosure, a huge oval wall with a perimeter of about 250 metres. In places it is almost eleven metres high and five metres thick, and it is the largest single ancient structure in the region.
paras.D: What makes the walls remarkable is the way they were built. The builders split granite into blocks by heating the rock with fires, then cooling it with water, and then they stacked the blocks in neat courses without any mortar. The walls curve gently, and some contain decorative patterns. Within the Great Enclosure stands a solid conical tower, about nine metres high, whose purpose remains a mystery. Some experts suggest that it was a symbol of a granary or of royal power.
paras.E: Among the most important finds are eight carved soapstone birds, each about forty centimetres tall, which stood on pillars in the Hill Complex. They show a bird with human-like features and are thought to represent a link between kings and ancestral spirits. The Zimbabwe Bird has become the national emblem, and it appears on the country's flag. Several of the birds were taken from the site in the early twentieth century, and some returned only after long negotiations.
paras.F: The decline of Great Zimbabwe seems to have begun in the fifteenth century. Historians suggest that the growing population exhausted the grazing land and the firewood, that the supply of gold in the region ran low, or that trade shifted to other routes. By around 1450, the city was largely abandoned and power moved to other centres. In 1986, UNESCO listed the ruins as a World Heritage Site, and the site now attracts thousands of visitors each year.

ps.title: Iron and Steel: The Metals That Built the Modern World

paras.A: Look around any city and you will see iron and steel: in the frames of buildings, the rails of railways, the hulls of ships, the engines of cars and the tools in every kitchen. Together, they are by far the most widely used metals in the world, and global production of steel is measured in billions of tonnes every year. Their importance is so great that historians even name entire periods of human history, such as the Iron Age, after them.
paras.B: Iron was first smelted, that is, extracted from its ore by heat, in the Middle East several thousand years ago. Early smelting furnaces could not reach the temperatures at which iron melts, so the metal emerged as a spongy mass, which had to be hammered repeatedly to remove impurities. The result, wrought iron, was tougher than bronze and could be made into weapons and tools. Because iron ore is much more common than copper or tin, iron gradually became affordable to ordinary farmers.
paras.C: Steel is iron with a small amount of carbon, usually less than two per cent. This addition changes the metal remarkably: it makes it far stronger and harder, while still allowing it to be shaped. For centuries, steel was made in tiny quantities and was expensive, used for swords and fine blades. The change came in 1856, when the English inventor Henry Bessemer developed a process that blew air through molten iron, burning away the excess carbon. The cost of steel fell dramatically.
paras.D: In a modern blast furnace, iron ore, coke (a form of coal) and limestone are fed in at the top, while hot air is blown in at the bottom. The coke burns and also removes oxygen from the ore, producing liquid iron, called pig iron. This is then taken to a converter, where oxygen is blown through it to reduce the carbon content, and other elements may be added to give the steel special properties. For example, adding chromium produces stainless steel, which resists rust.
paras.E: Steel production has a heavy environmental cost. The process uses large amounts of energy, and the chemical reactions release carbon dioxide, so that the industry is responsible for roughly seven per cent of global emissions, according to widely quoted estimates. One partial solution is recycling. Steel is the most recycled material in the world, and making new steel from scrap uses far less energy than starting from ore. However, there is not enough scrap to meet global demand.
paras.F: Researchers are now developing cleaner methods. One approach is to replace coke with hydrogen, so that the main by-product is water instead of carbon dioxide. Pilot plants in Sweden and elsewhere have produced small amounts of steel in this way, but the technology is expensive and depends on a large supply of clean electricity. Other experts hope to capture the carbon dioxide before it escapes. Whichever route is followed, the industry faces a major change in the next few decades.

paras.A: Artificial intelligence systems now write text, recognise faces, recommend medical treatments, decide which advertisements we see and, in some countries, help to select job applicants. As these systems become more powerful and more widely used, governments around the world are debating whether they should be controlled by law. Some argue that strict rules are essential to protect citizens, while others warn that heavy regulation could damage innovation and economic growth.
paras.B: Those in favour of regulation begin with the risks of harm. An AI system trained on past data may repeat the unfairness that is built into that data. For example, a recruitment tool might learn to favour men if most previous managers were men. Where such systems are used to decide who receives a loan, a job or a prison sentence, mistakes can seriously damage lives, and the people affected often cannot discover why a decision was made. Supporters of regulation say that clear rules on testing, transparency and accountability are the only way to prevent this.
paras.C: They also point to privacy and safety. Facial recognition can identify people in public spaces without their knowledge, which some regard as a threat to freedom. Others worry about false information: AI can now produce realistic images, voices and videos, making it easier to deceive voters or defraud individuals. Experts also note that voluntary codes of practice have rarely been enough in other industries, such as food or aviation, where safety standards only became effective when they were backed by the law.
paras.D: Opponents of strict regulation respond that the technology is changing so quickly that laws risk being out of date by the time they are passed. A rule that suits today's systems may be meaningless for tomorrow's. They also argue that complex regulation favours large companies, which can afford teams of lawyers, and makes it harder for small start-ups to compete. If one region sets demanding rules and another does not, companies and researchers may simply move to the more relaxed place, and the benefits will go elsewhere.
paras.E: There are also arguments about the benefits. AI is already helping doctors to detect diseases in scans, farmers to use water more efficiently and scientists to analyse data that would take humans years. Critics of regulation fear that excessive caution will slow such progress and deprive society of life-saving applications. Many suggest that existing laws on discrimination, consumer protection and privacy already cover many of the harms, and that the better course is to apply those laws carefully rather than to create an entirely new system.
paras.F: The writer believes that neither extreme is sensible. A complete absence of rules would leave citizens exposed in the high-risk areas, such as health, justice and employment, where errors are most costly. On the other hand, detailed rules for every use of AI would be impossible to enforce. The best approach, the writer suggests, is a flexible system in which the strictest controls apply to high-risk uses, and low-risk uses face only light requirements, with the rules reviewed regularly as the technology develops.

paras.A: The giraffe is the tallest animal on Earth. An adult male may reach five and a half metres in height, taller than a double-decker bus, and even a newborn calf is about 1.8 metres tall, roughly the height of a man. Giraffes live in the open woodlands and savannas of Africa south of the Sahara, where they are a familiar sight, moving gracefully among the acacia trees. Despite their fame, they are far less studied than elephants or lions.
paras.B: The most obvious feature, the long neck, contains only seven vertebrae, exactly the same number as in a human, but each one is greatly elongated and may be around 25 centimetres long. For many years, textbooks explained the neck as an adaptation for reaching high leaves. More recent researchers have proposed an alternative: the necks may have evolved in part through competition between males, who swing their heads at each other in fights called 'necking'. This is still debated.
paras.C: Having such a body creates serious problems for the circulatory system. The giraffe's brain is about two metres above its heart, so the heart must pump blood upwards against gravity. It is an exceptionally strong organ, weighing about ten kilograms, and produces roughly twice the blood pressure of a human. When the animal lowers its head to drink, special valves and a network of blood vessels at the base of the brain protect it from the sudden rush of blood.
paras.D: Giraffes eat the leaves, flowers and fruit of trees, particularly acacia, and an adult may consume as much as 30 kilograms a day. The animal uses a long, dark tongue, about 45 centimetres in length, to pull leaves from thorny branches. The dark colour is thought to protect the tongue from sunburn. Giraffes also get much of their water from their food, and so can go for several days without drinking, which allows them to live in dry regions.
paras.E: They are social animals, but their groups change constantly, and individuals come and go. Females tend to stay in loose groups with their young, and calves are sometimes left together in a 'nursery' guarded by one or two adults. Mothers give birth standing up, so the calf falls about two metres to the ground. Within an hour, it can stand and run. Lions are the main enemy of the young, and many calves do not survive the first year.
paras.F: Giraffe numbers have fallen sharply, by roughly a third in the last three decades, according to widely quoted estimates, because of the loss of habitat, hunting and conflict with humans. Scientists now recognise that there may be several species of giraffe rather than one, based on genetic studies, which makes the conservation of each group more urgent. In some places, projects that involve local communities in protecting wildlife have helped numbers to recover, offering some hope for the future.

qs.title: Questions 9–13

paras.A: A plant cannot walk, yet its offspring can travel across continents. The trick lies in the seed. If all the seeds produced by a tree simply dropped beneath it, the young plants would compete with their parent, and with each other, for light, water and nutrients. Over millions of years, plants have evolved a remarkable range of ways of sending their seeds away, a process known as seed dispersal.
paras.B: The simplest method uses the wind. Some seeds are extremely light, like the dust-like seeds of orchids, which can be carried for long distances. Others have special structures. The seeds of the dandelion carry a tiny parachute of fine hairs, and those of the maple tree have a wing that makes them spin like a helicopter as they fall, which slows their descent and lets the wind move them farther from the parent tree.
paras.C: Water is another carrier. The coconut is the most famous example: its fibrous husk is full of air and floats, and a coconut can drift in the sea for months, remaining able to grow when it is washed up on a distant beach. This explains why coconut palms are found on tropical islands all across the Pacific and Indian Oceans. Many plants along rivers and in wetlands also produce seeds that float. Rain can also help: in some desert plants, the seed capsule opens only when it is wet, so that the seeds are splashed away by raindrops at exactly the moment when the soil is damp enough for them to grow.
paras.D: Animals play a huge role. Many plants produce sweet, colourful fruits that are attractive to birds and mammals. The animal eats the fruit and later drops or excretes the seeds, often far from the parent, and in a convenient package of fertiliser. Other seeds, such as those of burdock, are covered with tiny hooks and cling to fur or clothing. The idea for the invention of Velcro came when a Swiss engineer, George de Mestral, studied burrs that stuck to his dog.
paras.E: Some dispersal methods are even more unusual. Squirrels and jays bury acorns and nuts as a store of food, and they forget some of them, which then grow into trees. Ants carry seeds with a nutritious attachment back to their nests, eat the attachment and discard the seed in a safe, rich place. A few plants, like the squirting cucumber, use explosive force: the ripe fruit bursts and shoots seeds several metres away.
paras.F: Dispersal matters not only for plants but also for entire ecosystems. When large animals disappear from a forest, the trees that rely on them to carry their big fruits may fail to spread, and the forest can change over time. Scientists studying tropical forests have warned that the loss of seed-carrying birds and mammals could reduce the ability of forests to store carbon and to move to cooler areas as the climate warms.

ps.title: Should Smoking Be Banned in Outdoor Public Places?

paras.A: In many countries, smoking in offices, restaurants and public transport has been banned for years, and the results have been widely welcomed. Now some governments are going further and proposing bans in parks, beaches, outdoor cafés and the areas outside hospitals and schools. The proposals have divided opinion. Supporters see them as a natural next step in protecting health, while critics regard them as an unnecessary intrusion into personal freedom.
paras.B: The main argument for an outdoor ban is the protection of others. Although smoke disperses quickly in open air, studies have shown that a person standing close to a smoker, for example at a crowded café table or at a bus stop, may be exposed to levels of pollution comparable to those found indoors. Children, pregnant women and people with asthma are especially vulnerable. Supporters argue that no one should be forced to breathe tobacco smoke simply because they wish to enjoy a park. They add that the benefit would also be felt by workers, such as waiters and lifeguards, who spend long hours outdoors.
paras.C: A second argument is about example. When children see adults smoking in public, they may come to regard it as normal, and studies suggest that young people who see a lot of smoking are more likely to start. Banning smoking in places where families gather, such as playgrounds and beaches, helps to change social attitudes. Supporters also note that discarded cigarette ends are the most common form of litter in the world, polluting beaches and harming wildlife, so a ban could benefit the environment.
paras.D: Opponents begin by questioning the evidence of harm. They say that the risk from outdoor smoke is very small compared with the risk to the smoker, and that bans are therefore based more on distaste than on science. They also argue that smoking is a legal activity, and that adults should be free to engage in it, provided they do not harm others, for example by staying away from other people. Prohibiting it in all open spaces, they say, treats smokers as outcasts.
paras.E: There are practical objections as well. A ban in a large park would be difficult and expensive to enforce, and police time might be better used on serious crime. Some smokers might simply move to residential streets, making life worse for people who live there. Others warn that people who are addicted to nicotine, often those on low incomes, would be punished by fines instead of being given help to quit.
paras.F: The writer is not convinced by either extreme. A ban on smoking in all open spaces seems excessive, but there are good reasons to protect children and other groups. The writer therefore supports restrictions in limited areas: playgrounds, school gates, hospital entrances and crowded outdoor eating areas. Accompanying this with free support for people trying to give up smoking would make the policy fairer and, in the long run, more effective than punishment alone.

ps.title: Merchants and Caravans of Central Asia

paras.A: The name 'Silk Road' suggests a single highway, but in reality it was a vast web of trade routes that for well over a thousand years linked China with India, Central Asia, Persia and the shores of the Mediterranean. The term itself is surprisingly recent. It was popularised in 1877 by a German geographer, Ferdinand von Richthofen, who wanted a convenient label for the ancient connections between East and West. Travellers of the time would never have used it, and few of them journeyed the full distance.
paras.B: The routes began to take shape in the second century BC, when the Han emperor of China sent an envoy named Zhang Qian to look for allies in the west. He was away for about thirteen years, and although he failed to win allies, he returned with detailed reports of rich and unknown lands. The Chinese court soon recognised the value of these contacts, particularly the chance to obtain strong horses from Central Asia. Official trade followed, and merchants quickly followed the soldiers.
paras.C: Silk was the most celebrated cargo. For centuries, only the Chinese knew how to make it, and the Romans paid enormous prices for the fabric, which they believed grew on trees. However, the caravans carried far more than silk. Spices, precious stones, glass, ivory, tea and porcelain moved in different directions, and so did ideas. Buddhism travelled from India to China along these paths, Islam later spread eastwards, and important inventions such as paper and, later, gunpowder passed from China to the West.
paras.D: Very few merchants travelled the entire route. Goods were usually passed from trader to trader, with each person selling to the next, and prices increased at every step. Camels, especially the sturdy two-humped Bactrian camel, were the preferred animals for the deserts and mountains. Along the way, travellers rested at caravanserais, which were inns with walled courtyards where animals and goods could be kept safe. Oasis towns such as Kashgar and Samarkand grew rich by supplying water, food and protection.
paras.E: The journey was dangerous. Caravans crossed some of the world's harshest deserts and highest mountain passes, and risked attacks by bandits. Disease also travelled with the merchants. Many historians believe that the plague known as the Black Death, which killed millions of people in the fourteenth century, was carried from Asia to Europe along trade routes. In the thirteenth century, the Venetian Marco Polo made the long journey to China, and his later account made Europeans aware of the wealth of the East.
paras.F: The Silk Road declined gradually. When the Mongol empire broke up, travel became less safe, and from the fifteenth century, European sailors opened sea routes to Asia that were cheaper and carried more goods. Many oasis cities lost their importance. Today, however, the idea has returned to public attention, and China has announced large projects of roads and railways that it calls a new Silk Road. Whether these will bring the shared prosperity of the original network remains a subject of debate.

paras.A: A volcano is an opening in the Earth's crust through which molten rock, ash and gas escape from deep below the surface. There are roughly 1,500 potentially active volcanoes on land, and many more under the sea. Some are gentle and produce slow rivers of lava, while others explode with a force greater than any human-made weapon. Volcanoes are dangerous, yet they have also shaped the planet, creating islands, mountains and even the atmosphere.
paras.B: Most volcanoes are found along the edges of the great plates that make up the Earth's surface. The most active zone is the so-called 'Ring of Fire' around the Pacific Ocean, which has roughly three quarters of the world's active volcanoes. In these places, one plate slides beneath another and melts, creating magma that rises through cracks. A few volcanoes, such as those of Hawaii, lie over 'hot spots' in the middle of plates, where a column of hot rock rises from deep inside the Earth.
paras.C: Volcanoes differ in shape and behaviour. Shield volcanoes, like Mauna Loa in Hawaii, have wide, gentle slopes built up by runny lava, and their eruptions are usually not violent. Composite volcanoes, such as Mount Fuji, are steeper and are made of alternating layers of lava and ash. Their magma is thick and sticky and traps gas, so the pressure builds until the volcano erupts explosively. If the top collapses into the emptied chamber, it leaves a vast crater called a caldera.
paras.D: History records some devastating eruptions. In 1815, the Indonesian volcano Tambora erupted with such force that the ash blocked sunlight, and the following year, 1816, became known in Europe and North America as the 'year without a summer', with failed harvests and famine. In 1883, the explosion of Krakatoa was heard nearly 5,000 kilometres away, and it caused giant sea waves, which killed tens of thousands. More recently, Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines erupted in 1991, and the cloud of gas it released cooled the entire planet by about half a degree for a year or so.
paras.E: Despite the dangers, millions of people live near volcanoes. One reason is that volcanic ash breaks down into exceptionally fertile soil, which is why farms flourish on the slopes of Mount Etna in Sicily and in parts of Java. Volcanic heat can also be used: in Iceland, geothermal power stations provide a large part of the country's heating and electricity. Furthermore, volcanic landscapes attract tourists, and the minerals that come from them include sulphur, and valuable gems.
paras.F: Scientists cannot yet predict exactly when a volcano will erupt, but they can often give a warning. Instruments called seismometers detect the small earthquakes that occur when magma moves, while other devices measure changes in the shape of the mountain and the gases it releases. Warnings have saved many lives, including those near Pinatubo, where tens of thousands of people were evacuated before the main eruption. Education and evacuation plans remain the best protection for those who live in the shadow of a volcano.

ps.title: Is Working from Home the Future?

paras.A: Before 2020, only a small minority of employees in most countries worked from home regularly. When offices closed during the pandemic, millions of people were suddenly obliged to do so, and many discovered that they liked it. Now that restrictions have ended, employers and workers are arguing about how much remote work should continue. Some companies insist that staff return to their desks, while others have abandoned offices altogether, and the debate shows no sign of ending.
paras.B: Supporters of remote work begin with the benefits for employees. Without a daily commute, people save time and money, and surveys regularly show that many would be willing to accept lower pay in return for the freedom to work from home. Parents and carers find it easier to combine their jobs with other duties, and people with disabilities gain access to jobs that might otherwise be out of reach. A number of studies have found that employees working from home are at least as productive as those in offices.
paras.C: Employers also gain. Companies that need less office space can cut their costs substantially, and they can hire people from anywhere in the country, or even the world, rather than only from those who live near the workplace. Some firms report that staff who work from home are less likely to leave, which reduces the expense of recruiting and training replacements. In addition, fewer commuters means less traffic and pollution, which is a benefit for the whole of society.
paras.D: Critics, however, point to problems. Working at home can be lonely, and some people find that the boundary between work and the rest of their lives disappears, so that they work longer hours and struggle to switch off. Not everybody has a quiet space at home, and young employees living in small shared flats are in an especially difficult position. Moreover, a number of managers argue that creativity depends on casual conversations in corridors and at coffee machines, which are hard to recreate on a screen.
paras.E: Careers may also be affected. Several studies suggest that workers who are seen less in the office are less likely to be promoted, since managers tend to favour those they meet in person. New employees may find it difficult to learn from colleagues without observing how they behave and speak. There are concerns, too, about fairness: jobs such as nursing, teaching and construction cannot be done remotely, and those who must still travel to work may feel resentful of colleagues who do not.
paras.F: The writer concludes that the best solution is probably neither entirely at home nor entirely in the office. Many organisations are experimenting with 'hybrid' arrangements in which staff spend two or three days a week in the workplace, meeting colleagues for projects and discussions, and the remaining days working alone on tasks needing concentration. The writer believes this combination offers most of the advantages of both, but adds that it works only if managers judge people by the results of their work, not by the hours they are visible.

paras.A: Easter Island, called Rapa Nui by its inhabitants, is one of the most remote inhabited places on Earth. It lies in the Pacific Ocean, about 3,700 kilometres from the coast of Chile, to which it belongs, and the nearest inhabited island is more than 2,000 kilometres away. Triangular in shape and just 164 square kilometres in area, it is famous for nearly 900 giant stone figures, known as moai, that stare inland from platforms along the coast.
paras.B: Polynesian settlers are generally thought to have reached the island somewhere between 800 and 1200 AD, travelling in large double-hulled canoes. Their descendants built a complex society divided into clans, each led by a chief. The moai were probably made to honour important ancestors, and they were believed to protect the living. The majority face inland, looking over the villages, while a small group of seven on one platform are the only ones that face the sea.
paras.C: The statues were carved from soft volcanic rock at a single quarry, the Rano Raraku crater, where hundreds more lie unfinished. The average moai is about four metres tall and weighs around twelve tonnes, but the largest completed example is almost ten metres high and weighs about 80 tonnes. Workers used stone tools called toki to carve each figure while it was still attached to the rock, and then detached it and slid it down the slope for the finishing work.
paras.D: How the statues were moved to platforms up to 18 kilometres away has long puzzled visitors. Early theories proposed that the islanders rolled them on logs. A more recent experiment suggests, however, that the moai could have been 'walked' upright: teams pulling on ropes tied around the head rocked the statue from side to side, advancing it a little with each swing. Local oral traditions say that the statues 'walked', and this explanation, which has been tested with a concrete replica, fits that story.
paras.E: For many years, a popular account held that the islanders destroyed their own environment by cutting down all the palm trees to move the statues, and that the society collapsed as a result. This story is now questioned. Some researchers argue that rats, which arrived on the canoes of the first settlers, ate the palm seeds and prevented forests from growing again. The population, they say, may have remained stable until European contact, and that it was the arrival of foreign diseases and slave raids in the nineteenth century that caused a catastrophic decline.
paras.F: The first European visitor was the Dutch explorer Jacob Roggeveen, who arrived on Easter Sunday in 1722 and gave the island its name. By 1877, only around 110 islanders remained alive. Since then the population has recovered, and today around 7,000 people live there, many of them working in tourism. Conservation has become a priority, because wind, rain and the feet of visitors threaten the statues. Many of the moai have been restored, and in 1995 the island was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

qs.title: Questions 9–13

paras.A: The eye is among the most complex organs in the human body, and certainly one of the most precious. Through it, we gather a large share of everything we know about the world: the faces of friends, the words on a page, the colours of a sunset. Yet the eye itself is a small organ, a ball just over two and a half centimetres wide, and it is protected by a bony socket, by the eyelids and by tears that wash away dust.
paras.B: Light first meets the cornea, the transparent dome at the front of the eye. The cornea bends the incoming rays and does most of the focusing work. Behind it is the coloured iris, which contains a muscle that controls the size of the central opening, the pupil. In bright light the pupil shrinks to limit the amount of light entering, while in the dark it opens wide. The colour of the iris, which may be brown, blue, green or grey, depends on the amount of a pigment called melanin.
paras.C: Behind the pupil lies the lens, a clear, flexible structure that makes the fine adjustments to the focus. To look at a nearby object, small muscles make the lens rounder; to look at something far away, they flatten it. With age the lens becomes stiffer, which is why many people over forty need reading glasses. The space inside the eye is filled with a clear, jelly-like substance called the vitreous humour, which helps the eye to keep its shape.
paras.D: The image falls on the retina, a thin layer of tissue lining the back of the eye. The retina contains around 120 million cells known as rods, which work in dim light but cannot detect colour, and about six million cones, which work in bright light and detect colour. Cones are concentrated in a tiny central area called the fovea, where vision is sharpest. When we read, we move our eyes so that each word falls on the fovea.
paras.E: The retina converts light into electrical signals, which travel along the optic nerve to the brain. The image formed on the retina is actually upside down, and the brain turns it the right way up. Each eye sees a slightly different view, and the brain combines the two to give a sense of depth. Where the optic nerve leaves the eye, there are no light-sensitive cells, creating a 'blind spot' that we do not notice because the brain fills in the missing information.
paras.F: Several common problems affect sight. In short-sightedness, the eyeball is slightly too long, so distant objects look blurred, while in long-sightedness, the opposite occurs. Both can be corrected with glasses, contact lenses or laser surgery. Cataracts, a clouding of the lens, are a leading cause of blindness in the world, but they can be treated by replacing the lens with an artificial one. Regular eye tests, which can detect disease early, are therefore important for everyone.

paras.A: A generation ago, most people bought clothes a few times a year. Today, thanks to cheap prices and rapidly changing styles, many shoppers buy a new item every week. This model, known as 'fast fashion', depends on producing trendy clothing quickly and cheaply, and it has made fashion accessible to nearly everyone. However, a growing number of critics argue that its true costs are hidden, and are paid by workers and by the planet. The debate raises a simple question: can clothing be both cheap and fair, or does a low price always mean that someone, somewhere, is paying more than they should?
paras.B: The first concern is the environment. Producing clothing uses huge amounts of water: it is often estimated that a single cotton shirt requires thousands of litres. Dyeing and finishing fabrics release chemicals into rivers in countries where regulations are weak. Synthetic fibres such as polyester are made from oil, and every wash releases tiny plastic particles into the water system. The industry as a whole is widely believed to be responsible for several per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions.
paras.C: Waste is another problem. The speed of the system makes it worse, since some shops now offer thousands of new designs every month. Because the clothes are cheap, and often poorly made, they are quickly thrown away. In many countries, millions of tonnes of textiles are sent to landfill each year, and only a small share is recycled. Charity shops cannot cope with the volume, and large quantities of unwanted garments are exported to developing countries, where they may overwhelm local markets and end up in huge dumps.
paras.D: Social issues also arise. Many garments are made in factories where wages are very low and conditions can be unsafe. The collapse of the Rana Plaza factory building in Bangladesh in 2013, in which more than 1,100 workers died, drew worldwide attention to the issue. Since then, some brands have signed safety agreements, but campaigners say that progress is uneven, and that workers still have little power to demand better treatment.
paras.E: Defenders of fast fashion offer a different view. They point out that the industry provides millions of jobs, many of them for women who would otherwise have few opportunities to earn a wage, and that these jobs have helped some countries to develop. Low prices, they add, matter greatly to families on small incomes, who cannot afford expensive clothes. They also note that many companies are now investing in recycled fibres and greener production.
paras.F: The writer accepts that fast fashion brings benefits but argues that the present system is not sustainable. Real change, the writer suggests, requires action from all sides. Governments could demand that companies take responsibility for the waste they create. Brands should pay fair wages and make clothes that last. Consumers also have a role, by buying fewer items, repairing clothes and choosing second-hand garments. If everyone does a little, the writer concludes, fashion can remain affordable without costing the earth.

ps.title: Machu Picchu: The Lost City of the Incas

paras.A: High in the Andes mountains of Peru, at an altitude of about 2,400 metres, lies one of the most spectacular archaeological sites in the world. Machu Picchu sits on a narrow ridge between two peaks, with steep green slopes falling away to the Urubamba River far below. Built in the fifteenth century, it was abandoned about a hundred years later and was never found by the Spanish conquerors, which is one reason why it survived in such good condition.
paras.B: The city was constructed around 1450, during the reign of the Inca emperor Pachacuti, who built an empire that stretched along the western coast of South America. Most scholars believe that Machu Picchu was a royal estate, a retreat for the emperor and his family and a place for religious ceremonies. At any time, only about 750 people lived there, mostly servants and specialist workers who maintained the estate, while the royal family visited during certain seasons.
paras.C: The Incas were master engineers. Their builders cut granite blocks so precisely that the stones fit together without mortar, and not even a knife blade can be pushed between some of them. This technique helped the walls to survive earthquakes, since the stones can move slightly and settle back into place. Hundreds of terraces were cut into the hillsides, to provide level ground for crops and also to prevent landslides during the heavy rains. A system of stone channels carried fresh spring water through the city.
paras.D: The site is divided into an agricultural zone and an urban zone. The agricultural part consisted mainly of terraces, where maize, potatoes and coca leaves were grown, and some storage buildings. The urban zone contained temples, palaces and houses. The most famous building is the Temple of the Sun, whose windows are aligned with the sun at the time of the winter solstice, showing the Incas' interest in astronomy. Close by, a carved stone known as the Intihuatana is thought to have been used as a kind of sundial.
paras.E: For centuries after its abandonment, Machu Picchu was known only to local farmers. In 1911, the American explorer Hiram Bingham, a lecturer at Yale University, was led to the ruins by a local boy. Bingham photographed the site and published his findings in a magazine, which made it famous around the world. He believed, wrongly, that he had found the 'lost' city of Vilcabamba, the last refuge of the Incas. Many of the objects he removed were returned to Peru by Yale in the following century.
paras.F: Today, Machu Picchu is a World Heritage Site and one of the New Seven Wonders of the World, and it receives well over a million visitors a year. This has created problems, such as erosion of the paths and pressure on the fragile environment. The authorities have introduced daily limits on tickets and require visitors to follow fixed routes. Many travellers walk to the site along the Inca Trail, a four-day hike through mountains and cloud forest, but this too is limited to a small number of walkers per day.

ps.title: Coral Reefs: Gardens of the Sea

paras.A: Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they are home to roughly a quarter of all marine species. This extraordinary diversity has earned them the nickname 'the rainforests of the sea'. Reefs also protect coasts from storms, provide food for hundreds of millions of people, and support tourism worth billions of dollars. They are, however, among the most threatened ecosystems on Earth, and scientists warn that a large share of the world's reefs could be lost within a few decades if present trends continue.
paras.B: What looks like a rock or plant is actually an animal. Corals are tiny creatures, called polyps, related to jellyfish and sea anemones. Each polyp is only a few millimetres across and has a soft body with a ring of tentacles. Most reef-building corals take calcium from sea water and use it to form a hard skeleton of limestone, and over centuries, the skeletons of countless generations pile up to form the reef. The Great Barrier Reef, in Australia, is made up of nearly 3,000 separate reefs and stretches for about 2,300 kilometres.
paras.C: Reef-building corals depend on a partnership with microscopic algae that live within their tissue. The algae use sunlight to make sugars by photosynthesis and give most of them to the coral, which in return provides the algae with shelter and nutrients. The algae also give corals their bright colours. Because the algae need sunlight, reefs grow in shallow, clear, warm water, usually less than 50 metres deep and between the latitudes of 30 degrees north and south of the equator.
paras.D: The greatest threat is warming of the sea. When the water is too hot for a long time, the corals become stressed and expel their algae, and without them the coral turns white, a process called bleaching. A bleached coral is not dead, and may recover if the water cools, but if the stress continues, it starves. Mass bleaching events, once rare, have become more frequent, and the Great Barrier Reef suffered several in recent years.
paras.E: Other pressures add to the problem. Absorbing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere makes the oceans more acidic, and this makes it harder for corals to build their skeletons. Pollution from farms and cities brings nutrients and sediment that smother the reef, while overfishing removes the fish that keep the algae on the reef under control. In some places, fishermen have used dynamite, which destroys the reef within seconds.
paras.F: Still, there is some hope. Marine protected areas, where fishing is limited, have allowed reefs to recover. Scientists are growing corals in nurseries and planting them on damaged reefs, and some are searching for heat-resistant types that could survive in warmer seas. However, experts stress that these efforts will succeed only if carbon emissions are cut quickly, since no amount of local action can protect a reef from a warming ocean.

paras.A: For more than two hundred years, zoos have attracted visitors who want to see animals they would never meet in the wild. Today, over 700 million people are estimated to visit zoos and aquariums each year. But attitudes are changing. Many people now feel uneasy about keeping wild animals in cages, and some argue that zoos should be closed. Defenders reply that modern zoos play an essential role in protecting nature, and that the debate should be settled by evidence about animals' welfare and conservation results, not by feelings alone.
paras.B: The strongest argument for zoos is conservation. Some species, such as the Arabian oryx and the California condor, were saved from extinction by breeding programmes in zoos, and animals bred in captivity were later released into the wild. Zoos also co-operate across the world to manage the genetic health of endangered species, so that small populations do not suffer from inbreeding. In addition, many zoos pay for conservation projects in the animals' natural habitats.
paras.C: A second argument is education. Seeing a living tiger or elephant has a stronger effect on children than watching a film, and zoos say that such experiences inspire people to care about wildlife. Zoos also provide opportunities for scientists to study animals' behaviour, diet and diseases closely, which is difficult in the wild. The knowledge gained has helped to improve veterinary care for both captive and wild animals.
paras.D: Critics reject these claims. They point out that only a small percentage of zoo animals belong to endangered species, and that very few captive-bred animals are ever released, since there may be no safe habitat left for them. Surveys of visitors also suggest that most people spend only a few minutes at each enclosure, and the evidence that zoo visits change behaviour in the long run is weak. Critics argue that money would be better spent on protecting habitats directly.
paras.E: The most serious criticism concerns welfare. Large animals that roam long distances in the wild, such as elephants, polar bears and orcas, often show signs of stress when confined, including repeated pacing and swaying. Some die younger in captivity than in the wild. Critics say that no enclosure, however large, can satisfy the needs of such animals, and that keeping them for entertainment cannot be justified. Several countries have already banned wild animals in circuses.
paras.F: The writer believes that the answer lies between the two extremes. Zoos that fail to meet high standards should be closed, and species that clearly suffer in captivity should no longer be kept. However, well-run zoos that concentrate on endangered species, provide spacious natural enclosures and put their money into conservation in the wild deserve support. In future, the writer suggests, zoos may become smaller in number but more important in purpose, acting as 'arks' for those species that cannot yet survive outside.

paras.A: Venice is unlike any other city in the world. Built on a group of 118 small islands in a shallow lagoon in north-eastern Italy, it has canals instead of streets and boats instead of cars. There are more than 400 bridges linking the islands, and the only way to travel between most neighbourhoods is on foot or by boat. For centuries, the city was one of the richest and most powerful in Europe, and its beauty attracts about twenty million visitors a year.
paras.B: According to tradition, the city was founded in 421 AD by refugees from the mainland who were fleeing invading tribes. The marshy islands, which were hard to attack, offered safety. To build on the soft ground, the settlers drove millions of wooden piles, mostly of oak and alder, deep into the mud. Stone platforms were laid on top of them, and the buildings were erected on these. Because wood does not rot when it is completely covered in water, the piles have lasted for centuries.
paras.C: Over time, Venice became a republic that was ruled by an elected leader called the doge, and it grew rich on trade with the eastern Mediterranean. Venetian merchants brought spices, silk and other luxuries to Europe, and the city's great shipyard, the Arsenal, was said to be able to build a ship in a single day. At its height, in the fifteenth century, Venice had a navy of hundreds of ships, and its coin, the ducat, was accepted across the known world.
paras.D: The city's architecture reflects this wealth. The most famous square, St Mark's, is surrounded by the Basilica, with its golden mosaics, and the Doge's Palace, the seat of government. The Grand Canal, about three kilometres long, winds through the centre of the city in the shape of a reversed S, and is lined by over 170 palaces. Traditional boats called gondolas, which are rowed by a single gondolier standing at the back, still carry tourists, although most residents now use motorised water buses.
paras.E: Venice also has serious difficulties. The city is slowly sinking, partly because groundwater was pumped out in the twentieth century, and sea levels are rising. Floods called acqua alta, which happen when high tides combine with strong winds, have become more frequent, and in 2019 the water reached its highest level for more than fifty years. To protect the city, engineers have built a system of mobile barriers across the lagoon entrances, known as MOSE, which can be raised when a flood is expected.
paras.F: Another problem is the pressure of tourism. Many visitors come for just a day and spend little, while the number of permanent residents has fallen from about 175,000 in 1951 to fewer than 50,000 today. Housing is expensive, and many apartments have been turned into holiday rentals. Large cruise ships, which once passed close to the historic centre, have been banned from the lagoon. The city has also begun to charge a fee for day visitors in an attempt to control numbers.

paras.A: Almost all life on Earth depends on a process that happens quietly in the leaves of plants. Photosynthesis is the way in which plants, algae and some bacteria turn sunlight into chemical energy. The word itself comes from Greek and means 'putting together with light'. The food that we eat, the oxygen that we breathe and even the fossil fuels that we burn all trace their origin back to this process.
paras.B: In simple terms, a plant takes in carbon dioxide from the air through tiny holes in its leaves called stomata, and water from the soil through its roots. Using the energy of sunlight, it combines these to make glucose, a type of sugar, and releases oxygen as a waste product. The glucose is used immediately for energy or converted into starch and stored, or built into the plant's cellulose, which forms its structure.
paras.C: The process takes place in tiny structures within plant cells called chloroplasts, which contain the green pigment chlorophyll. Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light most effectively, but reflects green light, which is why leaves look green. In autumn, many trees stop producing chlorophyll, and the yellow and orange pigments that were hidden beneath the green become visible, giving the season its colours.
paras.D: The first experiments on the subject date back to the seventeenth century. The Belgian scientist Jan van Helmont grew a willow tree in a pot for five years and found that although the tree gained about 74 kilograms, the soil lost only a few grams. He concluded, correctly, that most of the tree's mass came from the water. Later, in the 1770s, Joseph Priestley discovered that a plant could 'restore' air that had been used up by a burning candle, and another scientist showed that light was necessary.
paras.E: Photosynthesis is affected by several factors. Increasing the amount of light speeds up the process until a certain point, after which other factors become limiting. A rise in temperature increases the rate up to a limit, but extreme heat damages the enzymes involved. The concentration of carbon dioxide is also important, which is why some commercial growers add the gas to their greenhouses to increase the crop. Shortage of water causes the stomata to close, and this stops carbon dioxide from entering.
paras.F: The importance of photosynthesis is difficult to exaggerate. Without it, there would be no food chains, no forests and no animals as we know them. It produces the oxygen that makes up about 21 per cent of the atmosphere, and it removes carbon dioxide, so forests and the oceans' tiny algae are vital in controlling the climate. Today, scientists are trying to copy the process in the laboratory, in 'artificial leaves' that use sunlight to split water into hydrogen, which can be used as a clean fuel. If they succeed, humans will learn from plants how to make energy without polluting the world.

paras.A: Few topics divide parents, teachers and students as sharply as homework. In many countries, children as young as six are expected to spend an hour or more each evening on schoolwork, and older students may do several hours. Some education systems, in contrast, have limited or abolished homework in primary schools. The question is whether the extra work genuinely helps children learn, or whether it simply makes family life more stressful.
paras.B: Supporters of homework say that it reinforces learning. Practising a skill, such as solving mathematics problems or learning vocabulary, is an effective way to remember it, and doing so at home gives students more time than lessons alone. Homework also helps students to develop good habits, such as planning, working independently and meeting deadlines, which will be useful in higher education and employment. Some teachers add that homework allows parents to see what their children are learning.
paras.C: However, research on the benefits is mixed. A number of large reviews have concluded that homework has a clear positive effect on the achievement of older students in secondary school, but little or no effect on the results of primary pupils. Even for older students, there appears to be a limit: after about two hours a night, the extra time produces little benefit. The quality of homework matters more than quantity, and long repetitive tasks may do more harm than good.
paras.D: Critics raise concerns about stress and fairness. Children who spend several hours each evening on schoolwork have less time for sport, music, play and sleep, all of which are important for health and development. Surveys in some countries have found that many students report headaches, tiredness and anxiety linked to homework. Moreover, children from wealthier homes tend to have a quiet room, a computer and parents who can help, while others may lack these resources, so that homework can widen the gap between rich and poor.
paras.E: Some schools have adopted a middle path. Instead of sending home large quantities of exercises, they set short, meaningful tasks, such as reading a book for pleasure, interviewing a relative or preparing a presentation. Others run homework clubs, in which students can complete their tasks at school with the help of teachers, so that those with difficult home circumstances are not disadvantaged. A few schools have introduced the 'flipped classroom', in which pupils watch a lesson at home and practise the exercises at school.
paras.F: The writer concludes that homework should not be abolished, but that it should be reduced and made more purposeful. For young children, daily reading is probably enough. In secondary school, tasks should be limited in length and clearly connected to lessons, and teachers should avoid setting work simply to fill time. The writer adds that schools should regularly ask students and parents how long homework takes, so that the policy can be adjusted to the real situation.

paras.A: Before the middle of the fifteenth century, books in Europe were copied by hand. Monks in monasteries and professional scribes spent months, even years, producing a single volume, so books were extremely rare and costly. A library of a hundred volumes was considered large, and most people never owned a book, and could not read one. All this changed around 1450, when a goldsmith from the German city of Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg, developed a system of printing that could produce books quickly.
paras.B: Printing itself was not new. Woodblock printing had existed in China for centuries, and Chinese and Korean printers had experimented with movable type made from clay and metal. Gutenberg's achievement was to combine several technologies into a practical system. He designed a mould that allowed him to cast large numbers of identical metal letters, using an alloy of lead, tin and antimony that melted at a low temperature and hardened quickly into a durable form.
paras.C: The letters were arranged in a frame to form a page of text, and then covered with ink. Gutenberg developed a new oil-based ink that stuck to metal better than the water-based inks that scribes had used. The paper was pressed against the inked type with a wooden press, adapted from the presses used by wine-makers. When the printing was done, the letters could be removed from the frame and used again to set the next page, which made the system efficient.
paras.D: His most famous work is the Gutenberg Bible, printed around 1455. Roughly 180 copies are believed to have been made, some on paper and some on vellum, and about 50 of them survive today. Each page has 42 lines of text in two columns, and the big initial letters were added by hand in colour. Gutenberg himself did not become rich. He borrowed heavily to fund the project, and after a lawsuit by his financial backer, he lost his printing equipment.
paras.E: Despite this, the idea spread with astonishing speed. By 1500, printing presses were operating in more than 250 European towns, and an estimated 20 million books had been printed, in a Europe whose population was perhaps 80 million. Venice became a major centre for the book trade. The price of books fell sharply, and for the first time, ordinary merchants, lawyers and craftsmen could afford to own them. Literacy gradually increased as a result.
paras.F: The consequences were enormous. Scientists could share their findings with exact diagrams and tables, which speeded up discoveries. Religious reformers such as Martin Luther used printed pamphlets to spread their ideas across Germany within weeks, helping to start the Reformation. Languages became standardised in spelling and grammar, and newspapers eventually appeared. Many historians rank the printing press with the invention of writing and the internet as one of the three great turning points in the history of communication.

paras.A: The Amazon is not the longest river in the world, a title that is disputed between the Nile and the Amazon depending on how rivers are measured, but it is without question the largest by volume. Every second, it discharges about 200,000 cubic metres of water into the Atlantic Ocean, which is more than the next seven largest rivers combined. It flows for around 6,400 kilometres from its sources in the Andes mountains of Peru to the sea in northern Brazil.
paras.B: The river is fed by more than a thousand tributaries, some of which are themselves among the biggest rivers in the world. Its drainage basin covers about seven million square kilometres, an area nearly as large as Australia, and includes parts of nine countries. Brazil contains the greatest share. During the rainy season, the water level can rise by as much as ten metres, flooding huge areas of forest, and in places the river becomes so wide that one bank cannot be seen from the other.
paras.C: The Amazon rainforest, which surrounds the river, is the largest tropical forest on Earth. It is home to an estimated ten per cent of all known species. A single hectare may contain several hundred types of tree, and new species of plants and animals are discovered every year. The river itself holds more than 2,000 kinds of fish, including the piranha, the huge pirarucu, and the Amazon river dolphin, which is pink in colour.
paras.D: Unlike many large rivers, the Amazon has hardly any bridges along its main course, since the forest is thick and few roads reach it. People rely on boats. Towns such as Manaus, a city of about two million inhabitants in the middle of the rainforest, can be reached by large ocean-going ships, even though it lies about 1,500 kilometres from the sea. Indigenous peoples have lived beside the river for thousands of years, and some groups still have almost no contact with the outside world.
paras.E: The forest also plays a role in the world's climate. Trees take in carbon dioxide, and the vast amount of water that they release from their leaves forms clouds and produces rainfall, in some cases hundreds of kilometres away. Scientists estimate that the forest stores the equivalent of many years of global carbon emissions. For this reason, the Amazon is sometimes called the 'lungs of the planet', although researchers point out that the forest uses much of the oxygen it produces.
paras.F: The Amazon is under threat. Large areas have been cleared for cattle ranching, soy farming and logging, and roads built into the forest bring more settlers. According to widely quoted estimates, around a fifth of the original forest has been lost. Some scientists warn that if too much is destroyed, the forest could reach a 'tipping point', after which it would dry out and turn into savanna. Conservation groups and governments are working to enforce protection, though progress has varied from year to year.

paras.A: For decades, only professional astronauts could travel into space. That has now changed. Since 2021, private companies have taken paying passengers on short flights above the edge of space, and a few wealthy individuals have spent days in orbit. Tickets cost many thousands, or even millions, of dollars, and companies say that prices will fall in the future. But is it right to spend resources on holidays in space, when the planet faces so many problems?
paras.B: Supporters argue that tourism is a way of financing innovation. The cost of reaching space has fallen significantly, largely because companies have developed rockets that can land and be used again. Each paying customer helps to fund the development of safer and cheaper vehicles, which in the longer term can benefit science, communications and satellites. In the past, they say, new transport technologies such as aeroplanes were also first used by the rich before becoming available to ordinary people.
paras.C: Supporters also emphasise inspiration. Astronauts who have viewed the Earth from orbit often describe a feeling of awe, known as the 'overview effect', in which national borders seem to disappear and the planet appears small and fragile. If many more people could have this experience, advocates say, they might become more concerned about the environment. Space tourism might also encourage young people to study science and engineering, and create a new industry with well-paid jobs.
paras.D: Critics respond with environmental concerns. A rocket launch burns large amounts of fuel and releases gases and tiny particles into the upper atmosphere, where they may remain for years and could affect the ozone layer. Researchers calculate that each passenger on a short flight may be responsible for much more carbon dioxide than a passenger on a long-distance aeroplane trip. Because only a handful of people can travel on each flight, they argue, the impact for each person is unusually high.
paras.E: There are also arguments of fairness. Critics regard space tourism as an indulgence for the extremely wealthy while billions of people lack clean water, healthcare and education. They suggest that public interest in space should be directed toward scientific missions that benefit all humankind, such as monitoring climate change. Safety is a further worry. Space travel remains inherently dangerous, and accidents involving paying customers could lead to a loss of public trust and strict new regulations.
paras.F: The writer takes a cautious view. Space tourism, the writer suggests, is unlikely to be a harmless pastime for a rich minority, and is also unlikely to solve the world's problems. It should be allowed to continue, but companies should be required to measure and report their emissions and to develop cleaner fuels. If they do so, the writer concludes, the industry may be able to justify itself by contributing real advances, but if not, public opinion is likely to turn against it.

paras.A: Beside the Yamuna River in the Indian city of Agra stands a white marble building that many people regard as the most beautiful in the world. The Taj Mahal was built by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan as a tomb for his beloved wife, Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631 while giving birth to their fourteenth child. The emperor was heartbroken, and he decided to create a monument that would preserve her memory for ever.
paras.B: Construction began in about 1632 and took roughly twenty years. Records suggest that around 20,000 workers were employed, including stone-cutters, painters, calligraphers and inlay specialists, who came from India, Persia and Central Asia. The marble was brought by oxen and elephants from quarries more than 300 kilometres away, and precious and semi-precious stones came from as far afield as Afghanistan and Sri Lanka. The architect is traditionally said to have been Ustad Ahmad Lahori, though historians are not certain.
paras.C: The design is based on perfect symmetry. The tomb stands on a raised platform, with a tall minaret at each corner, and is crowned by a central dome that is about 35 metres high. In front, a long garden is divided by water channels into four equal parts, a pattern that represents the gardens of paradise in Islamic tradition. The surfaces are decorated with verses from the Quran in black stone and with delicate flowers inlaid in coloured gemstones.
paras.D: One of the building's most admired qualities is the way it seems to change colour during the day. At dawn the marble looks soft pink, at midday it is a brilliant white, and in the light of the moon it appears to glow with a silvery blue. The four minarets lean slightly outwards, which, according to many guides, was a deliberate choice so that they would fall away from the tomb in an earthquake, though this explanation is not proved.
paras.E: Shah Jahan's later years were unhappy. In 1658, his son Aurangzeb took power and imprisoned him in the nearby Agra Fort, from where, according to tradition, he could look out over the river to the Taj Mahal. When he died in 1666, he was buried next to his wife. Their graves, which lie in a chamber beneath the dome, are the only part of the complex that is not symmetrical, since the emperor's tomb was added later at the side.
paras.F: Today the Taj Mahal is a World Heritage Site that attracts several million visitors each year. The monument faces a number of threats. Air pollution from nearby factories and traffic has turned the marble slightly yellow, and the authorities have restricted vehicles near the site and apply a clay mask to clean the stone. The river, which once flowed full beside the garden, has partly dried up, raising concerns about the foundations. Conservation work continues year after year.

paras.A: Spiders have been spinning silk for more than 300 million years, and the material they produce is among the most remarkable in nature. Weight for weight, spider silk is stronger than steel, yet it is also elastic and so light that a strand long enough to circle the Earth would weigh only a few hundred grams. Scientists have long dreamed of copying it for use in medicine, industry and clothing. The reason is simple: if a material that strong could be made cheaply and in large quantities, it would change the way many everyday objects are designed, from bandages to bicycle helmets, and from fishing nets to the cables of bridges.
paras.B: A spider does not make only one kind of silk. An orb-weaving spider, for example, may produce up to seven different types, each made in a separate gland and each designed for a purpose. Dragline silk, the thread that forms the frame of the web and acts as a safety line when the spider falls, is the strongest. Another type is sticky and coats the spiral threads to trap insects, while another wraps prey, and another protects the eggs.
paras.C: The silk begins as a liquid protein in the spider's body. When it is drawn out through tiny openings called spinnerets, the proteins line up and change from a liquid into a solid fibre in a fraction of a second. This happens at room temperature and uses only water as a solvent, which compares favourably with the manufacture of synthetic fibres such as nylon, which requires high temperatures and harsh chemicals.
paras.D: The properties of the silk come from its structure. Within the thread, tiny hard crystals are embedded in a stretchy, flexible material. The crystals give strength, while the elastic part allows the thread to stretch by up to a third of its length without breaking. A strand can absorb the energy of a flying insect hitting the web, which would snap a thread of equal thickness made from most man-made materials.
paras.E: The obvious difficulty is that spiders cannot be farmed like silkworms. Most spiders are aggressive and eat each other if they are kept together, and each produces only tiny amounts of silk. Researchers have therefore tried to produce the proteins in other organisms. Genes from spiders have been inserted into bacteria, yeast, plants, silkworms and even goats, whose milk then contains the silk protein. The protein can then be spun into fibres.
paras.F: These efforts have already brought results, and companies now make clothing and sports equipment with fibres based on spider silk proteins. Potential uses include stitches that dissolve inside the body, artificial ligaments, lightweight armour and very fine filters. However, producing the silk in large amounts at a competitive price remains a challenge, and so far, no manufactured fibre has quite matched the performance of the natural thread produced by a living spider.

paras.A: In many parts of the world, rates of obesity have more than doubled in the last forty years. The condition raises the risk of diabetes, heart disease and some cancers, and the cost of treating it puts a heavy burden on health services. Governments are searching for solutions, and one of the most discussed is a tax on foods and drinks that are high in sugar, fat or salt. Several countries have already introduced taxes on sugary drinks. Whether this approach is wise, fair and effective is now the subject of a lively argument among doctors, economists and politicians, and the answer may differ from one country to another.
paras.B: Supporters of such taxes argue that higher prices change behaviour. When tobacco was taxed heavily, smoking fell, and there is evidence that sugary drink taxes have had a similar effect, with some countries reporting that purchases fell and that manufacturers reduced the amount of sugar in their products to avoid the tax. In addition, the money raised can be used to fund health programmes, school meals or sports facilities, making the policy useful in two ways.
paras.C: Supporters also point out that the costs of poor diet fall on everyone. Taxpayers pay for treatment, and employers lose working days through illness. A tax, in this view, makes the price of food reflect its real cost to society. Because children are heavily influenced by advertising and by cheap and easily available snacks, the supporters add that individual willpower alone cannot be expected to solve the problem.
paras.D: Opponents give several objections. First, they say that such taxes are unfair to poorer families, who spend a larger share of their income on food and therefore bear the greatest burden. Second, it is difficult to decide which foods should be taxed. A product may be high in fat but also contain valuable nutrients, as cheese does, and a definition based on one ingredient can lead to odd results. Third, they argue that the effect on health is uncertain, since people may simply switch to other unhealthy products.
paras.E: Many opponents prefer other measures. Education about nutrition, clear labelling on packages, and the improvement of school meals, they say, respect personal freedom and encourage people to make better decisions. Some propose that governments should rather make healthy foods cheaper, with subsidies for fruit and vegetables, so that the poorest families can afford a good diet. Others point out that exercise is just as important as diet, and that towns should provide safe places to walk and play.
paras.F: The writer concludes that a tax on the most obviously harmful products, such as sugary drinks, is justified by the evidence. However, such a tax should not be the only policy, and the revenue should be spent in ways that help low-income families, for example by subsidising healthy food. ps.title: The Temple City of the Khmer

paras.A: In the jungles of northern Cambodia stands the largest religious monument in the world. Angkor Wat, which means 'City of Temples', covers an area of about 160 hectares, and it is surrounded by a moat nearly 190 metres wide. It was built in the first half of the twelfth century by King Suryavarman II as a temple to the Hindu god Vishnu, and it was intended to be his own funeral monument after his death. The name Angkor itself is generally thought to come from a Sanskrit word meaning 'city', and the surrounding region contains hundreds of other temples, which makes it one of the richest archaeological areas on Earth.
paras.B: The temple is a representation of the universe in stone. Its central towers symbolise Mount Meru, the home of the gods in Hindu belief, while the outer walls represent the mountains at the edge of the world and the moat the cosmic ocean. The highest of the five towers rises to about 65 metres above the ground. Approaching from the west along a long stone causeway, visitors pass through a series of galleries, each higher and more sacred than the last.
paras.C: Angkor Wat is famous for its carvings. Along the walls of the lowest gallery are more than 800 metres of bas-reliefs, shallow sculptures that tell stories from Hindu epics, including a huge scene known as the Churning of the Ocean of Milk. Elsewhere, more than 1,800 carved figures of celestial dancers, called apsaras, look out from the walls, and no two are exactly the same. The stone was cut from sandstone quarries about 40 kilometres away.
paras.D: The temple was part of a much larger city. Between the ninth and fifteenth centuries, the Khmer Empire ruled much of South-East Asia from Angkor, and archaeologists using laser scanning from aircraft have shown that the city was one of the biggest in the pre-industrial world, perhaps home to nearly a million people. It depended on an elaborate system of reservoirs and canals that stored water in the dry season and drained excess in the wet season.
paras.E: After the empire declined in the fifteenth century, the capital moved south, but Angkor Wat itself was never completely abandoned. Buddhist monks looked after the site, and the temple gradually changed from a Hindu to a Buddhist place of worship. Its fame spread to the West after the French naturalist Henri Mouhot visited in 1860 and published drawings. Roots of enormous trees, especially the silk-cotton and strangler figs, have since grown over many of the other temples nearby.
paras.F: The temple is now the symbol of Cambodia and appears on its national flag. It was added to the World Heritage List in 1992, and it attracts about two million foreign visitors a year. The great numbers bring difficulties, including the wearing of stone steps and the pumping of groundwater, which may weaken the foundations. Teams from many countries are working to repair the monuments, and the authorities have introduced rules to limit the damage.
