qs.title: Questions 9–13

paras.A: The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite and the brightest object in the night sky. It is about a quarter of the Earth's width, 3,474 kilometres across, and lies on average 384,000 kilometres away. This is close enough that light from the Moon reaches us in just over a second. Its gravity pulls on our oceans and creates tides, and for thousands of years it has shaped calendars, myths and navigation. Even today, with spacecraft and satellites, the Moon remains the only world beyond Earth that humans have visited, and it continues to raise questions that scientists cannot yet answer fully.
paras.B: How the Moon formed was long a mystery. Several early ideas, such as the suggestion that Earth captured a passing body, have been abandoned. The most widely accepted theory today proposes that, about 4.5 billion years ago, a planet-sized object, sometimes called Theia, struck the young Earth. The collision threw huge amounts of molten material into orbit, and this gradually gathered together to form the Moon. Analysis of rocks brought back from the Moon supports this idea.
paras.C: The Moon has no atmosphere to speak of and no liquid water on its surface, so there is no weather. Temperatures swing from about 120 degrees Celsius in the lunar day to about minus 130 degrees at night. Its surface is covered with craters made by meteorites over billions of years, and because there is no wind or rain to erase them, they are preserved. The dark patches that we see from Earth, called maria, are huge plains of cooled lava.
paras.D: The Moon always shows the same face to the Earth. This happens because it takes the same time, about 27 days, to rotate once on its axis as to orbit the Earth. The side that we never see from Earth, known as the far side, was first photographed by a Soviet spacecraft in 1959. It has many more craters and almost no maria. The 'phases' of the Moon do not come from the Earth's shadow, but from the changing view of the half that is lit by the Sun.
paras.E: Humans first walked on the Moon on 20 July 1969, when Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed with Apollo 11. Between 1969 and 1972, twelve astronauts walked on its surface, and they brought back about 380 kilograms of rock and soil. No one has returned since 1972. The Moon is slowly moving away from us, at a rate of around 3.8 centimetres a year, about as fast as a fingernail grows.
paras.F: Interest in the Moon is growing again. Spacecraft have found evidence of water ice in craters near the poles that are permanently in shadow, and ice could provide drinking water and fuel for future visitors. Several countries and private companies have announced plans for lunar landers, and space agencies talk of building a permanent base. Scientists argue that the Moon could serve as a testing ground and a stepping stone for missions to Mars.

ps.title: Is Nuclear Power the Answer to Climate Change?

paras.A: As countries try to reduce emissions of carbon dioxide, many are looking again at nuclear power. At present, nuclear plants provide about ten per cent of the world's electricity, and in some countries, such as France, they provide much more. Supporters say that nuclear energy is essential in the fight against climate change, while opponents argue that its dangers and costs outweigh its advantages. The debate is intense, and the arguments on each side are worth examining carefully, because the decisions made in the next few years will shape the energy supply for generations.
paras.B: The strongest argument for nuclear power is that it produces very little carbon dioxide during operation. A single plant can generate large amounts of electricity continuously, regardless of the weather, which sets it apart from wind and solar power, which depend on conditions. Supporters note that nuclear plants use only small amounts of fuel and take up little land. Studies comparing the whole life cycle of different energy sources typically place nuclear at a similar level to wind in terms of emissions.
paras.C: Supporters also dispute the claim that nuclear power is unsafe. Statistically, it has caused far fewer deaths per unit of electricity than coal, oil or gas, which pollute the air and kill many people each year. The accidents at Chernobyl in 1986 and Fukushima in 2011 were serious, but supporters say that modern reactor designs include passive safety systems that shut down the reactor without human intervention. New small modular reactors may also be cheaper and quicker to build.
paras.D: Opponents begin with the problem of waste. Used nuclear fuel stays dangerously radioactive for tens of thousands of years, and although it can be stored in sealed containers, few countries have built permanent underground repositories. Critics ask whether it is right to leave such a burden to far-distant generations. They add that plants may be targets of attack, and that nuclear technology can be misused to make weapons.
paras.E: Cost is a second concern. New nuclear plants have often been completed years late and billions over budget, and critics note that the price of wind and solar power has fallen sharply, while the price of nuclear has not. Money spent on nuclear plants, opponents argue, would be better invested in renewable energy, batteries and efficiency, which can be installed quickly. Building a plant also takes a decade or more, which may be too slow to help the climate in the next twenty years.
paras.F: The writer suggests that the choice is not between nuclear and renewables but between nuclear and fossil fuels, at least in countries with little hydroelectric power. Existing plants, the writer argues, should be kept open as long as they are safe, since closing them tends to increase the use of coal and gas. Building new plants is more questionable, because of their cost, and should be judged case by case, in the light of the real alternatives available.

ps.title: Mount Everest: The Roof of the World

paras.A: Mount Everest, on the border between Nepal and Tibet, is the highest mountain above sea level on Earth. Its summit is 8,849 metres high, according to the latest joint measurement by Nepal and China, and it continues to rise by a few millimetres a year as the two great plates beneath it push against each other. The mountain is known as Sagarmatha in Nepal and Chomolungma in Tibet, and was given its English name in 1865 in honour of Sir George Everest, a former surveyor-general of India.
paras.B: For many years, the mountain was believed to be out of reach. The first serious attempts to climb it were made by British expeditions in the 1920s. In 1924, George Mallory and Andrew Irvine disappeared near the top while trying to reach the summit, and whether they got there is still debated. Mallory's body was found in 1999, but the camera that might have settled the question was not. His famous answer to the question of why he wanted to climb it was simply, 'Because it's there'.
paras.C: The summit was finally reached on 29 May 1953 by the New Zealander Edmund Hillary and the Sherpa climber Tenzing Norgay, members of a large British expedition led by John Hunt. The two men spent only about fifteen minutes on top, and Hillary took a photograph of Tenzing. Both became world famous. Hillary later devoted much of his life to building schools and hospitals in Nepal, and Tenzing became the director of a mountaineering school in India.
paras.D: Climbing Everest is dangerous because of the altitude. Above about 8,000 metres, the air contains only about one third of the oxygen found at sea level, and the region is known as the 'death zone', where the human body cannot adapt. Climbers who do not use bottled oxygen risk altitude sickness, frostbite and exhaustion. Temperatures can fall below minus 40 degrees, and winds can blow at over 150 kilometres an hour. Most climbers need weeks of acclimatisation, moving up and down the lower slopes so that their bodies produce more red blood cells.
paras.E: In recent decades the mountain has become far more accessible. Commercial companies guide paying clients up the mountain, supported by teams of Sherpas who fix ropes and carry equipment. Several hundred people reach the summit in a good season, and by now more than 6,000 have done so. The Sherpas take the greatest risks, and many have died in accidents such as the avalanche of 2014, which killed sixteen guides. Their work has led to calls for better insurance and wages.
paras.F: Success has brought new problems. On busy days, long lines of climbers wait to pass narrow sections of the route near the top, which wastes oxygen and increases the risk. Tonnes of rubbish, including tents, bottles and oxygen cylinders, have been left on the slopes, and in recent years, teams have been paid to collect it. Climate change is melting the glaciers, making the Khumbu Icefall more unstable. Authorities are now discussing stricter permits and rules about experience.

paras.A: Bats are the only mammals that can truly fly, and they are far more numerous and varied than most people realise. There are more than 1,400 species, which is about one fifth of all mammal species, and they live on every continent except Antarctica. Some are as small as a bumblebee, weighing under two grams, while the largest, the flying foxes, have wingspans of up to 1.7 metres. Despite this variety, bats are often misunderstood and feared.
paras.B: A bat's wing is really a modified hand. The four long fingers support a thin, elastic membrane of skin that stretches to the body and legs. This structure makes bats extremely manoeuvrable, allowing them to turn sharply to catch insects in mid-air. Some species can fly at speeds of over 90 kilometres an hour, and one common species is thought to be able to cover long distances during seasonal migrations. During the day, most bats roost, hanging upside down in caves, trees and buildings.
paras.C: Most small bats find their way and catch prey by echolocation. The bat produces high-pitched sounds, too high for humans to hear, and listens to the echoes that bounce back from objects. From the time taken for the echo to return and its quality, the bat builds a detailed picture of its surroundings, including the size, shape and even the texture of an insect. A bat can detect an object as thin as a human hair. Contrary to a popular saying, bats are not blind, and many species see quite well.
paras.D: The ecological value of bats is huge. Many species eat insects, and a single small bat can consume thousands of mosquitoes and other insects in a night, which helps to protect crops and reduces pests. A colony in a large cave may eat many tonnes of insects each year. Other bats feed on nectar and fruit, and in doing so they pollinate flowers and spread seeds. In tropical forests, some trees, including wild bananas and agave plants, depend on bats to reproduce.
paras.E: Bats also have some extraordinary abilities. Though small, many live for a long time; some species have been recorded as living for more than thirty years, which is unusual for animals of their size. They also appear to carry many viruses without becoming sick themselves, and scientists are studying their immune systems in the hope of learning new ways to fight disease. Only three species of vampire bat feed on blood, and these live in Latin America.
paras.F: Unfortunately, many bat populations are in decline. Habitat loss, the use of pesticides, wind turbines and disease have all taken a toll. In North America, a fungal disease called white-nose syndrome has killed millions of bats since 2006. Because they breed slowly, usually producing only one baby a year, populations are slow to recover. Conservationists protect roosts, put up bat boxes and teach local people about the animals' value.

ps.title: Should There Be a Minimum Age for Social Media?

paras.A: Social media platforms are used by billions of people, and many children join as soon as they can. Although most services officially require users to be at least thirteen, surveys suggest that a large number of younger children use them with false birth dates. Concerns about mental health, bullying and exposure to harmful material have led several governments to propose stricter age limits, including a complete ban for those under sixteen. The proposal has generated strong feelings on both sides, and parents, teachers, technology companies and young people themselves often disagree about what the best policy would be.
paras.B: Those who favour a higher age limit begin with mental health. Some studies link heavy social media use with anxiety, depression and poor sleep among teenagers, especially girls. Constant comparison with the carefully edited images of others can damage self-esteem, and notifications interrupt homework and rest. Supporters say that adolescence is a sensitive period of development, and that society has set age limits for other products, such as alcohol and tobacco, that can harm the young.
paras.C: Supporters also stress safety. Children may be contacted by strangers who intend to harm them, may see violent or inappropriate content, and may become victims of online bullying that follows them home. Because platforms are designed to keep users scrolling for as long as possible, it is argued, children cannot be expected to control their use. A legal age limit would put responsibility on companies, in the same way that shops are responsible for who they sell goods to.
paras.D: Opponents answer that a ban would be difficult to enforce. Young people are skilled at finding ways around restrictions, and checking the age of every user would require the collection of identity documents or facial scans, which raises serious privacy concerns for adults too. If children are pushed away from the major platforms, they may move to smaller, less regulated sites with fewer protections, making the problem worse instead of better.
paras.E: They add that social media also has benefits. For young people who feel isolated, for example because of where they live or their identity, online communities can offer support and friendship. Social media can also be a source of information, creativity and political engagement. Critics of a ban argue that education would be a better solution: children should be taught how to use the internet critically and safely, and parents should be supported in setting limits at home.
paras.F: The writer is cautious. The evidence on mental health is troubling, but it is not yet clear that social media directly causes the problems, rather than simply being used more by children who are already unhappy. The writer therefore supports a modest increase in the minimum age to fifteen or sixteen, combined with stronger rules requiring companies to remove harmful content and to switch off addictive features for young users. Such a package would be easier to enforce, the writer concludes, than an outright ban.

paras.A: On the morning of 24 August in the year 79 AD, the people of the Roman town of Pompeii, near the Bay of Naples, were going about their usual business. Nothing warned them that the mountain rising behind the town, Vesuvius, was about to erupt. Most of them did not even know that it was a volcano, since it had been quiet for centuries. Within twenty-four hours, Pompeii and its neighbour Herculaneum were buried, and their inhabitants killed or driven away.
paras.B: We know the details of the eruption largely because of a young Roman, Pliny the Younger, who watched from across the bay and described what he saw in two letters. He wrote that a tall cloud rose from the mountain in the shape of an umbrella pine tree. His uncle, Pliny the Elder, commander of a fleet, sailed across to rescue people and died on the shore. Volcanologists now call this kind of explosive eruption 'Plinian' in his honour.
paras.C: During the first hours, ash and small pieces of rock called pumice fell on Pompeii like heavy rain. Roofs collapsed under the weight, and many residents fled. Others took shelter in their homes. Early the next morning, the column of gas and ash collapsed, and fast-moving clouds of burning gas and ash, known as pyroclastic surges, rushed down the slopes at speeds of over 100 kilometres an hour. Those who remained were killed almost instantly. Estimates of the dead in Pompeii vary, but are usually put at about 2,000.
paras.D: The town lay under around four to six metres of ash and pumice, which preserved it in remarkable detail. Rediscovered by accident in the late sixteenth century, and properly excavated from 1748, it has revealed streets, shops, bakeries, theatres and baths. Walls are covered with paintings and writing, including advertisements and election slogans. In some houses, floor mosaics and even loaves of bread have survived. Pompeii gives a more complete picture of daily life in a Roman town than any other site.
paras.E: One of the most striking discoveries concerns the victims. As the ash around the bodies hardened and the bodies decayed, they left hollow spaces in the ground. In the 1860s, the archaeologist Giuseppe Fiorelli had the idea of filling these spaces with liquid plaster. When the plaster set and the surrounding ash was removed, it revealed the exact shapes of people and animals in their last moments. Such casts have made the tragedy very real to visitors.
paras.F: Pompeii is now one of Italy's most visited sites, with almost four million visitors a year. Its preservation is a constant struggle. Rain, sun and the damage caused by tourists have all led to collapses, and in 2010 a famous building known as the House of the Gladiators fell down. The authorities have invested in repairs and in new technology, such as drones for monitoring. Vesuvius, meanwhile, is still active, and more than half a million people live in its danger zone.

ps.title: Why We Sleep: Sleep and Memory

paras.A: We spend about a third of our lives asleep, and for centuries scientists assumed that sleep was merely a time of rest. In fact, the brain remains very active at night, and research over the last fifty years has shown that sleep is essential for health, mood and, above all, learning. People who are deprived of sleep, even for a single night, think more slowly, make more mistakes and find it harder to remember new information.
paras.B: Sleep is not a single state. During the night, we move through repeated cycles, each lasting around ninety minutes. Each cycle includes periods of light sleep, deep sleep, and a stage called REM, or rapid eye movement sleep, in which the eyes move rapidly behind closed lids and most vivid dreams take place. Deep sleep is more common in the first half of the night, while REM sleep becomes longer towards morning, which is one reason why cutting sleep short can be harmful.
paras.C: The link between sleep and memory has been tested in many experiments. In a typical study, volunteers learn a list of words or a skill in the evening and are then tested the next morning. Those who have slept well usually perform better than those who stayed awake for the same period. It appears that during sleep, the brain replays the day's experiences, strengthening important connections between nerve cells and moving memories from temporary storage to long-term storage.
paras.D: Different kinds of sleep seem to help different kinds of memory. Deep sleep is particularly important for facts and events, such as vocabulary and historical dates. REM sleep seems to help with skills and emotional memories, and may help the brain to make creative connections between ideas. Some researchers claim that people who sleep after learning are more likely to find a hidden pattern in a problem, though findings of this type are still being debated.
paras.E: Sleep also appears to clean the brain. During deep sleep, spaces between the brain's cells widen, allowing fluid to wash away waste products that build up during the day. One of these is a protein associated with Alzheimer's disease. Although more research is needed, scientists suspect that years of poor sleep may raise the risk of such conditions. Sleep also supports the immune system, the heart and the control of body weight. Over a lifetime, a person who sleeps well is likely to enjoy better health, a better mood and a sharper mind than one who regularly goes without.
paras.F: Most adults need between seven and nine hours of sleep each night, whereas teenagers need around eight to ten. Many people get less. Experts recommend a regular schedule, a cool, dark bedroom and avoiding screens and caffeine in the hours before bed. Sleeping pills are generally a short-term solution. For students, the advice is clear: staying up all night to revise is likely to do more harm than good, since sleep after studying helps to fix what has been learned.

paras.A: Tourism is one of the largest industries in the world. Before the pandemic, more than a billion international trips were made each year, and the industry accounted for roughly one in ten jobs worldwide. For many countries, particularly small islands and developing nations, tourism is the main source of foreign income. Yet there is a growing debate about whether the benefits truly reach local people, and whether they are outweighed by the costs. The answer matters, because millions of families depend on the industry for their income, and because decisions about how to develop it are often made quickly and are difficult to reverse.
paras.B: Supporters point first to jobs and income. A hotel or resort creates work for cleaners, cooks, drivers, guides and guards, and tourist spending supports local shops, farmers and craftspeople. In regions with few other opportunities, such as remote coasts and mountain areas, tourism may be the only way of earning a living without migrating to cities. Taxes paid by visitors and businesses can fund roads, schools and hospitals that also benefit local residents.
paras.C: Supporters also argue that tourism can protect culture and nature. When visitors pay to see wildlife or historic buildings, communities have a financial reason to preserve them. In some African countries, for example, income from safaris has persuaded governments to protect large areas of land. Traditional crafts, music and festivals which might have died out can survive because tourists want to buy and see them.
paras.D: Critics reply that the benefits are often exaggerated. In many destinations, a large share of the money paid by tourists leaves the country, a problem known as 'leakage'. Foreign-owned hotels and airlines take the profits, and food and drink are imported. Most of the jobs available to local people are low-paid, seasonal and without security, while the better positions go to outsiders. Studies suggest that in some resorts, only a small fraction of the price of a package holiday remains in the local economy.
paras.E: There are other costs. Tourism can drive up the price of land, housing and food, pushing out local residents, as has happened in cities such as Barcelona and Venice. Water and energy are used heavily by hotels, and in dry regions this can cause shortages for villagers. Environmental damage, such as the erosion of paths and pollution of beaches, can destroy the very attractions on which the industry depends. Residents may also feel that their customs are turned into entertainment.
paras.F: The writer argues that tourism is neither good nor bad in itself; the outcome depends on how it is managed. Benefits for local people are greatest when tourism is small in scale, when locals own the businesses, and when visitors stay in local guesthouses and eat local food. The writer suggests that governments should set limits on numbers, require businesses to hire and buy locally, and use tourist taxes to fund services. Travellers, too, can help by choosing responsible operators.

paras.A: Today, billions of people carry telephones in their pockets, and the idea of speaking to someone far away seems perfectly normal. In the middle of the nineteenth century, however, it would have seemed like magic. Messages could travel long distances only by the telegraph, which used electric pulses to send coded signals along wires, and which needed trained operators. Several inventors, working independently, dreamed of sending the human voice instead, and the race to be first would bring fame, fortune and some of the most bitter legal arguments in the history of technology.
paras.B: The man most often credited with the invention is Alexander Graham Bell, who was born in Edinburgh in 1847 and later moved to North America. He taught deaf children to speak, as his father and grandfather had done before him, and his knowledge of sound and speech influenced his experiments. In Boston, he worked with a young engineer, Thomas Watson, who built the equipment. Together, they tried to build a machine that would turn the vibrations of the voice into electrical signals.
paras.C: The breakthrough came on 10 March 1876. In the next room, Watson heard Bell's voice through the apparatus say, 'Mr Watson, come here, I want to see you.' The transmitter used a thin membrane that vibrated when Bell spoke, and the vibrations varied the strength of an electric current in a wire. At the other end, the receiver converted the changing current back into sound. Bell had patented the device a few weeks earlier, on 7 March.
paras.D: Bell was not the only inventor in the race. On the very same day that Bell filed his application, another inventor, Elisha Gray, filed a notice of his own design. The dispute that followed produced years of legal battles. In 2002, the United States Congress passed a resolution recognising an Italian immigrant, Antonio Meucci, who had built a voice communication device years before, as the first to develop the idea, although the claim remains disputed among historians.
paras.E: The telephone spread rapidly. In 1877, Bell and his partners formed a company, and by 1880 there were about 50,000 telephones in the United States. The first telephone exchanges, run by operators who connected calls by hand with plugs and cables, appeared in the late 1870s. Automatic exchanges, which allowed subscribers to dial numbers themselves, were introduced in the 1890s. The first transatlantic telephone cable was laid in 1956, allowing a few dozen simultaneous calls.
paras.F: Over the next century, the telephone was transformed. Wires gave way to optical fibres and satellites, and in 1973, an engineer at Motorola, Martin Cooper, made the first call from a handheld mobile phone. The invention of smartphones in the first decade of the twenty-first century turned the device into a pocket computer with a camera, a map and access to the internet. Bell himself, it is said, never had a telephone in his study, because he considered it a distraction from his work.

paras.A: Wetlands are areas where water covers the soil, either all year or for part of it. They include marshes, swamps, bogs, mangrove forests and the edges of lakes and rivers. For centuries, many people regarded such places as useless wasteland, to be drained and turned into farms or building land. Scientists now recognise them as some of the most valuable ecosystems on Earth, although it is estimated that around a third of the world's wetlands have disappeared since 1970. This loss has consequences for water, wildlife and climate that people are only beginning to understand.
paras.B: One of their most important functions is controlling floods. A wetland acts like a giant sponge, soaking up rainwater and releasing it slowly. When a river overflows, the wetland spreads the water over a wide area, lowering the peak of the flood downstream. Cities that have destroyed their wetlands often suffer worse flooding, and some are now trying to restore them. Coastal wetlands, such as mangrove forests, also protect the land from storm surges and waves.
paras.C: Wetlands also clean water. As water moves slowly through reeds and other plants, sediment settles on the bottom, and many pollutants, including nitrogen and phosphorus from fertilisers, are absorbed by plants and microbes. Some towns have built artificial wetlands to treat sewage naturally, which can cost less than a conventional plant. In this way, a wetland provides a service which, if it had to be replaced by machines, would be extremely expensive.
paras.D: These habitats are very rich in wildlife. They provide breeding grounds for fish and shellfish, and many ocean fish spend part of their lives in coastal marshes and mangroves. Millions of migratory birds depend on wetlands as resting and feeding places on their long journeys, and a single marsh may be visited by hundreds of species. Frogs, dragonflies and many plants also depend on the wet conditions. Wetlands cover only about six per cent of the land but support a far greater share of species.
paras.E: Wetlands are also important to the climate. Peat bogs, which form from partly decayed plants in waterlogged ground, cover only about three per cent of the Earth's land but store more carbon than all the world's forests together. When they are drained, the peat dries and rots or burns, releasing large amounts of carbon dioxide. Protecting and restoring peatlands is therefore regarded as one of the most cost-effective ways of limiting climate change.
paras.F: In 1971, representatives of several countries met in the Iranian city of Ramsar and agreed on a treaty to protect wetlands, which is now known as the Ramsar Convention. More than 170 countries have joined it, and over 2,000 sites have been designated as wetlands of international importance. Restoring damaged wetlands is possible, though it takes time and money. In many places, projects have shown that when water is allowed to return, plants and animals come back surprisingly fast.

paras.A: In a number of countries, including Germany and Norway, university students pay little or nothing in tuition fees. In others, such as the United States and Britain, students may graduate with debts of tens of thousands of pounds or dollars. The question of who should pay for higher education has become a political issue in many places. Should it be a public service, paid for by taxes, or a personal investment for which graduates should pay? Each answer has its defenders, and each carries consequences for fairness, for public budgets and for the choices that young people make about their futures.
paras.B: Supporters of free education argue that it promotes equality of opportunity. If students must pay high fees, young people from poorer families may decide not to attend, or choose a cheaper course rather than the one best suited to them. A system funded by taxes, in contrast, allows people to be admitted on the basis of ability and not wealth. Some also say that the fear of debt discourages graduates from taking lower-paid but valuable jobs, such as teaching or social work.
paras.C: Supporters also emphasise the benefits for society. Graduates generally earn more, pay more tax and tend to be healthier and more active in their communities. A well-educated workforce attracts businesses, drives innovation and strengthens the economy as a whole. As these gains are shared by everyone, they argue, it is fair that everyone contributes to the cost. In their view, higher education should be treated like schools, roads and hospitals: a public good rather than a private product.
paras.D: Opponents answer that free tuition is unfair in another way. Taxpayers, including those who never went to university, would be paying for a qualification that mostly benefits the graduate through higher lifetime earnings. Because students from wealthy families are still over-represented at universities, free tuition may in practice subsidise the better-off. Opponents prefer a system in which graduates repay the cost after they start earning, only if their income reaches a certain level.
paras.E: There are practical objections as well. Governments with limited budgets may be forced to limit the number of places or reduce the quality of teaching if they pay all costs. Some countries with free tuition have overcrowded lecture halls and long waits for popular courses. Fees, opponents say, make universities more responsive to student needs, and encourage students to think carefully about what they study and whether they will use the qualification.
paras.F: The writer finds merit in both positions. The existing evidence suggests that the main obstacle for poorer students is not the fee itself, particularly when repayments depend on income, but the cost of living while studying. The writer therefore proposes keeping income-based repayment but combining it with generous grants for students from low-income families, so that nobody is prevented from studying by lack of money. In this way, the cost would be shared by graduates and society, as the benefits are.
